profiles.label: BMW M Roadster & M Coupe (Z3 M, E36/7 & E36/8, 1998-2002)
profiles.framing: A characterful fair-weather weekend and daily driver, NOT a collector or investment car. The buyer values reliability, condition, driving engagement, value, and proximity to Carmel / Monterey / Bay Area. All Z3 M cars are factory manual. Identify the engine: 1998-2000 = S52 (more robust); 2001-2002 = S54 (rod-bearing design flaw, VANOS failures common and costly).
profiles.weak_points: REAR SUBFRAME / trunk-floor differential-mount cracking or tearing (worst on the M; inspect from below AND the trunk spot welds; reinforcement plates are the fix). S54: rod bearings (preventive replacement with upgraded bearings + oil analysis), double-VANOS failures. S52: cooling system, VANOS rattle. Finned differential mounts. Valve-cover and oil filter housing leaks. Rear trailing-arm bushings. Window regulators. Convertible-top mechanism (roadster). Cluster pixels. Cracked dashboard. Rust at rockers/floors.
profiles.immediate_repairs: cooling-system refresh, tires, fluids, oil analysis (S54)
profiles.repairs_12mo: rod bearings (S54, if not documented), VANOS service, rear subframe reinforcement, clutch if worn
profiles.market_notes: M coupes are the most valuable Z3 variant by a wide margin, with S54 coupes at the top. Documented rod-bearing and subframe work materially raises value. Mileage matters less than documentation on these cars.
profiles.catchup_notes: Cooling regardless of mileage; S54 rod bearings; VANOS; motor/trans mounts; rear shock mounts; tires by date; soft top; A/C. Salvage cars need pre/post-loss photos, invoices, the branding reason, measurements, airbag confirmation, CA smog feasibility, and a specialist PPI covering collision repair and the rear structure.

profiles.label: Lexus GX470

profiles.label: Acura NSX / NSX-T (NA2, 1997-2005, incl. 2002-05 facelift)
profiles.framing: The NA2 is the 3.2L C32B / 6-speed manual evolution of Honda's aluminum mid-engine car. It is a usable, reliable exotic that suits Carmel back roads and Highway 1 day trips, provided the age-related maintenance has been done. Because prices now sit firmly in collector territory, the buyer should pay for proof rather than mileage. That means accident-free aluminum structure, original or documented paint, a timing belt service dated within about 7 years, and a clean EPS/ABS/SRS scan. Low-mile cars that have mostly sat are not automatically better than well-serviced 40-70k mile drivers.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt, water pump and tensioner. Honda's interval is roughly 90-105k miles or about 7 years, and on low-mile NSXs age is almost always the trigger. Many 'garage queens' are overdue. A specialist job runs about $2,500-4,500 with water pump, tensioner, cam and crank seals, and possibly the thermostat. Require a dated receipt naming the parts replaced, and ideally the belt date tag in the engine bay. 2) Valve clearance. The C32B uses screw-type adjusters that need periodic checks. Ticking at idle or an unknown history means budget $800-1,500. 3) Oil seepage. Valve cover gaskets, spark plug tube seals, cam seals and the rear main seal weep with age. Drips onto the exhaust in the mid-engine bay cause smoke and smell. Valve covers cost $600-1,200; a rear main seal with the transaxle out costs $2,500-4,000+. 4) Cooling system. Long coolant lines run from the front radiator to the mid-mounted engine, and hoses, plastic radiator end tanks and the bleeding procedure all matter. Look for crusty residue at the front radiator and the engine-bay hose junctions, and overheating in traffic. A refresh with hoses and radiator runs about $1,200-2,500. 5) Electric power steering. Manual NA2s have EPS; faults include torque sensor, motor or control unit failure, shown by an EPS warning light, notchy or heavy assist, or a rack boot leak. Rack or unit replacement costs $2,000-5,000+ and parts can be slow. Require a scan with no stored EPS codes. 6) ABS modulator, pump and wheel speed sensors. An ABS light or pump buzz on startup points here. Modulator replacement costs $1,500-4,000. 7) Aluminum body and chassis. Repairs require aluminum-capable shops and proper parts. Poor collision work, filler over aluminum, or bent subframes and rails are the biggest value killer, and a clean Carfax proves nothing. Inspect with a non-ferrous (eddy-current) paint gauge; magnetic gauges read nothing on aluminum. Also check the front nose and bumper for refinish, which is common and acceptable if disclosed. 8) Galvanic and filiform corrosion where steel fasteners meet aluminum panels, at door bottoms, sills, and under the rear wing and engine cover. 9) Targa roof leaks. Shrunken roof and door weatherstrips, plus clogged drains, cause water in the footwells or behind the seats, wind noise and roof rattles. Seals cost $500-1,500 for a full set, and water can damage the SRS, ECU or carpets. 10) Power windows. Window regulators, motors and the master switch fail, showing as slow or crooked glass or glass not indexing to the seal. Expect $400-900 per side. 11) Climate control. The NA1 was worse for climate control display/LCD pixel loss and capacitor leakage in the climate unit, gauge cluster and SRS/ECU boards, but early NA2s are now old enough to be affected. Air conditioning (R134a) also suffers from compressor and condenser wear. Repair is $400-2,500 depending on fault. 12) Suspension bushings and alignment. Worn front lower control arm compliance bushings cause braking shimmy and clunks, and worn rear toe links and bushings matter too. The NSX is very alignment- and tire-sensitive, and mismatched or aged tires make it nervous. Bushings run $800-2,000, plus a specialist alignment. 13) Clutch hydraulics and synchros. The 6-speed transaxle is robust (the early snap-ring issue was a 1991-era 5-speed problem), but check the clutch master and slave cylinders, the clutch engagement point, and 2nd/3rd grind from abuse or track use. A clutch job runs $2,500-4,500. 14) Lighting. On 2002-05 cars the HID ballasts and bulbs fail ($300-900 per side). On 1997-01 cars the pop-up headlight motors and linkages wear. Modifications such as aftermarket exhaust, coilovers, intakes or ECU changes deserve scrutiny for whether the originals are included and any tune is reversible.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Expect a full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, coolant flushed and properly bled, brake and clutch fluid, and transaxle fluid if undated. Replace the timing belt, water pump and tensioner if there is no receipt within roughly 7 years. Replace tires if the DOT date code is older than about 6 years. Add a new battery or tender, since NSXs are hard on small batteries when stored. Finish with a 4-wheel specialist alignment and an AC performance check or recharge.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Likely items include valve cover and plug tube seals, targa and door weatherstrips, and roof drain cleaning. Expect at least one window regulator or motor. Front compliance bushings and rear toe links may be due. Brake pads and rotors may need doing if the car is glazed from sitting. Older dampers, or mismatched aftermarket shocks, may need replacing. Possible jobs are an HID ballast (2002-05) or headlight motor (1997-01), a climate display repair, and a valve clearance adjustment if undocumented.
profiles.market_notes: The 2002-05 fixed-headlight facelift cars command a strong premium over 1997-01 pop-up cars. The 2005 model year and rare colors (Imola Orange, Long Beach Blue, Rio Yellow, New Formula Red, Zanardi Edition) trade at the top, often with large odd-color premiums. Manuals dominate value; the automatic NA2 kept the 3.0L/4-speed and sells at a notable discount. Mileage bands matter (under 15k is collector-grade; 30-70k with full records is the driver sweet spot). Original paint, low owner count, complete Acura dealer or NSX specialist records, and stock exhaust and suspension (or originals included) add significant value. Undisclosed collision repair on aluminum or heavy modification are major discounts.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most NA2s are low-use cars that have sat. Rubber seals, hoses, the timing belt, tires and fluids age out regardless of mileage. Even a 13k-mile example often needs $4,000-8,000 of catch-up work (belt service, fluids, tires, weatherstrips, AC) before it is a trustworthy coastal driver. Budget a known NSX specialist for the PPI and first service; Northern California has several.

profiles.label: Alfa Romeo 105/115 Series Coupe (Giulia Sprint GT / 1750 & 2000 GTV)
profiles.framing: This is the classic Bertone twin-cam coupe: a small, light, mechanically simple Italian GT that rewards a driver on Carmel Valley Road, Laureles Grade, or a Highway 1 run far more than its 130ish horsepower suggests. For this buyer it is a weekend and fair-weather car, not a commuter — the value proposition is a documented, rust-free, correctly-sorted example that can be driven hard for 200 miles without drama, not a shiny car hiding filler. On a 105 the body and the restoration paperwork are the whole ballgame; the mechanicals are all rebuildable and well-supported (Centerline, Alfaholics, Classic Alfa, Wes Ingram), but structural rust is what turns a $75k car into a $30k car. Coastal Monterey humidity and salt air mean a garage, a battery tender, and disciplined post-drive care are part of ownership.
profiles.weak_points:
Structural rust is failure point number one and it is never limited to one spot: inner and outer sills (rockers), the box section under the front floors, the front suspension/shock tower mounts, the rear spring perches and rear shock upper mounts inside the trunk area, the battery tray and the metal under it, headlight bucket bottoms, the lower A-pillar/door hinge area, spare-tire well, rear valance and lower rear quarters behind the wheel arches, and the sail panel/rear window surround. Bodged repairs are normal — expect fiberglass, seam sealer and filler over rot. A proper sill and floor job is $8k–$20k+ in labor and panels; a full strip-and-paint on a straight shell is $20k–$35k, and rust discovered after purchase routinely runs past the car's value. Demand in-process photos of bare metal, not just finished paint.

The 1,962cc twin-cam is an aluminum block with cast-iron wet liners, and the classic failure is head gasket / liner-seal seepage: coolant loss with no external leak, pressurizing overflow tank, bubbles in the expansion tank, or coolant smell at the dipstick. Cars run hot in traffic at 60k–100k miles are prime suspects. A reseal with new liner O-rings and a skim is $4k–$7k; a full rebuild with liners, valve job and bearings is $10k–$18k at a specialist.

Overheating in general: original narrow radiators, tired water pumps, a tiny two-blade fan and a corroded head make the 2000 marginal in stop-and-go heat. Aluminum radiator, new pump, correct thermostat and an electric fan are near-mandatory upgrades — look for receipts, and watch the gauge in traffic during the test drive.

Timing chain tensioner and chain wear: a rubber-shoe tensioner and a two-row chain that rattle on start-up or at 1,500–2,500 rpm. A neglected chain can jump. Tensioner/chain/guides with cam timing reset: $1,200–$2,500 with the head on; often done during any top-end work. Also expect valve-guide wear (blue smoke on overrun, oil consumption over ~1 qt/1,000 mi) and hardened valve-cover and cam-cover gasket leaks on any car with unknown top-end history.

Oil pressure and bottom-end health: hot idle should hold roughly 15–25 psi and 50–60+ psi at 3,500–4,000 rpm on the dash gauge. Low hot pressure means worn bearings/oil pump and a rebuild bill. The oil pressure gauge inset in the tach is original; verify with a mechanical gauge if possible.

Fuel system: a US 1974 2000 GTV left the factory with Spica mechanical injection. Many have been converted to Weber 40 DCOE/DCOM carbs (as this example was). Spica cars need a specialist and a properly rebuilt pump ($2,500–$4,000 at Ingram) plus a working thermostatic actuator or they run rich, stumble and foul plugs; Weber-converted cars need documented jetting, correct linkage, and a proper distributor/ignition curve or they'll be lumpy below 2,000 rpm and hot-start poorly. Original Spica hardware set aside with the car is worth real money; a Weber conversion with no paperwork on tuning is a red flag. Old original steel tanks rust and clog filters — a replacement tank or documented tank cleaning is a plus.

Transmission: the 5-speed is stout but second-gear synchro is the known wear item — crunch or lockout on a warm 2nd-gear downshift is normal-ish and means a rebuild eventually ($3,000–$5,500). Also check for weak 1st/2nd detents, a worn shift linkage/tunnel bushing giving vague throw, and rear main/gearbox front seal seepage.

Driveline and rear suspension: two-piece propshaft with a center support bearing and rubber flex coupling (vibration at 50–70 mph if tired, $400–$900), rear trailing-arm and reaction-trunnion (T-bar) bushings that go soft and cause rear-end steer and clunks, and rear axle/diff whine. Limited-slip units are desirable; rebuilt-diff receipts matter.

Brakes: all four discs with an ATE/Bonaldi vacuum servo that is a known failure item — long pedal, hiss, or the servo dumping fluid. Rebuilt servos are scarce ($700–$1,500 exchanged) and many cars get a modern master/booster substitute. A
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (engine oil, gearbox, diff, brake fluid flush, coolant with correct mix); replace all rubber fuel lines and inline filters regardless of claimed age; new tires if the date codes are over 6 years old even with good tread; carb or Spica sync/tune and ignition timing with a fresh distributor cap/rotor/plugs/wires; adjust valve clearances and verify cam timing/chain tensioner noise; brake system check with attention to the servo, flex hoses and rear caliper drag; check and re-torque head, then pressure-test the cooling system for early liner/head-gasket seepage; correct any grounding/charging gremlins and fit a battery cutoff and tender; reseal cam covers and check for oil weeps around the timing cover; alignment and toe check after any suspension work; seatbelt and lighting
profiles.repairs_12mo: Second-gear synchro or full gearbox rebuild if any crunch appears; propshaft center support bearing and flex coupling; brake servo rebuild or conversion to a modern master/booster; wheel bearings and rear trailing-arm/T-bar bushings if not documented; radiator/water pump/electric fan upgrade if still original; fuel tank cleaning or replacement and sender calibration; distributor rebuild or electronic ignition (123/Marelli replacement); exhaust from the manifold back if original; window regulators, door seals and weatherstrip renewal to stop coastal water ingress; localized paint/rust touch-up at sills, wheel arches and battery tray as things reveal themselves; possible Spica pump rebuild or carb rebuild kit; speedometer/tach cable and gauge servicing.
profiles.market_notes: Within the 105/115 family, step-nose 1600 Sprint GT/GTV and the 1750 GTV generally out-trade the later 1974–76 2000 GTV, and GTA/GTAm cars are a different market entirely; US-market 1974 cars carry the big bumpers and Spica injection, so Euro-spec conversions and Weber swaps are common and split buyers. Price is driven almost entirely by documented rust-free structure and the quality/receipts of the bodywork, then by color (Verde/AR greens, Giallo Ocra and rare originals over red), original-spec details (Campagnolo alloys, LSD, correct dash and seats), and completeness of records — mileage barely moves the needle on a 50-year-old car. Sorted, restored driver-quality 2000 GTVs trade broadly in the $45k–$70k band, with concours or freshly and verifiably restored cars reaching $75k–$95k; note that restoration cost ($130k here) is not recoverable, so a fresh high-dollar refurbishment sold at $75k is the market working in the buyer's favor if the receipts are real. Unrestored 'ran when parked' cars at $20k–$35k are usually $40k+ of work away from the same place.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 50-year-old car needs a rubber-and-fluids reset regardless of the story: fuel lines, brake hoses and fluid, coolant hoses, engine mounts, suspension bushings, and date-expired tires. Even a freshly refurbished example typically needs 500–1,000 shakedown miles with a specialist on call to chase carb/ignition tune, minor oil weeps, electrical grounds and water leaks. Budget annual valve-clearance and carb/injection sync service plus a garage with a dehumidifier or car cover for coastal Monterey humidity.

profiles.label: Alfa Romeo 1900C Sprint by Touring (First Series, Tipo I & Tipo II)
profiles.framing: This is a 1950s Italian coachbuilt grand tourer. For a Carmel-based driver it is best used on Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and Monterey Car Week tours, not as daily transport. The hand-formed Superleggera alloy-over-steel body, the twin-cam engine, and coachbuilt trim cannot be replaced like a production car's parts, so structural integrity, authenticity (CDA build data versus what is actually on the car), and the quality of the last restoration matter far more than odometer readings. Buy the best-documented body and drivetrain you can find. Cosmetics and a nice interior are the cheapest things to fix on this car.
profiles.weak_points: ['Galvanic corrosion of the Superleggera body. The aluminum panels are rolled over small-diameter steel tubes and attached to a steel platform, and the aluminum corrodes where it touches steel. Look for blistering, white powdery corrosion, or paint lifting along wheel-arch lips, door bottoms, the edges of the hood and decklid, and around the headlamp and grille openings. Coastal fog and salt air in Carmel accelerate this if the car lives outdoors. Local panel and tube repair runs about $10k-$30k. A full body-off alloy and frame restoration runs $80k-$200k or more. Ask for bare-metal restoration photos.', 'Rot in the steel platform and floor. The 1900 is unitary below the beltline, so sills, floor pans, jacking points, the trunk floor, the spare-wheel well, and the battery tray all rust. Front and rear suspension pick-up areas are critical. Undercoating or fresh paint can hide filler and patch panels, so it must go on a lift with a magnet and moisture meter. Structural floor and sill work typically costs $15k-$50k.', 'Poor or mixed-quality earlier restorations. Many cars passed through low-cost restorations in Europe, South America, or the US decades ago. Look for thick filler over aluminum, which aluminum does not hold well, so it shows as cracking and ripples. Also check for mismatched panel gaps, steel patch panels let into alloy skins, and door and hinge misalignment. Doors that sag or need slamming suggest frame or hinge-pillar problems. Ask who did the bodywork and get the photo record.', 'Tipo 1308 twin-cam four (1,884 cc, roughly 100 hp, cast-iron block, alloy hemi head, chain-driven cams). Common faults are timing-chain stretch and tensioner wear (a rattle at idle or on decel), valve-guide and seal wear (blue smoke on overrun), and head-gasket or water-jacket corrosion in the alloy head from years of neglected coolant. Cam and valve-cover leaks are common; the example listing records repairs to both. Pistons, liners, bearings, and chains come through a small pool of specialists. A proper rebuild runs $30k-$60k and takes months. Get a compression or leakdown test, oil-pressure readings hot and cold, and the rebuild invoice with machine-shop details.', 'Non-original or replacement engines. Many cars now carry a replacement 1308 unit, a sedan 1306 unit, or a later 2.0 L Super Sprint unit, as in the example listing. Several of these are good drivers but they lower value. Compare the engine number to the Centro Documentazione Alfa Romeo (CDA) certificate. Look for sedan-type parts mixed in, and confirm the cylinder head and block numbers actually belong together.', 'Carburetion and fuel system. Original single or twin-choke Solex setups and period Weber or Abarth twin-carb kits all need careful synchronization and float setting. Worn throttle shafts cause hesitation and a hunting idle. Old fuel tanks shed rust and varnish. Cloth-braided and rubber fuel lines degrade under ethanol fuel, which creates a real fire risk near the hot exhaust manifold. Carb rebuild and sync costs $1.5k-$3k; tank clean, coat, or replacement plus lines costs $1.5k-$4k.', 'Cooling margin. The original radiator and thermostat setup is marginal in slow summer traffic at Monterey events. Look for creeping temperatures, a weeping water pump, and silted radiator cores. Overheating an alloy head risks warping and head-gasket failure. Radiator recore or upgrade plus pump rebuild runs about $1.5k-$3.5k.', 'Gearbox originality and wear. First-series Sprints were generally delivered with a 4-speed, often with a column change. Many now carry a later Alfa 5-speed floor-shift conversion, as in the example listing. Check for synchro crunch (especially 2nd), jumping out of gear, column-shift linkage slop, and the quality of any tunnel or crossmember modification made for a 5-speed swap. Gearbox rebuilds run $6k-$15k, and gears for early boxes are scarce.', 'Live rear axle and differential. Look for whine or clunk on and off throttle, pinion and axle-seal leaks ont
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full brake hydraulic service: wheel cylinders, master cylinder inspection or rebuild, hoses, fluid flush, and shoe adjustment.', 'Replace tires older than about 6-8 years regardless of tread (check Cinturato date codes), and balance the wire wheels.', 'Fuel system safety work: replace rubber and cloth-braided lines, add or replace the fuel filter, inspect the tank for rust, and check carb float levels and needle valves.', 'Ignition tune-up: points, condenser, plugs, cap, and rotor; set timing and dwell; synchronize the carburetors.', 'Cooling system flush with correct coolant, new hoses and clamps, thermostat check, and pressure test.', 'Engine oil and filter change; gearbox and differential oil change with correct non-aggressive gear oil.', 'Valve clearance check and timing-chain tensio
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Reseal chronic oil leaks: cam and valve covers, timing cover, rear main if weeping onto the clutch, and pinion and axle seals.', 'Front suspension bushings, kingpin or trunnion service, and steering-box adjustment or rebuild.', 'Radiator recore or upgrade and water pump rebuild if temperatures creep at idle or in traffic.', 'Generator or voltage regulator rebuild and targeted wiring repair or partial harness replacement.', 'Brake drum refinishing or relining if out of round or if liners show cracking.', 'Clutch hydraulics or linkage service; plan for a clutch if engagement is high or it slips.', 'Corrosion treatment at alloy-to-steel contact points, cavity wax in sills and floors, and a dehumidified indoor storage plan.', 'Gauge recalibration or repair (Veglia speedometer, tach, oil pres
profiles.market_notes: Value is driven first by authenticity: original matching-numbers engine and gearbox, original color per the CDA certificate, and complete correct Touring trim. Then come body quality and restoration documentation. Replacement engines, color changes, unknown total mileage, and missing original parts can depress values substantially, as the reserve-not-met result in the example listing suggests. Tipo I versus Tipo II details, Mille Miglia and touring-event eligibility or history, concours awards, and period-correct options such as Abarth carburetion or Borrani wheels move buyers. The later 2.0 L 1900C Super Sprint and examples from other coachbuilders (Pinin Farina, Ghia, Zagato) are priced as distinct markets and should not be used as direct comps.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a freshly refurbished, low-use example usually needs brake hydraulics, a fuel-line and tank review, a cooling flush, fresh tires, and an ignition and carb setup within the first months. Cars that sat after a show-quality refresh often develop seal leaks and sticking brakes once driven regularly. Budget for a specialist who knows 1900-series Alfas, and for indoor dehumidified storage to slow galvanic corrosion in the coastal Carmel climate.

profiles.label: Alfa Romeo GTV6 Callaway Twin Turbo (116 Series, c. 1984–1986)
profiles.framing: This is a dealer-installed period tuner car. Roughly 35 GTV6s received Callaway Engineering's twin-IHI-turbo, intercooler and Microfueler package over the stock Busso 2.5 V6 and rear five-speed transaxle. For a Carmel-based driver who wants documented, unmodified cars, 'original' here means intact, functioning Callaway hardware with a verifiable Callaway certificate and serial. A stock GTV6 with aftermarket turbos is not the same car. The real questions are whether the boosted engine has been kept healthy (compression, head and liner sealing, turbo oiling, correct fueling) and whether the 40-year-old Alfetta-platform body, driveline and inboard rear brakes are sorted. California smog and registration feasibility for a turbo-kit car, possibly Canadian-market, must be settled before money moves.
profiles.weak_points: ['Callaway fueling and boost control. The Microfueler adds fuel under boost on top of the factory Bosch L-Jetronic, and its failure or a bad adjustment is the classic way these engines die (lean under boost, detonation, holed piston or burned valve). Parts are essentially unobtainable, so a dead unit means specialist electronic repair or re-engineering. Budget $1,500–5,000 to diagnose and restore correct function, or $15,000–30,000+ if it has already hurt the engine. Ask for any wideband air-fuel and boost data, records from a known Alfa or Callaway specialist, and confirmation the car has always run on premium fuel.', 'Busso V6 head gaskets and wet-liner sealing. The 2.5 uses wet cylinder liners sealed by base O-rings, plus head gaskets that carry boost on this car. Symptoms are coolant loss, oil in the coolant, coolant in the oil, white smoke, pressurized hoses and overheating. Expect $4,000–8,000 for a head-gasket and liner reseal, and $15,000–25,000+ for a full rebuild by a Busso specialist. Ask for compression and leak-down numbers and a combustion-gas (block) test.', 'Timing belt, tensioner and water pump. The single long belt drives both cams, and the 12-valve Busso should be treated as an interference engine. Age matters more than miles: replace every 3–4 years or 30k miles, whichever comes first. Cost is $1,500–2,800 with the water pump, tensioner and idler. A low-mileage car that sat for years almost certainly needs it regardless of odometer. Ask for a dated receipt.', 'Valve guides, rockers and cam wear. Early Busso engines are known for valve-guide wear (smoke on startup or overrun). The exhaust-side rocker and cross-pushrod valvetrain can wear and tick, and boost adds heat and stress. A top-end refresh is $4,000–8,000. Watch for blue smoke at startup and on lift-off.', 'Turbochargers, oil feed/return lines and heat damage. The IHI turbos can coke their bearings after hot shutdowns, leak oil through their seals (smoke, oil in the intercooler piping) or develop shaft play. Rebuilds run $1,500–3,000 per turbo, and Callaway-correct parts are rare. Under-hood heat also cooks rubber fuel lines, vacuum lines, wiring insulation and the turbo oil-return hoses. Check for blue or white smoke under boost, wet intercooler couplers and brittle hoses near the manifolds.', 'Exhaust and turbo manifolds. Cast manifolds and crossover pipes crack with heat cycling, and studs break, causing ticking on cold start and soot tracks. Expect $800–3,000, more if Callaway-specific pieces must be repaired rather than replaced.', 'Fuel system fire risk and L-Jetronic faults. Old injector hoses, the fuel pump, the pressure regulator and the cold-start valve age out, and any leak sits next to hot turbo plumbing. Air flow meter wiper wear, a failing fuel-pump relay or ECU relay, and poor grounds cause stumbles and hot-start problems. A full hose and rubber refresh is $600–1,500. The AFM is $500–1,500 to rebuild or replace.', 'Body rust on the 116 platform. Inspect the sills and jacking points, front floors and footwells, windshield and scuttle base, A-pillar bases, door bottoms, rear arches, spare-wheel well and trunk floor (the battery lives in back, so look for acid damage), the lower edge of the hatch, and the de Dion and transaxle mounting areas. Structural repair runs $5,000–30,000+. Ask for underside photos on a lift, ideally of bare or clean metal, and a paint-meter reading.', 'Rear transaxle and clutch. Second-gear synchro wear causes crunching on fast shifts, the long shift linkage loosens through worn bushings, and output-shaft seals weep. The clutch sits at the rear and has to carry Callaway torque, so heavy slip under boost is a red flag. A clutch job is $1,500–2,500; a transaxle rebuild is $3,500–7,000.', "Driveshaft flex discs and center bearing. The two-piece propshaft with rubber flex couplings ('donuts') and center support cracks with age and torque, causing vibration, clunks on throttle changes and, if a disc fails, driveline dam
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace age-expired tires; the 205/55R15 fitment on OZ three-piece wheels needs fresh rubber before any spirited driving.', 'Do a timing belt, tensioner, idler and water pump service unless there is a dated receipt within about 3 years.', 'Complete the fuel- and oil-rubber refresh: any remaining injector and supply hoses, vacuum lines, turbo oil-return hoses and the cold-start valve hose.', 'Change fluids: engine oil and filter, transaxle oil, coolant (with a pressure test) and clutch fluid if not done with the recent brake flush.', 'Inspect the driveshaft flex discs and center bearing, and replace them if they are cracked.', 'Verify Callaway fueling with wideband AFR and boost logging, and correct any lean condition before driving it hard.', 'Inspect the inboard rear calipers for drag o
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front suspension refresh: upper ball joints, control-arm bushings, tie rods and a torsion-bar ride-height adjustment.', 'De Dion slider and bellows plus Watts-link bushings.', 'Inboard rear brake caliper rebuild and new pads and rotors if they are contaminated.', 'Exhaust and turbo manifold stud repair or crack repair.', 'Cooling-system catch-up: radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, fan switch and heater valve.', 'Turbo oil feed line and seal inspection, plus a turbo shaft-play check.', 'Air-conditioning service or R-12 conversion, depending on current state.', 'Shift linkage bushings and a 2nd-gear synchro assessment.', 'Cosmetic and comfort items: sunroof mechanism, window regulators, gauge senders.']
profiles.market_notes: Verified Callaway provenance drives value: the certificate of authenticity, serial number, intact Callaway induction, intercoolers, Microfueler and hood scoop, plus a documented chain of ownership. Comparable Callaways bring roughly double to triple a top stock GTV6, recently around $50k–80k for the best examples. Condition and originality of the Callaway-specific parts matter more than mileage. A car with missing or replaced Callaway electronics, or an engine rebuilt without specialist records, takes a heavy discount. Low miles from a car that sat many years should not command a premium unless sitting-damage catch-up (belt, rubber, seals, fuel system) is documented. Red over tan with original Recaros is a desirable spec. Export-market status (Canadian-market cars exist) and California smog feasibility materially affect what a California buyer should pay.
profiles.catchup_notes: Typical examples have low miles but long periods of sitting, so rubber, seals, belts, fuel components and brakes age out regardless of the odometer. Expect $4,000–10,000 of catch-up even on a well-presented car. The open-ended risk is a boosted Busso V6 that has been run lean or overheated: specialist engine work can reach $15,000–30,000, and irreplaceable Callaway electronics can push it higher.

profiles.label: Aston Martin Vantage (2025+ facelift, incl. Vantage S) Coupe & Roadster
profiles.framing: This is the heavily revised third-generation Vantage. The 2025 car gets a reworked AMG M177-based 4.0L twin-turbo V8 (656 hp; about 670 hp in the 2026 Vantage S), an in-house infotainment system, and a stiffer bonded-aluminum chassis. Every example uses the ZF 8-speed automatic, so the lack of a manual is not a demerit here. For a Carmel buyer it is a near-new, still-under-factory-warranty open GT for coastal and canyon driving, and the money questions are depreciation, warranty transferability, and California registrability rather than mechanical wear. What matters most is a clean, verifiable title chain, an undamaged and unrepaired aluminum body, current software and recall status, and an honest accounting of consumables like tires, brakes and the roof.
profiles.weak_points:
['Limited field history. The facelift launched for MY2025 and the Vantage S for MY2026, so there is little long-term failure data yet. Expectations below are extrapolated from the 2018-2024 Vantage, the DB12/DBX707 that share the updated powertrain and electronics, and the AMG M177 family. Factory warranty is 3 years/unlimited miles from the original in-service date. Confirm that date with an Aston dealer, because it is the main financial safety net.', 'Infotainment and electronics software. The new in-house touchscreen system shared with the DB12 has had early reports of screen freezes, slow boot, CarPlay/Android Auto dropouts, phantom ADAS and parking-sensor warnings, and 360-camera glitches. Most are fixed by dealer software flashes. Ask for proof that the latest software level and any campaigns have been applied. Out of warranty, a head unit or display module is a $4,000-8,000 item.', '12V battery drain and low-voltage faults. Astons of this era are sensitive to parasitic drain when parked. A weak battery produces cascading warnings, keyless-entry failures and roof or transmission messages that look far worse than they are. Low-mileage cars that sat are the most vulnerable. Check battery state of health and whether a maintainer was used. Battery replacement with registration costs $500-900.', 'Power soft top (Roadster). The Z-fold roof is quick but complex: electric/hydraulic actuators, microswitches, header latches and drain channels. Watch for:
  - hesitation or stopping mid-cycle
  - error messages
  - wind noise or water stains at the A-pillar and header
  - wet carpets behind the seats from blocked drains

  Actuator or hydraulic repairs run $2,500-6,000. Full top replacement (fabric and frame components) is $8,000-15,000.', 'M177-family twin-turbo V8. The basic engine is robust, but the hot-vee layout cooks components. Known family items:
  - coolant leaks at turbo coolant lines and plastic fittings
  - turbo oil feed/return seepage
  - coil packs and plugs stressed at high boost (misfire codes)
  - engine and transmission mounts on hard-driven cars

  Out of warranty, turbo replacement is $8,000-15,000. Look for any warranty claims in the dealer VIN history.', 'ZF 8-speed and electronic rear differential (E-diff). Both are generally durable. Harsh 2-3 or 3-4 shifts, flare on downshift, or clunks in tight parking-lot turns point to adaptation/software issues or E-diff problems. E-diff seal seepage has appeared on earlier Vantages. A transmission replacement out of warranty is $12,000-20,000. An E-diff unit is $6,000-10,000.', 'Brakes. Standard iron rotors are expensive but manageable: about $3,000-5,000 per axle at a dealer. Optional carbon-ceramic brakes cost $8,000-12,000+ per axle for rotors and pads, and they can be damaged by track abuse or improper wheel-mounting impacts. Confirm which system the car has from the build sheet and the rotor faces, and measure rotor condition.', 'Tires and 21-inch wheels. profiles.market_notes:
This Vantage depreciates steeply. Six-figure drops from the roughly $200k-230k+ sticker in the first year or two are normal, and the bid level in this listing reflects that. Price is moved by:
- S versus base trim
- carbon-ceramic brakes
- carbon packs
- Bowers & Wilkins audio
- desirable or Q-by-Aston paint
- remaining factory warranty term

Roadsters trade at a modest premium in sunny markets. Any accident, Carfax damage entry or evidence of panel repair on the aluminum body sharply hurts resale. Lien or title delays and out-of-state, non-California-certified cars also trade at a discount. One-owner, dealer-serviced, very low-mileage examples with transferable warranty and clean paint-meter readings command the strongest prices.
profiles.catchup_notes:
A 2025-2026 car needs little true catch-up. The real items are age-related rather than mileage-related:
- tires and the 12V battery degrading from storage
- the first time-based annual service coming due within 12 months of in-service
- applying any outstanding software and recall campaigns

In Carmel's salt-fog climate, budget for keeping the roof and brake hardware clean and garaging the car to protect the soft top and semi-aniline leather.

profiles.label: Audi RS4 Avant (B5, 2000–2001)
profiles.framing: The B5 RS4 is a 375 hp, Cosworth-developed twin-turbo 2.7 V6 (engine codes ASJ/AZR), six-speed manual, Torsen quattro wagon. Roughly 6,000 were built and none were sold new in the US, so every American car is a 25-year-rule import, usually from Japan or Europe. For a Carmel buyer who wants a usable, documented, unmodified driver, the first question is whether a gray-market 2000–2001 car can legally be registered and smog-certified in California. After that, what matters is proof of timing-belt and turbo-oiling health, and a verified odometer, because engine-out turbo work and scarce RS-specific parts can quickly exceed the car's purchase premium.
profiles.weak_points: ['California registrability is the largest non-mechanical risk. California has no 25-year emissions exemption. A 2000–2001 direct import generally needs CARB-pathway certification through a CARB-approved lab, often with emissions modifications, before DMV will register it. Budget roughly $5,000–15,000+ with uncertain timelines, and confirm feasibility before bidding, not after. Out-of-state titles (FL, etc.) do not carry over.', "Timing belt service on this interference engine includes the belt, water pump, thermostat, hydraulic tensioner, rollers and idler. Due every ~75k miles or ~5 years, and age matters more than miles on low-mileage imports. The front end goes into service position, so expect $2,500–4,500 at a specialist. With no dated receipt, assume it is due immediately, and treat a 20+ year-old belt on a 'low-mile' car as a real failure risk.", "Turbos are BorgWarner K04-family units, larger than the S4's K03s, mounted low in the valley-side and exhaust-side positions. They fail through oil coking, shaft play, seal leakage (blue smoke on boost or lift-off) and wheel damage. Replacement is typically engine-out and runs about $7,000–12,000 for a pair with OEM or quality rebuilt units plus new oil and coolant lines. Ask whether they are original or rebuilt, look for receipts, and test boost under load.", 'The turbo oil-feed banjo bolts contain fine mesh screens that clog and starve the turbos. The oil pickup tube and screen in the sump commonly clog with sludge or excess RTV, causing low oil pressure and bearing or turbo failure. Look for documentation that the screens were removed or replaced and that the pan was dropped and the pickup cleaned (roughly $600–1,500). Short service intervals with correct VW 502.00 synthetic matter a lot.', 'Valve cover gaskets, cam-chain tensioner gaskets and the rear half-moon seals leak oil onto the exhaust manifolds and turbos. This shows up as a burning oil smell and smoke from the engine bay after a drive, and as oil-soaked heat shields. Repair runs about $900–2,000 and is often paired with the timing belt job.', 'Vacuum, boost and breather hoses fail with age. The PCV/crankcase breather hoses go brittle, the Bosch diverter valves tear, and the N75 and boost hoses leak. Symptoms are boost leaks, lean codes, erratic idle, hesitation and low boost. Parts are cheap, but a full refresh runs about $400–1,200 in labor-heavy spots. Original rubber on a 2000–2001 car should be assumed due.', 'Ignition coil packs (2.7T-era coil failure and recall history) and plugs cause misfires under boost. Look for a coil record and a clean misfire count on a scan. Coils are about $40–100 each. Undiagnosed misfires can damage the catalysts, which also matters for California smog.', 'The clutch and dual-mass flywheel are expensive in this application. Check for slipping in 4th–6th at full boost, a high engagement point, DMF rattle at idle that changes with the clutch pedal, and judder. Replacement is about $3,000–5,000 with an OEM-spec clutch and flywheel.', 'The 01E six-speed and driveline are robust but not immune. Watch for worn 2nd/3rd synchros (grinding on fast shifts), sloppy shift linkage bushings, output and axle seal leaks at the gearbox and rear differential, and CV boot tears. Gear oil should be changed on a non-documented car. A gearbox rebuild runs $3,000–6,000 if synchros are gone.', 'The front four-link suspension (upper and lower control arms) and tie rods wear out. You get clunks over bumps, vague steering, uneven tire wear and shimmy under braking. Hydraulic engine and transmission mounts also sag and leak with age. A full arm kit with alignment is about $1,200–2,500, and mounts are about $600–1,200.', 'The cooling system has plastic-tanked radiators, plastic coolant flanges and pipes, an aging expansion tank and cap, and turbo coolant lines. These seep, crack or overheat, which is especially damaging on a twin-turbo engine. A preventive refresh runs about $800–2,000. Check for pink/purple
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Do a timing belt, water pump, thermostat, tensioner and roller service unless a dated receipt within ~4–5 years exists.', 'Change all fluids: engine oil and filter (VW 502.00 synthetic), coolant (G12-type), gearbox and rear differential oil, brake fluid, and power steering fluid if dark.', 'Inspect and clean the oil pickup tube and turbo banjo screens (drop the pan) if there is no record.', 'Refresh the vacuum, PCV breather, diverter valve and boost hoses. Smoke-test the intake for boost leaks.', 'Replace the oiled K&N filter with an OEM-type paper filter and inspect or clean the MAF.', 'Replace tires if date codes are over 6 years old, even with good tread. Set alignment.', 'Start the California CARB-lab and DMV registration process, including any emissions-equipment corrections and a f
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Replace valve cover, cam-tensioner and half-moon gaskets for oil leaks onto the manifolds.', 'Replace the front control arms, tie rod ends and sway bar links. Do an alignment.', 'Replace the hydraulic engine and transmission mounts.', 'Refresh the cooling system: radiator, plastic flanges, expansion tank and cap, hoses.', 'Replace coil packs if any are original or there are misfire counts. Address the secondary air pump and check valves if smog fails.', 'Replace the clutch and dual-mass flywheel if it slips or rattles.', 'Replace CV boots, axle seals, and the gearbox and rear differential seals as found.', 'Repair the instrument cluster or climate display pixels, the tailgate harness, and door lock microswitches as found.', 'Clean sunroof drains and check the wagon cargo area for water i
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven by originality (stock K04 turbos, no tune, factory exhaust and intake, original RS4 wheels and body panels), verified low mileage with credible export or auction-sheet documentation, and receipts for the timing belt and turbo-oiling work. Color matters strongly: Nogaro Blue Pearl and Imola Yellow command premiums, Misano Red and Avus Silver are solid, and plain black is less sought. Recaro seat condition (bolsters) and carbon trim affect value. Japanese-market cars often show lower miles and better cosmetics but need careful odometer verification. Euro cars with stamped service books trade on documentation. Cars that are tuned, accident-repaired in RS-specific panels, or lack California registrability trade at a meaningful discount for a California buyer, and clean low-mile examples are currently in the roughly $40k–75k band.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical import of this age has a 20+ year-old belt, brittle vacuum and breather rubber, original cooling plastics, and probably a sludged oil pickup, even if the mileage is low. Expect to spend roughly $5,000–9,000 in the first year to bring it to a reliable baseline, before any California certification costs.

profiles.label: Audi S3 Sedan (8V, 2015-2020 US; 2017+ facelift)
profiles.framing: The 8V S3 is a compact, fast, all-weather quattro sedan built on the VW MQB platform. It uses the EA888 Gen 3 2.0T and a dual-clutch S tronic, and no manual was offered in the US. For a Carmel-based daily driver, a stock, dealer-documented example is a genuinely quick and refined car with modest running costs, as long as the S tronic, Haldex coupling and cooling system have been maintained on schedule. The biggest variable is history: this is one of the most commonly tuned cars on the market, and a car that was flashed and then returned to stock is a different risk proposition than a true never-tuned car. In California, an untested tune is also a smog liability.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Coolant pump and thermostat housing (EA888 Gen 3 integrated plastic thermal-management module, mounted behind the intake): the single most common failure. It typically weeps or leaks between 40k and 80k miles. Look for pink or white crust under the intake on the exhaust/firewall side, a sweet coolant smell, a slowly dropping G13 level, or P0597/P2181-type codes. Expect $900-1,500 at an independent shop and $1,500-2,200 at a dealer. Check for a receipt or a TSB or warranty-extension replacement. 2) S tronic dual-clutch transmission: 2015-2016 cars use the 6-speed DQ250 wet-clutch unit, and 2017+ cars use the 7-speed DQ381 (0GC). Fluid and filter service is due every 40k miles ($400-700). A skipped service accelerates clutch-pack wear and mechatronic faults. Symptoms include harsh 1-2 or 2-3 shifts, low-speed shudder, clunks into reverse, flashing PRNDS, or limp mode. Mechatronic unit replacement runs $2,500-4,500, and a clutch pack runs $2,000-3,500. 3) Haldex Gen 5 AWD coupling: the fluid is often neglected (Audi interval roughly 40k miles or 3-4 years, $150-300). Old fluid kills the pump, and the car then quietly runs front-drive only. Pump replacement is $800-1,400. Look for Haldex fault codes and confirm the service in the records. 4) Turbo (IS20-family): wastegate rattle on cold start or decel is a known trait. It can be benign or progress to a loose wastegate actuator linkage. Turbo replacement is $2,500-3,800. Tuned cars run higher boost and wear turbos faster. 5) Tuning history: APR, Unitronic, IS38 swaps and DSG tunes are extremely common. Evidence includes a non-stock ECU or TCU software part number, an elevated flash counter, aftermarket intake or downpipe witness marks, and a missing or replaced catalytic converter. In CA, BAR smog checks now flag non-CARB-EO software, so a tune is both a reliability and a registration problem. 6) PCV/oil separator and cam cover area: the diaphragm fails less often than on Gen 1/2 engines but still occurs. Symptoms are a whistle or hiss at idle, lean codes (P0171) and rough idle. Repair is $300-700. 7) Ignition coils and spark plugs: plugs are due about every 40k miles. Coils fail randomly and produce misfire codes P0300-P0304. Repair is $150-450, and coils and plugs wear much faster on tuned cars. 8) Timing chain tensioner: the revised Gen 3 tensioner is far more reliable than the 2008-2012 design, but chain stretch is still worth checking via cam-crank correlation values on a scan tool. A failure is rare, but repair is $2,000-3,500. 9) Audi Magnetic Ride dampers (S Sport package cars): they can leak or fault, showing suspension warnings or a floaty or crashing corner. OEM replacement is $900-1,400 per corner installed, and non-MR swaps lose the feature. 10) Panoramic sunroof: clogged front or rear drains can put water in the footwell, headliner or electronics, and the roof can rattle or stall. Cleaning the drains is cheap, but water damage to modules is not. 11) Front suspension: the rear bushings on the front lower control arms and the lower engine/transmission pendulum (dogbone) mount wear. Symptoms are clunks over bumps and vibration on launch or at idle in gear. Expect $400-1,000. 12) Brakes and electronic parking brake: the S3 front rotors and pads are a fairly costly wear item ($700-1,200 per axle at an independent shop). The rear EPB caliper motors can fault. 13) Infotainment and electrical: Virtual Cockpit or MMI screen glitches, retracting-screen faults, and occasional battery-drain or BMS-coding issues after a non-coded battery replacement.

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Coolant pump and thermostat housing replacement if original and past 50k miles ($900-1,500)', 'Front brake pads and rotors depending on measured thickness ($700-1,200)', 'PCV/oil separator if idle whistle or lean codes appear ($300-700)', 'Lower engine/transmission pendulum mount and front control arm bushings if clunking ($400-1,000)', 'Ignition coil replacement as misfires appear ($150-400)', 'Magnetic Ride damper replacement if a fault or leak develops ($900-1,400 per corner)', 'Replace the 12V battery with BMS coding if original or weak ($250-400)', 'Replace summer tires, which wear fast on this car (235/35R19, $900-1,300 per set)']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by originality and documentation: a provably never-tuned, dealer-maintained, single-owner car commands a clear premium over the many tuned or 'returned to stock' examples. The 2017-2020 facelift cars (7-speed S tronic, updated LED lights, available Virtual Cockpit on Prestige) are preferred over 2015-2016, and Prestige trim with B&O and Virtual Cockpit or the S Sport package with Magnetic Ride adds value. Mileage bands matter at roughly 40k miles (first S tronic and Haldex service and plugs due), 60k miles (coolant pump window) and 80k miles or more (soft prices, turbo and mechatronic risk priced in). Clean-title 2019-2020 cars in the 40-60k mile range trade roughly in the mid-$20k to low-$30k range depending on trim and records.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2017-2020 S3 with 40-60k miles is at or past its first S tronic, Haldex, spark plug and brake fluid intervals, and is entering the coolant pump failure window. Even well-kept cars often need $1,500-3,000 of catch-up within the first year. Dealer 'oil service and top-off' visits do not imply that the 40k-mile driveline services were performed, so confirm each one by line item.

profiles.label: Audi S4 (B5, 2.7T twin-turbo, sedan & Avant, US 2000–2002)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, a B5 S4 Avant is a usable, analog quattro wagon with a twin-turbo V6. It suits Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road and still carries a dog and luggage. Most cars are now more than 20 years old, and the 2.7T's turbo, oil-feed, and timing-belt service history decides whether it is a joy or a money pit. Mileage matters less than records. A stock, documented, 6-speed car with recent turbo and timing-belt work is worth much more than a cheaper modified one. California smog compliance is a real gate for any tuned or out-of-state example.
profiles.weak_points: ['Turbochargers (twin Borg Warner K03, US APB engine). Oil coking in the turbo oil feed lines and the banjo-bolt screens starves the turbos. Symptoms include blue smoke on startup or under load, whistle or siren noise, oil in the intercooler piping, shaft play, and underboost. Original turbos past 100k are living on borrowed time, especially with short-trip use, long oil intervals, or a tune. Replacement is effectively an engine-out or deep front-end-service-position job, typically $4,000–7,000 for the pair with new feed and return lines. Look for receipts naming both turbos, new oil feed lines, banjo bolts, and gaskets.', 'Oil pickup tube and sludge. Coked turbo oil and degraded sealant can clog the oil pickup screen in the pan, causing low oil pressure and bearing or turbo failure. Any turbo job should include dropping the pan and cleaning or replacing the pickup tube. Ask whether this was done, and for oil analysis if available. Required oil is a full synthetic meeting VW 502.00, at 5,000-mile or shorter intervals.', "Timing belt service (interference engine). Audi's original interval was later shortened. Enthusiast and shop consensus is about 75k miles or 5–7 years, whichever comes first. The job should include water pump (preferably metal impeller), thermostat, hydraulic tensioner/damper, idler and tensioner rollers, and cam/crank seals. It requires front-end service position and runs $1,500–2,800. An undocumented belt on a car this old should be treated as due.", 'Valve cover gaskets, cam chain tensioner gaskets, and half-moon seals. These almost always seep on unrefreshed cars. Oil drips onto the exhaust manifolds and turbos, producing a burning smell and smoke at idle, and is a fire risk. A full refresh of both banks runs $700–1,400 and is often paired with the timing belt.', 'Vacuum, boost, and crankcase-breather leaks. Rubber vacuum lines, PCV and breather hoses under the intake manifold, intercooler couplers, and diverter valves (upgrade to the revised Bosch 710N-type part) go brittle with age. Symptoms are rough idle, underboost, lean or misfire codes, and oil in the intake. A smoke test is essential. Budget $300–1,200 depending on how deep the breather hose job goes.', 'Ignition and sensors. The 2.7T coil packs fail and cause misfires; Audi ran a coil-pack campaign on the 2001–2003 VAG turbo family. The MAF sensor (Bosch HFM) fails and causes hesitation and low power. The G62 coolant temp sensor gives erratic gauge readings or hard starting. The oil pressure sender also fails. Each is $100–600, but they stack up. Check misfire counters and the MAF reading with VCDS.', 'Cooling system aging. Expect leaks from the radiator plastic end tanks, coolant flanges, the expansion tank and cap, and upper and lower hoses. The turbo after-run coolant pump, if equipped and functional, matters for turbo longevity. A full refresh outside the timing belt job is $600–1,500.', "Clutch, dual-mass flywheel, and clutch hydraulics (6-speed 01E). Watch for a slipping or high-engaging clutch, DMF rattle or chatter at idle, and a leaking slave or master cylinder. Replacing the clutch and DMF is a transmission-out job at $2,000–3,500. Many cars have been converted to a single-mass flywheel, which is a modification to note. The listing's 'clutch due' is a common real-world state.", 'Tiptronic (ZF 5HP19) automatic. It works when stock, but internal clutch and valve-body wear shows as harsh or slipping shifts, especially with any power increase. A rebuild runs $3,000–4,500. For this buyer the 6-speed is strongly preferred.', 'Front multilink suspension. The eight aluminum control arms (four per side), especially the upper arms, wear their ball joints and bushings. Symptoms are clunks over bumps, vague steering, and uneven tire wear. A full kit installed with alignment is $900–2,000. Sway bar end links, strut mounts, and engine and transmission mounts (clunk on throttle transitions, excess vibration) are also typical.', 'Driveline and brakes. T

profiles.market_notes: The 6-speed manual Avant is the most sought-after B5 S4 configuration and commands a clear premium over sedans and Tiptronic cars (Tiptronic cars trade at a substantial discount). Documented turbo replacement, timing belt service, and stock or tastefully reversible condition move prices more than mileage alone. Rare colors such as Imola Yellow and Nogaro Blue Pearl bring more, while Brilliant Black and Light Silver are common. Clean low-mile manual Avants can bring several times the price of tired 100k+ mile driver-quality cars. Heavily modified or rusty examples, especially those with A-pillar bubbling or unknown turbo history, sell at steep discounts.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume most rubber and plastic on a typical B5 S4 is at end of life unless receipts show otherwise: vacuum lines, breather hoses, coolant hoses, suspension bushings, and gaskets. Plan for roughly $2,500–5,000 of catch-up work beyond the purchase price, even on a car that drives well. The timing belt, oil leaks, and a vacuum/breather refresh come first, with the turbos as the looming wildcard.

profiles.label: Audi Ur-Quattro (Typ 85, 10v/20v turbo coupe)
profiles.framing: This is a rally-icon halo car, not a rational fast coupe: 160-200 hp, heavy steering, turbo lag below 3,000 rpm, and a driving position out of a 1980 Coupe GT. For a Carmel-based driver it is a weekend Highway 1 and Laureles Grade car that can genuinely be used in the wet and on dirt roads, but it lives or dies on documentation, rust status, and whether the vacuum diff locks and CIS fuel system actually work. US-market cars are 1983-1986 (WR 2144cc, then MB 2226cc); anything else on a US title is a gray-market Euro import, which matters enormously for California registration and smog. Buy the best-documented, least-rotten example and accept that parts hunting is part of ownership.
profiles.weak_points: Rust is the first and last question. Check the front strut towers and their reinforcement plates, the floor pans under the carpet (especially the driver's footwell), the rear wheel arch lips and inner arches, the battery tray and the area under the master cylinder, the jack points and sills, the fuel filler area, the hatch lower corners, and the sunroof drain outlets at the base of the A-pillars where blocked drains dump water into the footwells. Strut tower or subframe-mount rot is structural and effectively terminal at these prices; arch repair alone is $3k-$8k done properly with correct panel fabrication. Cylinder head and head gasket on the 10-valve WR/MB engines: these heads crack between valve seats and warp if ever overheated, and a mid-1980s engine that has boiled once will telegraph it with coolant loss, combustion gases in the coolant, or mayonnaise under the oil cap. A head rebuild is $3,500-$6,000 and usable cores are getting scarce; 20v RR heads are worse. Cooling system is the enabler of that failure: original radiators, the plastic-tanked later units, brittle hoses, weak fan switches and the viscous/electric fan setup all fail with age. An aluminum radiator (2Bennett or similar) is a sensible, common upgrade rather than a red flag, but confirm the thermostat, fan switch, and temperature gauge all function. Bosch K-Jetronic / CIS-E fuel system: 40-year-old rubber fuel lines, the accumulator, warm-up regulator/control pressure regulator, cold-start behavior, and a gummed fuel distributor cause hot-start hesitation, rough idle, and rich running. A distributor rebuild is $700-$1,500 (Wayne Kuhn-type specialists); expect to replace every fuel hose in the engine bay and under the car as a fire-safety item, $600-$1,200. Vacuum-operated differential locks are the model's signature and its most commonly dead system: the center and rear lock actuator pods on the transaxle and rear diff perish, the vacuum reservoir and check valves leak, and the console knob/microswitches fail, so the car either won't lock or won't unlock. Budget $800-$2,000 to sort; demand video of both locks engaging and disengaging with the dash indicator lights. Hydraulic brake and steering system on 1983-1986 cars: a single pump feeds power steering and a brake pressure accumulator ('the bomb') using green mineral fluid (Pentosin/G002000). A dead accumulator gives a hard pedal after a few pumps ($400-$900), and leaking racks, hoses, and pump seals are routine; never let anyone put DOT brake fluid in this system. The MC/MB-era instrument cluster with the green LCD auto-check panel suffers dead segments, failing gauge voltage stabilizers, flaky speedo drives, and cracked circuit boards; cluster and stepper repair runs $400-$1,200 and cosmetic dash plastics are unobtainium. Wiring harness and grounds are brittle after four decades: the fuse/relay box, bulb-failure module, headlight and window switches, and door-lock pneumatics all misbehave; expect chasing gremlins rather than one fix. KKK K26 turbo with its oil feed and return lines: coking, shaft play, leaking wastegate diaphragm and boost hoses produce low boost or smoke; a rebuild is $1,500-$2,500 and the boost gauge/overboost fuel cut should be verified on a road test. Timing belt is non-negotiable maintenance on the I5 with water pump, tensioner, and seals; $800-$1,500 and a belt of unknown age is an immediate buy-day expense. The 016 five-speed transaxle wears second-gear synchro and pinion bearings (whine on overrun), the clutch and hydraulics are aging, and the hollow driveshaft/center support and CV boots leak grease. Finally, interior and trim: seat bolsters, headliner sag, door card vinyl, and the fragile console/switchgear are expensive or impossible to source correctly, and Euro-conversion cars (bumpers, lights, wing) are common enough that originality documentation moves money.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt, water pump, tensioner and cam/crank seals unless there is a dated receipt within 5 years/30k miles. Replace every rubber fuel line and the fuel filter, plus the brake/steering mineral-fluid flush and likely pressure accumulator. Tires almost certainly need replacing on date code regardless of tread (15" sizes, $900-$1,400). Full fluid service including transaxle and final drive, new battery, all coolant hoses, and a diff-lock vacuum system test and repair. Sunroof drain clearing and a proper alignment.
profiles.repairs_12mo: CIS fuel distributor and warm-up regulator rebuild or replacement to cure hot-start and mixture drift. Clutch and hydraulics if the pedal is high or engagement is slipping. Suspension refresh: struts, all control arm and subframe bushings, tie rods, and sway bar links ($2,500-$4,500). Instrument cluster repair, wiring/ground cleanup, and door-lock pneumatic servicing. Exhaust downpipe/manifold crack repair, turbo inspection or rebuild, and localized rust remediation at arches and battery tray before it spreads. A/C, if fitted, is usually dead and a conversion is $1,500-$2,500.
profiles.market_notes: Provenance and originality drive price more than mileage: documented US-market cars (664 claimed 1983 US examples), original paint or a known respray, complete records, and a working diff-lock system carry the top money, with strong results now $55k-$90k+ and outliers for 20v RR Euro imports and Sport Quattro tribute-free originals. Euro-conversion details (sloped H4 lights, small bumpers, added wing, Recaros, Ronals) are widely tolerated by this market and often bid up, but a documented-stock US car with factory seats and original wheels is the cleaner buy for a purist. Colors: Tornado Red, Mars Red, Zermatt Silver and Alpine White read correctly; black hides and then reveals bodywork. Rust history, a cracked head, or a California gross-polluter/smog problem discounts a car $10k-$20k because the repair economics are brutal.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a typical example needs a full 40-year catch-up pass: all fuel and coolant hoses, timing belt kit, mineral-fluid hydraulic system service, tires on date code, and diff-lock vacuum restoration in the first season. Bushings, cluster repair, and CIS recalibration follow in year one, and any deferred rust work should be priced at fabrication rates because correct panels are scarce.

profiles.label: BMW 02 Series (E10: 1600-2 / 2002 / 2002tii)
profiles.framing: This is a 2,200-lb, 100-hp analog sports sedan bought to be driven on Highway 1, Laureles Grade and Carmel Valley Road — not stored. For this buyer the car's value lives in its structure and its paperwork: a sorted, rust-free, honestly documented 2002 is a delightful weekly driver, while a pretty repaint over filled shock towers and spring perches is a five-figure hole. Because nearly every surviving 02 has been modified (Weber 32/36 or 38/38, headers, Ireland/Bilstein suspension, 15-inch wheels), the realistic test is not 'original' but 'reversible, well-chosen, and professionally installed, with the original parts and receipts on hand.' Five-digit odometers and 'Mileage Exceeds Mechanical Limits' titles mean condition and service history — not indicated miles — set the price.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural rust is the defining failure mode and it is age- not mileage-driven. The front strut/shock towers crack and rot where the tower meets the inner fender and at the spring perches; a car with bubbling or filler here needs $3,000–$10,000+ of metal work. Ask for bare-metal or undercarriage photos of both towers, and press on the perch with a screwdriver during a PPI.', 'Rear subframe mounting points, trailing-arm mounts and the rear shock towers under the parcel shelf rot from trapped water. Failure here is a safety item and is commonly hidden by fresh undercoating. Look for factory seam sealer and spot welds, not black rubberized spray.', "Rockers, front fender lower rear corners (behind the wheel, ahead of the door), battery tray and adjacent inner fender (acid), floor pans under the seats, spare tire well and the windshield/backlight surrounds under the chrome trim. Trim removal photos are worth more than any seller's statement; chrome-trim rust is a $2,000–$6,000 job with glass out and repaint.", 'M10 iron-block four is robust but the aluminum head cracks between the valve seats, especially 1975–76 US cars fitted with the EGR/thermal-reactor emissions exhaust that cooks the head. Symptoms: chronic coolant loss, combustion gases in the coolant, hot-start hesitation. Head rebuild $1,800–$3,500; complete engine rebuild $6,000–$9,000. Ask for a leakdown/compression test and a block test on the coolant.', 'Timing chain and plastic chain guides/tensioner wear with age; a rattle at cold idle or a chain that has worn a groove in the timing cover is a $700–$1,500 job on the cover, more if the cover is grooved through. Also expect weeping front and rear main seals and a dripping oil-pressure sender.', 'Cooling system is marginal by modern standards: original brass radiator, viscous/fixed fan, water pump and the notorious plastic-impeller failures on replacements, plus a thermostat housing that corrodes. Many good cars have already had an aluminum radiator/electric fan; verify the swap is properly shrouded and wired with a relay, not a toggle switch. Budget $600–$1,200 for radiator/pump/hoses/thermostat if undated.', 'Fuel system: original Solex 32/36 DIDTA carbs are worn out and rarely rebuildable to spec, so Weber 32/36 DGV or 38/38 conversions are near universal. A 38/38 with a hot cam is fun but often jetted rich — check for fuel smell, black plugs, and poor cold idle. Kugelfischer mechanical injection on the tii is the expensive one: pump rebuild $2,000–$3,500, and cold-start/enrichment gremlins are common if the car sits. Original rubber fuel lines and the tank sending unit/tank rust cause leaks and fuel-starvation; verify fuel lines have been replaced (a fire risk on these cars).', 'Ignition: Bosch distributor vacuum advance diaphragms fail (a listed fault on this example), points-era mechanical advance seizes, and 123/Pertronix conversions are common. Symptoms are pinging under load, poor part-throttle economy and weak hot restarts. $150–$450 to correct.', 'Steering and front suspension: the ZF worm-and-roller box develops play, the idler/pitman arms and tie rods wear, and front control-arm bushings and non-serviceable ball joints are consumables. Lowered cars on short springs eat ball joints and cause bump steer. Full front end refresh $1,200–$2,500; a rebuilt steering box is $500–$900 plus install.', 'Driveline: the rubber guibo (flex disc) and driveshaft center support bearing perish and cause launch clunks and a 40–60 mph vibration ($400–$800 done together). The differential mount and rear subframe bushings tear; half-shaft U-joints/CV boots leak.', "Getrag four-speed: second-gear synchro wear (crunch on a cold 1–2 upshift), worn nylon/plastic shift-tower bushings giving vague, rattly shifts, and leaking output and selector-shaft seals. A tower rebuild is cheap; a gearbox rebuild is $1,500–$2,500. Persistent 'weeping' from a gearbox usually means the front or rear seal and often a worn output shaft.", 'Brakes: sin
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid and filter service plus valve lash adjustment (0.006 in cold/0.008 in hot per spec) and a compression/leakdown baseline', 'Distributor service: new vacuum advance, points/condenser or electronic conversion, fresh cap/rotor/wires/plugs, and a timing and carb tune on a gas analyzer', 'Replace all rubber fuel lines from tank to carb, inspect the tank and sending unit for rust, and pressure-check for leaks (fire prevention)', 'Brake hydraulic refresh: flexible hoses, fluid flush, rear wheel cylinder/drum inspection and adjustment, booster and master function check', 'Address gearbox weeping: reseal output/selector shaft seals and rebuild the shift tower bushings if not already done', 'Guibo, driveshaft center support bearing and differential mount inspection and replacement as nee
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front end refresh: control arm bushings, ball joints, tie rods, idler arm, and an alignment with a corrected ride height', 'Steering box rebuild or adjustment to remove on-center play', 'Clutch hydraulics (master/slave) and, if the pedal is high or the throwout bearing whines, clutch and rear main seal while the box is out', 'Timing chain, guides, tensioner and front cover seal if history is unknown', "Heater box rebuild, blower motor and heater valve — the classic 'do it once with the dash out' job, combined with the cracked-dash replacement", 'Door/window seals, quarter-window seals, trunk and hood seals, and door card clip/regulator work to stop water intrusion', 'Wiring cleanup behind the dash: remove stereo/A/C splices, fuse box and ground refresh, alternator/voltage regulator check
profiles.market_notes: Round-taillight 'roundies' (1968–73) and especially tii cars carry a clear premium over 1974–76 square-taillight cars, and US 1974–76 cars with the big 5-mph 'diving board' bumpers are discounted unless converted to Euro bumpers. Documented, rust-free, honestly presented drivers in desirable period colors (Inka, Malaga, Verona, Agave, Amazon/Taiga green, Colorado, Chamonix) with a sunroof, factory-look interiors and a thick receipt file trade at the top; heavily modified cars with hot cams, big Webers and unknown mileage sell at the low end of the money regardless of cosmetics. Four-speed is the norm and expected; the ZF three-speed automatic is a significant value and desirability penalty. Expect $18k–$35k for good modified drivers, $35k–$60k+ for sorted original-spec roundies and tiis, with restoration receipts and metal-work photos moving price more than paint quality.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 50-year-old car needs its rubber and hydraulics renewed regardless of presentation: fuel lines, brake hoses and fluid, coolant hoses, window/door/trunk seals, motor and subframe mounts, guibo and center bearing, and tires older than six years. Plan a full ignition and carburetion tune plus valve lash and a cooling-system overhaul in the first season, and set aside for the dash-out heater box and cracked dash job that nearly every 02 eventually needs. profiles.label: BMW 135i Convertible (E88, N54 & N55)
profiles.framing: This is the cheap-thrills, short-wheelbase BMW: 300 hp turbo six in a small rear-drive chassis, and in E88 convertible form a genuinely usable top-down daily for Highway 1 and the Monterey Peninsula. For this buyer it is a driver, not an asset — E88 verts sit at the bottom of the 1-Series price ladder while carrying the same running costs as a much more expensive car. The whole exercise is buying maintenance history, not miles: a documented, unmodified, tune-free car with cooling, fuel and turbo work already paid for is worth several thousand dollars more than a cheap one. Salt-free California/Southwest history and a top that has been exercised and drained matter as much as the drivetrain.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Fuel system, N54 cars (2008–2010): the HPFP (high-pressure fuel pump) was the subject of multiple recalls and an extended 10yr/120k warranty that has now expired on every car; symptoms are long cranks, limp mode, 'Half Engine Power' warning, rough cold running. Replacement is roughly $900–1,400. Piezo injectors on N54 failed in waves (index 11/12 supersessions); a full set is $1,500–2,500 installed. 2) N55 cars (2011–2013) use solenoid injectors and a more robust pump but still fail individually — a misfiring cylinder usually means one injector at $250–450 plus labor. 3) Turbocharger wastegate rattle: N54 twin turbos develop wastegate flutter, N55's single twin-scroll turbo develops the same rattle in its electric wastegate actuator, typically past 60–90k miles; audible as a metallic buzz at light throttle 1,500–2,500 rpm and eventually underboost codes. Actuator alone $600–900, turbo replacement $2,500–4,000. 4) Cooling system is consumable, not durable: the electric water pump and thermostat are a 60–90k mile / 8-year item at $900–1,400 together; the plastic expansion tank, coolant hoses and the plastic thermostat housing crack with age. A car with no cooling records at 50k+ miles and 13 years should be assumed to need the whole job. 5) Oil leaks are near-universal by 60–80k: valve cover and VCG gasket ($600–900), oil filter housing gasket ($500–800, contaminates the belt if ignored), and the oil pan gasket ($1,200–1,800 due to subframe clearance). Look for oil on the exhaust manifold and a smell after a hard drive. 6) Direct injection carbon buildup on intake valves: expect walnut blasting every 60–80k miles, $500–900. Symptoms are rough cold idle, misfires under load, mild power loss. 7) The stock plastic charge pipe (both N54 and N55) cracks at the coupler and dumps boost; an aluminum replacement is a sensible, accepted fix — but confirm it accompanied a stock tune, not a boost increase. 8) Tuning/modification is the biggest hidden risk: heavily tuned N54/N55 cars suffer crank hub timing slip, burned pistons, and stretched rod bearings. Any car with a JB4/MHD/Cobb history, upgraded turbos, or a methanol kit should be treated as a rebuild candidate unless the tune history is fully documented and the crank hub pinned. 9) DCT (7-speed GS7D36SG) cars need a mechatronic/clutch fluid service every ~60k miles ($500–800); neglected units show shudder from a stop and eventually mechatronic sleeve leaks or clutch wear — $3,500–6,000 to fix. Manual cars: check clutch and the dual-mass flywheel ($1,500–2,200) and the notorious weak 6-speed synchro feel when cold. 10) Convertible-specific: hydraulic top cylinders and pump leak (fluid on the trunk liner or top well), microswitches/Hall sensors fail and cause the top to stop mid-cycle, and the roll-over bar deployment mechanism can seize. Top mechanism repairs run $800–3,000; a replacement top with glass window is $1,500–2,500 installed. 11) Blocked convertible/cowl drain tubes are the classic cause of wet front footwells and trunk, which then kills body modules and the FRM (footwell module) — a wet-carpet car is a $1,000+ electrical rabbit hole. 12) Suspension and rubber age out: front control arm bushings and rear trailing arm/rear shock mounts around 70–100k ($800–1,500 for a front refresh), plus run-flat-battered wheels and struts. 13) Electrical odds and ends: FRM module failure (windows/lights all dead, coding recovery ~$300–600), Comfort Access door handle sensors, iDrive/CIC screen and CD stereo faults, and the E88 dash leather delaminating around the airbag seam (cosmetic, $500–1,500 to re-wrap). 14) Brakes on M Sport cars use larger rotors and pads that wear fast if driven hard; budget $900–1,400 for a four-corner refresh.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including engine oil, brake fluid and (if DCT) transmission/mechatronic fluid; new coolant if age is unknown. Replace the cracked/aged plastic charge pipe and boost hoses if still stock. Clear and flush all four convertible/cowl drain tubes and dry/verify the trunk and footwells. Address any known oil weep (valve cover or filter housing gasket) before it fouls the belt. Fresh non-run-flat tires and an alignment; new wiper blades and cabin filter; battery test with registration if replaced. Expect $1,500–3,000 on a decent 50–70k mile car.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Electric water pump and thermostat if not documented ($900–1,400); intake valve walnut blasting ($500–900); one or more fuel injectors ($300–600 each installed); turbo wastegate actuator if rattle is developing ($600–900); front control arm bushings and possibly rear shock mounts ($800–1,500); brake pads/rotors ($900–1,400); convertible top hydraulic seal or microswitch repair ($400–1,200); oil filter housing and/or oil pan gasket ($500–1,800).
profiles.market_notes: Manual coupes (E82) command the strongest money and 135is/6MT cars are the top of the market; DCT convertibles are the value end — typically $3,000–6,000 behind an equivalent manual coupe. N55 cars (2011–2013) generally bring more than N54 for perceived fuel-system reliability, though N54 enthusiasts pay up for unmodified, well-documented examples. Miles matter less than binders: a 70k-mile car with pump/injector/turbo/cooling receipts beats a 45k-mile car with 'no records.' Rare colors like Marrakesh Brown over Terracotta, Le Mans Blue, and Alpine White with M Sport/Sport seats add appeal; heavily tuned, deleted, or accident-history cars are discounted hard and are difficult to resell.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 12–16 year old E88 needs a full age-based catch-up regardless of mileage: coolant system components, all gaskets and rubber hoses, suspension bushings, brake fluid and likely a battery, plus convertible top seals, drains and hydraulics. Low-mileage cars are often worse for rubber and top mechanisms because they have sat. Budget $3,000–5,000 in the first year on top of the purchase price to get a typical example to a trustworthy baseline.
