profiles.label: BMW 3 Series Convertible (E36: 318iC / 325iC / 323iC / 328iC)
profiles.framing: An E36 328iC is a light, communicative six-cylinder convertible for top-down coastal drives on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley roads. A five-speed manual is the enthusiast spec. At 25+ years old, the car's real condition is set by rubber, plastic, hydraulic and cooling-system age more than by mileage. A low-mileage example can still need a full catch-up, so for this buyer the priorities are documented cooling-system work, a fully functioning power top, verified mileage, and a stock, unmodified chassis. The US-market M52 2.8L uses an iron block, so the European Nikasil bore-wear issue does not apply; the head is aluminum and does not tolerate overheating.
profiles.weak_points: ['Cooling system: the plastic radiator end tanks, coolant expansion tank (cracks at the neck and seam), plastic thermostat housing, bleed screw, and water pump (original-style plastic impeller) all become brittle with age regardless of mileage. Failure is often sudden and comes with a cloud of steam. Overheating an M52 can warp the aluminum head or fail the head gasket, which costs roughly $2,500–5,000. Look for a dated invoice showing the radiator, expansion tank, water pump (preferably metal impeller), thermostat and housing, hoses, and the viscous fan clutch replaced within about the last 5–6 years. A full indie refresh is about $900–1,600.', 'Power convertible top hydraulics: the 328iC uses an electro-hydraulic pump, usually in the trunk, driving rams in the top frame. Rams and lines weep fluid, which shows as stains on the top fabric, headliner pad or rear seat, followed by slow or uneven operation. Ram rebuild or replacement plus fluid typically runs $800–2,500. Watch at least one full open/close cycle from cold, and check the trunk area around the pump for fluid.', 'Top fabric, plastic rear window and seals: the plastic rear window yellows, hazes or cracks at the fold line. Fabric wears at frame contact points, tension straps and cables fray, and weatherstrips shrink, causing wind noise and water leaks into the footwells and trunk. A new top runs roughly $1,500–3,000 installed; seals run $300–900. Carpet and trunk-floor dampness or a musty smell points to long-term leaks and possible electrical corrosion. A factory hardtop is a real plus.', 'Top electrics and window drop: the top module, microswitches, relays, and the tonneau or top-compartment lid latching can fail, leaving the top stuck partway. All four windows should index down and back up when the top cycles. Window regulators and motors (front and rear quarter) are common failures at about $200–500 per corner. Check the rollover-protection system, if equipped, for warning lights.', 'Front suspension: the front control arm (lollipop) bushings and ball joints wear out, as do inner and outer tie rods. Symptoms are shimmy under braking at 50–70 mph, vague turn-in, and clunks. Arms and bushings run about $500–1,000 installed, plus an alignment. Original bushings at this age are hard and cracked even at low mileage.', 'Rear suspension and subframe: rear trailing arm bushings (RTABs) crack and cause rear steer and clunks over expansion joints. Rear shock upper mounts tear, and the body-side mount area can crack. Rear subframe mount cracking, more famous on M3s and hard-driven cars, should still be inspected on any E36. Bushings and mounts run about $500–1,200; subframe mount reinforcement and welding runs $1,500–3,000.', 'M52 oil leaks and crankcase ventilation: the valve cover gasket and the oil filter housing gasket weep, dripping oil onto the exhaust manifold and belts and causing a burning smell. Oil pan gasket and rear main seal weeps also occur. A clogged CCV (crankcase vent) system raises crankcase pressure and pushes oil past seals. Gasket and CCV work runs roughly $300–900; a rear main seal is a transmission-out job, best done with the clutch.', 'Single VANOS on the M52: worn VANOS seals cause soft low-rpm torque, a rattle or diesel-like noise at idle or light load, and sometimes VANOS fault codes. A seal kit with labor runs about $250–600. Also check the idle control valve, MAF and O2 sensors, which cause rough idle, hunting, or lean or catalyst codes. These matter for California OBD-II smog.', 'Manual driveline: the clutch, flywheel (dual-mass flywheel chatter or rattle), slave cylinder and plastic clutch fork pivot wear. A clutch job with flywheel runs roughly $1,500–2,800. Shifter carrier bushings and selector rod joint wear make the shifter sloppy ($150–400 to fix). Also check the driveshaft flex disc (guibo), center support bearing and transmission mounts, which cause clunks or vibration on take-off ($300–800).', 'Mounts and steering: engine and transmissi
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, BMW-spec coolant, brake fluid flush, manual transmission and differential fluid, and power-steering fluid check or flush.', 'Cooling system refresh if there is no dated invoice from the last ~5 years: radiator, expansion tank, water pump (metal impeller), thermostat and housing, hoses, bleed screw, and a fan clutch inspection.', 'Replace tires if DOT codes are older than about 6 years, regardless of tread depth.', 'Convertible top service: check hydraulic fluid level and type, clean and lube the top linkage and seals, and verify all window indexing and latches.', 'Address any active oil leaks dripping onto the exhaust: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and CCV inspection.', 'Battery and trunk battery vent/cable check; scan for stor
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front control arms or bushings, ball joints and tie rod ends, plus a four-wheel alignment.', 'Rear trailing arm bushings, rear shock upper mounts, and rear subframe mount inspection or refresh.', 'Shifter bushing and carrier rebuild, guibo and center support bearing, and engine and transmission mounts.', 'VANOS seal kit, idle control valve cleaning or replacement, and O2 sensors as indicated by driveability or smog readiness.', 'Window regulators or motors and door card reattachment as they fail.', 'Top hydraulic ram reseal or replacement, or top fabric and plastic rear window replacement, if weeping or hazing was noted at purchase.', 'Clutch and dual-mass flywheel if slipping or chatter was noted; do the rear main seal at the same time.']
profiles.market_notes: Prices are driven by top condition and function, transmission (the 5-speed manual commands a clear premium over the automatic), documented mileage, and service records. A clean, documented sub-60k-mile manual 328iC can reach the high teens to low twenties. Average 120k+ mile cars trade far lower, often $5k–10k. A factory hardtop, Sport Package, desirable colors (Boston Green, Cosmos Black, Arctic Silver and similar), and un-faded original interiors add value. Unverified mileage, a worn top, overheating history, or modifications subtract materially, and a CARFAX with buyback, title, or odometer issues should cap the offer.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even at low mileage, a typical 1999 E36 convertible should be assumed to need the full cooling-system refresh, fluids, tires, and convertible-top hydraulic and seal attention unless receipts prove otherwise. Within the first year, expect a suspension bushing and mount refresh (front control arms, RTABs, shock mounts) and oil-leak gaskets. Budget roughly $2,500–5,000 of catch-up on an undocumented example, before any top fabric or clutch work.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series E30 (325e/325i/325is, M20 six-cylinder)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E30 325is is a compact, analog, rear-drive coupe meant to be driven on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road most weekends — light (2,700 lb), hydraulically steered, with a smooth M20B25 six and a shift linkage that rewards patience. It is not a fast car by modern standards; the appeal is transparency, small footprint, and a parts/knowledge ecosystem that makes long-term ownership realistic. Because these are now 35-40 years old, condition, rust history, and a paper trail matter far more than the odometer reading, and a documented, unmodified, uncracked-dash car with the sport seats and LSD is worth a real premium over a 'clean-looking' unknown. Coastal California living means salt air and damp — a car that has never lived in the Rust Belt is materially more valuable to this buyer than one that spent 30 years in Nebraska or the Northeast.
profiles.weak_points: 1) M20 timing belt and water pump: the M20B25 is an interference engine — a snapped belt bends valves and turns a $400 service into a $3,500-$6,000 head rebuild. Interval is 60k miles or 4-5 years, whichever comes first, and the water pump (early cars used a plastic impeller that disintegrates) and tensioner should go with it. Demand a dated receipt or photo of a chalk-marked belt; if there is no proof, assume it must be done immediately regardless of mileage. 2) Cylinder head cracking between the valve seats on early M20 heads (casting numbers 1277731 and 885) — symptoms are unexplained coolant loss, overheating, or a milky film; a later 1705310 or 1710891 head or a documented replacement is a plus. Head work runs $1,800-$3,500. 3) Cooling system generally: the plastic-neck radiator, expansion tank, thermostat housing, and hoses all become brittle at 25+ years. Any overheating episode on an M20 is a head-gasket/head-crack event waiting to happen. Budget $600-$1,200 for a full cooling refresh. 4) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and the front timing cover/oil pan seams weep on nearly every car; the rear main and oil pan gasket ($700-$1,200 with subframe drop on the pan) are the expensive ones. Check for oil pooling on the exhaust and on the crossmember. 5) Fuel system: the 30+ year old rubber fuel hoses under the car and at the tank, plus the fuel pump and accumulator, are a genuine fire risk on cars with unknown history. Original-looking cracked hoses = replace now, $300-$800. 6) Rust: shock towers (look under the strut mount hats in the engine bay for bubbling or cracking), the battery tray corner in the trunk, the rear subframe/trailing-arm mounting points and floor, rear wheel arches, jack points, sunroof drains and the panel under the rear window seal, and the seam behind the front fenders. A Midwest/Northeast car needs the underside and trunk floor photographed thoroughly. Structural shock-tower or subframe-mount rot is a walk-away or a $3,000+ repair. 7) Interior plastics: cracked dashboard is near-universal ($400-$900 for a good used one plus labor, more for a re-skin), sagging headliner, brittle door cards, failing window regulator clips, and disintegrating sunroof cassette parts. Sport seat bolsters on 325is cars split at the driver's outer bolster; the beige and Cardinal interiors are hardest to source. 8) Suspension and steering bushings: front control arm bushings and ball joints, rear trailing arm bushings (RTABs, cause of vague rear end and inconsistent toe), subframe bushings, sway bar links, and the steering box/center link/idler arm all wear out by 100k. A full front-and-rear refresh with shocks is $1,500-$3,000 installed. Note whether 'shocks replaced' also included struts, mounts, and bump stops or was just dampers. 9) Electrical: the instrument cluster and OBC use failure-prone capacitors and cracked solder joints — dead odometer gears (a black-and-white speedometer needle drift or stuck odo), dim pixel displays in the OBC/SI board, and the SI battery packs that leak onto the board. Cluster odometer gear repair $150-$400. Also check the sunroof motor, central locking pneumatics (early) or actuators, and the notoriously melting relay panel connections. 10) Getrag 260 transmission and driveline: synchros (especially 2nd) start to balk when cold at high miles, the shift linkage bushings and selector rod joint make the shifter sloppy ($100 in parts, big improvement), the giubo/flex disc cracks, the center support bearing collapses (vibration at 45-60 mph), and the guide tube/throwout bearing squeal precedes a clutch job. Clutch/flywheel/rear main combined job runs $1,400-$2,500. 11) Limited-slip differential: the 25% ZF LSD on a 325is wears out and behaves like an open diff; check for one-wheel spin and for gear whine or leaking diff cover/output seals. Diff rebuild or swap $800-$2,000. 12) Brakes and ABS: the ABS control unit and wheel sensors fail, the master cylinder and rear calipe
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt, tensioner, water pump, thermostat, and all coolant hoses unless there is dated proof within 4 years; full fluid service (engine, Getrag 260 with MTL, diff, brake fluid, coolant); replace all rubber fuel lines and check the fuel pump/accumulator; new tires if date codes exceed ~6 years regardless of tread (the Uniroyal Tigerpaws on the example car are a red flag for age); shift linkage bushings and selector rod; flex disc/giubo and center support bearing if there is any driveline vibration; front control arm bushings and ball joints; battery, belts, and a check/clean of the relay panel and grounds.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Rear trailing arm bushings and subframe bushings; rear shock mounts and bump stops; clutch, throwout bearing, guide tube and rear main seal if any squeal or slip; oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets; radiator if still original plastic-neck; instrument cluster odometer gears and SI board battery service; sunroof cassette lubrication and drain clearing; A/C evaluation and likely condenser/dryer/expansion valve refresh; LSD evaluation and possible clutch pack rebuild; dash cap or replacement dash and headliner if sagging; seat bolster repair.
profiles.market_notes: The 325is coupe with 5-speed and factory LSD sits near the top of the non-M E30 hierarchy, above 325i sedans and well above 325e/eta cars; convertibles and 325ix occupy separate niches. Documented low-mileage, unmodified, rust-free cars with original paint, intact uncracked dash, and books/window sticker/records bring the strongest numbers; a Carfax accident, a replaced fender tag, or a repaint drops a car into the driver-grade band. Delphin Gray, Alpine White, Diamond Schwarz and Zinnoberrot are safe; beige/Pearl Beige leather is desirable when clean but expensive to fix when it is not. Modified cars (M50/S52 swaps, coilovers, aftermarket wheels, non-original seats) can be cheaper to buy and are much harder to resell to the documentation-driven auction crowd; typical strong-driver money for a 90k-110k mile 325is is roughly $12k-$20k, with exceptional preserved examples going higher.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-40 year old E30 needs a systems catch-up regardless of mileage: every rubber item — coolant hoses, fuel lines, suspension bushings, engine mounts, tires — ages out on the calendar, not the odometer, and low-mileage cars are often worse for seized calipers and dried seals. Budget $3,000-$5,000 in the first year for timing belt/cooling, fuel lines, bushings, and fluid services even on a well-kept car, plus a contingency for the cluster, sunroof, and A/C.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series E30 Touring (318i / 320i / 325i wagon, grey-market import)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E30 Touring is a small, honest, analog rear-drive wagon that can actually be used — dog, bikes, Highway 1, weekend hauling — not a garage queen. Every one in the US is a personal or commercial import (the Touring was never federalized), so the paperwork trail and the California registration path matter as much as the mechanicals. A 318i with the M40B18 is the cheapest E30 engine to buy and the most expensive to ignore: it is a belt-driven interference four with a famous camshaft-wear problem, so service documentation outranks a shiny repaint. The realistic goal is a rust-free, documented, mechanically sorted 100–130k-mile example that needs $3–6k of catch-up rather than a cosmetically staged import with a fresh coat of paint over unknown history.
profiles.weak_points: 1) M40B18 camshaft and rocker wear: the M40's cam lobes and hydraulic lifters run marginal oil supply and wear badly if oil changes were stretched — symptoms are ticking that doesn't quiet after warm-up, weak top end, and metallic glitter in the oil filter. A cam, rockers, lifters and head refresh runs $1,800–3,500 installed; a full head is more. Ask for oil-change intervals and any cam/rocker receipt. 2) M40 timing belt: interference engine, belt plus tensioner every 4 years/40–50k miles regardless of miles driven. A snapped belt is bent valves and a $3,000+ job. Demand a dated belt/tensioner/water pump receipt; a faded fuse-box sticker from 2018 is not proof enough on a 2026 car. 3) Cooling system: plastic-neck radiator, plastic-impeller water pump, expansion tank and the thermo-time/temp sensors all fail on age, not miles. Full refresh (radiator, pump, thermostat, hoses, tank, belts) $700–1,200 DIY-parts, $1,500–2,200 shop. Overheating an M40 warps the head. 4) Rust, and this is the make-or-break on a Touring: front shock towers under the strut mounts, jacking points and sills, rear wheel arches, spare-wheel well and rear floor, battery tray, windshield/rear-glass surrounds, sunroof drains, and Touring-specific tailgate lower seam, hatch-glass hinge area and rear cargo floor. Bubbles at the tailgate seam or wet spare well usually mean $2,000–8,000 of real bodywork. A fresh repaint of unknown depth (as in this listing) is a reason to bring a paint gauge and a lift, not a reason to relax. 5) Instrument cluster: the SI-board Ni-Cd batteries leak and destroy the board ($200–500 rebuild), and the odometer gear strips — this is why so many E30s are TMU. A metric cluster on a US-titled car also means every gauge reading and any recorded mileage is a conversion estimate. 6) Suspension bushings and mounts: front control-arm bushings, rear trailing-arm bushings (RTABs), strut and shock mounts, sway-bar links and rear subframe mounts are all consumable at 100k+; a full bushing/mount refresh is $1,200–2,500. Cheap entry-level coilovers (Raceland and similar) commonly ride harshly, leak within a season and often come with wrong spring rates and no corner balancing — budget $1,200–2,000 for OE-height Bilstein/Sachs plus springs to put it back. 7) Steering: E30s use a recirculating-ball box; play at center, a weeping box, and worn idler arm/center link/tie rods are normal at this age. Box $400–900, linkage $300–600. The listing's fresh power-steering pump/reservoir suggests a prior leak — ask what leaked and whether the rack lines and box were addressed. 8) Driveline: guibo (flex disc), center support bearing, driveshaft U-joints and differential mounting bushing all perish; symptoms are a shudder off-throttle and a clunk on shift. $500–1,100 to do properly. 9) Clutch hydraulics and clutch: slave and master cylinders leak with age (a slave was just replaced here — ask whether the master and line went too); clutch job on a 318i $900–1,500. 10) Fuel and idle: Motronic-era idle control valve, crankcase breather hose, fuel pump/filter and 30-year-old rubber fuel lines in the rear — a hard-starting or hunting idle is usually ICV or vacuum leaks. Rear fuel-line replacement is cheap parts, fire risk if ignored. 11) Interior aging: cracked dash top, sagging headliner (Touring headliners are large, $400–800 retrim), brittle door-card vinyl, failing window regulators, sticky switchgear and dead cargo-cover mechanisms. Touring-specific trim and cargo pieces are hard to source in the US. 12) Touring-specific electrics: the tailgate wiring loom runs through rubber conduit at the hinge and chafes/breaks — dead rear wiper, dead rear defrost, or dead hatch lock; repair is tedious but cheap. Rear wiper motors and the separately-opening glass hinges seize and corrode. 13) Rear self-leveling: some European Tourings carry Nivomat-type self-leveling rear dampers; failed units sag and replacement is expensive, and cars converted to conventional shocks may stil
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt, tensioner, water pump, thermostat and accessory belts unless there is a dated receipt inside 4 years/40k miles; full cooling-system refresh including radiator, hoses and expansion tank; fresh oil with a filter cut-open inspection for cam debris; four tires (2016/2018 date codes are hard-expired and dangerous); brake fluid flush, pads/rotors and a rear caliper check; clutch master cylinder and line if only the slave was replaced; fuel filter and inspection/replacement of rear rubber fuel lines; ICV clean and vacuum-hose replacement; headlight/turn-signal and taillight function check for US road legality; and the California registration/BAR referee process — budget time and fees, and be ready to revert Euro lighting.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Replace the budget coilovers with OE-height Bilstein/Sachs and correct springs, plus new strut/shock mounts and bearings; front control arms and bushings, RTABs, sway-bar links, tie rods and idler arm/center link; steering box or box rebuild if play persists; guibo, center support bearing and differential mount; instrument cluster SI-board battery removal/rebuild and odometer gear; headliner retrim and driver's seat/door-card repair; sunroof drain cleaning and reseal; A/C system evaluation (R12-era system, likely needs conversion or delete); exhaust hangers and possibly a rear muffler section; and a paint-depth-guided investigation plus repair of any rust found at the tailgate seam, jacking points or shock towers.
profiles.market_notes: Six-cylinder Tourings (325i, and especially 325iX all-wheel drive) trade at a clear premium over the four-cylinder 318i, and manuals over automatics; within 318i cars the earlier M40 and later M43 are similar money. Documented, unmolested, original-paint imports with a clean import file and a straightforward registration path bring the most; fresh repaints, TMU metric clusters, budget coilovers and replica M-Tech II kits suppress value with knowledgeable buyers even when they attract auction bidders. Desirable colors (Alpine White, Lachs Silber, Diamantschwarz, and period blues) and factory options like a sunroof, sport seats and the rear cargo cover help; a $18–22k result for a modified 318i Touring is essentially paying a rarity/novelty premium, since a similar-money 325i sedan or coupe is far better sorted. Records matter more than mileage on these — a 150k-mile car with a folder beats a 100k TMU car with a shine.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-year-old import needs a full fluids/rubber/cooling reset regardless of what the ad says: belts, hoses, radiator, pump, fuel lines, brake and clutch hydraulics, tires, and all suspension bushings and mounts. On a modified example add reversing cheap coilovers to OE-height quality dampers and correcting anything the body kit installation disturbed. Budget $4,000–6,000 of catch-up in year one on a good car and treat the import/registration process as a separate project with its own timeline.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series Touring (E91 328i / 328xi Wagon)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E91 is the classic do-everything answer: a normally aspirated inline-six wagon with a real manual option, hatch practicality for Monterey Peninsula weekends, and enough chassis feel to make Highway 1 and Laureles Grade worth driving. It is a $10k–$25k car with $60k-car maintenance costs, so the value case lives or dies on records: cooling system, VANOS, gaskets, suspension, and (on autos) transmission fluid. Because it is a driver, not an investment, condition and documented catch-up work matter more than mileage. In California the emissions story is decisive — SULEV N51 cars, engine swaps, and deleted/tuned hardware all interact with biennial smog and BAR rules.
profiles.weak_points: Cooling system is the signature E9x expense: the electric water pump and its associated thermostat are effectively a 60–90k-mile wear item, and failure is often abrupt (limp mode, overheat warning). Budget $900–$1,400 installed for pump plus thermostat; ask for a dated invoice, not 'recently done.' The plastic coolant expansion tank, upper/lower hose necks, and radiator end tanks go brittle by 10–12 years and weep or split; a full refresh is $600–$1,200. The N52's magnesium-alloy block is durable but leaks: the valve cover (plastic, warps) and its gasket, the oil filter housing gasket, and the oil pan gasket are near-universal by 90–130k. Valve cover $500–$900; oil filter housing gasket $500–$900 and important because oil drips onto the serpentine belt — a shredded belt can be pulled into the front crank seal and cause catastrophic damage. VANOS solenoids and the VANOS bolts/exhaust adjustment unit cause rough cold idle, a 2A87/2A82 code and lazy throttle; solenoids are cheap, a full VANOS unit is $800–$1,500. The DISA intake flap valve can shed its plastic pivot into the intake — $250–$400 to replace, cheap insurance. Valve stem seals are the classic N51/N52 sin: a puff of blue smoke on cold start or after long idle, especially on California SULEV N51 cars, and a head-off-optional-but-expensive job at $2,000–$3,500. Watch smog readiness monitors and NOx-related codes on N51 cars. Wagon-specific: the tailgate glass hinges crack and the rear hatch wiring loom chafes inside its rubber boot, causing dead wiper, dead lock, dead lights and intermittent tailgate release; hinges $400–$900, loom repair $200–$500. Rear light cluster and hatch seals leak into the spare-wheel well — pull the trunk floor and look for standing water, rust, and a corroded battery cable or amplifier if so equipped. Panoramic roof cassettes are heavy and troublesome: blocked drains dump water into the headliner and A/B-pillar carpets, and the cassette slide/cable can fail ($1,000–$2,500). Suspension bushings are consumables: front control arm/thrust arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings and rear shock mounts all knock and wander by 80–120k; a full front and rear refresh is $1,200–$2,500. Rear wheel bearings and front hub bearings hum by 100k, $400–$700 each corner. Electrics: the FRM footwell module can brick during a low-voltage jump or battery swap, taking out lights and windows ($300–$800 to repair/recode); the FSU/blower final stage resistor kills fan speeds; and the battery must be registered when replaced or charging strategy cooks the new one. On manuals, the shift shaft seal leaks gear oil onto the underbody, the clutch delay valve is commonly deleted, and clutch plus dual-mass flywheel is $1,800–$3,000. On the 6HP19 automatic, the 'lifetime' fluid is not — unserviced units at 120k+ show flare and harsh 2-3 shifts; fluid and pan/filter service is $500–$800 and the mechatronic sleeve/adapter leak is a common $600–$1,200 job. Finally, run-flat tires and 18-inch wheels crack rims and beat the bushings; check for bent/repaired wheels and consider non-runflats.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Oil service with a real BMW-spec 5W-30, coolant condition test and expansion tank/hose inspection, full fault-code scan with freeze-frame, battery test and registration if replaced, serpentine belt and pulleys if any oil-filter-housing weep is present, DISA valve inspection, sunroof drain flush, tailgate loom and hinge inspection, alignment plus four matched tires if staggered/mismatched, and rear brake pads/rotors (BMW pads wear rears first).
profiles.repairs_12mo: Electric water pump and thermostat if not documented within 60k miles, valve cover gasket and oil filter housing gasket, front control arm bushings and possibly rear shock mounts/trailing arm bushings, VANOS solenoid cleaning or replacement, automatic transmission fluid and pan/filter (or manual shift shaft seal), one or two wheel bearings, expansion tank and radiator hoses, and window regulator or FSU blower resistor as they surface.
profiles.market_notes: Manual-transmission 328i wagons are the enthusiast currency here and carry a meaningful premium over slushbox cars — a clean documented 6-speed can bring double an equivalent automatic. Sport package with the proper seats, xDrive (valued in snow markets, less so in Carmel), Montego Blue/Space Gray/Alpine White over saddle or black, and non-panoramic roofs all help; heavy modification, engine swaps, salvage history, and 150k+ miles compress value fast. Records are worth more than mileage: a 130k car with a folder of cooling, VANOS and suspension invoices should outbid a 90k car with no history. Cars with California-legal emissions status (stock N51/N52 with intact CARB-legal hardware) are worth a clear premium locally because a swapped or tuned car may be unregisterable without a BAR referee sticker.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 110–140k-mile E91 is due for a cooling-system refresh, the standard trio of oil leaks (valve cover, filter housing, pan), and a round of front and rear bushings — plan $3,000–$5,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year unless invoices prove otherwise. Rubber and plastic are the real age items on a 13–18 year old car: hoses, mounts, sunroof drains, hatch loom, and window regulators. Buying the car with the thickest documented folder is cheaper than buying the lowest-mileage example.

profiles.label: BMW 318i / 318is / 318iC (E30, US-market 1984–85 M10 and 1991–93 M42)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, an E30 318i is a light, simple, analog manual BMW for Highway 1, Carmel Valley and Laureles Grade. It should be bought for chassis honesty and paperwork, not for power. The 1984–85 cars use the 101 hp M10 eight-valve engine and are the cheapest way into a stock E30. The 1991–92 318is and 1991–93 318iC use the 16-valve M42 and are the most desirable 318s. Many 318i shells have been used for M20, M50 or S52 swaps, like the example listing. Treat those as out of scope for a documented, unmodified purchase. A 1985 car registered in California must pass smog, and a swap without a BAR referee label, such as an OBD2 S52 converted to OBD1, can be unregisterable. What matters most is rust-free metal, a verifiable mileage story, cooling and timing health, and an unmodified, emissions-intact drivetrain.
profiles.weak_points: ["Odometer and instrument cluster (1984–87 especially): the plastic odometer drive gears in the speedometer strip, so the odometer freezes while the car keeps accumulating miles. The Service Interval (SI) board's NiCd batteries also leak or die, causing erratic temperature, fuel and tach gauges and dead SI lights. Very low claimed mileage on a 40-year-old E30 should be assumed wrong until proven otherwise. Documentation to look for: dated service receipts, CA smog history (BAR/DMV records) showing odometer progression, and any cluster-swap notes. Gear kit $100–250. SI board repair $150–400.", 'M10B18 valvetrain (1984–85 318i): the screw-and-eccentric rocker adjusters need valve adjustment roughly every 10–15k miles. Neglect causes ticking, burnt exhaust valves and low compression. Rocker arms and shafts wear, and cracked rockers are a known M10 failure. The single-row timing chain and tensioner can rattle at cold start at high mileage. Documentation to look for: valve-adjustment receipts and a compression test with even cylinders (roughly 150–170 psi, within 10%). Valve adjustment $150–300. Head refresh $1,800–3,000.', 'M42 timing chain guides and tensioner (1991–93 318is/318iC): the plastic chain guides embrittle and break, often at 100–150k miles or from age alone. Symptoms are rattle at startup or on deceleration. Guide debris can starve the oil pickup or let the chain jump. Documentation to look for: a receipt for guides, rails and tensioner. Job cost $1,200–2,500 at an independent shop.', 'M42 head gasket and top-end leaks: the M42 has a known head gasket weakness, typically at the rear cylinders, from overheating or from age on the original gasket. Symptoms are coolant loss, oil in coolant, or white smoke. Cam cover and spark-plug-tube seals leak oil into the plug wells, causing misfires. The oil filter housing gasket also weeps. Documentation to look for: head gasket receipt with the updated gasket and a head-flatness check. Head gasket job $1,500–2,800. Cam cover seals $200–400.', 'Cooling system (all): plastic radiator end tanks crack, the expansion tank splits at the seams, and the water pump impeller and bearing fail. The thermostat housing, heater hoses and heater valve leak. The mechanical fan clutch weakens and the auxiliary fan or its temperature switch fails. Overheating warps the aluminum M10 and M42 heads. Documentation to look for: a cooling overhaul receipt within about 5 years or 30k miles. Overhaul $800–1,500. Head repair after an overheat $1,500–3,000+.', 'Fuel hoses and fuel delivery (all): original rubber fuel hoses under the intake and at the fuel rail crack. This causes a raw-fuel smell and is a genuine engine-bay fire risk. The main in-line pump and in-tank transfer pump weaken, causing hot-start or long-crank issues. The air flow meter flapper track wears, causing hesitation and poor idle on M10 L-Jetronic cars. The idle control valve, cold-start valve and O2 sensor are also wear items. Documentation to look for: a receipt for full fuel hose replacement. Hoses $200–500. Pumps $300–700. AFM $200–500 used/rebuilt.', 'Rust (even CA cars): check the following areas. Clogged sunroof drains rot the sunroof panel surround and the A-pillar bases. Also check the lower windshield frame corners, rear wheel arch lips and rocker/jacking points. Look at the front valance and fender bottoms behind the splash guards, the battery tray area, the rear shock towers in the trunk, and the trunk floor under the spare. Previous rust repair or accident damage often hides under fresh paint. Documentation to look for: undercarriage and sunroof-area photos on a lift. Small localized repair $1,500–3,000. Structural or sunroof-surround repair $4,000–10,000+.', 'Rear suspension and subframe: soft or torn rear subframe bushings, trailing arm bushings and diff mount cause clunks, wheel hop and vague rear steering. Rear shock mounts tear and the upper shock tower sheetmetal can crack, especially with stiff aftermarket shocks. Docum
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter, coolant, brake fluid flush, manual transmission and differential oil, power steering fluid.', 'Replace all rubber fuel hoses in the engine bay and the fuel filter unless receipts are recent.', 'Inspect the cooling system and replace suspect items: expansion tank, radiator (if original or with stained end tanks), thermostat, hoses and cap.', 'Service the valve train: valve adjustment on the M10, or cam cover and spark plug well seals on the M42.', 'Replace tires older than about 6 years regardless of tread, and do an alignment check.', 'Replace belts, check the battery, and clean or replace the main ground straps.', 'Replace the failed front window regulator, and fix the SI board or odometer gear if the gauges are erratic or the odometer is not a
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Rear subframe, trailing arm and diff mount bushings, plus rear shock mounts, with shock tower reinforcement.', 'Front control arm bushings, ball joints, tie rods and struts/shocks as a set.', 'Guibo, driveshaft center support bearing, and engine and transmission mounts.', 'Clutch master and slave cylinders and a shifter bushing refresh; clutch if slipping or high engagement.', 'Water pump and fan clutch if not documented; full cooling overhaul if not already done.', 'M42 timing chain guides and tensioner if undocumented; M10 timing chain tensioner if rattling.', 'Fix oil leaks: oil pan gasket, timing cover, oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets.', 'Interior age items: dash cap or replacement, headliner, seat bolster repair.']
profiles.market_notes: The 1991 318is coupe (M42, sport seats, LSD, spoiler) is the most valuable 318. Clean examples bring roughly $12–25k, and 318iC convertibles land somewhat lower. The 1984–85 M10 318i, especially sedans, is the cheapest E30: roughly $4–10k for drivers and $12k+ only for exceptional, documented, low-verified-mileage cars. Price is moved most by a documented, unmodified example with original bumpers and paint, plus proof of no rust and verifiable mileage. Manual commands a premium over automatic, and desirable colors like Alpine White, Diamond Black, Henna Red and Lachssilber help. Swapped cars like the example ($16k with an S52) sell to a different market based on build quality. For this buyer they carry heavy discounts for CA smog and registration risk and unknown workmanship, and they fail the unmodified preference.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a typical 30–40-year-old E30 needs a full rubber refresh unless receipts prove otherwise. That means fuel hoses, cooling system, suspension and subframe bushings, guibo and center bearing, clutch hydraulics, and brake hoses. Budget roughly $3,000–6,000 over the first year for catch-up work on a sound, rust-free car. Add the risk reserve for head gasket or timing work on M42 cars, or for hidden rust.

profiles.label: BMW 325i / 328i / 323i Convertible (E36, US 1994–1999)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer this is a top-down coastal cruiser and Highway 1 driver: a smooth inline-six, rear drive, and a power soft top, ideally with the 5-speed manual. In the US the E36 convertible began in model year 1994; a '1992 325i Convertible' is almost certainly an E30, so verify chassis by VIN before applying this profile. What matters most is proof that the plastic-heavy cooling system has been refreshed, a fully functioning and leak-free top, and a dry, rust-free floor and trunk. Engine internals are durable when the car has never been overheated.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Cooling system is the number-one killer. The radiator has plastic end tanks, and the expansion tank, the water pump (often with an early plastic impeller), the thermostat and housing, the viscous fan clutch, the hoses and the plastic bleeder screw all fail on age rather than mileage, typically every 60–80k miles or 8–10 years. A full overhaul runs $900–1,600. An overheat that warps or cracks the aluminum head (M50TU and M52) costs $2,500–4,500. Look for dated receipts covering radiator, pump, thermostat and expansion tank, and ask directly about any overheat history. 2) Single VANOS (M50TU in the 1994–95 325i, M52 in the 328i and 323i): worn seals cause a rattle and lost low-end torque. A seal kit is $300–800 installed. Rattle at idle or from 2,000–3,000 rpm points to the VANOS or the timing chain guides. 3) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket (it can drip onto the exhaust and the alternator), oil pan gasket and rear main seal. Gaskets run $200–600; a rear main seal is best done alongside a clutch job. 4) Convertible top mechanism. The E36 top is electromechanical rather than hydraulic, with an electric motor, drive cables and flex shafts, a tonneau lid lock and microswitches, plus a top control module. Stripped drive gears, worn cables, misadjusted latches or a failed module stop the cycle midway. Repairs run $400–1,500, and a used module or motor is $200–600. 5) Top fabric and rear window: shrunken or torn canvas, a cloudy or cracked plastic rear window, and failing seam stitching. A quality canvas installed costs $1,500–3,000, with frame pads, cables and seals extra. 6) Water intrusion from worn top seals, window seals and blocked drains soaks the footwell carpets and trunk. It rusts the floor pans, battery and spare-wheel areas and damages wiring. Rust in the rockers, jacking points and the rear wheel-arch lips also appears, and coastal fog and salt air make this worse. 7) Rollover protection system: the pop-up rear roll bars and their sensor or module can log faults or fail to deploy. Check that the warning light self-tests and goes out, then scan for codes; module or sensor repairs run $300–1,000. 8) Rear suspension: rear trailing arm bushings (RTABs) and the upper rear shock mounts wear out (clunks and a vague rear end), and the rear diff mount and rear subframe mounts also deteriorate. Expect $500–1,200 together. Inspect the subframe mount areas for cracks. 9) Front suspension: control arm inner bushings (shimmy under braking), ball joints, tie rod ends and sway bar links. A refresh is $600–1,200. 10) Manual drivetrain: plastic clutch slave and master cylinder lines, worn shifter carrier bushing and selector rod bushings (sloppy shift), and the driveshaft flex disc (guibo) plus center support bearing (vibration on takeoff). Shifter and guibo work runs $300–900; a clutch is $1,200–2,000. 11) Automatic (ZF 5-speed in six-cylinder cars): slow or harsh shifts and limp mode at age. A fluid and filter service plus adaptations is about $300, while a rebuild is $2,500–3,500. 12) Electrical gremlins: pixel loss on the instrument cluster and OBC/check-control LCDs, a failed blower final-stage resistor (fan stuck on high or dead), door and trunk lock actuators, and power window regulators including the rear quarter windows. Most fixes are $100–500 each, but they add up. 13) Interior UV damage from top-down use: cracked dash, faded door cards and rear deck, worn leather bolsters, and a sticky or failed top switch or console. 14) Factory hardtop, if fitted: check the seals, latches, the rear defroster connector and that the hardtop stand is included. A damaged hardtop is expensive to replace.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Without dated receipts, plan on a full cooling system overhaul: radiator, expansion tank, water pump with a metal impeller, thermostat and housing, fan clutch, hoses and bleeder screw. Also change all fluids (engine oil, coolant, brake fluid flush, manual gearbox and differential oil, or automatic fluid and filter). Replace the valve cover gasket and the oil filter housing gasket if weeping, and fit new spark plugs and filters. Replace any tires older than 6 years, and clear and lubricate the top drains and seals. Do a full top-cycle lubrication and adjustment, and scan and clear codes including the rollover protection system. Budget $1,800–3,500.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Refresh the rear suspension (RTABs, upper shock mounts, diff mount) and the front control arm bushings and ball joints, ideally with new shocks and struts and an alignment. Do VANOS seals if rattly, the driveshaft guibo and center support bearing, and shifter bushings plus a clutch slave/master if the pedal feels soft. Expect a window regulator or two, plus top cable or motor adjustment or repair and possibly top canvas or rear window replacement. Smaller items include the blower final-stage resistor, lock actuators and cluster pixel repair. Budget $2,000–5,000 depending on how much is deferred.
profiles.market_notes: Driver-grade E36 convertibles commonly trade around $5k–12k, and well-documented, low-mileage manual cars reach $15k–20k. The M3 convertible (1998–99) is a separate, higher tier. Value moves on a manual gearbox (a significant premium), a factory hardtop (about $1,000–2,500), the 328i's M52 over the 325i or 323i, Sport package or M-tech trim, a top condition that needs no immediate work, documented cooling and suspension refreshes, and attractive colors with clean leather. The example listing (1992, Calypso Red, hardtop, $25,250) reflects E30 convertible pricing, which runs well above E36. Don't use it as an E36 comp.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 25–30-year-old example has some combination of an original cooling system, tired suspension bushings and a top that has been neglected or damaged by water. Expect $3,000–6,000 to bring an average car to reliable daily-driver standard. Carmel's coastal fog and salt air make stopping water ingress and inspecting the underbody especially important.

profiles.label: BMW 328i Convertible (E93 LCI, retractable hardtop)
profiles.framing: This is a top-down Highway 1 / Carmel Valley Road cruiser, not a track toy: the LCI E93 pairs the naturally aspirated N52 inline-six (no HPFP, no injector, no turbo/wastegate drama that plagues the 335i N54/N55) with a three-piece folding steel roof that is the single most expensive thing on the car. For this buyer the right example is a documented, unmodified, garage-kept coastal car whose roof has been exercised regularly and whose water-management drains are clean and dry. Value lives in service records and a dry trunk floor, not in mileage; a 51k-mile car is age-limited rather than wear-limited, so rubber, fluids, gaskets and hydraulics govern the first-year budget. Treat it as a ~$5k-per-decade maintenance car that happens to be cheap to buy.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Roof hydraulics and roof control module: the RHT uses a hydraulic pump in the left rear quarter feeding cylinders for the tonneau, roof segments and latches. Cylinders and lines weep after 8-12 years, leaving pink/amber fluid stains on the trunk liner or rear parcel area; a single cylinder is $600-1,200 installed, a pump plus multiple cylinders and reseal can run $2,500-5,000. Ask for the roof's cycle history and any INPA/ISTA fault log from the CTM/convertible-top module. 2) Microswitches, Hall sensors and hardtop latch motors: the roof will refuse to operate and flash a warning if any one of a dozen position sensors mis-reports; diagnosis is labor-heavy ($200-600 just to find it), individual switches $150-400. A car sold with "roof works but sometimes needs a second try" is a car with an unresolved sensor. 3) Water management: plenum and A-pillar drains, the rear bulkhead channels and the trunk-lid drains clog with Monterey pine needles and coastal debris, dumping water into the footwells, under the rear seat, into the spare-tire well and onto the roof module and amplifier. Look for stained/damp trunk carpet, corrosion on module connectors, musty smell, or a car that has had the carpet shampooed. Remediation of soaked modules is $1,000-3,000+. 4) N52 valve cover and gasket: the plastic valve cover warps and the gasket hardens by 70-100k or 10 years, dripping onto the exhaust manifold (burning-oil smell, smoke at idle after shutdown); gasket $500-900, full cover $900-1,400. 5) Oil filter housing gasket: classic N52 leak that drips onto the alternator and belt; $400-800, more if the alternator is contaminated. 6) Lower oil pan gasket: aluminum pan requires front subframe/axle drop, $1,200-2,000 — the leak BMW independents warn about, so verify the front of the block and pan rail are dry. 7) Electric water pump and thermostat: N52's electronically controlled pump is a known 60-100k / 8-12 year failure, often without warning (overheat, limp home). Pump plus thermostat $900-1,500 installed; demand a receipt or plan on doing it preemptively. Also inspect the expansion tank (cracks at seams) and upper radiator hose neck. 8) VANOS solenoids and eccentric shaft (Valvetronic) sensor: rough cold idle, hesitation, 2A82/2A9E/2AB0 codes; solenoids $300-500, eccentric shaft sensor with gasket $600-1,200 (its seal is also an oil leak source into the harness). 9) DISA/intake manifold adjuster and crankcase vent hoses harden with age, causing lean codes and whistle; hoses and adjuster $250-600. 10) Front suspension: front control arm (thrust arm) bushings clunk over expansion joints by 70-90k or by age, $450-850 the pair; rear shock mounts, integral-link and trailing-arm bushings follow. Sagging rear on a low-mile car usually means tired springs/mounts, not shot shocks. 11) ZF 6HP19/6HP21 automatic: BMW's "lifetime" fluid is not; a car with no drain-and-fill by 60-80k is a candidate for harsh 1-2 shifts and torque-converter lockup shudder. Service with pan/filter $500-800; mechatronic sleeve/adapter and pan gasket leaks are common and cheap to fix early, expensive if the fluid runs down. 12) Electrical housekeeping: original battery is dead weight by now, and any replacement must be registered to the IBS/DME or the alternator cooks it; blower final-stage resistor, cigarette-lighter-circuit dramas, and CIC/iDrive nav module quirks are common. 13) Frameless door glass and rear quarter windows: regulators and the auto-drop function fail, glass mis-indexes and wind-noise/leaks follow; regulator $400-800. Also confirm the wind deflector and trunk luggage partition/divider are present — the roof will not cycle without the partition properly stowed. 14) Recalls and age items: verify the Takata driver airbag inflator recall and any roof-related service bulletins are closed at a BMW dealer, and treat the run-flat tires as consumables by date code — 2013-era low-mile cars frequently ride on 8-year-old, hard, cracking run-flats ($1,200-1,800 a set).
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: engine oil with BMW-spec 5W-30, brake fluid flush (2-year interval, almost always overdue on a low-mile car), coolant condition check; new AGM battery properly registered if the current one is original or undated. Date-code check on tires with replacement of anything over ~6 years (likely the full set of run-flats). Clear and flush all roof/plenum/trunk drains, replace the microfilter/cabin filter, reseal or clean roof weatherstrips and lubricate the RHT rubbers per BMW procedure. Scan all modules (DME, CTM roof module, DSC, airbag) and resolve stored roof faults; fix any weeping valve-cover or oil-filter-housing gasket before it contaminates the belt and alternator. Expect $1,800-3,500 all-in.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Preemptive electric water pump plus thermostat if there is no receipt ($900-1,500). Valve cover gasket or cover replacement and oil filter housing gasket if not already done ($700-1,800 combined). ZF 6HP drain/fill with pan and filter ($500-800). Front control arm bushings and an alignment ($500-900). One or two roof hydraulic cylinders or a latch motor/microswitch ($600-1,800). Serpentine belt, pulleys and idlers, plus spark plugs and coils if not documented within 60k ($600-1,000). Possible rear shock mounts, window regulator, or blower final stage ($400-900).
profiles.market_notes: Price is set first by roof condition and documentation, then by color and options: a car with roof-service receipts and a dry trunk is worth $2,000-4,000 more than a visually identical car with a hesitant top. 328i convertibles trade well below 335i asks and are the smarter buy given the NA six's simpler fuel system; manual-transmission E93 328i cars are genuinely rare and carry a modest enthusiast premium but sell to a narrower audience. Premium/Sport/Cold Weather packages, navigation, and a warm, uncommon interior (Saddle Brown, Coral Red) over a non-silver body lift the top of the range; under-60k-mile California cars with BMW dealer CBS history are the ceiling, while 100k+ cars, lease returns with no records, or any car with musty smell/curbed wheels/aftermarket springs sit at the bottom.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 51k-mile 2013 is age-limited, not wear-limited: assume original brake fluid, original battery, decade-old run-flats, hardened coolant and vacuum hoses, and roof seals/hydraulics that have sat more than they have moved. Budget a one-time $2,000-3,500 catch-up covering fluids, tires, battery with registration, drain cleaning and seal service, then plan the water pump, valve cover gasket and ZF fluid service across the first 12-18 months.

profiles.label: BMW 330Ci Convertible (E46, 2001–2006)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, this is a top-down Highway 1 and Carmel Valley cruiser with a smooth, durable M54 inline-six and genuinely good steering. It should be a reliable daily-capable driver once the predictable E46 wear items are caught up. The engine is not the main risk. The real risks are the plastic cooling system, oil leaks and crankcase ventilation (CCV), the convertible-specific hydraulic top and water-ingress problems, and the E46 rear subframe mounting area. Documented cooling and top service plus a clean structural inspection matter far more than low miles alone, and a manual with records is the sweet spot.
profiles.weak_points: ['Cooling system (the #1 E46 failure). The plastic radiator end tanks, expansion tank and bleeder screw, thermostat housing, hoses, water pump (early units had plastic impellers) and the viscous fan clutch or auxiliary electric fan all age out. Plan on replacement roughly every 60–80k miles or 8–10 years regardless of mileage, so low-mile cars are not exempt. One overheat can warp or crack the aluminum head. Look for a dated receipt covering radiator, expansion tank, water pump and thermostat. A full refresh runs about $900–1,600 at an independent shop.', 'Oil leaks. The valve cover gasket leaks, and the plastic valve cover itself can crack. The oil filter housing gasket weeps onto the serpentine belt, and a softened belt can shred and be pulled behind the crank pulley into the front main seal, which is a major failure. The oil pan gasket also seeps with age. Valve cover job: $350–700. Oil filter housing gasket: $250–500. Oil pan gasket: $600–1,000.', 'Crankcase ventilation (CCV) system. The separator and hoses under the intake manifold clog and crack. Symptoms are oil consumption, smoke at startup, vacuum-leak codes (lean codes P0171/P0174), whistling, and a dipstick that pops up or a tight oil cap under vacuum. Expect $400–800 at a shop, since the intake manifold must come off. The M54 is also known for some piston-ring oil consumption, so ask the owner about quarts per 1,000 miles.', 'Intake and VANOS. The DISA valve flap can break and drop into the intake, and its O-ring leaks ($150–350). Double-VANOS seals harden, causing lost low-end torque and rough idle ($200–500 with seal kit). Expansion-type crankshaft and camshaft position sensors fail with age, causing hard starts and stalling ($100–300 each).', 'Belt drive. The plastic idler and tensioner pulleys crack, and tensioner dampers weaken. Replace them with the belts as a set ($250–450). Listen for chirps or a wobbling pulley at idle.', "Convertible top hydraulics. The trunk-mounted hydraulic pump and especially the main lift cylinders and tension-bow cylinders leak. Hydraulic fluid can stain the headliner, rear seat and trunk, and the top becomes slow, stalls mid-cycle or won't latch. Cylinder rebuild or replacement: $500–1,500. Pump: $600–1,200. Full fabric top replacement: $1,500–3,000. The glass rear window can also separate from the fabric. Run the top through several complete cycles and look for fluid at the cylinders and on the headliner.", "Convertible water ingress. Clogged top drain channels and tired seals let water into the footwells and trunk. That water can corrode the trunk-mounted battery area, the top control module and wiring, and cause mildew under the carpets. Carmel's coastal fog and moisture make this worth checking even on garaged cars. Diagnosis plus drain or seal work: $200–800. Water-damaged modules can add $500–1,500.", "Rollover protection and convertible safety electronics. The pop-up rear rollover bars (ROPS cassettes) and their sensors, plus the front seat occupancy sensor mat, are common sources of an airbag (SRS) warning light. An occupancy mat replacement is $300–800. The front seats carry integrated seatbelts and power easy-entry mechanisms that also wear. A car with an SRS light can't be considered sorted.", "Rear subframe mounting area. The floor-pan mounting points can crack on all E46 variants. It is most notorious on M3s and hard-launched manuals but has been documented on non-M cars. Symptoms are clunks on throttle changes, visible cracks or torn sealer around the mounts, or rear alignment that won't hold. A proper reinforcement-plate repair is $1,500–3,500. Inspect underneath and from inside the trunk.", 'Front suspension. The front control arm (lollipop) bushings wear, often by about 60k miles and sooner on age, causing vague steering and shimmy under braking. Control arm ball joints, inner tie rods and sway bar links also wear. Bushings alone run $300–700; arms plus bushings run $700–1,200. The original rubber bushings are fine
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline if undocumented in the last 1–2 years: engine oil and filter, coolant, brake fluid (2-year interval), manual transmission fluid or 5L40-E automatic fluid and filter, differential fluid, power steering fluid, and convertible top hydraulic fluid level check', 'Cooling system refresh if there is no receipt within roughly 60–80k miles or 8–10 years: radiator, expansion tank, water pump, thermostat, hoses, bleeder screw, and fan clutch or auxiliary fan check', 'Serpentine and A/C belts with idler and tensioner pulleys if age is unknown', 'Valve cover gasket and oil filter housing gasket if any seepage is present; inspect the belt for oil contamination', 'CCV system replacement if there is oil consumption, smoke, a lean code or the oil-cap vacuum symptom', 'Clear the conver
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front control arm bushings, possibly with arms or ball joints, plus a four-wheel alignment', 'Rear trailing arm bushings and rear shocks with upper mounts if original', 'Engine and transmission mounts, driveshaft flex disc and center support bearing inspection or replacement', 'Convertible top hydraulic cylinder reseal or replacement once leaks or slow operation appear', 'DISA valve O-ring or replacement, and VANOS seal kit if low-end torque is soft', 'Window regulator(s), blower motor resistor, or cluster pixel repair as they fail', 'Crankshaft and camshaft position sensors if hard-start or stall symptoms appear', 'Oil pan gasket and differential output seals if seeping', 'Clutch, dual-mass flywheel and slave cylinder on a manual with high or unknown clutch life; fluid and filter servic
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission is the biggest price lever: a clean 5-speed and especially a 6-speed ZHP Performance Package convertible commands a clear premium over automatics. Sport Package (sport seats, M-style wheels, firmer suspension), the 2004–2006 facelift styling, a factory hardtop (worth roughly $1–2k), desirable color combinations, and verified low mileage push cars up. Typical driver-grade examples at 90–150k miles trade around $6–11k. Exceptional low-mile manuals with records can reach $15–20k, as in the example at $17,500 and 33k miles. Documented cooling system, top hydraulics and suspension work is worth real money, while cars with top malfunctions, SRS or ABS lights, or an overheat history should be discounted by the full repair cost or passed over.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most E46 convertibles are now 20+ years old, so plan for the plastic cooling system, belt-drive pulleys, gaskets, CCV and suspension bushings on age even if mileage is low. Low-mile garage cars often need more rubber and seal catch-up than higher-mile, well-maintained ones. Budget roughly $2,000–4,000 in the first year to bring a typical undocumented example to a reliable baseline, less if receipts show the cooling, CCV and top hydraulics already done.

profiles.label: BMW 335is (E92 Coupe / E93 Convertible, N54)
profiles.framing: The 335is is the send-off N54 car: 320 hp / 370 lb-ft on overboost, upgraded cooling, M Sport suspension and seats, offered only as a coupe or retractable-hardtop convertible with a 6-speed manual or 7-speed DCT. For this buyer it is an enthusiast bridge car — a fast, analog-feeling, daily-usable GT that is cheap to buy and expensive to neglect. What matters most is a documented, never-tuned N54 with paper on the high-pressure fuel pump, injectors, turbo wastegates and cooling system, and (on the E93) a hardtop that cycles perfectly with dry drain paths. A sorted example is a genuine driver; a deferred-maintenance example will hand back the purchase discount within a year.
profiles.weak_points: 1) HIGH-PRESSURE FUEL PUMP (N54 HPFP, Bosch): the signature failure. Symptoms are long crank, rough cold idle, limp mode and codes 29E1/29E2/29F1/30FF. BMW's extended coverage (10yr/120k) has expired on all of these cars. Expect $900–$1,400 installed; want a receipt showing the latest index part number. 2) PIEZO FUEL INJECTORS: index 11/12 injectors leak and cause misfires, rough cold start, fuel smell and washed-down cylinders. Replacement is $180–300 each plus labor — a full set with decoupling elements and labor is $1,800–2,800. Ask which index is installed and when. 3) TURBO WASTEGATE RATTLE: the twin small turbos develop wastegate flapper/bushing wear — a diesel-like rattle at 1,200–2,000 rpm and, later, underboost codes (30FF, 2B2A/2B2B, boost deviation) and limp mode. Rebuilt or new turbos run $2,500–4,500 installed; this is the single biggest budget item on a high-mile or tuned car. 4) CARBON BUILD-UP ON INTAKE VALVES: direct injection with no port wash; misfires, rough idle and lost power by 50–70k miles. Walnut blasting is $500–900 and is due roughly every 40–60k. Low-mileage but old cars still coke up from short trips. 5) CHARGE PIPE / BOOST PLUMBING: the OEM plastic charge pipe and the boost solenoid o-rings crack, usually announced by a pop and sudden limp mode; $250–600 to fix with an aluminum pipe. Any tuned car is far more likely to have already blown one. 6) COOLING SYSTEM: electric water pump and thermostat are wear items at roughly 60–90k miles or 8–10 years ($1,100–1,700 for the pair installed); the 335is also carries extra radiators/oil cooler, and the plastic expansion tank, radiator neck and coolant hoses go brittle with age. The radiator fan module (as replaced on the example car) is a known failure. 7) OIL LEAKS: valve cover and valve cover gasket (the cover itself cracks and the integrated CCV/PCV fails — $700–1,200), oil filter housing gasket ($500–900), and oil pan gasket ($800–1,500 because the subframe drops). Look for oil on the exhaust manifold/turbo area and a burning smell. 8) VANOS / SOLENOIDS AND ELECTRIC WATER PUMP-ADJACENT ELECTRICS: VANOS solenoid rattle codes (2A82/2A87), and an aged main battery that must be properly registered — an unregistered battery slowly cooks the alternator/IBS system. 9) E93 RETRACTABLE HARDTOP: hydraulic pump and cylinders leak into the trunk, microswitches and the CTM throw "top inoperative" errors, and the trunk partition must be latched. A full top repair is $1,200–3,500; hydraulic cylinder resealing alone is ~$1,500. 10) WATER INTRUSION: clogged roof and cowl drains dump water into the footwells and under the seats, where the junction box, seat modules and airbag sensors live. Damp carpet, musty smell or corroded connectors is a walk-away-level problem. 11) DCT (GS7D36SG) SERVICE: fluid and filter every ~50k miles or 5 years ($600–900); neglected units get harsh low-speed engagement and eventually mechatronic/clutch faults ($3,000+). Manual cars need clutch and slave/master cylinder attention around 70–100k. 12) SUSPENSION AND RUBBER: front control-arm bushings and rear trailing-arm/guide-rod bushings wear by 60–80k ($700–1,400), and the M Sport shocks are typically tired by 90k. Run-flat 19s beat up the chassis and the wheels bend on potholes. 13) TUNED-CAR RISK: a flashed or JB4 car raises the odds of sheared crank hub (crank timing slip, catastrophic), grenaded turbos, cracked charge pipe and stretched rod bolts. Absence of a tune history — and an ECU read showing stock calibration — is worth real money. 14) LOW-MILEAGE-CAR RISK: cars like the example (11k miles, 14 years old) have age-failed rubber and seals — tires with old date codes, dry-rotted coolant hoses, hardened top seals, stale brake and DCT fluid, and fuel system parts that fail shortly after being woken up.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: engine oil with OEM filter, brake fluid flush, DCT fluid/filter or manual gearbox oil, coolant condition test. Tires if date codes are over 6 years regardless of tread, plus alignment. Battery test and proper registration/coding if replaced. Cooling system pressure test with replacement of any brittle hose, expansion tank or the radiator fan module. Walnut-blast the intake valves if there is no record within 40k miles. Replace the plastic charge pipe with an aluminum unit and refresh the boost-solenoid o-rings. Diagnose and fix any oil weep at the valve cover or oil filter housing. On an E93: clear and flush all four roof/cowl drains, cycle the top 10+ times, inspect the trunk for hydraulic fluid. Full ISTA/INPA fault-memory read and clear, then re-drive.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Expect one or more of: HPFP replacement if not already documented ($900–1,400); an injector or a matched set with decoupling elements ($400–2,800); water pump and thermostat if original or over ~8 years ($1,100–1,700); valve cover/gasket and oil filter housing gasket ($1,200–2,000 combined); front control-arm and rear guide-rod bushings ($700–1,400); spark plugs and coils on a 40k/5-year interval ($400–700); and, on a car that already rattles, turbo wastegate repair or replacement ($2,500–4,500). E93 owners should budget for hydraulic cylinder reseal or a top microswitch/sensor over the first year or two.
profiles.market_notes: The 335is carries a clear premium over a same-year 335i and is the most desirable non-M N54 E9x; 6-speed manual coupes bring the strongest money and the DCT convertible the softest, with the E93's extra weight and top complexity knocking value relative to the coupe. Documented, never-tuned cars with HPFP/injector/turbo receipts and a clean Carfax sell for real premiums over cheap, boosted, tuned examples — the spread between a sorted car and a project is often larger than the price of the repairs. Low-mileage time-capsule cars (under 25k) command collector-adjacent asks but must be discounted for age-related catch-up and multi-year Carfax service gaps; strong colors (Alpine White, Space Grey, Le Mans Blue, Black Sapphire) with Coral Red or Oyster interiors and the correct 19-inch Style 225 wheels help, while worn/repainted panels, aftermarket exhausts/intakes and missing keys hurt.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2011–2013 335is is now 12–15 years old, so age — not mileage — drives the first bills: brittle coolant hoses and expansion tank, hardened top and window seals, aged tires and brake fluid, and a fuel system that often fails shortly after a long-stored car is put back into service. Budget $2,500–4,000 in the first six months for fluids, cooling refresh, tires, carbon service and a charge-pipe/boost-plumbing update even on a low-mileage, well-presented example, and treat the HPFP/injectors and wastegates as scheduled expenses rather than surprises.

profiles.label: BMW 525i Touring (E39, M54 2.5L, 2001–2003)
profiles.framing: The 525i Touring is a comfortable, well-balanced rear-drive wagon for daily driving and coastal and Highway 1 trips out of Carmel. It is not a collectible. Its value to this buyer depends on whether the plastic-heavy cooling system, the 'lifetime-fill' GM automatic, and the M54's crankcase-ventilation and oil-leak issues have been handled, or can be handled affordably. Prioritize documented, unmolested, rust-free, accident-free examples with a clean scan and a current California smog pass. Treat cosmetic 'M Sport' add-ons, aftermarket head units, and coil-spring conversions as condition and wiring questions, not value adds.
profiles.weak_points: ["Cooling system (the biggest killer). The M54 uses a plastic-neck radiator, a plastic expansion tank, a plastic coolant bleeder screw, a water pump (early units had plastic impellers), an electronically mapped thermostat, and an aging fan clutch or auxiliary fan. Plan on replacing these every 60–80k miles or 6–8 years. One serious overheat can warp the aluminum head or crack it near the coolant passages, which costs $2,500–4,500. A full refresh (radiator, tank, pump, thermostat, hoses, bleeder) runs $900–1,600 at an independent shop. Look for dated receipts that name each part. A single 'replaced radiator' line is not enough.", "Automatic transmission (GM 5L40-E in the 525i). BMW called the fluid 'lifetime fill,' so many cars have never had a fluid and filter service. Symptoms include harsh or flared 2–3 shifts, delayed engagement, slipping, shudder on light-throttle cruise, and transmission failsafe or limp mode. The aging crimped transmission cooler lines also seep. A drain-and-fill with filter costs $300–500; cooler lines cost $250–500. A rebuild or used unit costs $2,500–4,500. Ask for service records, and test it cold and hot. If a high-mileage, never-serviced transmission shifts well, a first fluid change is still a mild gamble. Do it gently, with the correct spec fluid.", 'Crankcase ventilation (CCV) system. The oil separator and hoses under the intake manifold harden and clog. Symptoms are oil consumption, oil in the intake boot, rough idle, a whistle, lean codes P0171/P0174, and strong suction at the oil filler cap or dipstick. The job costs $400–900 because the intake manifold must come off. A good shop will do the DISA valve and dipstick-tube O-ring at the same time. Ask for receipts showing the CCV was replaced, ideally with the intake manifold gasket.', 'DISA valve. The flap pivot pin in the intake resonance valve wears and breaks, causing a rattle at idle and a loss of mid-range power. In the worst case, the flap pieces get sucked into the engine. A replacement or updated unit costs $150–450 installed. Inspect it or have it replaced if the history is unknown.', 'Oil leaks. Common sources are the oil filter housing gasket (it leaks onto the serpentine belt, and a softened belt can shred and be pulled behind the crank seal), the valve cover gasket and its grommets (oil on the exhaust manifold), the oil level sensor O-ring, and the oil pan gasket. Costs: oil filter housing gasket $250–500, valve cover gasket $250–450, oil pan gasket $600–1,000. Check the belt edges and the front of the engine for oil wetness.', 'VANOS (variable valve timing) seals and the VANOS solenoid. The dual-VANOS O-rings harden with age, causing rough idle, weak low-end torque, and cam position codes. A seal kit costs $300–700 installed, more if the oil pump disc or rattle needs attention. Ask whether the seals have been done, and when.', 'Front suspension. The thrust arm (tension strut) bushings and the lower control arm ball joints wear, causing shimmy or wobble under braking at 50–70 mph, clunks, and uneven tire wear. Inner and outer tie rods also wear. This is often due by 80–120k miles. Expect $600–1,400 for quality parts (Lemförder/Meyle HD) plus an alignment. Ask for receipts with part brands.', 'Rear self-leveling air suspension (Touring-specific). Most US Tourings have rear air springs, a compressor and valve block, and a ride-height sensor. The rubber bags crack and leak, the compressor wears out or burns its relay, and the rear sags overnight or after loading. Bags cost $300–700 a pair installed, a compressor $400–900. Many cars have been converted to coil springs, which is a modification you should disclose and check for proper ride height. Look for an even stance and listen for the compressor running repeatedly.', 'Tailgate wiring harness (Touring-specific). The wires in the rubber boots at the hatch hinges fatigue and break. This causes intermittent loss of the rear wiper, hatch or glass release, license lights, rear defroster,

Inspect the transmission cooler lines for seepage.', 'Cooling system inspection and probable refresh if there are no records in the last 60k miles or 6 years: radiator, expansion tank, water pump with metal impeller, thermostat, hoses, bleeder screw, and a fan clutch check.', 'Diagnostic scan of all modules (engine, transmission, ABS/DSC, SRS, light check module, air suspension, instruments) and clearing of legitimate faults. Confirm smog readiness monitors.', 'Insp

profiles.market_notes: Tourings command a clear premium over 525i sedans. The 540i Touring sits above the 525i Touring, and a rare factory 5-speed manual 525iT brings a notable premium over the far more common automatic. Documented cooling-system and transmission service, a clean (non-salvage) accident-free history, rust-free California provenance, and sub-100k mileage move prices most. Most examples trade roughly in the mid-single to low-double thousands, and exceptional low-mile documented cars go higher. Aftermarket M Sport bumpers, wheels, and head units add little or subtract for this buyer. Carfax damage entries, worn interiors, and unknown transmission history pull prices down.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 20-plus-year-old 525i Touring with incomplete records needs $2,000–4,500 of catch-up work. This usually covers the cooling refresh, CCV and DISA, oil leak gaskets, transmission service, front suspension arms, and rear air suspension or tailgate harness work. Budget it in addition to the purchase price rather than assuming any single receipt covers it.

profiles.label: BMW 640i / 640i xDrive Gran Coupe (F06, N55)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel-based driver, the F06 640i Gran Coupe is a quiet, comfortable four-door GT for Highway 1, Peninsula errands, and long freeway runs. It is not a sports car or a collectible. Depreciation makes the purchase price cheap, but running costs stay at BMW-flagship levels, so buy the best-documented, least-modified, leak-free example rather than the cheapest one. xDrive adds little on the Central Coast and adds a transfer case, a front differential, and a much costlier oil pan gasket job, so a well-kept RWD 640i is often the smarter buy. Any car imported from out of state must pass a California smog check, and loud or deleted exhausts can draw equipment tickets.
profiles.weak_points: ['Electric coolant pump and thermostat (N55, Pierburg). Typical failure window is 60-110k miles or 8-10 years. Symptoms are a yellow or red coolant warning, reduced power, and the radiator fan roaring at shutdown. Replace pump and thermostat together, about $1,000-1,700 at an independent shop. Ask for receipts showing a genuine or OE-supplier pump and the thermostat part number. Repeated pump replacements in a short span, or the dealer still logging cooling faults afterward, point to wiring, connector, fan, or air-in-system problems that need explaining.', 'Oil filter housing gasket (OFHG). Usually seeps by 60-90k. Oil drips onto the serpentine belt and alternator area. A degraded belt can shred and get pulled behind the crank pulley into the front main seal, which turns a $400-800 gasket job into a $1,500+ repair. Look for receipts for the OFHG and a belt replaced at the same time.', 'Valve cover and gasket (plastic cover with integrated PCV). The gasket hardens and the cover can crack or warp, leaking onto the exhaust manifold with a burning-oil smell after drives. PCV failure causes whistling, rough idle, or lean codes. Cost is $800-1,400 with a new cover. Look for receipts and fresh, dry engine photos, not a pressure-washed engine bay.', 'Oil pan gasket, especially on xDrive. The front axle shaft passes through the oil pan, so the job requires dropping the front subframe and steering rack and pulling the axle. That runs $1,200-2,200 on xDrive versus roughly $500-900 on RWD. Common weep by 80-100k. Require underside photos of the pan rail and a lift inspection.', 'Turbo wastegate rattle (N55 single twin-scroll turbo). The wastegate actuator linkage wears, causing a metallic rattle at cold start, on decel, or at light throttle around 1,500-2,500 rpm. Boost-related codes (P0299) may or may not set. A full turbo replacement is the real fix at $2,500-4,500, with $200-600 band-aid clips as an option. Also watch for the plastic charge pipe cracking at the throttle-body end, which causes boost loss and limp mode. That is a $150-400 fix, and an OE replacement keeps the car stock.', 'Ignition coils and spark plugs, plus intake-valve carbon. Plugs are due every 45-60k. Weak coils cause misfires under boost, mostly at highway on-ramp load. Expect $350-700 for plugs and coils. Direct injection carbon on the intake valves causes rough cold idle and misfire codes at 90k+. Walnut blasting costs $500-900. VANOS solenoids can stick, causing rough idle and cam timing codes, at $200-450.', "ZF 8HP automatic (8HP45 in 640i). Fluid is marketed as 'lifetime' but should be changed every 60-80k with BMW's pan/filter unit. The plastic mechatronic adapter sleeve and the pan gasket weep fluid, which slowly starves the unit. Symptoms are harsh 2-3 or 3-2 shifts, delayed engagement, or a flare on downshifts. Expect $500-900 for service with a new sleeve and $4,000-7,000 for a replacement transmission. Look for a fluid-service receipt with the sleeve replaced.", 'xDrive transfer case (ATC 35L) and front differential. Mismatched tire sizes, brands, or tread depths, plus old fluid, wear the clutch pack. Symptoms are binding or crow-hopping in tight parking-lot turns, a shudder on gentle acceleration, or xDrive and DSC warnings. The actuator motor costs $350-800 and a full transfer case $2,500-4,000. Look for transfer case fluid service records and evidence that all four tires were replaced as a matched set.', "Front suspension: thrust or tension rods, lower control arm bushings, and front strut mounts. The F06's weight (about 4,300 lb with xDrive) wears these out by 70-100k. Symptoms are clunks over driveway lips, steering-wheel shimmy under braking, and inner tire wear. Expect $900-1,800 for the front arms plus an alignment. Curb strikes also bend arms and can damage the xDrive front axle and CV boots.", 'Adaptive Drive (active roll stabilization with dynamic dampers), if equipped. Stabilizer actuators, the valve block, or lines leak hydraulic fluid. Sym
