Reset the condition-based service (CBS) data and shorten the interval to about 7,500 miles.', 'Full ISTA (dealer-level) scan of all modules. Clear or diagnose stored faults and confirm the AGM battery health and registration.', 'Brake fluid flush if not done in the last 2 years.', 'Correct active oil leaks found at inspection: oil filter housing gasket plus serpentine belt, and the valve cover if weeping.', 'Spark plugs if there is no record within 45-60k miles. Replace coils if misfire counters show activity.', 'Inspect the plastic charge pipe and replace it with an OE-style part if it is cracked or brittle.', 'On xDrive, transfer case fluid service. Verify all four tires match in size, brand, and wear.', 'Four-wheel alignment check, especi
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['ZF 8HP transmission service with a new pan/filter and mechatronic adapter sleeve if there is no record by 60-80k.', 'Front thrust/tension arms and lower control arm bushings, plus an alignment: about $900-1,800.', 'Oil pan gasket if weeping: $1,200-2,200 on xDrive.', 'Electric coolant pump and thermostat if original or undocumented, plus a cooling system plastics refresh.', 'Brake pads, rotors, and wear sensors on one or both axles: $700-1,400 per axle at an independent shop.', 'Front and rear differential fluid service on xDrive.', 'Intake valve walnut blasting if cold-idle roughness or misfires appear at 90k+.', 'Possible door latch or soft-close actuator, headlight module, or battery replacement as electronics age.', 'Wastegate rattle remediation if present and worsening.']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven mainly by condition, documentation, and modification status. Clean, stock, well-recorded cars bring a meaningful premium over modified or accident-reported ones. The 2016+ LCI facelift (full-LED lights, updated interior and iDrive) and the M Sport, Executive, Driver Assistance Plus, Bang & Olufsen, and M Sport Edition equipment add value, while xDrive versus RWD is roughly a wash nationally and less relevant in coastal California. Mileage bands matter. Sub-60k cars bring strong money. The 80-110k range is where cooling, gasket, and suspension bills arrive, so records showing those jobs done justify paying up. Any Carfax accident entry, aftermarket exhaust, or tuning is grounds for a substantial discount or a pass.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-year, 80-100k-mile F06 640i has deferred the N55 gasket trio (oil filter housing, valve cover, oil pan), plus 'lifetime' transmission and xDrive fluids, aging cooling plastics, and worn front suspension bushings. Unless records show this work, budget about $3,000-6,000 of catch-up maintenance in the first year on top of the purchase price.

profiles.label: BMW 7 Series E38 (740i / 740iL / 740i Sport, 1995-2001)
profiles.framing: The E38 740i is a large, quiet, hydraulic-steered luxury sedan that drives smaller than it is. The 740i Sport (1998-2001) adds firmer suspension, contour seats, and M Parallel wheels, which makes it a strong long-distance driver for Highway 1 and trips to the Bay Area or LA. US cars were automatic only (ZF 5HP24), so any manual or S62 car is a swap and conflicts with the buyer's preference for unmodified examples. Swaps also need a California BAR referee label to stay smog-legal. What matters most is an honest, verifiable mileage history, a recently refreshed cooling system, and evidence on the M62 V8's timing-chain guides and valve stem seals. Those two jobs decide whether the car is a bargain or a money pit.
profiles.weak_points: ['Cooling system (all years, critical at any age): the plastic radiator end tanks, expansion tank, thermostat housing, upper and lower hoses, water pump (often a plastic impeller), bleeder screw, viscous fan clutch, and auxiliary electric fan all fail with age. An overheat can warp the aluminum heads. Ask for receipts for a full refresh within the last 4-6 years or about 60k miles. Undocumented, budget $1,200-2,500 for a full refresh at a California independent shop.', 'M62/M62TU timing-chain guides and tensioner (typically 100k+ miles, or earlier on cars with long oil-change intervals): the plastic upper guides crack and drop fragments into the oil pan. The symptom is a rattle on cold start or at about 1,500-2,500 rpm under light load. Left alone, the chain can jump and cause valve damage. Repair requires removing the front of the engine and costs roughly $4,000-7,000 at a shop. Look for receipts, or have a mechanic pull the valve covers and inspect the upper guides.', 'Valve stem seals (M62 family, often from about 90k miles): look for blue smoke on cold start or after extended idle (for example, pulling away from a light after sitting in traffic) and rising oil consumption. Shop repair runs about $1,500-2,500 with the heads in place and $3,000-5,000 with the heads off, which is often combined with timing-guide work. Insist on a true cold-start video or watch a cold start in person.', 'Rear coolant transfer pipe, valley pan gasket, and intake gaskets (M62/M62TU): the O-rings and gaskets under the intake manifold leak coolant down the back of the block and onto the bellhousing. This is often misdiagnosed as a head-gasket or water-pump leak. Repair is $1,200-2,000 because the intake has to come off. Check the rear of the block and the bellhousing for crusty coolant residue.', 'Oil leaks (all years): valve cover gaskets and spark plug tube seals, the oil filter housing gasket, timing cover gaskets, the oil pan gasket, and the oil level sensor all seep. Valve covers cost $600-1,200, oil filter housing $300-600, and the oil pan $800-1,500. Oil dripping onto the exhaust is a fire and smell concern.', 'M62TU-specific items (1999-2001): VANOS solenoid O-rings and seals cause rough idle, cam-timing fault codes, and low-end hesitation ($300-700). The electronic throttle body (EML) can put the car into limp mode with the EML light on ($500-1,200). Crankcase ventilation (CCV) hoses and the oil separator cause vacuum leaks and lean codes ($300-700).', '1995-1996 M60 Nikasil bores: high-sulfur US fuel attacked the Nikasil cylinder coating, causing hard starts, rough cold running, and low compression or high leakdown. Many affected engines were replaced under warranty with Alusil short blocks. Before buying a 1995-1996 car, get paperwork for the replacement or a passing leakdown test.', 'ZF 5HP24 automatic transmission: it was sold with so-called lifetime fluid but needs fluid and filter (pan) service every 50-60k miles. Look for harsh 2-3 or 3-4 shifts, flare on upshift, delayed engagement, or limp mode. A fluid service costs $400-700 and a rebuild $4,000-6,000. Ask for fluid service receipts and scan the transmission control module (EGS) for stored faults.', 'Driveline: the driveshaft flex disc (guibo) and center support bearing wear, causing a clunk on takeoff and vibration at 50-70 mph ($600-1,200). The rear differential mount and rear subframe bushings wear and cause a clunk on throttle changes ($800-1,800).', 'Front suspension and steering: the thrust arms (tension struts) and their fluid-filled bushings, the lower control arms, the center link, idler arm, and tie rods, plus play in the recirculating-ball steering box. Symptoms are wandering, a shimmy under braking, and uneven tire wear. A front-end rebuild costs $1,500-3,000 and a steering box $800-1,500. The 740iL and 750iL rear self-leveling suspension adds risk of sagging shocks and pump failure ($1,000-2,500); the 740i Sport uses conventional sport suspension.', 'Display pixel f
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, coolant drain and fill with BMW coolant and a proper bleed, brake fluid flush, power steering fluid, differential oil, and a 5HP24 fluid and filter service if there is no receipt from the last 50-60k miles.', 'Cooling system refresh if undocumented: radiator, expansion tank, water pump, thermostat, hoses, and fan clutch.', 'Engine air filter and cabin filters, a full code scan of all modules, and a battery health check, with a new AGM battery in the trunk if it is aged.', 'Fix any vacuum leaks found (CCV hoses, intake boots) and any active oil leak dripping on the exhaust.', 'Tires if over 6 years old or unevenly worn, followed by an alignment after any steering or suspension work.']
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front suspension and steering refresh: thrust arms, control arms, tie rods, center link, and idler arm.', 'Valve cover gaskets, the oil filter housing gasket, and possibly the oil pan gasket.', 'Driveshaft flex disc (guibo) and center support bearing; rear differential mount if clunking.', 'Rear coolant pipe and valley pan gasket if seepage is found.', 'VANOS solenoid seals and CCV system on 1999-2001 M62TU cars.', 'Window regulators, door lock actuators, trunk harness repair, and pixel repairs on the cluster, OBC, and climate control displays as they appear.', 'Contingency for timing-chain guides and valve stem seals if a cold-start rattle or smoke develops.']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven mainly by condition, verified mileage, and documentation. A well-kept, recorded 740i Sport typically sells well above an average 740iL. 1999-2001 facelift cars (xenon headlights with corona rings, M62TU engine) and the Sport Package (Style 37 M Parallel wheels, contour seats, Shadowline trim) bring the most money, and Imola Red, Jet Black, and Orient Blue over a contrasting interior help further. S62 and manual swaps sell at enthusiast-auction premiums, but they are modified cars with verification and smog-compliance burdens. Rollback flags, cluster swaps, and accident history should discount any car heavily. Undocumented 750iL V12 cars are cheap for a reason and carry much higher repair risk.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most E38s now have 100k-200k miles and 25-plus years of deferred rubber and plastic. Expect a cooling refresh, gaskets, suspension bushings, and driveline mounts unless receipts exist, which typically means $3,000-6,000 of catch-up work on an average car. Timing guides and valve stem seals are the big-ticket unknowns, and documented work on either is worth paying more for.

profiles.label: BMW M3 (E46, S54)
profiles.framing: This is the last naturally aspirated, hydraulically steered M3 — a 8,000-rpm S54 with a real 6-speed and a chassis that rewards a canyon run over Highway 1 or Laureles Grade far more than it rewards a spreadsheet. For a Carmel driver this is a weekend-plus-occasional-commute car: coastal salt air is mild, but marine damp punishes soft tops, subframe seam sealer, and neglected cooling systems. What matters most is documentation of the four expensive E46 M3 stories — rod bearings, rear subframe mounts, VANOS, and cooling system — because a cheap car with none of those records is not cheap. The convertible is heavier, softer, and worth meaningfully less than a coupe, so it should be bought as a driver, never as an appreciation play.
profiles.weak_points: Rear subframe mounting point cracking is the defining E46 M3 flaw: the four floor-pan mounting points and the surrounding sheet metal tear away from the trunk floor, most commonly on cars over ~60k miles, with harder-driven and clutch-dumped cars failing earlier. Symptoms are a clunk on throttle transitions, cracked seam sealer visible under the trunk carpet and above the differential, and in bad cases a visibly deformed floor. Proper repair is a reinforcement plate kit (CMP, Redish, Vorshlag) welded in — $2,500–$5,000 done right; look for photos of the weld-in job, not just "seam sealer looked fine." Rod bearings are the headline engine risk: BMW's original spec left marginal clearance, and while catastrophic failure is less common than internet lore suggests, prophylactic replacement with new-spec (or aftermarket ACL/King) bearings and new rod bolts is a $1,500–$3,000 job, done in-car. Ask for a receipt with the date, mileage, part numbers, and ideally a Blackstone oil analysis showing low lead/copper; an unknown-history 90k car with no bearing history should be priced with that job assumed. VANOS is a wear item, not a maybe: the exhaust hub bolts can back out, the intake/exhaust solenoid pack seals harden, and the high-pressure oil line rots — symptoms are a rattle at idle, loss of low-end torque, and codes for VANOS position. Beisan seal/rattle-fix kits and hub reseal run $800–$2,000 with labor; the earlier-recall single VANOS hub was addressed by BMW on many 2001–2003 cars, but verify. Cooling system is a full-replacement item every 60–80k miles or 8–10 years: plastic-impeller water pump, thermostat, expansion tank, radiator, hoses, and the notorious plastic thermostat-housing/coolant necks — $1,200–$2,000 as a package. The listing example shows a 2022 pump/thermostat at 78k, which covers the two biggest pieces but not necessarily the radiator or expansion tank. SMG II cars add a hydraulic pump ($1,500–$2,500), accumulator, and clutch position sensor to the risk list; manuals are strongly preferred and command more money. Clutch and dual-mass flywheel typically go together at 80k–120k for $2,000–$3,000; a chattering pedal-up rattle or shudder on take-up is the tell. Valve adjustment is a genuine S54 maintenance item every 30k miles or so ($600–$1,000 with shims) and is very often skipped — ask for it by name; a car with no valve adjustment record in 60k miles is a red flag on overall care. Oil consumption of a quart per 1,500–2,000 miles is normal-ish; more than that with blue smoke on overrun points at valve stem seals or worse. The CDV, rear shock mounts, front control arm bushings (FCAB), and rear trailing arm bushings are all $600–$1,500 suspension refresh items that most 20-plus-year-old cars need, and worn RTABs mimic subframe clunk. Convertibles add their own list: the power soft-top hydraulic cylinders and pump leak fluid onto the trunk carpet, the top's rear window and seams shrink and leak, the roll-over bar deployment system and its microswitches misbehave, and the tonneau/flap motors are expensive one-off parts — budget $1,500–$4,000 for a top replacement plus mechanism repairs. Electrical gremlins are routine: pixel loss in the instrument cluster and OBC ($200–$400 to repair), failing final stage resistor for the blower, a dying cluster stepper motor, sticky interior trim/soft-touch coating, and a glovebox latch that only works with the key (as noted in this listing) is a classic worn-latch item. Finally, the front control arm/steering rack bushing wear plus 20-year-old rubber engine and trans mounts make the car feel vague — cheap individually, but they add up fast.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (oil with the correct 10W-60 or a quality modern equivalent, brake, clutch, diff with LSD additive) if not documented within a year; front brake pads and likely rotors as flagged by the seller's technician ($600–$900); the cracked A/C belt plus serpentine belt, tensioners and pulleys ($400–$700); a proper subframe inspection with the trunk carpet and rear undertrays removed, and immediate scheduling of reinforcement if any cracking is found; battery registration and confirmation of the recently installed battery; VANOS rattle assessment and Beisan seal kit if the idle rattle is present; convertible top hydraulic leak check and soft-top seal/hinge lubrication; valve clearance check if there is no record within 30k miles.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Rod bearing and rod bolt replacement if there is no documented prior service (budget $2,000–$3,000 and treat it as scheduled, not optional, at 90k with a history gap); completion of the cooling system — radiator, expansion tank, upper/lower hoses, coolant necks — since only the pump and thermostat are documented; clutch and dual-mass flywheel if any shudder or high engagement point is noted ($2,000–$3,000); front control arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings, rear shock mounts and possibly all four dampers ($1,200–$2,500); soft-top replacement or rear-window repair if the material is shrunken or the seams are separating ($1,200–$2,500); instrument cluster pixel repair; new tires if the current set is over six years old regardless of tread; interior refresh items — driver's bolster reuph
profiles.market_notes: Coupes command a clear premium over convertibles — often 25–40% for equivalent condition — and 6-speed manuals are worth substantially more than SMG cars, with an SMG-to-manual swap history usually a net negative unless fully documented. The Competition Package (ZCP, 2005–2006, with 19-inch CSL-style wheels, quicker rack, and cross-drilled rotors) and Laguna Seca Blue, Phoenix Yellow, and Imola Red over Cinnamon or Kiwi carry the strongest desirability; black over black is the most common and least differentiated combination. Documented rod bearings, a welded subframe reinforcement, a recent cooling system, and a valve adjustment history can swing a car by $6,000–$10,000 against an unknown-history equivalent, which is exactly the value of paperwork on this model. Mileage matters less than records below about 120k, but Carfax gaps, rust-belt titles, and salvage/branded history all cut hard.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 20-plus-year-old S54 needs a systematic catch-up regardless of mileage: all rubber cooling components, belts and pulleys, suspension bushings, engine and transmission mounts, and every fluid on a documented interval. On this specific convertible, add the soft-top hydraulics and fabric to that list, and treat rod bearings and the remaining cooling components as scheduled work rather than contingencies given the ownership gap and the 2012-purchase, low-annual-mileage storage pattern.

profiles.label: BMW M4 / M4 Competition (F82 Coupe & F83 Convertible, 2015-2020)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, the F82 M4 is a fast, usable, four-seat coupe for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and occasional longer trips. A clean, unmodified Competition car is a strong real-world driver if three things check out: the S55 drivetrain has not been tuned, the DCT or manual gearbox has been looked after, and the car has not lived on a track or drag strip. Factory-stock software matters doubly in California. The BAR smog check verifies ECU calibration IDs, so a tuned car that was flashed back to stock can still cause headaches. The engine's press-fit crank hub also punishes cars that were tuned and launched. Unlike the S65 V8 E92 M3, rod bearings are not a pattern failure here. The money risks are the DCT, the crank hub on abused cars, cooling-system plastics, and the expensive consumables: staggered tires, M Compound rotors, and carbon-ceramic brakes if fitted.
profiles.weak_points: ['Crank hub (S55 timing/crank sprocket hub): the crank hub is a friction/press fit rather than keyed. Under high torque, especially tuned cars with aggressive launches or missed shifts, it can slip. That knocks cam timing out, and outcomes range from a misfire or no-start to valve-to-piston contact and a $15k-25k+ engine. A truly stock car driven normally has low but non-zero risk. Look for: confirmation the car was never tuned, and ideally a clean timing check. If the car was ever tuned, look for a receipt for a pinned or keyed aftermarket hub (e.g., Bimmer Hub, Vargas), typically $1,500-3,000 installed at an S55 specialist.', "DCT (Getrag 7-speed M-DCT, GS7D36BG): BMW lists the fluid as 'lifetime,' but specialists recommend a fluid and filter service every 40k-50k miles (about $500-900). Failure signs include harsh or slurred low-speed engagement, flare on 1-2 or 2-3, 'Drivetrain malfunction' or 'Transmission malfunction' messages, and refusal to engage reverse. Mechatronic unit or clutch pack faults run $4k-8k, and a used or reman transmission $8k-14k. Seepage at the mechatronic connector sleeve/adapter seal is common, roughly $400-900 to reseal. Some low-speed clunk and a lurchy creep are normal DCT character; slipping and fault codes are not. Look for: DCT service invoices with mileage, a clean transmission fault memory on ISTA, and a smooth cold-start test drive including reverse and parking-lot maneuvers.", '6-speed manual (if equipped): the clutch and dual-mass flywheel wear faster on cars that were launched or tuned. Watch for a high or slipping engagement point, chatter, or DMF rattle at idle. Clutch plus flywheel runs $2,500-4,500. Also check for a sticky or notchy 2nd/3rd shift and for leaks at the clutch slave cylinder. Wheel hop from hard launches on manual cars also damages the driveshaft and diff mounts.', 'Carbon-fiber driveshaft (one-piece CFRP prop shaft): it is strong in normal use but can be damaged by wheel hop, curb strikes or improper jacking. It is expensive to replace, about $3,500-6,000. Signs are driveline vibration at speed or clunks under load or off throttle. Look for: underbody photos showing no impact damage, and no evidence of drag-strip or launch abuse.', 'Charge pipe (plastic, turbo to throttle body): the OEM plastic pipe cracks or blows off at couplers, especially at higher boost. That causes sudden power loss, limp mode and boost-deviation faults. The repair is cheap, about $300-700 with an aluminum replacement, but a car already fitted with an aluminum pipe often signals a past tune. Look for: OEM pipe present and intact, and no boost-leak codes in history.', 'Oil leaks (valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, oil pan gasket, turbo oil feed/return lines, front crank seal): these are common from about 50k-80k miles or 6+ years old. Valve cover gasket runs $600-1,200, oil filter housing gasket $400-800 and oil pan $800-1,500. Oil from the filter housing gasket can drip onto belts and the exhaust. Look for: underbody photos with the undertray removed, receipts for any gasket work, and no burning-oil smell after a test drive.', 'Cooling system: this includes the plastic expansion tank and fittings, the main mechanical water pump, and the electric auxiliary pumps for the indirect charge-air cooler (low-temperature) circuit. The auxiliary radiators in the front bumper are also exposed to road debris. Expansion tank or hose failure runs about $300-800, an auxiliary electric pump $400-900 and the main water pump $1,000-1,800. Watch for coolant-level warnings, sweet smell, or charge-air-temperature/power-reduction faults. Look for: coolant service receipts, dry crusty-free fittings, and ISTA fault memory free of coolant-pump or charge-air-temperature entries.', "Ignition (spark plugs and coils): BMW's interval for the direct-injected turbo engine is long. Specialists change plugs about every 30k miles stock, and much sooner if tuned, at $300-600. Worn plugs lead to misfires that kill coils,

profiles.market_notes: Competition Package cars (444 hp, standard from 2019 in the US) are worth meaningfully more than base 425-hp cars. The 2018+ LCI updates also add value (LED headlights, revised taillights, NBT Evo iDrive). The 6-speed manual carries a few-thousand-dollar premium among enthusiasts and is rarer in late Competition cars. The CS, GTS and special editions are separate collector-tier markets. Unmodified, one-owner, dealer-serviced cars with documented DCT service and no tune history sell at a clear premium. Cars that were tuned and returned to stock, or have unexplained aluminum charge pipes or downpipes, are heavily discounted by informed bidders. Mileage bands matter: under 30k miles commands top money, 30k-60k is the core market, and 60k-80k+ cars trade at a discount but are the sweet spot for a driver if the records are good. Desirable colors are Yas Marina Blue, Austin Yellow, Sakhir Orange, Le Mans Blue and Individual paints, along with the Executive Package, adaptive LEDs, carbon-ceramic brakes in good condition, and transferable extended warranty coverage. Visibly worn CCBs, track history or salvage branding crater value.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2018-2020 example at 50k-70k miles has usually had only CBS oil changes at about 10k-mile intervals. Expect to catch up DCT fluid, diff fluid, spark plugs, coolant plastics and an initial reseal of the valve cover or oil filter housing gasket, budgeting about $1,500-3,500 if nothing is broken. Staggered tires and M Compound brakes are the recurring big-ticket consumables. Plan another $2k-4k within the first year for tires, rotors and pads, depending on condition.

profiles.label: BMW M6 (F12/F13/F06, S63Tü twin-turbo V8)
profiles.framing: The F1x M6 is a heavy, very fast grand tourer. It is well suited to Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and runs to LA or Tahoe, but it costs as much to run as a supercar no matter how cheap it is to buy. Low auction prices reflect real risk in the S63Tü engine: rod bearings, timing chain, and hot-V leaks. They also reflect how quickly neglect compounds on a car whose original owners often followed BMW's long oil intervals. For this buyer, the right car is accident-free and unmodified, so it passes a California smog software check without question. It should have records for oil changes every 5k miles or so, plus documented rod bearing and fluid work. A cheap car with collision history, mods, and thin records is usually the most expensive M6 to own.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rod bearings: The S63B44T0 uses tight bearing clearances, and failures are documented on F10 M5 and F1x M6 cars. They tend to appear between roughly 50k and 100k miles, especially on cars run on BMW's 10k-mile or one-year oil intervals, or tracked and launched frequently. A preventive replacement with OEM or coated shells and new rod bolts costs about $3,000-5,500 at an independent shop. A spun bearing means a replacement engine at $15,000-25,000+. Look for a dated invoice naming the parts. Also look for oil analysis showing low lead and copper, and a 5k-mile oil change habit.", 'Timing chain, guides, and VANOS: Chain stretch and guide wear are accelerated by extended oil intervals and short-trip use. Symptoms are a rattle for a few seconds on cold start and camshaft/crankshaft correlation or VANOS faults. A fix is a major job, usually $7,000-12,000 at an independent shop because of access in the engine bay. Ask whether timing adaptation values have been read with ISTA or similar BMW-level software.', 'Valve stem seals and oil consumption: The S63Tü is better than the N63, but some cars puff blue smoke on startup after sitting or at idle. Others use more than 1 quart per 1,500 miles. Seal replacement runs $6,000-9,000. Ask the owner directly about top-offs between oil changes.', 'Piezo injectors, coils, and plugs: Misfires come from a failing piezo injector ($300-450 each plus coding) or worn coils and plugs. Plugs are due roughly every 30-40k miles on a tuned or hard-driven car. A plug-and-coil job runs about $800-1,500. Check the misfire counters per cylinder on a scan. A recent coil and plug job is good, but ask whether it was triggered by a misfire that could point to an injector.', 'Hot-V cooling and turbo lines: The turbos sit inside the V, which cooks the coolant hoses, turbo coolant and oil feed/return lines, and their gaskets. There are three water pumps: the main pump, an auxiliary electric pump, and a low-temperature intercooler circuit pump. Each costs about $600-1,500 to replace. Expansion tanks and bleeder screws crack. Symptoms are a sweet coolant smell, low-coolant warnings, or white crust in the valley. A turbo replacement for wastegate rattle or seal failure is $6,000-10,000 for the pair.', "Oil leaks: By 8-12 years old, valve cover gaskets get brittle, and the job costs $1,200-2,500 because of hot-V access. Other common leak points are the oil filter housing gasket, oil pan gasket, crankcase vent lines, and vacuum lines. A puddle under the front of the car, like in the example listing, needs a lift inspection, not a seller's assurance.", 'Fuel system: Look for high-pressure fuel pump faults, injector seal leaks, and fuel line or connector leaks, signaled by a raw fuel smell in the engine bay. A prior fuel leak repair, as in the example, needs an invoice showing what was replaced. Check the VIN for open recalls and service campaigns at a BMW dealer.', "Getrag 7-speed M DCT: The gearbox is generally robust. Mechatronic failures cause limp mode, sudden neutral, or no-engage, and cost $4,000-8,000. Clutch wear comes from repeated launch control use. Leaks can appear around the mechatronic connector and cooler lines. BMW calls the fluid 'lifetime', but a service every ~50-60k miles ($500-900) is good practice. Many cars have never had one. Undocumented 'flushes' are not proof of service. Scanned clutch adaptation values give real evidence of wear.", 'Active M Differential: The differential has an electronically controlled clutch pack. Look for actuator or seal leaks, whine or clunk on and off throttle, and diff fault codes. A fluid service is about $250-400. A replacement unit is $3,000-5,000+.', 'Brakes: The cars weigh about 4,200 lb and the standard steel brakes are large compound/drilled rotors. They crack at the drill holes and wear quickly. A full set of pads and rotors costs about $2,500-4,000 at an independent shop. Optional carbon-ceramic rotors cost $10,000+ to replace, so measure their wear. Old brake

profiles.market_notes: These cars depreciated hard, and neglected, high-mileage, accident-history, or modified DCT coupes trade in the low-to-mid teens. Clean, documented, unmodified examples bring a meaningful premium. Value rises with the Competition Package (575 hp from 2014, 600 hp from 2016), the rare 6-speed manual, carbon-ceramic brakes, Executive Package, Individual paint, and especially receipts for rod bearings, DCT and diff fluids, and timing work. Collision history, tunes or emissions mods, and gaps in service records cut value sharply. Convertibles and Gran Coupes follow the coupe but appeal to different buyers.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 2012-2014 car is now 10+ years old, and the heat-soaked hot-V will have hardened its coolant hoses, turbo line seals, valve cover gaskets, and vacuum and vent lines. Most cars still have 'lifetime' DCT, differential, and coolant fluids and original rod bearings at 60-90k miles. Expect a $4,000-8,000 catch-up in the first year even on a decent example.

profiles.label: BMW M6 / M635CSi (E24, S38 shark)
profiles.framing: This is the top-shelf shark: a hand-assembled S38 four-valve six in a heavy, elegant 1980s GT that drives like a fast tourer rather than a scalpel. For this buyer it is a weekend and coastal-road car that can plausibly do a 300-mile day — Carmel to Cambria and back — and that will be kept for many years rather than flipped. What matters most is honest sheetmetal, a documented top-end (valve clearances, timing chain, cooling system) and an interior that is still complete, because every one of those three is expensive or nearly impossible to fix properly after the fact. Mileage matters less than whether the car has been used and maintained; a 38k-mile car that sat is often a bigger bill than a 110k-mile car with a folder.
profiles.weak_points: 1) S38B35 top end: shim-under-bucket valve adjustment is a real service item every 30–40k miles or ~5 years, and it is labor-heavy — expect $1,200–2,500 with shims. A noisy, tappy top end plus no adjustment record is a near-certain bill. 2) Timing chain and guides: single-row chain with plastic guides and a hydraulic tensioner; guides embrittle with age regardless of mileage, and rattle on start-up or at idle is the tell. Chain/guides/tensioner is a $2,500–4,500 job because the front of the engine comes apart. 3) Head and head gasket: the S38 head is effectively unobtainium — cracked or warped heads from one overheat event can total the car's economics ($6,000–12,000+ if a usable head must be sourced). Any coolant-loss or overheat story needs hard evidence of resolution. 4) Cooling system as a system: brass/plastic radiator end tanks, water pump with plastic impeller on some units, viscous fan clutch, aux fan, thermostat, expansion tank, and all hoses. If it hasn't been done in 10 years, budget $1,500–2,500 and do it before driving. 5) Fuel system: dual pumps (in-tank transfer plus main), accumulator, filter, and rubber supply/return hoses that harden and weep — a genuine fire risk on 35+ year-old cars. Cold-start hesitation, long cranking, or fuel smell means $800–2,000. 6) Motronic and sensors: 1.0/1.3 DME, air-flow meter, crank/reference sensors, aging grounds and harness connectors; cracked or repaired engine-bay harness insulation on late cars. Driveability gremlins here are chased in hours, not parts. 7) Individual-runner throttle bodies: six butterflies, worn linkage bushings and cracked rubber boots cause uneven idle and vacuum leaks; rebuild kits and sync labor $600–1,500. 8) Self-leveling rear suspension (SLS): factory-fitted to M6/M635CSi, and the accumulators, pump, and high-pressure hoses leak. Full OE restoration is $2,500–5,000 if parts can be found; most cars have been converted to conventional Bilstein/spring setups, which drives fine but is a small purist demerit and should be documented, not discovered. 9) Rust: inspect front strut/shock towers, cowl and windshield surround (leaking seals rot the plenum), rear window lower channel and trunk shelf, sunroof drains, trunk battery tray, jacking points, floors, rear subframe mounting points, and lower fenders behind the brightwork. E24 rear window channel repair is a $3,000–8,000 bodywork exercise done properly. 10) Interior unobtainables: cracked dash top (NLA, $1,500–3,500 for a good used/recovered unit), Nappa sport seat bolster wear and failed power/headrest motors, sagging headliner, dead OBC/check-control pixels, and brittle interior trim clips. Silver Gray and Natur leather show wear more than black. 11) Driveline: Getrag 280 with weak 2nd-gear synchro, worn shift platform bushings, clutch slave/master cylinders, driveshaft flex disc (guibo) and center support bearing, plus a 25% ZF LSD that seeps and can whine. Clutch job $1,800–3,000; guibo/center bearing $700–1,200. 12) Brakes and ABS: early Bosch ABS pump/module and sensors, seizing rear calipers and parking-brake mechanisms on cars that sat, and rotors that are getting scarce. Full refresh $1,500–3,000. 13) TRX metric wheels: 415mm basketweaves require Michelin TRX tires at roughly $500–700 each and they are commonly 10+ years old and hard/date-expired even with tread. Check date codes; budget $2,500 for tires or plan a period-correct 16in/17in alternate set while keeping the TRXs. 14) A/C and climate: R12 systems long since converted or dead; Behr box flap servos, blower, and evaporator replacement means dash-out labor — $2,000–3,500 to make genuinely cold. 15) Sat-car maladies specific to sub-50k-mile examples: flat-spotted or date-expired tires, varnished fuel system, dried-out seals, weeping hydraulics, stuck A/C compressor, and a wiring harness that has never been heat-cycled. Records of periodic use matter more than the odometer.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Complete fluid service (engine oil, gearbox, differential, brake fluid flush, coolant); new fuel filter plus inspection/replacement of all rubber fuel hoses and pump check; tires if date codes exceed ~6 years; full cooling-system inspection with thermostat, hoses, expansion tank and fan clutch as needed; valve clearance check and adjustment if no record within 5 years/30k miles; timing chain noise assessment and guide replacement if any rattle; brake hydraulic overhaul and rear caliper/parking-brake freeing on a low-use car; battery, belts, wipers, all bulbs and check-control faults; sunroof and windshield/rear window seal drainage clean-out.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch hydraulics or clutch if pedal feel/records are marginal; driveshaft flex disc and center support bearing; front control-arm bushings, tie rods, and rear trailing-arm/subframe bushings; throttle body bushings and full sync; shocks/springs if the SLS delete hardware is old or if original SLS units are weeping; A/C rebuild for reliable cold air; dash top and headliner cosmetics; OBC/instrument pixel and SI-board battery repair; differential and gearbox seals; exhaust center section or rear muffler rust-through.
profiles.market_notes: Federalized US M6 (1987–88, 256hp, big bumpers, airbag wheel on later cars) and Euro M635CSi (286hp, slim bumpers, often gray-market) trade on different terms — Euro cars appeal to purists but carry import/compliance paperwork risk, while clean US cars are the safer documented buy. Price is driven by mileage bands (sub-50k commands a strong premium, 60–110k is the sweet spot for drivers, 130k+ needs an exceptional file), rust-free southern/western history, original TRX wheels present even if unused, intact and uncracked dash and seats, and a thick service folder showing valve and chain work. Strong colors (Zinnoberrot, Royal Blue, Bronzit, black over Natur/Silver Gray) beat silver and gray; documented full respray or accident history and SLS conversions shave money but rarely kill a good car. Expect roughly $35–55k for solid drivers, $60–90k+ for low-mile or concours-documented examples, with all-manual supply meaning the only real transmission question is a Euro automatic M635CSi, which trades well below manual cars.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-plus-year-old car needs a systematic catch-up regardless of odometer: all rubber (fuel, coolant, vacuum, body and glass seals), full brake and clutch hydraulics, cooling system, tires, and a valve/chain assessment — realistically $6,000–12,000 over the first year unless receipts prove it was already done. Low-mileage survivors trade paint and interior quality for dried-out seals and varnished fuel systems, so budget the same money in different places. Prioritize drainage and seal work early, because water intrusion at the windshield, rear window, and sunroof is what turns an expens

profiles.label: BMW X5 (E70, incl. 2011+ LCI)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E70 is a comfortable, well-built all-weather family hauler for Monterey Peninsula duty: Highway 1, Sierra ski trips, Costco runs, and the occasional dirt road to a trailhead — not a collectible. The whole game is picking the right drivetrain (N55 six over N62/N63 V8, diesel only with a thick file) and the right maintenance history, because a cheap E70 is the most expensive kind. Low mileage helps but does not excuse age: rubber, gaskets, coolant-system plastics and electronics fail on a calendar, not an odometer. Budget the purchase price as roughly two-thirds of the real first-year number.
profiles.weak_points: Engine choice dominates the risk profile. The N62/N62TU 4.8-liter V8 (2007–2010 4.8i/xDrive48i) is known for valve stem seal failure — blue smoke on cold start and after long idles, a $4,000–7,000 heads-off job — plus alternator bracket gasket oil leaks, coolant transfer pipe (valley pan) leaks requiring intake removal, and timing chain guide wear past ~100k; many 'cheap' E70s are these cars. The N63 twin-turbo V8 (2011–2013 xDrive50i) is worse: hot-vee turbochargers cooking oil, valve stem seals, timing chain and fuel injectors, with BMW's own 'Customer Care Package' rework; without documentation of that campaign or an equivalent rebuild, walk. The N55 (2011–2013 xDrive35i) is the sane pick but has its own list: oil filter housing gasket leaking onto the belt (do it with the belt, $600–1,000), valve cover / cover gasket seeping ($700–1,200), VANOS solenoids and a wastegate rattle at idle that eventually needs a turbo ($2,500–4,000), plastic charge pipe cracking, and an electric water pump plus thermostat that is a 70–90k mile wear item ($1,100–1,600 installed). The N57 diesel (2009–2013 35d) delivers great range but EGR cooler recalls/fires, swirl-flap-free but glow-plug, DPF regeneration, DEF/SCR heater and turbo actuator issues make $3,000–5,000 single repairs routine; only buy one with full dealer history. Across all cars: the transfer case (ATC 700/500) actuator motor and servo gear strip, producing 4x4/drivetrain warnings and a shudder — $1,200–2,500 for a remanufactured unit. Front suspension thrust/control arm bushings and rear upper links are consumables every 60–80k ($900–1,800 a pair of ends). The optional rear self-leveling air suspension (standard on 7-seat and many Sport cars) fails at the air springs and compressor, $700–1,800 per corner-ish; M Sport cars with Adaptive Drive add Active Roll Stabilization hydraulic pump/valve block and EDC dampers that leak — ARS faults can run $2,000–4,000 and often get bodged by deleting them. Panoramic sunroof drains clog and soak the headliner and the FRM/footwell module or LCM under the dash; a drowned FRM shows as dead windows, lights and mirrors ($600–1,200 plus programming). The tailgate wiring loom in the rubber boot chafes and kills the rear wiper, lock or camera. The ZF 6HP/8HP is strong but 'lifetime' fluid is a myth — look for a drain/fill with a new pan-filter around 60–80k ($500–900); a shudder at low speed on a 100k+ car often means mechatronic sleeve/valve body. Also common: oil pan and rear main seal weeps on high-mile examples, coolant expansion tank and radiator end-tank cracks, iDrive CCC head unit failures on 2007–2010 cars, battery/IBS registration ignored by quick-lube shops, and run-flat tires that destroy ride quality and wheels on Carmel-area frost-heaved pavement.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid reset: engine oil with the correct LL-01 spec, transfer case fluid, front/rear differential fluid, transmission drain-and-fill with pan/filter if not documented in the last 50k, brake fluid, and coolant if older than four years. New battery with proper registration if the existing one is undated. Fresh non-run-flat tires in the right load rating (nearly every E70 needs this), plus an alignment. Expect an oil filter housing gasket and/or valve cover gasket seep to need addressing, sunroof drain cleanout, cabin and engine air filters, spark plugs and coils if over 60k since last, and wiper/bulb/warning-light cleanup. Scan all modules and clear stored faults, then re-scan after 200 miles.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Front thrust-arm and control-arm bushings, possibly rear upper links, and an alignment. Electric water pump and thermostat if original or over ~80k. Brakes with wear sensors all around. Ignition coils and plugs on the N55, a charge pipe upgrade if the plastic original is still in place, and VANOS solenoid replacement if rough cold running appears. Possible transfer case actuator, rear air spring(s), or an ARS/EDC damper on Adaptive Drive cars. Sunroof cassette service, tailgate loom repair, and A/C service on a car this age. Realistic first-year spend on a clean N55 car: $2,500–4,500; on a V8 or diesel, double it.
profiles.market_notes: Configuration and paperwork move price far more than odometer: 2011–2013 LCI xDrive35i (N55) cars with the M Sport or Sport Activity package, panoramic roof, and a documented dealer service file bring a strong premium over pre-LCI 4.8i/48i V8s, which are effectively bottom-of-market at $6k–12k because of the valve-seal and cooling-system liability. Third-row and diesel examples are niche — diesels draw a small torque-hungry crowd but scare most buyers. Low-mileage 'time capsules' like the 31k example trade at collector-ish premiums ($20k+) that an ordinary 90–120k driver cannot justify; the value sweet spot is a 70–110k mile LCI 35i with recent water pump, gaskets, and suspension work at $10k–15k. Neutral exteriors with black or beige interiors sell best; a Carfax with accidents, a salvage brand, or a gap in service records takes 20–30% off.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a 30k-mile 2013 is a 12-plus-year-old German SUV: coolant hoses, expansion tank, sunroof drain seals, air springs, engine and transmission mounts and tires all degrade on age, and lightly used cars often have original 'lifetime' transmission and transfer case fluid. Plan a full fluid and rubber catch-up plus a battery with registration in the first month, and treat the water pump/thermostat as due regardless of miles if it is original.

profiles.label: BMW X5 xDrive50i (F15, N63TU V8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the F15 50i is a fast, comfortable, all-weather family and road-trip SUV for Highway 1, Carmel Valley, and Tahoe runs. It is not something to appreciate. The cheap purchase price is the bait. The real cost is the N63TU twin-turbo hot-V V8, which is solid only when it has had short oil-change intervals and its known leak and oil-consumption items have been addressed. Buy the records and the engine condition first and the options second. Budget as if one major engine-bay job is coming within two years.
profiles.weak_points: ['Valve stem seals (N63TU): the seals harden from hot-V heat, causing a blue smoke puff at cold start or after idling at lights, plus rising oil consumption. This becomes common from about 70k miles or 8+ years, worse on cars with long-interval oil changes. Look for invoices for seal replacement or an oil-consumption test. Cost is about $3,500-6,000 at an independent shop, and more if done together with timing chains.', 'Timing chains and guides: the N63TU improved on the original N63 but still stretches chains, especially with 10k-15k-mile oil intervals. Symptoms include cam-correlation faults (2A82/2A87 family), a rattle at cold start, and rough idle. Ask for a cam/crank correlation readout from ISTA. Cost is about $4,000-7,500, and it is often combined with valve stem seals.', 'Turbo oil feed and return lines and turbo coolant lines: the O-rings and crush washers seep into the hot V, causing a burning-oil or coolant smell and residue on the turbos and downpipes. Common from 60k miles onward. Cost is about $1,200-2,500 per side-pair at an independent.', 'Valve cover gaskets and integrated PCV: the plastic covers and gaskets leak onto the exhaust manifolds, and cracked covers or failed PCV cause lean codes and whistling. Common from 70k-100k miles. Cost is about $1,500-3,000 for both banks.', 'Cooling system: the thermostat (often replaced around 80k), the electric auxiliary coolant pump for the turbos and charge-air circuit, the low-temp intercooler pump, the expansion tank, and the many plastic hose connectors in the V. Coolant loss can be slow and hidden under the engine cover and belly pan. Individual items run about $300-1,500. Overheating risks the turbos and heads.', 'Fuel injectors and ignition: the N63TU uses solenoid injectors, which are less troublesome than the earlier N63 piezos but can still leak or drip. That causes misfires, a fuel smell, or oil dilution. Spark plugs should be replaced about every 30k-40k miles, and coils fail with age. Plugs and coils run $500-1,200. A full injector set runs about $2,500-4,000.', 'Turbochargers: wastegate rattle on decel or cold start, oil seepage, and boost-deviation faults. Turbo life depends heavily on oil-change history and cooldown habits. Replacement is about $5,000-9,000 for both, since the job is in the V.', "ZF 8HP70 transmission: the gearbox is robust, but BMW calls the fluid 'lifetime'. By 80k-100k miles it needs a pan/filter and fluid service, about $500-900. The mechatronic connector sleeve and pan can leak. Watch for harsh 2-3 shifts or flare when cold, and ask for service records.", 'Transfer case (ATC45L) and actuator: aged or original fluid causes binding or shudder in tight parking-lot turns, and the actuator motor can fail. A fluid change is about $200-300. An actuator is about $400-800. A transfer case replacement is about $2,500-4,000.', 'Suspension (where equipped): rear air springs and the compressor leak or age out, causing the rear to sag overnight or air-suspension warnings. About $800-1,800. Dynamic Drive or active roll stabilization uses hydraulic lines and a valve block that can leak, about $1,500-4,000. Front thrust arm and control arm bushings wear on all cars, about $800-1,500.', 'Electrical and battery: the large AGM battery must be registered with the car, and weak batteries cause cascading faults. The NBT head unit, CID screen, surround-view cameras, and soft-close door actuators can fail. Repairs are about $400-3,000. A full module scan is the only reliable check.', 'Body and interior: panoramic roof drains clog, causing water in the footwells or headliner. Split-tailgate struts and the latch soft-close weaken. Dakota leather cracks on the driver bolster. Rust-belt cars can show subframe, brake/fuel line, and exhaust hanger corrosion. Corrosion repair can range from minor to $2,000+.']
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Oil and filter service, then shorten the interval to 5k miles or 6 months going forward', 'Full ISTA/module scan with fault-memory clearing and battery registration check; replace the AGM battery if it tests weak (about $350-500)', 'Spark plugs (and coils if misfire history) unless documented within the last 30k miles', 'Brake fluid flush if not documented within 2 years; inspect and fit the included front pads and rotors if near limit', 'Transfer case fluid and front/rear differential fluid service if no record', 'Coolant level and pressure test; inspect the auxiliary and intercooler pumps and the V-area hose connectors', 'Engine and cabin air filters, wiper blades, and a tire age/condition check (run-flat or conventional)']
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Valve cover gaskets and PCV if seeping (both banks)', 'Turbo oil feed/return line and coolant line seals if hot-V residue is present', 'ZF 8HP transmission pan/filter and fluid service if never done', 'Front thrust arm and control arm bushings, plus an alignment', 'Rear air springs and/or compressor if equipped and showing sag', 'Auxiliary electric coolant pump or intercooler pump if weak or faulted', 'Panoramic roof drain clearing and seal check before rainy season', 'Driver seat bolster leather repair or recolor', 'Monitor oil consumption and cold-start smoke; plan for valve stem seals and timing chains if trending worse']
profiles.market_notes: 50i prices sit only slightly above the 35i, despite much higher running costs. Steep depreciation makes $7k-$15k examples common. Value is driven far more by documented engine work than by options. Proof of valve stem seals and timing chains, or 5k-mile oil records, is worth thousands. M Sport, Executive package, Driver Assistance Plus, Dynamic Handling (adaptive dampers and Dynamic Drive), Bang & Olufsen, and third-row seating add modestly. Under 60k miles carries a premium. The 80k-120k band is where major N63TU jobs cluster and prices should reflect that. Rust-belt history and long-interval dealer-only service records (15k-mile oil changes) deserve a discount.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 8-10-year-old F15 50i at 80k-110k miles was likely serviced on BMW's long 10k-15k oil intervals. Assume never-changed 'lifetime' fluids (transmission, transfer case, differentials), aging hot-V rubber seals and plastic coolant fittings, and possibly original plugs and coils. Plan about $2,000-4,000 of baseline catch-up beyond the risk reserve. Rust-belt imports to coastal California need an extra underbody look, since salt damage does not reverse.

profiles.label: BMW Z3 Coupe (E36/8, incl. M Coupe)
profiles.framing: The 'clown shoe' is a short-wheelbase, stiff-shell hatchback built on E36 Z3 running gear — a genuinely rare, characterful weekend and back-road car for Carmel/Highway 1 and Laureles Grade duty, not a commuter. For this buyer it is an enthusiast bridge car: manual, unmodified, documented, and bought on chassis integrity rather than on shine. Values now split sharply between the S52/S54 M Coupe and the 2.8/3.0i coupe, so verifying exactly which car is in front of you is step one. Because the E36/8 has a known structural weak point (rear subframe mounting area), evidence of a clean underbody inspection outranks cosmetics, mileage, or 'like new' claims.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Rear subframe mounting points: the trunk floor sheetmetal where the rear subframe bolts up can crack, tear, or deform — the single most important E36/8 issue, disproportionately on M Coupes and any car driven hard or on sticky tires/lowered stiff suspension. Symptoms are hairline cracks radiating from the four mount cups, paint flaking, sealant splitting, or a 'clunk/wander' under load. Reinforcement plates (Redish, Vincebar, or BMW dealer plates) welded in run $2,000–$4,000; repairing already-torn metal $4,000–$7,000+. Look for photos of the trunk floor with carpet and spare tire out, and receipts naming the shop and plate kit. 2) Cooling system (M52TU 2.8 and M54 3.0i): plastic-necked radiator, expansion tank, thermostat housing, and water pump with plastic impeller are all life-limited at 60–100k miles or ~10–12 years, whichever comes first — regardless of odometer, a 25-year-old car on original cooling parts is a roadside failure waiting to happen. Full refresh $900–$1,800. A cooked M52TU/M54 head from an overheat is a $4,000+ event. 3) VANOS: rattle at idle/light throttle, lazy low-end torque; seal kit (Beisan) $200 DIY, $700–$1,200 at a shop. S54 M Coupes have the more complex, more expensive double-VANOS. 4) S54 rod bearings (2001–2002 M Coupe only): the well-known interval item; without a documented bearing service (~$2,000–$3,500 with rod bolts and oil analysis), assume it's due. Also check for the BMW VANOS/rod-bearing recall history and oil-pump nut/shaft. 5) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and oil pan gasket all weep by 80–120k miles; $400–$1,200 each depending on access. Look for oil on the exhaust manifold and burning smell. 6) Crankcase ventilation (CCV/oil separator) on M54 3.0i and M52TU: clogged separator causes smoke, rough idle, and can pull the dipstick out; $400–$800. 7) Driveline mounts and bushings: rear differential bushings and diff mount, driveshaft flex disc (guibo) and center support bearing, and rear trailing arm bushings all age out and cause clunks and driveline shudder; $800–$2,000 to do the set. Original diff-mount failures also contribute to subframe stress. 8) Rear hatch and glass sealing: the coupe leaks into the spare-tire well through the hatch seal, third brake light, and taillight gaskets — pull the trunk carpet and look for staining, rust, or a musty smell; the water also feeds subframe corrosion. Hatch struts sag ($100). 9) Interior electrics/trim: instrument cluster pixel loss (cluster rebuild $150–$350), sticky soft-touch coating on console/vents, sagging headliner, window regulator clips, and glovebox/ashtray plastics. Parts for coupe-specific trim (rear side glass, hatch, cargo cover, rear panels) are scarce and expensive. 10) ABS/ASC module and wheel-speed sensors: dashboard triangle plus ABS light; module rebuild $250–$500, sensors $100 each. 11) Secondary air pump and DISA valve (M54): CEL codes P0491/P0492 and a rattling DISA flap; $250–$600. 12) Clutch and hydraulics: clutch typically 100–140k miles; slave/master cylinders leak with age. Clutch job $1,400–$2,200 due to transmission removal. 13) Suspension bushings and shocks: front control arm bushings, rear shock mounts (RSMs) and their reinforcement, and 25-year-old dampers — a full refresh with quality parts is $1,500–$2,500. Many coupes have been lowered on coilovers with big wheels, which accelerates subframe and RSM damage. 14) Rust: California cars are usually clean, but East Coast/Midwest examples rot at the rear fender arches, rockers, jack points, trunk floor seams, and the subframe area itself — this is a specific problem for the listed New York car. Bushing replacement is not evidence of structural soundness; the trunk-floor welds and differential mounting area are a separate inspection and a separate repair (https://www.autoengineering.com/portfolio/bmw-z3-rear-subframe-mounting-points-repair/).
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full underbody/trunk-floor inspection with the carpet and spare out, and reinforcement plates if any cracking is found ($2,000–$4,000). Complete cooling-system refresh if not documented within 8 years/60k miles (radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, hoses, water pump) $900–$1,800. All fluids including differential and manual gearbox, plus brake fluid flush ($400–$700). New tires if the 19s are period no-name rubber, and ideally a return to a correct-offset 17-inch M Coupe/OEM-style wheel and OE-spec suspension ($1,500–$3,000). Reseal the hatch/taillight gaskets and clear the trunk drains ($200–$500). Battery, wipers, and a full pre-drive brake inspection.
profiles.repairs_12mo: VANOS seal kit and DISA/CCV service ($700–$1,500). Valve cover and oil filter housing gaskets ($700–$1,400). Guibo, center support bearing, diff and trailing arm bushings ($1,000–$2,000). Shocks and rear shock mounts if not recently done ($1,200–$2,000). Cluster pixel repair and window regulator clips ($300–$600). On a 2001–02 S54 car, budget rod bearings and a valve adjustment ($2,500–$4,000). Clutch and hydraulics if the pedal is high or shudders ($1,600–$2,200).
profiles.market_notes: The market is bimodal: S52/S54 M Coupes are collector cars ($45k–$100k+ depending on year, color, and records), while 2.8/3.0i coupes are enthusiast cars typically $18k–$32k, with the 2001–02 3.0i manual at the top. Documented subframe reinforcement, a rust-free Western car, factory wheels, and a thick service file add real money; lowered coilovers, 19-inch wheels, aftermarket exhaust, and repainted or Bondo'd rear arches subtract it. Rare factory colors (Imola Red, Estoril Blue, Titanium Silver, Hell Red) and clean two-tone leather help; black-on-black with modifications is the commodity spec. Automatic 2.8 coupes trade at a meaningful discount and are hard to resell; low mileage without records is worth far less than average mileage with them.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 25-year-old, low-mileage example needs age-based rather than mileage-based work: every cooling component, all rubber (hoses, bushings, guibo, motor and trans mounts), fuel lines, brake fluid and possibly calipers, tires regardless of tread, and seals that have dried out from sitting. Budget $3,000–$5,000 in the first year on a nice non-M coupe just to make it a trustworthy Highway 1 driver, plus the subframe reinforcement if not already done.

profiles.label: BMW Z3 Roadster & Coupe (E36/7, E36/8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Z3 is a cheap-to-buy, analog, rear-drive weekend roadster for Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road — hydraulic steering, a real handbrake, an inline-six, and a top that drops in fifteen seconds. A 2002 is the last and best year: M54 2.5i/3.0i engines, updated interior, and the wide rear track. It is emphatically not an investment car (M Roadster/M Coupe excepted), so buy the best-documented, unmolested six-cylinder manual you can find and treat the purchase price as the smaller half of the equation. Coastal fog, salt air, and a 20+ year old convertible top mean condition and storage history matter more here than mileage.
profiles.weak_points: Rear subframe mounting points: the single most important Z3 issue. The floor pan sheet metal around the four differential/subframe mounts tears and cracks, especially on 2.8/3.0i/M cars and any car that saw autocross, hard launches, or a heavy tow hitch. It is often invisible until you pull the trunk carpet and spare and inspect the sheet metal from above, or get under the car and look at the seams around the mounts. Repair is a welded reinforcement kit (Turner/Redish Motorsport/AKG plates) at roughly $2,000–$4,500 depending on how far the tears have propagated; ignoring it eventually means a floor pan section. Ask for photos of bare metal at all four mounts. Cooling system: M52TU/M54 cooling parts are plastic and time-expired at 20 years — radiator end tanks, expansion tank, thermostat housing, water pump (plastic impeller on some), and the radiator neck all fail without warning and an overheat can warp the aluminum head ($3,000+). A full cooling refresh is $700–$1,200 in parts and should be treated as a maintenance interval, not a repair; look for receipts within the last 8 years/60k miles. VANOS: M52TU/M54 single/double VANOS uses O-rings and seals that harden, producing a diesel-like rattle at idle, weak low-end torque, and rough cold running; seal kits are $150 in parts, $600–$900 installed, and a rebuilt unit is $1,000+. Crankcase ventilation (CCV/oil separator): the M54's CCV diaphragm and heater hoses crack, causing high crankcase vacuum, whistling, oil consumption, sucked-out rear main seal, and rough idle; $400–$700 to do properly with all the hoses. Oil filter housing gasket and valve cover gasket: near-universal leaks by 100k, oil drips onto the exhaust manifold and makes the classic BMW hot-oil smell; $300–$600 each. DISA valve (M54): the intake manifold flap pivot fails and can shed plastic into the engine; rebuild kit or replacement, $150–$350. Convertible top: the rear plastic window yellows, cracks and separates from the fabric; the top itself shrinks and the frame pivots seize. A quality Haartz cloth top with glass window installed is $1,200–$2,000, and a torn rear window on a coastal car means a wet interior and a rusting floor. Check the drain channels behind the seats. Rust and water intrusion: inspect rocker panels below the doors, the rear wheel arch lips, the seams under the sill trim, the trunk floor/spare well, and the battery tray (battery lives in the trunk on the passenger side); trunk lid seal and taillight gaskets leak and quietly rot the trunk pan. Electrical/interior: instrument cluster and OBC LCD pixel loss (a $150–$250 refurb), failing door lock actuators/microswitches, window regulators, and the notorious brittle interior trim; the headliner in the Coupe sags. Seats: driver's seat bolster and base foam collapse, and the seat frame bushings squeak; a re-foam and reupholster is $600–$1,200. Suspension/steering: front control arm (thrust arm) bushings and tie rods are 60–80k-mile items that cause shimmy under braking; rear shock mounts crack; original dampers on any surviving example are long dead. Budget $1,200–$2,000 for a full front-end and damper refresh. Driveline: hydraulic clutch master/slave cylinders weep and leave a soft pedal ($300–$500); the rear differential bushing and the driveshaft center support bearing/flex disc (guibo) fail with vibration at 60–80 mph ($500–$900). Fuel: level sender and in-tank pump failures give erratic gauge readings and hot-start issues. Secondary air pump and its check valve fail and throw P0491/P0492 codes that will block a smog pass — plan $400–$700. Finally, the 1.9L four (M44) is slow, weaker in resale, and shares the timing chain guide and cooling issues without the six's charm; a four-cylinder 2002 does not exist in the US, so a 2002 will be a 2.5i, 3.0i, or M.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full cooling system refresh (radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, water pump, hoses, cap) unless documented recent; oil service with a proper BMW filter; CCV/oil separator and hose set on the M54; oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets if seeping; convertible top rear window or full top if cracked/hazed plus clearing the top-well drains; four matching date-coded tires (age-outs are common on low-mile cars); front control arm bushings and tie rods if there is any shimmy; battery and trunk battery-tray cleanup; brake fluid flush.
profiles.repairs_12mo: VANOS seal service if the rattle is present; DISA valve rebuild; shocks/struts and rear shock mounts; clutch hydraulics; driveshaft flex disc, center support bearing and differential bushing; secondary air pump/valve if a smog code appears; instrument cluster pixel repair; door lock actuators and window regulator; seat foam/bolster repair; soft-top frame pivot service and re-lube; exhaust flex section or rear muffler; subframe reinforcement plates preemptively if the car is a 3.0i/M and shows early stress marks.
profiles.market_notes: Six-cylinder manuals carry the market: a documented 2002 3.0i manual with a hardtop, sport package and clean floors is the top of the non-M range, while automatics and the 2.5i sell noticeably softer. M Roadster and especially M Coupe live in a separate, much higher tier and demand S54 rod-bearing and subframe evidence. A factory hardtop adds $1,500–$2,500, and desirable colors (Steel Blue, Topaz Blue, Imola/Hell Red, Titanium Silver) with a contrasting or well-preserved interior move cars fast; grey/black on black with a tired top is the discount end. Records and rust-free southwestern/coastal-garaged provenance are worth more than a low odometer, and mileage below 60k mostly matters for the cosmetics it implies.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2002 Z3 is a 20+ year old car whose rubber, plastic, and fabric are all time-expired regardless of mileage: expect to spend $3,000–$5,000 in the first year on cooling system, CCV, gaskets, suspension bushings, dampers, tires, and likely the convertible top. None of it is exotic and most is DIY-friendly, but budgeting for it up front is the difference between a delightful cheap roadster and a rolling disappointment.

profiles.label: BMW Z4 Roadster (E85, 2003–2008; incl. 2.5i/3.0i M54 and 3.0i/3.0si N52)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, an E85 Z4 3.0i with the six-speed manual is a low-cost, analog-feeling roadster for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laureles Grade. It is a real driver, not a collectible. What matters most is a documented cooling-system and crankcase-ventilation history on the M54 engine, healthy electric power steering, a convertible top and trunk free of water intrusion, and a clean underside with no hidden accident repair. Expect the car to pass a California smog check with all OBD readiness monitors set. For an out-of-state purchase, the car needs to pass smog at CA registration, so verify readiness before money changes hands.
profiles.weak_points: ["Electric power steering (EPS) column: the column-mounted motor and torque-sensor assembly is the signature E85 fault. Symptoms include a notchy or 'sticky' feel just off center, heavy steering, intermittent loss of assist, and an EPS or steering warning light. It is common on 2003–2005 cars at any mileage. Repair runs about $900–1,500 for a rebuilt or used column installed, and $2,500+ for a new BMW unit. Ask for steering-column receipts, and check NHTSA and BMW campaign status by VIN.", 'M54 cooling system (2003–2005 2.5i/3.0i): the plastic expansion tank, radiator end tanks and neck, plastic-impeller water pump, thermostat and upper/lower hoses become brittle with age. Failures are age-driven more than mileage-driven, typically every 60–80k miles or 8–10 years. A full refresh costs about $900–1,600 at an independent shop. Look for a dated receipt listing the radiator, expansion tank, water pump, thermostat and hoses. Overheating an M54 risks a warped head or cracked block, so undocumented original cooling parts on a 20+ year-old car are a red flag.', "Crankcase ventilation (CCV) system: the oil separator and hoses under the intake manifold clog or crack. Symptoms are oil consumption, blue smoke at startup, lean codes (P0171/P0174), a rough idle, a whistle, or the dipstick or oil cap being sucked down. Repair costs about $350–700 because the intake manifold must come off. That intake-off access is also the time to replace the DISA O-ring and idle control valve gaskets. Look for a CCV receipt, ideally with 'intake gaskets' listed.", 'DISA valve (M54): the plastic flap inside the intake-manifold DISA unit can loosen and break off. In the worst case it gets ingested into the engine. Symptoms are a rattle at idle, a flat spot around 3,000–4,000 rpm, and codes. Expect $150–400 for a new DISA valve or a quality repair kit plus O-ring. Check for a receipt or have it inspected at the PPI.', 'M54 oil leaks: valve cover gasket (and cracked plastic valve covers), oil filter housing gasket, and oil pan gasket. Oil dripping onto the exhaust manifold or alternator causes burning smells and belt or alternator damage. Budget about $250–600 for the valve cover, $250–450 for the oil filter housing gasket, and $600–1,000 for the oil pan. Request photos of the underside and valve-cover area.', 'VANOS seals (M54 double VANOS): hardened seals cause loss of low-end torque, a rough cold idle, and hesitation. The fix is a seal kit, about $350–700 installed, and it is very common past 80k miles or 15 years. The VANOS solenoids and oil feed-line banjo seals can also leak.', 'N52 engines (2006–2008 3.0i/3.0si): the electric water pump and thermostat fail without warning. Budget $900–1,300 and treat them as a wear item around 70–100k miles. Other N52 issues are oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets, eccentric-shaft (Valvetronic) sensor faults, and lifter tick at cold start. Look for a water-pump receipt on any 2006+ car.', 'Convertible top hydraulics and water intrusion: the power top pump, hydraulic lines and cylinders can leak. The top-drain channels behind the seats clog with leaves and debris. The result is water in the trunk, battery well and footwells, which can corrode connectors and modules. Pump rebuild or replacement runs $500–1,500. Fabric wear at the fold lines, rear-window seam separation, and seal shrinkage add $1,200–2,500 for a new top installed. Coastal fog and rain in Carmel make this especially important.', "Front suspension: worn front control-arm (thrust/'lollipop') bushings and ball joints cause clunks over bumps, shimmy under braking, and vague steering. Replacing arms and bushings costs about $400–900. Rear shocks, shock mounts and trailing-arm bushings wear similarly, especially on Sport Package cars on 18-inch wheels.", 'Rear subframe mounting area: the E85 rear axle shares E46-derived architecture. Subframe-mount cracking is far less common than on the E46 sedan, but it is worth a lift inspection on any car driven hard.
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service unless documented within 12 months: engine oil and filter, brake fluid flush, manual transmission fluid, rear differential fluid, and coolant (BMW blue, with a correct bleed procedure).', 'Cooling-system refresh (radiator, expansion tank, water pump, thermostat, hoses, and cap on the M54) if there is no receipt from roughly the last 8 years or 70k miles.', 'Clear the convertible top drains and check the trunk floor and battery well for moisture; dry them and treat any corrosion.', 'Address any active oil leaks found at the PPI, most commonly the valve cover gasket or oil filter housing gasket.', 'Scan for stored codes and confirm all smog readiness monitors are set before California registration; fix CCV or secondary-air faults if present.', 'Replace the damaged windsh
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['CCV / oil separator replacement with intake gaskets, DISA O-ring or valve, and idle control valve cleaning, if not documented.', 'VANOS seal kit if there is cold-idle roughness or a low-rpm torque loss.', 'Front control-arm bushings or arms, and rear shocks and shock mounts if original or clunking.', 'Valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket and spark plugs if over 60k miles; inspect ignition coils.', 'Clutch slave cylinder and clutch-delay-valve removal or replacement; shifter bushing refresh for a crisper shift.', 'Convertible top hydraulic fluid check, pump inspection and seal conditioning; plan for top fabric or rear-window seam repair if worn.', 'Headlight lens restoration and xenon bulb or ballast replacement if dim or flickering.', 'Belts, idler and tensioner pulleys if not d
profiles.market_notes: A six-speed manual 3.0i commands a clear premium over automatic, SMG and 2.5i cars. The Sport Package (sport suspension, Dynamic Driving Control, 18-inch Style 107 wheels) and the Premium package add value. 2006–2008 3.0si cars sell for more because of their 255-hp N52, but they are not as much of a step up as the separately priced Z4 M Roadster. Documented cooling, CCV and EPS work, a healthy top, one-owner history and sub-60k miles are what push a car from about $8–12k into the $14–20k range. Interesting color combinations, such as bright colors over contrasting or Dream Red leather, also help. Accident history, cloth-top damage, SMG and a missing service history pull prices down sharply.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 20+ year-old E85s, even low-mile ones, still need a cooling-system refresh, CCV and intake gaskets, front control-arm bushings, and convertible-top drain and seal work. Low-mile cars that sat for long periods also commonly need rubber, gasket, belt and fluid catch-up. Budget roughly $2,000–4,000 in the first year for an undocumented example.
