profiles.label: BMW Z8 (E52, incl. Alpina V8 Roadster)
profiles.framing: The Z8 is a hand-assembled aluminum-spaceframe roadster with the E39 M5's S62 V8 and Getrag 6-speed. It is a collector-grade car even when bought as a driver. For a Carmel buyer who wants a documented, unmodified car to use on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley roads, the deciding factors are structural integrity, title and odometer history, and S62 health. Cosmetics and trim come after those. Mechanical parts are mostly shared with the M5 and are serviceable, but body, lighting, and trim parts are scarce and costly, and aluminum collision repair is a specialist job. That makes a car's history worth more than its shine.
profiles.weak_points: ['Aluminum spaceframe and body damage or poor repair. The Z8 frame and panels are aluminum and need aluminum-qualified repair procedures; conventional steel-shop repairs, pulled rails, or filler-heavy panels hurt both value and safety. Inspect the jacking points, front rails, sills, and suspension pickup areas for crush damage, kinks, cracks, or non-factory welds and rivets. Improper lifting damage at the jack pads is common. Look for galvanic corrosion (white powdery oxide) where steel fasteners or brackets meet aluminum. Ask for a lift inspection report with photos. Real structural repair can run $15k-$50k or more, and parts may be unavailable.', 'Title and odometer history. Some Z8s carry manufacturer-buyback, lemon-law, salvage, or rollback flags. Some cars spent time in Canada, where the clusters were switched between km and miles. BMW stores mileage in the cluster, the keys, and some control modules, so a dealer-level scan can help corroborate it. Demand the buyback reason (state lemon-law paperwork or the BMW NA case file) and a continuous service timeline. An unexplained brand typically cuts value by 40-60%.', 'S62 throttle actuator. The electronic throttle actuator (shared with the E39 M5) has plastic internal gears that wear. Symptoms are a limp-home mode, an EML warning light, and throttle fault codes. Replacement is about $1,200-$2,500 for a new or rebuilt unit plus labor. Ask whether it has been replaced or whether an improved-gear repair kit was fitted.', 'S62 double-VANOS. Watch for solenoid and seal wear, high-pressure VANOS oil line seepage, and cam-adjustment fault codes. Symptoms are rough idle, low-rpm hesitation, power loss, and a rattle on cold start. A seal and solenoid refresh runs about $1,500-$3,500, and a full unit rebuild more. Look for receipts and clean adaptation and fault readings on a BMW-capable scan tool.', 'S62 timing chain guides and tensioners. The upper plastic guides crack and the tensioners weaken with age and heat cycles, more so on cars over about 80k miles or cars that sat for long periods. Symptoms are cold-start chain noise and guide debris in the oil pan or filter. Guide and tensioner replacement runs about $3,500-$6,500. A failure that goes unaddressed can destroy the engine, which costs $25k-$40k or more to rebuild or replace.', 'S62 rod bearings and oil consumption. They are less notorious than on the S54 or S65 but still a concern on high-mileage or track-used cars. Preventive bearings cost about $3,000-$5,000. Oil analysis (watch copper and lead) and a consumption record are useful. Excessive consumption can also point to worn valve stem seals or rings.', 'Cooling system. The plastic radiator end tanks, expansion tank, water pump, thermostat and housing, and hoses age out regardless of mileage. Overheating an aluminum V8 risks warped heads. Check the date of the last full refresh; an engine-out-quality cooling overhaul runs about $1,500-$3,500. Partial work, such as a thermostat alone, is common.', 'Oil leaks. Common sources are the valve cover gaskets, oil filter housing gasket, oil pan gasket, and timing cover. Expect $500-$2,500 depending on the source. Most are age-related on low-use cars.', 'Clutch, dual-mass flywheel, and clutch hydraulics on the Getrag 6-speed. Symptoms include a high engagement point, chatter, DMF rattle at idle, a soft or sticking pedal, and slave or master cylinder leaks. A clutch and flywheel job runs about $3,500-$6,000. Hydraulics alone are about $500-$1,200. Also check for differential and transmission seep.', 'Neon taillights and side indicators. The Z8 uses neon tube lamps whose ballasts or tubes fail. Symptoms are dim, flickering, or dead segments. Replacement assemblies are expensive and supply is limited (roughly $800-$2,500 or more per assembly, sometimes no longer available), so repair specialists exist. Verify all lamp functions.', 'Wheels, tires, and the no-spare setup. The car left the factory on run-flat tires with no spare. Most owne
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service unless documented within 12 months: engine oil and filter, coolant, brake fluid, clutch fluid, transmission and differential oil (about $800-$1,500)', 'Replace tires older than 5-6 years, and decide between a run-flat or conventional tire plus inflator kit', 'Battery and charging check; Z8s that sit often have weak batteries and parasitic drain', 'Belts, idler and tensioner pulleys, and a cooling-hose inspection with replacement of anything cracked or soft', 'Clear and diagnose any stored throttle, VANOS, or MAF fault codes; address throttle actuator limp-mode faults', 'Alignment and a check of suspension bushings for obvious wear or clunks', 'Soft-top hydraulic and latch check, and seal conditioning to stop leaks before the coastal winter', 'Repair or replace failed n
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Cooling system refresh if undocumented: radiator, expansion tank, water pump, hoses (about $1,500-$3,500)', 'Valve cover, oil filter housing, and oil pan gaskets as leaks dictate (about $500-$2,500)', 'VANOS seal and solenoid service if fault codes or rough low-rpm running appear (about $1,500-$3,500)', 'Timing chain guide inspection, and replacement if noisy or high mileage (about $3,500-$6,500)', 'Front control arms, thrust arm bushings, and shocks as needed (about $1,500-$4,000)', 'Clutch, dual-mass flywheel, and hydraulics if engagement is high or DMF rattle is present (about $3,500-$6,000)', 'Soft top and headliner replacement if fabric is shrunk or torn or the headliner is sagging (about $4,000-$8,000)', 'Interior leather repair or re-trim on the dash and gauge pod (about $1,000-$4
profiles.market_notes: Clean-title, documented, unmolested cars with the factory hardtop command a large premium. Branded, buyback, rollback-flagged, or poorly repaired cars trade at a steep discount and are harder to resell. Mileage bands matter: under 10k miles is collector territory, 10-40k is the core market, and over 60k is driver-grade. Rare colors (Topaz Blue, Le Mans Blue, Black, Red) and contrasting interiors bring more than the common Titanium Silver. The 2003 Alpina V8 Roadster has its own premium despite being automatic. Complete records, the hardtop, a matching interior, a working phone and original items, and an honest frame report move the price most.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most Z8s are low-use cars that sat, so age-related catch-up is typical even at modest mileage. That usually means fluids, cooling plastics, gaskets, tires, bushings, and soft-top hydraulics. Budget $5k-$15k in the first year for a well-kept example, and plan for more if records are thin or the history is clouded.

profiles.label: Biagini Passo (1990–1993, Golf Mk1 Cabriolet body / Golf Mk2 Country Syncro drivetrain)
profiles.framing: The Passo is a low-volume Italian coachbuilt oddity, with an estimated production of fewer than 100 to about 300. It pairs a reworked VW Golf Mk1 Cabriolet unibody with the 1.8 EA827 engine, 020-family five-speed manual and Syncro AWD of the Mk2 Golf Country, hung on a Biagini-specific subframe. For a Carmel buyer it is a quirky, slow, open-air soft-roader for Highway 1, Carmel Valley and dirt fire roads, not a serious off-roader or an appreciating asset. The VW mechanicals are serviceable and mostly cheap. The real risks are the unique Biagini body and chassis parts, which are effectively unobtainable, the health of the Syncro driveline, cabriolet-body rust, and whether a non-US-certified 1991 import can legally be registered in California at all.
profiles.weak_points: ['California registration and emissions compliance. This was never a US-certified vehicle, and many examples, including the reference car, came in from Europe under the 25-year rule. Federal import eligibility does not equal California eligibility. CARB/DMV treat a 1991 gasoline vehicle as smog-required, and a non-certified direct import can face a costly CARB-lab modification and certification process, or may not be registrable at all. Out-of-state titles (e.g., CT, IL) prove nothing about CA eligibility. Documentation to seek: any prior California registration, an existing CA referee or BAR determination, the federal import paperwork (HS-7, EPA 3520-1), and the emissions label or catalyst presence. Without a clear path, the car is a $0 asset in California regardless of condition.', 'Syncro viscous coupling and rear final drive (Golf Country / Mk2 Syncro-derived). The viscous coupling stiffens with age and causes binding, tire scrub and crow-hop in tight, slow turns on pavement. Alternatively it goes weak and the car is effectively FWD. Golf Syncro-derived rear drives also use a freewheel that is locked out in reverse, and a failed freewheel or lockout gives clunks or no rear drive. Test: tight full-lock circles in a parking lot, then a jack-one-rear-wheel or slippery-surface traction check. Repair band: used/rebuilt coupling or rear drive roughly $800–2,500 installed, more if parts must come from Europe.', "Angle drive / transfer case and propshaft. The PTO angle drive on the 020-family transaxle leaks and develops bearing whine. The multi-piece propshaft's center support bearing and rubber couplers dry out on a 30+ year-old car, giving vibration at 40–60 mph and clunks on throttle transitions. Look for receipts showing all three driveline fluids (transaxle, angle drive, rear final drive) were changed, not just engine oil. Propshaft bearing/coupler work runs about $400–1,200. An angle drive rebuild runs about $800–1,800.", 'Biagini-specific subframe and lifted geometry. The custom subframe and lift (claimed ~10.2 in clearance) are unique, low-volume fabrication. Inspect for cracked welds, crushed sections from off-road use, corrosion at mounting points, and DIY repairs. The added ride height steepens CV angles, so torn boots and clicking outer or plunging inner CVs are common. CV axle replacement runs about $250–600 per corner. Any structural subframe repair is custom fabrication, typically $1,000–3,000+.', 'Golf Mk1 Cabriolet body rust. Check floor pans under carpets (soft-top leaks soak them), rocker/sill seams, the A-pillar and windshield frame base, the battery tray area, front strut towers, rear wheel arches behind the flares (the flares trap mud and water), the spare well, door bottoms, and the base of the roll bar. A Cabriolet shell relies on its sills and floor for stiffness. Visible bubbling usually means much more underneath. Rust repair runs $2,000–10,000+, and a rotted A-pillar or sill is often a walk-away.', 'Unique body panels and trim. The redesigned hood, front fenders, wheel-arch flares, drop-down tailgate, brush guard, swing-out spare carrier, Biagini badging and console plaque have no aftermarket supply. Fiat Panda Mk1 headlights and Fiat Ritmo side markers are obtainable in Europe but slow and costly to import. Any accident damage to these parts means one-off fabrication. Photograph and verify completeness, then budget generously for even minor collision repair.', "Soft top, zippered rear panel and tailgate sealing. The Golf Cabriolet top frame was carried over, but the glass rear window was replaced by a zippered plastic panel to suit the tailgate. Zippers fail, panels cloud and tear, and the top-to-tailgate seal leaks, which feeds floor rust. Off-the-shelf Mk1 Cabrio tops need trim-shop modification for the Passo's rear. Budget about $300–800 for a rear panel and $1,500–3,500 for a full custom top.", '1.8 EA827 8-valve engine (likely single-point injection, ~89–98 hp depending on version; verify the eng

profiles.market_notes: This is a thin, illiquid market with few public sales, so comparable pricing is noisy. Values swing mainly on structural rust condition, completeness of the Biagini-unique parts (hood, fenders, flares, tailgate, brush guard, spare carrier, Panda headlights, badging), and whether the Syncro driveline works as designed. Documentation of European history, import paperwork and a clean registration path in the buyer's state add real value. Aftermarket wheels, seats and tuner-brand pieces may help on an enthusiast auction site but reduce appeal to originality-focused buyers. Mileage matters less than rust and drivetrain health because odometers are hard to verify. For a California buyer, an example already registered in CA or with a documented CARB pathway is worth substantially more than an identical car titled elsewhere.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a typical imported example has an unknown maintenance history. Plan on a full baseline: timing belt, all three driveline fluids, brake hydraulics, cooling system and fuel/vacuum rubber, roughly $2,000–4,000 at an independent VW shop. Any rust, soft-top or unique-panel deficiencies are on top of that, and are the items most likely to exceed the risk reserve.

profiles.label: Chevrolet C/K Pickup "Square Body" (1973-1987 pickups; R/V carryover through 1991)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, a square-body C10 is a simple, fixable, honest driver truck for coastal errands, hauling and weekend use. It is not a precision machine. Nearly every mechanical part is cheap and available, so what matters is how much rust and structural damage the truck has, whether its identity is correct, and how many previous owners' hacks you inherit. California registration is the big model-specific factor. 1976-and-newer gasoline trucks need a smog check at every transfer and every two years, with a visual inspection of original emissions equipment. 1973-1975 trucks are exempt, so smog compliance should drive both which year you buy and how much you pay.
profiles.weak_points:
['California smog compliance (1976+ gasoline only). Light-duty C10s from 1975 onward came with a catalytic converter, EGR, PCV, an evap canister and, on many, an AIR pump. These parts are often removed or replaced with uncertified aftermarket intakes, carbs and headers. A truck missing equipment fails the visual inspection outright. Restoring a 1977 350 to compliance (cat, EGR, air pump plumbing, a correct Quadrajet, CARB-EO parts) runs $800-3,500, and some hot-rodded trucks are effectively unregisterable without a referee visit. 1981+ trucks add Computer Command Control (E4ME electronic Quadrajet, O2 sensor, ECM), which is harder to diagnose. Out-of-state trucks must pass at initial California registration. Diesels from 1997 and older are exempt.', 'Cab rust. The classic failure points are:
- cab corners behind the doors
- rocker panels
- door bottoms
- floor pans under the seat and in the footwells

The floors usually rot from cowl-vent and windshield-gasket leaks that wet the carpet and jute pad. Also check the lower windshield channel and the cab mounts and cab support structure. Patch panels are cheap, but professional repair runs $1,500-4,000 per side for corners and rockers and $1,500-3,500 for floors. Rust hidden under fresh paint is the biggest value trap.', 'Front fender and bed rust. Mud packs into the rear lower front fenders and rots them, along with the inner fender and core support. On the bed, check the bed floor, the front bed rail and the inner wheelhouses, plus the bed crossmembers, especially under long-term caps or toolboxes. Replacement fenders are $150-400 each plus paint. A Fleetside bed floor or wheelhouse repair runs $800-2,500.', 'Frame cracks at the steering gear mount. The driver-side frame rail can crack around the steering box bolts, and the bolts loosen, particularly on trucks with oversized tires or lifts. Symptoms are clunking and steering wander. Also inspect the rear spring hangers and crossmembers for rust-through. A frame plate/brace kit plus welding costs $300-1,200.', 'Steering looseness from:
- a worn Saginaw recirculating-ball box
- a deteriorated rag joint (flex coupler)
- the idler arm, pitman arm and tie-rod ends
- ball joints and control-arm bushings

Typical symptoms are vague, wandering steering and dead play at center. Full front-end refresh parts are $400-900. A box replacement is $250-600 plus labor.', 'Timing chain wear on the small-block (250 I6, 305 and 350 V8). The factory nylon-toothed cam gear wears and sheds teeth, which lets timing jump and drops debris into the pan. Typical failure point is 60-100k miles if never replaced. Look for a receipt for a double-roller timing set. Repair runs $400-900. Smog-era 350s (roughly 8.5:1 compression, around 165 hp in 1977) also commonly have worn valve guides that cause oil smoke, plus intake, valve cover and rear main seal leaks.', 'Quadrajet carburetor (M4MC/M4ME, and E4ME from 1981) problems:
- Worn throttle-shaft bushings cause vacuum leaks and an erratic idle.
- Leaking well plugs drip fuel into the intake, causing hard hot starts and fuel smell.
- Secondary air-valve tension and choke pull-off diaphragms go out of adjustment or fail.

A quality rebuild with bushings runs $350-700. Swapping to an aftermarket carb usually breaks California smog legality unless it carries a CARB EO.', 'Automatic transmission wear. TH350 (common in C10) and TH400 (heavier trucks) are durable, but watch for:
- a vacuum modulator that fails and gets pulled into the engine, causing white smoke and low fluid
- kickdown cable or switch problems
- pan and tailshaft leaks

The 700R4 overdrive (1981+) is far more fragile. Its TV cable adjustment is critical, and a misadjusted cable burns the 3-4 clutches. Rebuild costs are $1,800-3,000 for a TH350 and $2,500-3,800 for a 700R4.', 'Rear axle and 4x4 driveline. The C10's GM 10-bolt (8.5") rear axle usually has pinion seal leaks, axle bearing noise and C-clip wear. K-series trucks add a

profiles.market_notes:
Price is driven by:
- rust-free structure, especially an original West Coast truck
- trim level (Silverado/Cheyenne > Scottsdale > Custom Deluxe)
- short-bed Fleetside (a clear premium over long beds)
- 4x4 K10 over C10
- factory V8 and factory A/C
- documented originality

In California, 1973-1975 trucks carry a smog-exemption premium over otherwise similar 1976+ examples. Taste-specific custom paint, mismatched-year front clips and heavy aftermarket parts shrink the buyer pool, so trucks like the example tend to stall around $7-12k. Clean original or well-restored short-beds bring $20-45k, and pro-built restomods go higher.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical square body has decades of deferred maintenance and amateur fixes. Plan on $1,500-3,500 to catch up rubber, brakes, ignition, carburetor and front-end wear, plus fuel-sender and wiring gremlins. Hidden rust under recent paint and California smog-equipment restoration on 1976+ trucks are the two items most likely to blow the budget, so budget for them before bidding.

profiles.label: Chevrolet Camaro IROC-Z (3rd Gen, 1985-1990)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the IROC-Z is a period-correct V8 driver: a lowered, stiffly sprung 1980s GM F-body with a simple, very cheaply serviced small-block. It is not a precision sports car. Value and enjoyment depend on three things. First, a verified genuine IROC (B4Z) with its original drivetrain. Second, a solid unibody free of rust and of poorly repaired accident damage. Third, an engine and emissions system that can pass a California biennial smog check as delivered. Mechanical parts are cheap and plentiful. Rust, bodywork, clones and smog-illegal modifications are what turn a $20k car into a money pit.
profiles.weak_points: ["Authenticity and drivetrain mix-ups are common. Many 'IROCs' are Z28s or base cars dressed up with IROC wheels, decals and ground effects. Verify RPO B4Z and the engine and transmission codes on the SPID label (glovebox lid or console lid), and check that the VIN 8th digit matches the engine. Engine codes: F = LB9 305 TPI, G = L69 305 HO, H = LG4 305 4bbl, 8 = L98 350 TPI, E = LO3 305 TBI. The model-year availability matters. In 1985-86, TPI came only with the 700R4 automatic, and the L69 HO came only with the 5-speed. The L98 350 (1987-90) was automatic-only. A 'factory' TPI 5-speed 1985, or a 350 5-speed, is a red flag.", "Rust is the body killer. Check these areas: lower hatch corners and the hatch floor/spare well; rear quarter wheel lips; rockers behind the plastic ground effects, which trap water and dirt; floor pans under the seat tracks; strut towers and cowl; the windshield frame lower corners; and the T-top drain channels. Expect $3k-15k+ for proper metal repair. Underbody 'corrosion visible' in a listing deserves photos of rails, floors and the rear spring perches before bidding.", 'Accident damage and unibody fatigue are common. These cars were driven hard and frequently crashed. Look for uneven panel gaps, overspray, and rippled or replaced core supports and frame horns. The front frame rail can crack around the steering-box mounting bolts, from flex and from impacts. Most cars lack subframe connectors, so high-mileage cars show door sag, creaks, cracked windshields and T-top leaks. A professional rail and steering-box mount inspection is mandatory. Repair runs $500-2,500 depending on cracking.', 'TPI (Tuned Port Injection) has several known faults, all usually inexpensive. Vacuum leaks occur at the plenum, runner and lower intake gaskets, causing high idle, hunting or lean codes ($300-900 to reseal). Injectors drip or clog, especially on earlier cars ($300-700 for a refurbished set). The 1985-87 cold-start injector and thermo-time switch can leak and flood the engine on hot restarts. The 1985-89 MAF sensor and its burn-off relay fail, causing stalling and hesitation ($150-400; 1990 cars switched to speed-density). The in-tank fuel pump, relay and oil-pressure backup switch also fail, causing no-start or long crank ($300-700). Look for receipts for injector and fuel-pump service.', "Cooling and gauge problems are common. The aged radiator (often plastic tanks), water pump, heater hoses and the electric cooling-fan relay/switch can all fail. Temperature and oil-pressure senders and gauge-cluster connections are flaky, so an 'inoperable temp gauge' is often just a $30 sender. However, it can also hide a car that has been overheated with no warning. Confirm the fan cycles at temperature, and check for coolant in the oil from lower intake gasket seepage. Cooling refresh: $500-1,200.", 'Small-block 305/350 wear items are routine but inevitable. Valve stem seals harden, causing blue smoke at startup. The timing chain stretches, and some factory cam gears have nylon-coated teeth that shed debris into the oil pan. The rear main seal and oil pan gasket leak (two-piece rear main seal through early 1986). Distributor HEI module and pickup coil failures cause hot stalling. Timing set: $400-800. Seals and gaskets: $500-1,500. A tired 305 rebuild: $4,500-7,500.', 'The 700R4 automatic is the big-ticket drivetrain risk. Its TV (throttle valve) cable must be adjusted correctly, or line pressure falls and the 3-4 clutch pack and band burn up. TPI swaps and intake work often leave it misadjusted. Known failures include the sunshell, the 3-4 clutches and torque-converter lockup (TCC) solenoid/switch faults. Symptoms are slipping into 4th, flare on the 2-3 shift, harsh or late shifts, and no lockup. A rebuild runs $2,800-4,500. Look for fluid and filter service records and any rebuild receipt with a shop name.', 'The Borg-Warner T-5 manual (L69 and later LB9 5-speed cars) is marginal behind a V8. Watch for worn 2nd/3rd synchros, a g

Service the front calipers and the rear drums or discs.', 'Replace tires older than six years. Original-size 245/50R16 tires are available, but date codes are often 5+ years old on low-mile collector cars.', 'Replace serpentine/V-belts, radiator and heater hoses, and the thermostat. profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by authenticity and condition. A documented, rust-free, unmodified B4Z car with original paint and low verified mileage brings roughly $20k-40k+. Clean drivers usually trade around $10k-18k. Clones, swapped drivetrains, rusty cars and smog-non-compliant cars are heavily discounted. Desirability rises with the L98 350 (1987-90), the LB9 TPI 5-speed (1987-88), and G92 performance axle/four-wheel disc cars. Convertibles (1987-90), T-tops, original window stickers or RPO documentation, and single-owner history all add value. Carbureted LG4 and LO3 TBI cars are worth less. Automatics are normal for TPI cars and are not penalized much. Reported accidents, repaints and visible underbody corrosion take a meaningful bite. For a California buyer, a car that has already passed a CA smog check is worth a premium over an out-of-state car with unknown emissions compliance.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even low-mile IROCs have usually sat for long periods. Assume all rubber has aged out: tires, hoses, belts, brake hoses, bushings and weatherstrip. Also assume fluids are stale and the in-tank fuel pump and senders are of questionable health. Budget $2,500-5,000 in the first year to bring a typical example to reliable-driver standard, before any rust, A/C or transmission surprises.

profiles.label: Chevrolet Chevy II / Nova (2nd gen, 1966–1967)
profiles.framing: The 1966–67 Chevy II Nova is a light, simple compact that, in V8 sport-coupe form, makes a fun classic for weekend runs on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road. Any trained classic-car mechanic can maintain it, and reproduction parts support is excellent. This buyer wants a documented, factory-correct car, so the job is mostly separating honest, rust-free original or sympathetically restored cars from the far more common restomods, SS clones and engine swaps (the example listing, with its 502/TCI/Mustang II build, is exactly the type to avoid). Look for a sound unibody and front subframe, a verifiable drivetrain, and a brake and suspension system that has been properly refreshed rather than modernized.
profiles.weak_points:
Unibody rust is the dominant risk on this generation. The likely spots are the floor pans under the carpet (worst near the rockers and under the front footwells), the trunk floor and its drop-offs, the rocker panels, and the lower rear quarters behind the wheels. Small bubbles there usually mean much worse rust underneath, and a proper floor/trunk/quarter repair runs $8k–25k+. Look for photos taken during any restoration that show bare metal.

The rear frame rails and the front mounts of the rear leaf springs are a structural weak point. Rot or cracking there, often hidden under undercoating, compromises axle location. Rail sections cost $1.5k–5k installed, and they must be inspected on a lift.

The front subframe (bolt-on stub frame) to firewall/cowl mounting area can corrode. Collision damage can also distort the subframe, causing alignment that won't stay in spec and uneven tire wear. Check the mount bushings and bolts and the condition of the frame horns. Correcting a tweaked subframe on a frame machine costs $1k–3k.

Water leaks from the cowl vent and plenum and from the rear-window lower channel on hardtops rot the cowl, kick panels and rear package-tray area. Wet carpet, musty smell or rust stains around the rear glass are red flags. Cowl repair is $2k–6k; a rear-window channel repair with glass reset is $1k–3k.

The mono-leaf rear springs used through 1967 allow axle wrap and wheel hop, especially on V8 and 327 cars, and they sag with age. Check ride height, spring eye bushings and the axle seating. Correct replacement springs are $400–900 plus labor.

Front suspension and steering wear: the coil spring sits above the upper control arm in a tower, and the bushings, ball joints, idler arm, tie rods and manual steering box wear loose. Symptoms are wander, clunks, and steering-wheel play above roughly 2 inches. A full front-end rebuild with alignment runs $1.5k–3.5k, and steering-box rebuild or replacement $400–1,200.

Brakes: four-wheel drums were standard (front discs were a rare 1967 option). The 1966 cars have a single-circuit master cylinder; 1967 got the federally mandated dual master. Drums fade and pull, and old wheel cylinders and rubber lines leak. A full hydraulic refresh (master, wheel cylinders, hoses, shoes, hardware, turned drums) is $800–2k. Ask for receipts and the brake fluid service date.

Drivetrain authenticity is the major value risk. SS and L79 327/350hp clones are common, and many cars are on a replacement small block. Original-ness is only partially encoded: the VIN series digits identify six-cylinder vs V8 and Nova vs SS series, the cowl/trim tag gives body and paint, and the engine pad stamp gives a date-plus-suffix code that should be plausible against the VIN build date. Have a marque specialist decode the photos before paying an SS or L79 premium.

Engines: the 230 and 194 sixes and the 283 and 327 V8s are robust, but tired examples show worn valve guides (blue smoke on startup), timing-chain stretch, rear main seal and oil pan gasket leaks, and overheating, especially in V8 cars running original-size radiators. Get compression or leak-down numbers. A small block rebuild runs $6k–12k, a six $4k–8k.

Transmissions: the Powerglide 2-speed is durable but slurs and leaks with age (rebuild $1.5k–3k). The Muncie 4-speed and 3-speed manuals pop out of gear or grind when the synchros and bushings wear (rebuild $1.5k–3.5k). Clutch linkage (Z-bar) bushings wear, causing a heavy or vague pedal.

The rear axle on these cars is a light-duty 10-bolt. A whine, clunk on take-up or a leaking pinion seal is common, and a rebuild is $1.2k–2.5k. Many have been swapped to 12-bolts or 9-inch housings, which is a deviation from factory.

The electrical harness is about 60 years old. Brittle insulation, previous-owner splices, a corroded fuse box, a weak generator/alternator and charging problems are typical. Partial repair is $300–1.5k; a reproduction harness installed runs $1.5k–3.5k. Any burned smell or melted co

profiles.market_notes: Price is driven mainly by verifiable drivetrain and trim. Documented SS sport coupes, especially factory L79 327/350hp four-speed cars, command big premiums ($80k–150k+ for proven examples), while six-cylinder or base V8 Powerglide driver-grade cars often trade at $25k–50k. Restomods like the example listing can bring $100k+, but they sit in a different market that is irrelevant to this buyer's preference for factory-correct cars. Documentation (build sheet, protect-o-plate where present, decoded trim tag/VIN/engine pad, rust repair photos), rust-free California or Southwestern history, original paint or quality respray in a factory color, and a manual transmission all add value; SS clones, filler-heavy bodies and non-matching drivetrains cut value sharply.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most examples need a full rubber-and-fluids refresh: brake hydraulics, fuel lines, hoses, bushings, weatherstrip and tires. They also typically need a front-end rebuild and carburetor and ignition sorting to be reliable drivers. Budget $3k–8k for catch-up on a nominally good car, more if rust or wiring issues surface once the carpets and undercoating come up.

profiles.label: Chevrolet Corvette (C3, 1968-1982) — Chrome/Rubber Bumper Coupe
profiles.framing: For this buyer the C3 is a weekend Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road cruiser — a cheap-to-own, easy-to-service American GT with real presence, not a numbers-matching investment. A 1973 L48 four-speed is the sweet spot of the affordable end: the last year of the chrome rear bumper, 190 net horsepower, and a chassis that is genuinely pleasant on coastal two-lanes if the bushings, steering, and brakes have been sorted. Because parts are plentiful and cheap and nearly every job is DIY-accessible, the real risk is not mechanical failure but hidden structural rot in the birdcage and frame, plus decades of accumulated bodge repairs under fiberglass and paint. Documentation, a lift inspection, and honest paint history matter far more than mileage on a five-digit, exempt-title odometer.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Birdcage rust: the steel 'birdcage' skeleton under the fiberglass — windshield surround, A-pillars, T-top header, door hinge pillars, and the area under the rear window trim — rots from water intrusion and is the single most expensive C3 failure. Symptoms are bubbling/cracking gel coat at the windshield corners, doors that sag or won't latch, T-tops that leak or won't seal. Proper repair means glass out, fiberglass cut, steel fabricated: $6,000-$20,000. Look for photos of the windshield pillar corners with trim removed and any receipts for windshield replacement (a shop that did it recently will have seen the steel). 2) Frame rot at the rear kickup over the axle and at the #4/#5 body mount area: the boxed frame traps mud and rusts from the inside. Poke it. Weld-in repair sections are $150 each but installation is $2,500-$6,000; a rotted rear kickup is a car-killer at this price point. 3) Body mount bushings: 8 rubber-and-steel mounts that crush and rot, causing door gaps to close up, cowl shake, and squeaks. Kit is ~$200, labor 8-12 hours ($1,200-$2,000) because the bolts and cages almost always fight you. 4) T-top and rear window leaks: original weatherstripping is 40+ years old; water goes straight into the birdcage and the rear compartment. Wet carpet or a musty smell is a red flag, not a detail item. Full seal kit $400-$800 plus fitting. 5) Rear suspension: the trailing arm bearings (tapered rollers on a spindle) fail from age and lack of grease, causing rear wheel wobble and uneven tire wear; rebuilt arms with shims are $700-$1,200 a pair installed. The transverse leaf spring bushings, strut rod bushings, and half-shaft U-joints are all wear items — a full rear rebuild runs $2,000-$3,500. 6) Steering: worn steering box, idler arm, and rag joint give the classic C3 'vagueness' and clunk; a quick-ratio box rebuild plus linkage is $800-$1,500. Power steering control valve and slave cylinder leak onto the crossmember — very common and messy. 7) Brakes: the four-wheel disc system's calipers were originally riveted and prone to piston seizing and internal leakage; unsleeved rebuilt calipers will fail again. Stainless-sleeved calipers plus hoses, rotors, and a master cylinder are $1,200-$2,200. Check for a brake pedal that slowly sinks or a rear that drags. 8) Fuel system and vapor: original steel tanks rot; the 1973-era emissions plumbing, EGR, and vapor canister are usually deleted or non-functional. A leaking Quadrajet base (warped throttle body, cracked fuel inlet) is nearly universal — a proper rebuild by a Q-jet specialist is $500-$800. 9) Engine: the 350 L48 is durable but at 50+ years expect rear main and oil pan gasket seepage, intake manifold end-seal leaks, a tired timing chain (nylon-toothed factory gears strip — listen for retard/rattle), and worn valve guides showing as startup smoke. A refresh-in-car (timing set, gaskets, seals) is $1,500-$2,500; a full rebuild $6,000-$9,000. Original camshafts are mild; many cars have been re-cammed. 10) Cooling: these run hot with the small radiator opening, especially non-A/C cars with a clutch fan. Verify a correct shroud, a working fan clutch, and no boil-over in traffic. Aluminum radiator conversion $500-$900. 11) Wiring and grounds: 50-year-old harness, headlight vacuum system, and wiper-door vacuum actuators. Pop-up headlights that are slow, uneven, or stuck are a vacuum-leak diagnosis job; hardware/actuator kits $300-$600. Dash gauges, tach drive, and clocks (the listing's clock is dead — normal) are commonly non-functional. 12) Transmission/driveline: the Muncie/Saginaw four-speed is stout but second-gear synchro wear and pop-out are common; rebuild $1,500-$2,500. Check for a correctly working clutch cross-shaft with fresh bushings — worn ones make the clutch heavy and vague. 13) Fiberglass repair history: check under the car and inside wheel wells for filler, mismatched bonding strips, and pressed-in repairs from prior collisions. 1973-era 'pressed' body panels shrin
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (engine, trans, diff — the diff is chronically neglected); new brake hoses, fluid flush, and inspection/likely replacement of at least one seized caliper; tires (most C3s wear old date-coded rubber even with tread — the Cooper Cobras here should be date-checked and probably replaced, ~$700); T-top and windshield/rear-window seal refresh to stop birdcage water intrusion; carburetor tuning and timing set correctly for modern fuel; wheel alignment plus tightening of front end/steering linkage; exhaust leak repair (the black soot above the exhaust noted in the listing usually means a leaking manifold or header collector); battery/charging and ground-strap cleanup; seat belt and lighting function check for CA registration.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Body mount bushing replacement if any are crushed; rear trailing arm bearing service and half-shaft U-joints; steering box, idler arm, and rag joint refresh to remove play; power steering control valve/slave cylinder reseal; radiator and cooling system upgrade or recore for California summer traffic; rear main and oil pan gasket attention if seepage is more than a film; likely Q-jet rebuild or replacement if not recently done; interior odds — door hinge pin/bushing kit (doors sag), window regulators, dash gauge or wiper-door vacuum repairs; possible clutch and rear main done together.
profiles.market_notes: Chrome-bumper cars (1968-1972) and big-block/LT-1/L82 cars carry big premiums; the 1973 is a hybrid year (body-color front, chrome rear) and sits at the low end with 1974-1982 rubber-bumper cars. Manual transmission adds roughly 15-25% over an automatic, matching-numbers and documented low mileage adds more, and correct original color plus a period-correct interior matters — a repaint away from the trim-tag color (Blue Green to red here) suppresses value. Sub-$25k buys a driver-quality L48 four-speed; $30k-$45k buys a documented, correct-color, records-rich example; body/frame rot or a bad repaint history takes 30-40% off. Rally wheels, Positraction, tilt-tele column, A/C, and side pipes are positive; T-tops are standard on coupes and a leaking set is a discount.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 50-year-old car has had deferred rubber-and-seal work regardless of cosmetic presentation: budget the first season for all four brake corners, tires by date code, body mounts, T-top and glass seals, and a full front-end/steering refresh. Recent receipts for fuel system and ignition (as here) are welcome but address the easy end; the expensive, unglamorous items are structural steel, suspension bushings, and water sealing.

profiles.label: Chevrolet Corvette Convertible (C5, 1998–2004)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the C5 convertible is an open-top LS1 V8 driver for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laguna Seca weekends. It has a simple, durable pushrod V8, a transaxle layout that gives good balance, and parts that are cheap and plentiful. The engine is rarely the problem. The money goes to electrical and module gremlins, the torque-tube and transaxle driveline, aging F45 dampers, and convertible-top sealing. A documented, unmodified 6-speed that passes California smog cleanly, with the known C5 failure points already addressed on paper, is worth a meaningful premium over a cheaper car with a modified, undocumented history.
profiles.weak_points: ["Electronic Steering Column Lock (ESCL), most common on 1997–2001: the column lock motor or sensor fails. Symptoms are a 'SERVICE COLUMN LOCK' DIC message, a no-start, or a car stranded with the wheel locked. GM addressed this with a campaign (later recall/special coverage), so run the VIN for open recall status and look for receipts showing the GM update or a replacement column lock. Typical cost is $300–900 for a part plus labor. Aftermarket bypass modules (~$100–200) are common and functional, but they are a modification you should know about.", 'Harmonic balancer wobble or separation, especially on 1997–2001 LS1s: the elastomer ring delaminates, causing belt walk, chirp, a wobbling outer ring, and eventually a thrown belt that takes out the water pump and alternator drive. Repair runs $300–700 with an OEM or quality balancer and requires the proper crank bolt. Ask for the receipt and the brand, and confirm the new crank bolt was torqued correctly. The example car documents this repair, which is a plus.', 'Fuel level sending units in the dual saddle tanks fail. Symptoms are a gauge reading erratically, stuck full or empty, or a sudden drop. This was worsened by high-sulfur fuel in the early-to-mid 2000s and GM extended coverage at the time. Replacing one or both senders costs about $500–1,400 because the tanks must be accessed. Verify the gauge tracks properly through a fill-up.', "EBCM (ABS/Active Handling module) failure: 'SERVICE ACTIVE HANDLING', 'SERVICE ABS' and 'SERVICE TRACTION CONTROL' messages, often intermittent at first. A mail-in rebuild costs about $200–450; a new unit plus programming costs considerably more. Scan the ABS module for stored codes rather than trusting a dark dash.", 'Clutch and torque-tube driveline (6-speed): clutch replacement requires dropping the torque tube and transaxle, so expect $1,800–2,800 at an independent shop. Torque-tube coupler and bushing wear causes clunks on and off throttle and driveline rattle at idle. The clutch slave cylinder and hydraulics leak or soften, and some cars have the known clutch-pedal-hang-at-high-rpm issue. Ask for any clutch receipts and when the work was done.', 'Rear transaxle and limited-slip differential: output shaft and side seals weep, and the LSD clutches chatter in tight turns if the fluid or GM limited-slip additive is neglected. A full transaxle or differential rebuild is a $2,500–4,500 low-frequency risk. Look for documentation of a differential fluid change with GM friction modifier and inspect for gear oil on the axle shaft area.', "F45 Selective Real Time Damping (the 'continuously variable adaptive dampers' option): the electronic shocks leak or fail and are expensive or scarce. New or remanufactured units cost $300–650 each, and a full set with labor runs about $1,500–2,500. Many owners convert to passive shocks, which disables the system and sets a code or warning. Check for leaking shock bodies and a 'SERVICE RIDE CONTROL' message.", "Convertible top and body sealing: the manual top's fabric shrinks or tears, rear window seals and bows age, and windshield-header and door glass weatherstrips harden. Water then enters the footwells and behind the seats, where it can corrode connectors and the window/valet circuits. Carmel fog and UV accelerate mildew and fabric wear. Top replacement costs about $1,200–2,500 installed. Check the carpet padding for dampness and the latch operation, and look for the window-drop (window valet) function working on door open.", "Interior electrics: sport seat bolster bladders and their pump fail (seat bladders 'do not inflate' is classic). Headlight motor gears strip, giving a winking or stuck headlamp, fixed with a $20–60 gear kit or $150–350 motor. Window motors and regulators fail, as do door handle microswitches. Gauge cluster LCD, DIC and HVAC displays fade or lose pixels; cluster repair runs about $150–450.", 'LS1 engine habits: some 1999–2001 LS1s consume oil (up to about 1 qt per 1,500–2,000 mi is tolerat
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil, brake and clutch hydraulic fluid flush (they share a reservoir), transaxle fluid, and differential fluid with GM limited-slip additive.', 'Coolant drain and refill with fresh DEX-COOL if the service date is unknown.', 'Replace tires if they are more than 6 years old by DOT code, and carry a plug/inflator kit since there is no spare.', 'Load-test the battery and inspect the battery tray and terminals for corrosion.', 'Verify steering column lock status and address it if it is not documented as updated or replaced.', 'Clean and treat the convertible top and weatherstrips, and clear the drains; dry out and fix the source of any damp carpet.', 'Inspect the drive belt, tensioner, and idler pulleys, and confirm the harmonic balancer is not wobbling.', 'Read the
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Water pump, idler and tensioner pulley replacement if weeping or noisy.', 'Spark plugs and plug wires if the service history is unknown or the wires show heat damage.', 'Front and rear suspension bushings, ball joints, tie-rod ends, and a four-wheel alignment.', 'F45 shock replacement or rebuild if damping is weak or a shock is leaking.', 'Clutch slave cylinder and hydraulic refresh, or clutch replacement if engagement is high or slipping.', 'Fuel level sender replacement if the gauge is erratic.', 'Sport seat bladder pump or bladder repair.', 'Gauge cluster or HVAC display repair if pixels are fading.', 'Convertible top fabric or rear window seal replacement if leaking or shrunken.', 'Knock sensor replacement if codes recur.', 'Fuel filter and air filter replacement.']
profiles.market_notes: Manual 6-speed convertibles command a clear premium over the much more common 4L60E automatics. Clean, documented sub-50k-mile examples trade roughly in the high-teens to mid-$20k range, while average 70–120k-mile cars sit lower. Later 2001–2004 cars, with 350 hp, revised electronics and fewer column-lock issues, bring more, as do the 2003 50th Anniversary and 2004 Commemorative Edition convertibles, Z51 or F45 option cars, and desirable colors like Torch Red, Millennium Yellow and Magnetic Red. Aftermarket audio, shifters, exhaust and LED lighting rarely add value and can deter buyers who want stock cars. A stack of receipts showing the column lock, balancer, EBCM and top issues resolved, plus a clean California smog history, moves price more than cosmetic perfection.
profiles.catchup_notes: Any C5 is now 20–27 years old, so plan on rubber and wear items regardless of mileage: tires, hoses, belts and pulleys, suspension bushings, weatherstrips, top fabric, and all fluids including DEX-COOL. Low-mileage cars that sat often need tires, fuel senders, TPMS sensors, seat bladders, and a hydraulic clutch refresh before they are reliable drivers. Budget $1,500–3,500 for catch-up beyond the purchase price.

profiles.label: Chevrolet Corvette Stingray & Grand Sport (C7, LT1, 2014–2019)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, the LT1 C7 is a usable, comfortable 460-hp grand-touring sports car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the occasional Laguna Seca spectator weekend. It is not a garage queen, and its running costs are reasonable for the performance. The priorities are an unmodified, unboosted engine and driveline; original wheels free of cracks or bends; and a clean, documented fluid history. Z51 dry-sump cars especially need correct oil service, and 2015+ automatics need 8L90 fluid service. This profile covers the LT1 Stingray and Grand Sport only. The supercharged LT4 Z06 and ZR1 have distinct cooling and supercharger risks and should be evaluated separately.
profiles.weak_points: ['OEM wheel cracking and bending. This is the signature C7 problem, most common on Z51 and Grand Sport wheels (19-inch front, 20-inch rear) running low-profile run-flats. Cracks start on the inner barrel and often show up as a slow leak or a vibration at 60–75 mph. Replacement OEM wheels cost roughly $600–1,200 each. Welding or straightening a cracked wheel is not acceptable. Pothole-heavy local roads make this a live risk, so ask for inner-barrel photos of all four wheels and any wheel-repair invoices.', "8L90 eight-speed automatic (2015–2019 only). Symptoms are torque-converter shudder at light throttle between 25 and 80 mph, harsh 1-2 and 2-3 shifts, and clunks; the problem was the subject of litigation. GM's fix is a fluid exchange to Mobil 1 LV ATF HP under its service bulletins, costing $350–600. Torque converter replacement runs $2,500–4,500 and a transmission replacement $5,000–8,000. Look for a dated fluid-exchange receipt that names the fluid. The 2014 automatic is the older 6L80 six-speed, which is more robust but can still flare and shift harshly with old fluid.", '7-speed manual (TR6070) clutch hydraulics. The clutch pedal can stick to the floor or go soft in high heat or after hard driving, caused by fluid boiling or an air-contaminated hydraulic system. The fix is a pressure bleed or an updated master cylinder and line, about $300–900. A worn clutch is a $2,500–4,000 job because the torque tube and transaxle must come out. Test for slip in 6th and 7th gear at low rpm and wide-open throttle, and get records of any clutch or hydraulic work and of whether the car has been tracked or tuned.', 'LT1 AFM/DOD lifter failure. Cylinder-deactivation lifters can collapse or stick, causing a persistent tick, misfires (P0300–P0308), or a flat cylinder. The C7 is less prone to this than GM trucks with the same family of engines, but it does happen. Lifters alone cost about $2,500–3,500; with a cam wiped by lifter damage, $4,000–6,000. An AFM delete requires a tune, which counts as a modification. Normal direct-injection injector and fuel-pump ticking is not a fault. Get misfire-counter data from a scan and any engine-work invoices.', 'Z51 dry-sump oil system. The external tank must be checked hot and idling, with a specific fill and check procedure. Quick-lube shops routinely overfill or underfill these cars, which can lead to oil being pulled into the intake, smoke, or starvation under cornering loads. Look for oil changes performed by a dealer or Corvette-savvy shop using dexos-spec 5W-30, at roughly 5,000–7,500 miles or annually, with no long gaps.', 'Water pump and cooling system. LT1 water pumps commonly weep from the weep hole or gasket, typically between 50,000 and 90,000 miles or after 8–10 years, and repair costs $700–1,200. Also inspect the coolant hoses, the reservoir cap, and the Dex-Cool condition. Most original-coolant cars from 2014–2016 are overdue for a coolant flush. Look for any coolant service record and any pump replacement.', "Electronic limited-slip differential (Z51 and Grand Sport). Problems include axle and pinion seal leaks, 'Service Active Handling' and stability faults, and clutch-pack chatter in tight turns with old fluid. Fluid service costs $150–300, seals $300–800, and actuator or clutch rebuild work $1,500–3,500 or more. Ask for a dated differential fluid change record that confirms GM-spec fluid.", "Magnetic Ride Control dampers (optional on Z51, standard on Grand Sport 2LT/3LT in many builds). Dampers leak oil at the shaft or throw 'Service Suspension' codes. Replacements cost roughly $800–1,300 each installed. Non-MRC cars have conventional dampers that are much cheaper to replace. Inspect all four dampers for wet bodies.", 'Front-end vulnerability. The low front splitter, the air dam and the A/C condenser behind the grille take rock and curb damage. Bent or holed condensers cause weak A/C and cost $900–1,600 to replace. The underside of the splitter, the front crossmember and the rocker pi
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace run-flat tires if older than about 6 years or unevenly worn: $1,600–2,400 per set, plus a four-wheel alignment at $150–250.', 'Engine oil and filter, using the correct dry-sump procedure on Z51 cars and dexos-spec 5W-30, if the history is unclear: $150–250.', 'Brake fluid flush if more than 2–3 years old or unknown: $120–200.', 'Differential fluid with GM-spec lubricant, plus manual transmission fluid or 8L90 fluid exchange with Mobil 1 LV ATF HP if not documented: $250–700 combined.', "Rear battery load test, with AGM replacement if 4+ years old ($250–400), and add a battery tender for Carmel's typical low-use weeks.", 'Clean and verify the engine and cabin air filters, and confirm A/C performance and condenser condition.', 'Full-module scan, then address stored codes, TPMS sens
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Coolant flush with Dex-Cool on original-coolant cars ($180–300), and a water pump if a weep develops ($700–1,200).', 'Front and rear brake pads and rotors depending on wear: $800–1,800 for a full axle set on Z51 slotted rotors.', 'MRC damper replacement if any are weeping: $800–1,300 each.', 'Clutch hydraulic bleed or updated master cylinder and line if the pedal sticks in heat: $300–900.', 'eLSD or axle seal leaks: $300–800.', 'Exhaust valve actuator, door release switch or hatch strut replacements: $200–700 each.', 'Interior rattle chase and roof seal refresh: $200–500. Dash leather repair if shrinkage worsens: $1,500–3,000.', 'Spark plugs and coil inspection on high-mileage examples (plug interval about 97,500 miles): $350–600.', 'Refinish an exposed carbon roof or hood if the clear c
profiles.market_notes: Unmodified Z51 3LT coupes with the 7-speed manual, low mileage and full records command the top of the Stingray market, and Grand Sports (2017–2019) carry a clear premium above that. Modified, tuned or supercharged cars, cars with Carfax damage, convertibles and high-mileage automatics trade at meaningful discounts. A boosted, damage-history car at auction is often $8–15k below a clean stock equivalent, and that discount is earned. 2015–2016 8L90 automatics without fluid-exchange documentation are discounted for shudder risk. 2014 first-year cars sell slightly below 2015+ cars, which added the Performance Data Recorder and other updates, while 2019 Grand Sports and special editions sit at the top. Desirable options include Z51, MRC, NPP exhaust, front lift, Competition Sport seats and the carbon packages. Bright or uncommon colors such as Laguna Blue, Long Beach Red, Admiral Blue and Sebring Orange help modestly, and original factory wheels on the car matter.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2014–2016 C7 is now 9–12 years old and often still has its original coolant, brake fluid, differential and transmission fluid. Many also carry aged run-flat tires, a tired rear battery and weeping seals. Budget roughly $1,500–3,000 in fluids, battery, tires and alignment to reset the baseline, even on low-mileage cars that have mostly sat.

profiles.label: Chevrolet SS (Holden VF Commodore-based, 2014–2017)
profiles.framing: The SS is a low-volume, Australian-built, rear-drive V8 family sedan (about 12,900 US units). For a Carmel buyer it is a comfortable, roomy daily driver with real performance and a mostly proven GM drivetrain, not an investment piece. What matters most is a stock, untuned LS3 that will pass California smog, a healthy 6L80 automatic or TR6060 manual, a quiet rear differential and bushings, and evidence that it was not launched hard or drifted. A 2014 was automatic-only and had no Magnetic Ride. An automatic on a 2014 is factory-correct, not a compromise, even though manual 2015–2017 cars are the enthusiast pick.
profiles.weak_points: 1) 6L80E automatic: torque converter clutch shudder at light throttle between 25 and 50 mph, usually from 40k–90k miles. A fluid exchange with current-spec Dexron VI sometimes fixes it. If it persists, a converter replacement runs about $1,500–2,800. The bigger risk is failure of the 3-5-R clutch pack or the valve body / internal TEHCM module. Symptoms are flare on the 2-3 or 3-4 shift, harsh engagement, or loss of reverse or 3rd–5th gears. A rebuild or reman unit costs about $3,500–6,000 installed. GM calls the fluid 'lifetime,' so look for a documented fluid exchange by roughly 60k and check for weeping cooler lines at the radiator. 2) Rear differential and cradle bushings: the clutch-type limited-slip diff needs fluid with friction modifier. Neglect shows up as chatter or groan in tight parking-lot turns. Hard launches wear the diff and rear cradle bushings and cause wheel hop, a clunk on throttle on/off, and drivetrain slack. Bushings run about $600–1,300 installed and a diff rebuild about $1,800–3,200. Pinion seal leaks are also common. Look for a diff fluid change with LS additive (this listing shows one at 62.8k). 3) Front tension rod (caster arm) bushings, the hydraulic 'radius rod' bushings shared with the VE/VF Commodore. They crack and leak from about 40k–80k, causing a clunk over bumps, shimmy or vibration under braking, and vague steering. Expect $400–900 per pair installed. Strut top mounts and lower ball joints wear in the same window. 4) Magnetic Ride Control dampers (2015–2017): they leak or throw suspension fault messages with age. OE dampers cost about $700–1,200 each plus labor, and cheaper non-MRC conversions trigger warnings. 2014 cars use conventional FE3 dampers, which are far cheaper to replace. 5) LS3 valvetrain: the SS LS3 has no cylinder deactivation (AFM), so lifter collapse is less common than on AFM GM V8s. Lifter or rocker trunnion wear, ticking, and cam lobe damage still occur on high-mileage or hard-revved cars. Lifters, guides and gaskets run about $2,500–4,500, more if the cam is damaged. Listen for a persistent tick when warm and look for misfire codes. 6) LS exhaust manifold bolts break or loosen, causing a cold-start tick that fades as the engine warms. Repair costs about $400–1,200 depending on extraction. 7) LS3 water pump weeps from about 80k–120k (check for dried coolant at the pump weep hole and the front of the engine), about $500–900. Ignition coils, plugs and O2 sensors are typical 60k–100k items, about $300–900. 8) Sunroof drains clog, leaving headliner stains near the A-pillar and water in the footwells. Water can reach under-carpet wiring and modules. Clearing the drains is cheap; electrical corrosion and mold are not. This example has a documented leak and headliner stain. 9) Brembo front brakes: big rotors and pads cost about $700–1,100 per axle with quality parts. Pedal vibration from uneven pad deposits or thin rotors is common. 10) Staggered 19-inch performance tires (245/40 front, 275/35 rear) wear fast on a 4,000-lb V8 sedan, about $1,200–1,800 per set. Rear wear patterns reveal burnouts and alignment issues. 11) Electrical and infotainment: the MyLink touchscreen can become unresponsive or ghost-touch, and HUD or Bose amp faults occur. Starters fail at around 70k–90k, about $400–700. Weak batteries cause odd body-control faults. 12) Modification culture: many SS sedans have been tuned or fitted with headers, cams, catless exhaust or cold-air intakes. A flashed PCM, a missing cat, or a non-CARB-approved part means a failed California smog test and possible abuse. A converter swap or drag launches multiply transmission and diff risk. 13) Run the VIN through NHTSA/GM for open recalls. Australian-sourced body and trim parts can be slow or expensive (headlights, fascias, Holden-specific trim), which matters for any collision-repaired car.
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline if undocumented: engine oil (dexos, 5W-30), 6L80 fluid exchange, rear diff fluid with LS friction modifier, brake fluid flush (and clutch fluid on manuals), coolant check or replacement', 'Clear the sunroof drains, then dry and inspect under the carpets and headliner for moisture or mildew (mandatory on this example)', 'Replace the front tension rod bushings and/or strut mounts if there is a clunk or shimmy under braking', 'Replace tires if mismatched, aged over 6 years, or showing burnout wear; four-wheel alignment', "Remove front side window tint to meet California's 70% VLT rule; fix minor trim like the broken sun visor hinge", 'Battery and charging system test; engine and cabin air filters; wiper blades', 'Complete California registration and smog: confirm stock c
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['LS3 water pump and thermostat if weeping (common past 80k)', 'Front Brembo pads and rotors as wear dictates', 'Rear cradle and diff bushings if clunk or wheel hop is present', 'Magnetic Ride dampers on 2015–2017 cars if leaking or throwing faults; conventional dampers and struts on 2014 cars past 80k–100k', 'Plugs and coils around 90k–100k if not already done; PCV and valve cover gasket seepage', 'Engine and transmission mounts on high-mileage cars', 'A/C service or condenser if cooling is weak', 'Exhaust manifold bolt repair if a cold-start tick develops']
profiles.market_notes: Transmission is the biggest price driver: 2015–2017 TR6060 manuals carry a clear premium, and low-mile manuals are priced as near-collectibles. 2016–2017 cars bring more for the refreshed fascia, standard bimodal exhaust and Magnetic Ride. Mileage bands matter sharply: under 30k, 30k–70k, and 70k-plus driver-grade cars like this 83k 2014 automatic, which trades well below the low-mile tier. Stock, documented, unmodified cars in less common colors bring more than tuned cars or common silver, black and white. Visible tunes, headers, or heavy mods often reduce value to a California buyer because of smog compliance.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 70k–90k SS has never had a transmission fluid exchange and is due for front tension rod bushings, a water pump, plugs and coils, and tires. Budget $1,500–3,000 for that baseline on top of the purchase price. Out-of-state cars also need California smog prep and tint correction. Hard-launched or tuned cars can add rear bushings, a diff rebuild, or transmission work.

profiles.label: Chevrolet Tahoe (GMT900, 2007–2014)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the GMT900 Tahoe is a durable, body-on-frame utility vehicle. Its jobs are towing, hauling family and gear, and covering Highway 1 or the Sierra in comfort. Value comes from a healthy 5.3L V8 (ideally with lifter and oil-consumption history), a sound transmission, a dry and rust-free underbody, and a clean California smog path. A documented, stock LT 4x4 from a dry state is the sweet spot. Modified powertrains create real registration risk in California and should be discounted heavily.
profiles.weak_points: ['Active Fuel Management (AFM/DoD) lifter failure on the 5.3L (LMG/LC9/LH6) and 6.2L (L9H). A collapsed or stuck AFM lifter, usually on cylinders 1, 7, 4 or 6, causes a ticking or knocking tick, a misfire code (P0300/P0301/P0307 etc.) and a bent pushrod. Lobe wipe is possible. Most common from 90k–160k miles, and worse with long oil-change intervals. Repair ranges from $2,500 to $4,500 for cam, lifters, guides and gaskets, or $3,000–$5,500 as a full AFM delete with tune. A delete needs a CARB-legal calibration question answered in California. Look for receipts naming lifters, a camshaft or AFM, plus consistent 5k-mile oil changes.', 'Oil consumption tied to AFM. The AFM pressure-relief valve in the oil pan sprays oil onto the cylinder walls, and the rings stick. The PCV/valve-cover design adds to it. Symptoms are a quart per 1,000–2,500 miles, oil-fouled plugs (often cylinders 1, 7 and 8), and blue smoke on startup. Remedies range from a $150–$400 valve-cover/PCV fix or baffle, to a ring job at $3,000+, to replacement catalytic converters ($1,200–$2,500 per side, which California requires to be CARB-compliant). Ask about consumption and look at the plugs.', 'Transmission depends on year. 2007–2008 5.3L trucks mostly used the 4L60E. It has a weak 3-4 clutch pack, sun shell and servo, with slipping or flare on the 2-3/3-4 shift and loss of 3rd/4th. A rebuild runs $2,800–$4,000. 2009+ (and 6.2L) trucks use the 6L80E. It is stronger, but known for torque-converter clutch shudder (feels like rumble strips at 35–55 mph), harsh 1-2 or 3-4 shifts, valve body/TEHCM (internal control module) faults and pump bushing wear. Costs run $1,200–$2,500 for a converter, $800–$1,500 for a valve body/TEHCM, and $3,500–$5,500 for a rebuild. Look for fluid-change receipts (Dexron VI) every 50k miles.', "Transfer case. The front-axle actuator and transfer-case encoder motor fail and trigger a 'Service 4WD' message, a flashing 4WD switch, or failure to engage 4LO. Costs are $350–$900. The NV246 AutoTrac (AUTO 4WD) clutch pack can shudder in turns if the fluid is old. Ask for proof of transfer-case fluid service (AutoTrak II) every 50k miles.", "Broken exhaust manifold bolts on the 5.3L and 6.2L, usually the rear driver-side or front passenger-side bolts. This causes a cold-start tick that fades as the engine warms. It is often misdiagnosed as a lifter problem. Repair is $400–$1,200 per side, depending on broken-stud extraction. Note that this listing's long-tube headers replace the factory manifolds, which removes this failure point but creates a California legality problem.", 'Cracked dashboard top pad. Nearly universal on sun-exposed GMT900s, with cracks around the defrost vents and passenger airbag seam. A cap overlay costs $150–$300. A correct dash pad replacement runs $800–$1,500 installed. Not mechanical, but it signals UV exposure and affects resale. Get photos of the full dash top in daylight.', 'Corrosion of brake lines, fuel lines and rear auxiliary A/C lines along the frame rails and over the rear axle. This is a federal-investigation-level brake-line issue on GM trucks of this era. Steel lines rust through and cause sudden pedal loss. The long rear A/C lines leak refrigerant. Repairs run $800–$1,800 for brake lines, $500–$1,200 for fuel lines, and $600–$1,200 for rear A/C lines. This is less common on Texas and California cars, but the example listing discloses underbody corrosion, so get detailed underbody photos.', 'Cooling system. Water pump weep at the gasket and bearing, and plastic radiator end-tank cracks, are common from 90k–140k miles. Costs are $600–$1,000 for a water pump and $500–$900 for a radiator. Overheating on a high-mileage AFM engine risks the head gaskets. Look for coolant service records and pink Dex-Cool crust at the pump weep hole.', 'Oil pressure sensor and its screen in the valley under the intake area. It fails and gives an erratic or zero gauge reading. It is cheap to fix ($150–$350), but a low reading also worse
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline if records are missing: engine oil (dexos 5W-30), transmission fluid and filter (Dexron VI, partial drain), transfer case fluid (AutoTrak II), front and rear differential fluid, brake fluid flush ($600–$1,100 total)', 'Spark plugs and inspection of the coil boots and wires; read the plugs for oil fouling to gauge AFM oil consumption ($250–$450)', 'Engine air filter, cabin filter, serpentine belt and tensioner/idler pulleys if original or noisy ($150–$350)', 'Address any active codes (misfire, EVAP, 4WD service) and verify the smog-readiness monitors before the California registration deadline', 'Underbody inspection with cleaning and treatment of brake and fuel line surface rust; replace any pitted line sections ($200–$1,500)', 'Tires and alignment if mismatched or ol
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Water pump and/or radiator replacement on a 100k+ mile truck without records ($600–$1,600)', 'Front hub bearings, control-arm bushings, ball joints or intermediate shaft as wear appears ($400–$1,500)', 'Exhaust manifold bolt repair if a cold tick develops ($400–$1,200 per side)', "Transfer case encoder motor or front-axle actuator if 'Service 4WD' appears ($350–$900)", 'HVAC blend door actuator(s) and possibly a rear A/C line repair or recharge ($200–$1,200)', 'Rear shocks, or Autoride shock replacement or conversion on LTZ ($300–$1,800)', 'Possible torque-converter or valve-body work on the 6L80 if shudder or harsh shifts emerge ($800–$2,500)', 'Battery, alternator or starter replacement on an original-electrical truck ($200–$700)']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven mostly by mileage band (sub-100k commands a clear premium, and 150k+ is commodity pricing), 4WD versus 2WD, and condition of the dash, leather and underbody. LTZ adds a premium for the 6.2L, Autoride, 20-inch wheels and navigation. LT with the Z71, Heavy Duty Trailering or Convenience packages sits in the middle. 2007–2008 trucks with the 4L60E trade at a discount to 2009+ 6L80 trucks, and 2013–2014 models are the most sought after. Documented AFM lifter or cam replacement and transmission service are a positive. Supercharged or long-tube-equipped trucks are worth less to a California buyer because they may not pass smog without CARB EO parts, and a rust-free dry-state truck commands a premium over one from the Midwest or Northeast.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10–15-year-old GMT900 at 100k+ miles is overdue for transfer case, differential, transmission and brake fluid service. It is also often due for a water pump or radiator and front hubs or suspension bushings. Out-of-state examples need a careful underbody line inspection and a California smog-readiness check before purchase. Aftermarket intake, header or tune changes may need to be reversed to stock before the truck will pass.

profiles.label: Classic Roadsters Cobra Replica (owner-assembled fiberglass kit, Ford V8)
profiles.framing: This is an owner-assembled fiberglass Cobra kit from a second-tier maker, typically built on a steel ladder or tube frame with Ford donor or aftermarket running gear. It is a loud, hot, raw weekend car for Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not an appreciating collectible. Each car is effectively a one-off, so the builder's workmanship matters more than the badge. For a Carmel buyer, the deciding issue is usually whether the car can be legally registered and smogged in California. That gate comes before any mechanical question. The next priorities are documentation of the build, chassis integrity, and safety-critical assembly quality: steering, brakes, fuel, and wiring.
profiles.weak_points: ["CALIFORNIA REGISTRATION AND SMOG: This is the single largest risk. A replica titled with a post-1975 model year (e.g., '1998') is not automatically smog-exempt in CA. On transfer it goes to a BAR referee as a Specially Constructed Vehicle. Without an SB100 sequence number, it is generally held to the emissions standards of the engine's model year or the year of assembly. A carbureted crate 351W with side pipes and no cats, EGR or evap system will rarely pass late-1990s standards. SB100 certificates let the car be evaluated against the far looser standards of the year it resembles. They are limited to 500 per year and are not guaranteed. Budget roughly $300–1,000 for referee visits, brake-and-lamp, weight certificate and VIN verification. In the worst case the car cannot be registered at all. Side-exit exhaust may also exceed CA's 95 dB(A) limit (SAE J1492) at the referee.", "REBUILT/SALVAGE TITLE HISTORY: A branded title on a kit car may reflect real crash damage, or it may be a state-assigned-VIN paperwork quirk. Many states brand self-assembled vehicles 'rebuilt' or 'reconstructed.' You must learn which it is. Crash damage on a fiberglass body over a steel frame can hide bent frame rails or cracked suspension mounts under fresh gelcoat. CA also requires additional inspection for revived salvage. Frame straightening or section replacement runs $2,000–8,000+.", "CHASSIS AND WELD QUALITY: The frame is mild steel and of variable fabrication quality. Check for cracked or porous welds at the front suspension pickups, 4-link or 3-link rear brackets, engine mounts and roll-hoop mounts. Check for surface rust where the body sits on the frame and where moisture is trapped under carpet. Carmel's coastal fog and salt air accelerate this. Minor weld repair runs $300–1,500. Structural rework runs $3,000+.", 'FIBERGLASS BODY: Spider and stress cracks are common around door hinges and latches, hood and trunk corners, roll-bar penetrations, side-pipe cutouts and the front valance. Gelcoat crazing and print-through are normal at 20+ years. Proper glass and paint repair costs $800–2,500 per panel area. A full repaint costs $8,000–15,000. Uneven panel gaps or fresh paint in one area suggest collision repair.', 'ELECTRICAL AND WIRING: The harness is builder-installed, usually an aftermarket kit, with variable quality. Look for chafed wires passing through fiberglass, poor or missing grounds (fiberglass is not a ground path), undersized wire, missing fuses or relays on fans and lights, and added accessories tapped in (here a stereo head unit and Bluetooth soundbar). Intermittent gauges, fans not triggering, and dim lights are early signs. A professional rewire runs $1,500–4,000. Electrical fire is the real downside.', 'COOLING AND COCKPIT HEAT: Cobras have a small grille mouth, a tight engine bay, and a side-pipe heat soak problem. Overheating in traffic is a classic complaint. Watch for a temperature climb at idle, a missing or poorly fitted fan shroud, an undersized radiator, and a manual fan switch in place of a thermostatic relay. An aluminum radiator, shroud and quality fan run $700–1,500 installed. Floor and tunnel heat insulation runs $300–800. The side pipes will burn calves on entry and exit.', 'FUEL SYSTEM: Look for an aluminum tank or fuel cell with weeping seams or sender gaskets. Rubber lines from circa 2000 will be hard or cracked by now. Check line routing near exhaust or headers, and look for missing rollover or vent valves. Holley or Edelbrock carbs gum up from storage and ethanol fuel. A raw fuel smell is a red flag. Lines, filter and a carb rebuild run $400–1,200. A tank repair or replacement runs $600–1,500.', 'ENGINE (typically Ford 289/302/351 Windsor crate or rebuild): Low miles since the build often mean long storage. Flat-tappet cams can suffer lobe wear if run on low-ZDDP modern oil. Watch for intake gasket and rear main seal leaks, timing chain stretch, and header gasket and bolt leaks, which are very common with side

Plan a clutch if slipping.', 'Replace rear axle and pinion seals, and service the LSD clutch pack if chattering or ineffective.', 'Clean up wiring: proper grounds, fused accessory circuits, and chafe protection through fiberglass.', 'Upgrade cooling (aluminum radiator, shroud, higher-CFM fan) if the car runs hot in traffic.', 'Add heat and sound insulation to floor and tunnel. Add side-pipe heat shields.', 'Address minor fiberglass stress cracks before they propagate.', 'Refresh or replace soft top and tonneau snaps and fasteners.']
profiles.market_notes:
["Cobra replica values are driven mainly by the builder's reputation. Top-tier makers (Superformance, Kirkham, ERA, Factory Five) bring roughly $40k–150k. Older second-tier kits like Classic Roadsters typically trade in the high teens to low $30ks.", 'Within a tier, the main value drivers are:
- Build quality and photo- or receipt-documented assembly.
- Engine: a big-block FE or 427 brings more than a small-block 289/302/351W.
- Transmission: a TKO brings more than a T5.
- Brakes and suspension upgrades.', 'Title status is a major swing factor. A rebuilt or salvage brand typically discounts 20–40%. A car already registered in California with a smog-exempt or SB100 status commands a real premium, because CA registration of out-of-state replicas is uncertain.', 'Odometer miles mean little on these. Build date, storage conditions and evidence of shakedown sorting matter far more.']
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical example was built around 2000 and has covered very few miles since, so age, not mileage, drives the work list. Expect to replace tires, fuel lines, cooling hoses, all fluids and possibly coilover seals in the first season. Separately budget $500–1,500 and real time for California referee, smog and noise compliance, with the risk that the car cannot be registered at all.
