profiles.label: Factory Five Racing Mk4 Roadster (Cobra replica kit, all builds)
profiles.framing: This is a home-built or shop-built fiberglass Cobra replica on a Factory Five tube-frame chassis. The builder's skill matters far more than the model year or the odometer. For a Carmel driver it is a fair-weather canyon car with no top, no airbags and real cockpit heat. The questions that decide whether it is a joy or a project are build quality, verifiable documentation, and California registration status. 'Documented and unmodified' translates here to: a known builder, a build log, receipts for every major component, and a car still close to its as-built specification.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Builder quality is the number-one failure point. Look for wiring with poor grounds, unprotected harness runs near headers, insulation-piercing splice connectors, missing fuses or relays, and fuel lines chafing on frame tubes. Ask who built it: factory/FFR-referred pro builder, independent shop, or first-time home builder. Get the build log, photos taken during assembly, and the chassis number with MSO/title. Fixing a sloppy build can run $3k–$15k+. 2) Engine-bay cooling, especially with a supercharged Coyote packed into a bay designed around a small-block. Watch for heat soak, climbing coolant temps in traffic, an undersized radiator or fan, poorly bled systems that air-lock, and supercharger intercooler pump or heat-exchanger failures. Expect $1.5k–$4k for a radiator, dual fans, shroud and intercooler pump upgrade. 3) Transmission mismatch, which is critical on a '5-speed' supercharged Coyote. A Borg-Warner/Tremec T-5 cannot survive 500–700+ lb-ft. Confirm it is a TKO-500/600, TKO-600 RR or TR-3550 and not a T-5. A TKO swap with bellhousing, input-shaft spacer and shifter is $5k–$8k. Also check driveline angles: wrong pinion or transmission angles cause vibration and U-joint wear. 4) Coyote engine items, Gen1 2011–2014 and Gen2/3 2015+. Gen1 has cam-phaser and VCT tick. Some Gen2/3 engines show oil consumption. Check the Ford Performance Control Pack or standalone ECU (Holley Terminator, etc.) for the tune file, and confirm the supercharger is matched to injector size, fuel pump and tune. Fuel-system mismatches lean out cylinders, and engine replacement is $8k–$15k. 5) Fuel system. Coyote builds need a return or regulated returnless high-flow pump. Look for fuel-tank vent and charcoal-canister issues, raw-fuel smell in the trunk or cockpit, and pinched filler necks. Pump and line corrections run $800–$2.5k. 6) Cockpit and footbox heat from side pipes and headers. Look for missing or poor heat shielding (DEI, Lizard Skin) and burned shins from side pipes. Shielding and insulation runs $500–$2k. 7) Rear suspension, which comes in three types. a) The early 4-link solid axle can bind. b) For the 3-link plus Panhard bar, check bushings and Panhard mount welds. c) For IRS cars, check the 8.8 center section mounts, CV/axle boots and toe links. Bushing or mount repairs run $500–$2.5k, and IRS center-section work runs $2k–$4k. 8) Front suspension and steering. Some kits used 1987–2004 Mustang donor spindles. Problems include bump steer from rack height, worn tie-rod ends, Coyote headers clearing the steering shaft, and manual-rack effort. An alignment and corner-weight sheet should exist. Steering corrections run $400–$1.5k. 9) Brakes. Look for a mismatched master cylinder and calipers, no adjustable proportioning valve, a soft pedal from poor bleeding, and old flex lines on older builds. Expect $500–$2k. 10) Fiberglass body and paint. Check for stress cracks and spider-webbing at door hinges, hood corners, trunk hinge points and roll-bar penetrations. Also look for gelcoat crazing, panel gaps, and stripes or clear coat that are peeling or yellowing. Spot repair costs $1k–$5k, and a respray is $10k–$20k+. 11) Chassis, roll bar and body mounting. Inspect welds at the roll-bar base and suspension pickup points, aluminum panel rivets working loose, and body-mount rubbing. Look for corrosion where powder coat has chipped. 12) Clutch hydraulics on Coyote/TKO builds. Hydraulic throwout bearings leak and are a transmission-out job, $1.2k–$2.5k. On mechanical builds, check pedal-box geometry. 13) Wheels and tires. Spinner or knock-off-style wheels must be torqued and safety-wired or clipped correctly. Many low-mile kits sit on 8–15-year-old tires that look fine but are hard and dangerous. Tires run $1k–$1.8k. 14) California registration status. A kit car without a California SB100/SPCNS title and referee label, or with an engine and supercharger combo lacking CARB compliance, may be very difficult or impossible to register in California. O

profiles.market_notes: Price is driven mainly by builder reputation, drivetrain and paint quality, not mileage or year. Coyote 5.0 (supercharged carries a premium) and well-sorted 302/347/427W builds lead the market, with LS builds slightly behind. A TKO-600 or similar transmission is expected, and a T-5 behind big power is a discount. IRS and later 3-link chassis bring more than early 4-link cars. Show-quality paint with classic stripe combinations (Guardsman Blue/white, black/silver) adds value, and a full build log with receipts adds a lot. In California, a clean SB100/SPCNS title can be worth thousands over an out-of-state-only title. Typical driver-quality builds trade at roughly $35k–$60k, and pro-built supercharged Coyote cars $65k–$90k+.
profiles.catchup_notes: Kit cars often have low miles but long sit times. Expect aged tires, dried brake fluid, stale fuel effects, and hardened rubber in hoses and bushings even on a 'fresh' build. Budget for a thorough shakedown that re-torques every fastener and sorts the builder's loose ends (wiring, heat, cooling) before treating the car as a reliable driver.

profiles.label: Ferrari 360 (Modena, Spider & Challenge Stradale, 1999-2005)
profiles.framing: The 360 is the first modern, usable mid-engine V8 Ferrari. It has an aluminum spaceframe and a belt-driven 3.6L F131 V8, and the timing belts can be serviced without dropping the engine. For a Carmel driver it makes a great Highway 1 and Carmel Valley car, but it only stays affordable if the big-ticket wear items are documented: timing belts, F1 clutch, F1 pump, cam variators and exhaust manifolds. Because California smog applies to these OBD-II cars, an unmodified, smog-passing example with recent belts and a scanned clutch-wear reading is worth paying up for. A tuned car with uncertified exhaust is a registration and resale liability.
profiles.weak_points: ["Timing belts and tensioners. Ferrari specifies belt replacement on a time basis, roughly every 3-5 years regardless of mileage, and low-mile cars are not exempt. A belt or tensioner-bearing failure destroys valves. A proper major service (belts, tensioner bearings, accessory belts, often water pump and cam seals) runs about $3,500-$6,000 at an independent shop and $6,000-$9,000 at a dealer. Insist on a dated invoice naming the belts and tensioner bearings, not just 'major service'.", "F1 clutch wear. The F1 single-plate clutch typically lasts 15k-30k miles, much less with heavy parking-lot and reverse use. Replacement is about $4,500-$7,500 including flywheel inspection and throwout bearing. Wear must be read with a Ferrari SD2/SD3/Leonardo or a capable Autologic/Texa-type tool; seller 'it doesn't slip' claims are meaningless. Get a printout with clutch wear percentage or mm, kiss/engagement point and recent adaptation.", "F1 hydraulic pump, relay and accumulator. Signs of failure include the pump running continuously or audibly cycling at rest, a slow or no-engagement 'F1 fault' light, or the car refusing to go into gear. The pump is about $2,000-$4,000 installed, and the accumulator sphere is about $600-$1,500. A recently replaced pump (as in the example listing) is a plus, but confirm whether the relay and accumulator were also addressed and that the F1 fluid level is correct.", 'Cam variators (phasers). Worn variators rattle or clatter for a few seconds on cold start and can set cam-timing codes. Replacing both banks typically costs $3,000-$6,000, and it is best done alongside a belt service. Listen to a true cold start before the PPI shop warms the car up.', 'Exhaust manifolds and pre-cats, especially 1999-2001 cars. The thin-wall headers crack, producing a ticking noise on cold start, a burnt smell or exhaust leaks, and heat damage to nearby wiring and hoses. Later revised manifolds or quality aftermarket replacements solve it. Replacement is about $3,000-$6,000 for parts and labor. Catalytic converter and O2 sensor faults often follow misfires or tunes.', 'Sticky interior trim. The soft-touch coating on switches, vent surrounds, console, door pulls and the key fob turns tacky with age. Refinishing costs about $1,000-$3,000 for a full set, and individual parts can be swapped piecemeal. It is cosmetic, but universal and a negotiating point.', 'Dashboard and seat leather shrinkage. Dash leather pulls away at the windshield edge and vents, especially on cars that sat in the sun; the example listing shows pulled dash leather. A professional dash re-skin runs about $2,500-$5,000. Bolster wear on Modena comfort seats is common.', 'Cooling system. Look for water pump shaft-seal weeps, expansion tank cracks, aging hoses and clogged front radiators packed with debris. Seized or weak radiator fans cause high temps in traffic. Water pump service runs about $800-$2,000 if done standalone. Ask for photos of the front radiators with the bumper or undertray off.', "Front suspension and steering wear. Tie rods, lower ball joints and bushings knock or clunk over bumps and cause uneven tire wear. Sachs adaptive dampers leak and set suspension faults. Dampers run about $600-$1,200 each installed. Ride-height changes ('lowered' cars) can add rubbing and scraped splitters.", 'Oil leaks. Common sources are cam cover gaskets, cam seals and oil cooler lines. Engine-out leaks are rare but expensive. Inspect the belly pans and the rear of the engine bay, and expect gasket work of about $800-$2,500 on older, unmolested cars.', 'Electrical gremlins. Expect window regulators and motors that are slow or drop the glass (about $500-$1,200 per side), alternator and battery drain issues (these cars need a maintainer), dash warning lights from low voltage, and failing hood and trunk struts or release cables.', 'Spider-specific items. Check the electro-hydraulic top for pump and ram leaks, alignment and latching problems, and rear-window and top-fabric w

profiles.market_notes: The gated 6-speed manual commands a large premium, often 40-70%+ over an equivalent F1 car. F1 cars make up most of the supply and are the value play for a driver, provided clutch wear is documented. Challenge Stradale cars are a separate, collector-priced market; Modena cars wearing 'Challenge Stradale' replica parts are not CS cars and often sell for less than clean stock cars. Prices are driven by recent belt service with invoices, a clutch-wear printout, a complete stock configuration (especially in CA), desirable colors and options (Rosso Corsa, Grigio Titanio, Blu Tour de France, Daytona or carbon seats, Scuderia shields, Challenge grille), and condition of the interior coatings and dash. Mileage bands matter less than records: a well-serviced 20k-40k mile car is often a better buy than a 6k-mile car that sat for years.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 360s are now 20+ years old and many have sat with low annual miles, so rubber ages out regardless of the odometer. Expect belts, hoses, tires, battery, seals and interior coatings to need attention. Budget for a full belt and fluid service plus one major item (clutch, variators or manifolds) unless invoices show it was done recently.

profiles.label: Fiat 124 Sport Spider / Spider 2000 / Pininfarina Azzurra (US big-bumper cars, 1975-1985)
profiles.framing: This is a light, rev-happy twin-cam roadster for Carmel's back roads (Carmel Valley Road, Highway 1, Laureles Grade). It is cheap to run if the body is sound and the timing belt is current. Rust and deferred engine-cooling work are the two things that turn a $15k car into a money pit. In California, emissions legality matters as much as mechanical condition: 1976-and-later cars need a biennial smog check and a pass to register from out of state, so an intact or properly restored emissions system and a recent pass have real value. Model years break down as 1.8 carbureted (1975-78), 2.0 carbureted (1979-80), and 2.0 Bosch L-Jetronic fuel injection (1980.5-85). Judge each on its own fuel-system risks.
profiles.weak_points: ["Structural rust is the number-one deal-killer. Check the floor pans under the seats and pedals, inner and outer rockers/sills, and the lower front fenders behind the wheels. Also check the door bottoms, rear wheel arches, trunk floor and spare well, rear spring perches and trailing-arm mounts, and the base of the windshield frame/cowl. Leaking top seals and clogged drains rot floors from the inside. Carpets can hide perforation, and fresh undercoating or bedliner is a red flag. Cosmetic patching runs $1,500-4,000. Proper floor/sill replacement runs $6,000-15,000+ and usually exceeds the car's value. Ask for underside photos on a lift and any rust-repair invoices with photos.", 'The timing belt drives an interference engine (Lampredi DOHC). A failed belt or seized tensioner bearing bends valves, and a head rebuild runs $2,500-5,000. The belt and tensioner should be changed every 30k miles or about 4-5 years regardless of mileage, ideally with the water pump. Shop cost is about $600-1,200. Want a dated, mileaged receipt that names belt and tensioner. Assume none was done if undocumented.', 'Aluminum cylinder head, overheating, and head gasket: the head warps if the car overheats. Symptoms are milky oil, coolant loss, white exhaust, and pressurized hoses. Bucket-and-shim valve adjustment is often neglected, causing ticking or burnt exhaust valves. Valve adjust is $300-600, head gasket $1,500-2,500, warped or cracked head $3,000+. Look for compression or leakdown numbers and any head-work invoices.', 'Cooling system: original or tired radiators and plugged heater cores are common. The heater valve leaks onto the passenger floor, and heater core replacement means dash-out labor of $800-1,500. Thermostat, hoses, and fan switch (or electric fan on later cars) all age out. Check that the temp gauge stays mid-scale in traffic.', 'Carbureted cars (1975-80): US cars came with a 2-barrel Weber plus air pump, EGR, and on many cars a catalytic converter. Worn throttle shafts, vacuum leaks, and gummed jets cause hesitation and hard starting. Many cars were converted to a Weber 32/36 DGV or DGEV with emissions parts removed. That is drivable, but in California a 1976+ car with missing or modified emissions equipment can fail the visual smog check. Bringing it back to stock can cost $800-2,500 plus hunting for parts.', 'Fuel-injected cars (1980.5-85, Bosch L-Jetronic) suffer air-flow meter wear, brittle intake boots and vacuum hoses (lean running, high idle), failing cold-start valves and thermo-time switches, and weak in-tank or external fuel pumps. Old injector hoses and fuel lines are a fire risk. Expect $500-1,500 to sort a neglected FI car. The parts are shared with period VW/Volvo/BMW and are still available.', 'Electrical: the Italian fuse box with ceramic bullet fuses corrodes, and grounds go bad. You get intermittent lights, wipers, or gauges. The ignition switch, turn-signal/headlight stalk, and headlight relays also fail, and windshield wiper motors are weak. Points-type distributors (some carb cars) need regular attention. Usually $200-800 to sort, but chasing gremlins eats shop hours.', 'Five-speed gearbox: worn 2nd/3rd synchros grind on fast shifts, and shift-lever bushings wear out (sloppy shifter, $50-150 fix). Gearbox rebuild runs $1,500-2,500. The clutch is cable-operated. Cables stretch or snap, and a high or sticky engagement point means cable or clutch wear. Clutch job runs $800-1,400.', 'Rear axle: the live axle with coil springs, trailing links, and Panhard rod develops worn bushings (clunks and rear steer), pinion seal leaks, and diff whine. Bushings run $400-900 and a pinion seal $200-400. A noisy diff rebuild runs $1,000-1,800.', 'Steering and front suspension: the worm-and-roller steering box develops play or leaks, and the idler arm and tie-rod ends wear. Lower control arm bushings and ball joints wear, and engine and transmission mounts collapse, causing clunks and vibration. Expect $600-1,500 to refresh the fron
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Timing belt, tensioner bearing, and accessory belts unless there is a dated receipt within roughly 4 years/30k miles ($600-1,200)', 'Oil and filter, gearbox and differential oil, brake fluid flush, and coolant flush with a new thermostat', 'Replace tires older than about 6 years. Many cars carry old date codes despite good tread.', 'Replace rubber fuel lines, fuel filter, and vacuum hoses. Old hose on a hot twin-cam is a real fire risk.', 'Valve clearance check/adjust and a carburetor or FI tune with a fresh ignition baseline (plugs, cap, rotor, wires, timing)', 'Clean and treat the fuse box and main grounds, and confirm all lights, wipers, and gauges work', 'California smog check for 1976+ cars (and registration from out of state), with any emissions repairs it reveals', 'Inspect brake
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Coolant hoses, heater valve, and possibly radiator if original or scaled', 'Front suspension bushings, ball joints, tie-rod ends, and idler arm, plus a steering box adjustment', 'Rear axle link and Panhard bushings, and the diff pinion seal if weeping', 'Engine and transmission mounts', 'Clutch cable, and possibly a clutch if engagement is high or slipping', 'Shifter bushings, and possibly synchro work if 2nd/3rd grind', 'Convertible top, rear window, and weatherstrip replacement', 'Exhaust manifold studs/gasket or exhaust section repairs', 'Fuel pump, and on FI cars the air-flow meter, cold-start, and intake boot refresh', 'Rust-proofing: clear drains, cavity wax, and treatment of any small surface rust before it spreads in coastal air']
profiles.market_notes: Prices have climbed sharply. Rough examples still trade at $5-9k and driver-quality cars at $10-16k. Exceptional, documented, low-mile cars can reach $20-25k at auction, though results swing wildly with bidder turnout. Rust-free history and documented timing-belt and cooling work move price more than mileage. The 1980.5-82 fuel-injected 2000 and the 1983-85 Pininfarina Azzurra are favored for drivability and trim, while the 1975-78 1.8 carb cars are cheapest. The rare 1981-82 Legend Turbo commands a premium. Automatics (offered from 1979) and heavily modified or emissions-deleted cars are discounted. In California, a 1976+ car with a recent smog pass or intact emissions equipment is worth meaningfully more than one that can't be registered without work.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even well-kept examples are 40-50 years old. Expect to replace aged rubber across the car: fuel and brake hoses, coolant hoses, bushings, mounts, and top seals. Plan on a timing belt unless it is freshly documented, plus a full fluid and brake refresh. In Carmel's damp, salty coastal air, budget for rust prevention (drains cleared, cavity wax) and garage storage to keep a sound body sound.

profiles.label: Ford Bronco (First Generation, 1966–1977 "Early Bronco")
profiles.framing: For this buyer the early Bronco is a weekend-and-errand toy that has to actually drive to Big Sur, Laureles Grade, and the beach without drama — not a trailer queen and not a show car. Because almost none survive unmodified, the realistic goal is a documented, coherently built truck: rust-free structure, one shop's fingerprints on the driveline, and receipts that explain every deviation from stock. The single biggest determinant of long-term cost is metal — body mounts, frame rails at the shock towers, rear quarters and floors — followed by whether the builder solved the known weak links (steering, brakes, cooling, wiring, fuel) or just bolted on lift and tires. A restomod with a crate engine and an overdrive-less or freshly rebuilt automatic is acceptable here; an undocumented 'built motor' with mystery fabrication is not.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rust is the defining issue and it is structural, not cosmetic. Check the rear quarter panels and inner wheel arches, the floor pans (especially under the driver's-side fuel tank on 1966–77 trucks that retain the under-seat tank), the tailgate skin and its lower corners, the rear crossmember, the windshield frame lower corners, and the cowl/kick panel area. Full quarter replacement with blend paint runs $3,000–$8,000 per side; a body-off metal restoration is $60,000–$150,000. Look for panel-gap irregularity, seam sealer that hides filler, and magnet/thickness-gauge evidence.", "Frame and body-mount corrosion. The front frame rails rot at the shock-tower/coil-spring mounts and at the radius-arm rear mounts; cracks propagate there from lift and oversize tires. Rotted body mounts let the tub shift and the doors stop closing. Weld-in frame stiffeners or repair plates are common and should be documented — new mounts and rail repair is $1,500–$5,000 of labor. Get clear underbody photos, not just 'no rust' claims.", '\'Bronco lean\' and worn front suspension. Sagging driver-side coil spring, tired radius-arm bushings, and a worn track bar / drag-link joint produce lean, wander, and shimmy-into-death-wobble at 45–60 mph, badly amplified by 33s and a 2.5" lift. Springs, bushings, shocks, and a full front end joint refresh is $1,200–$3,000; lifts done without correcting steering geometry or drop pitman arm create permanent bump steer.', 'Steering. Factory 1966–75 Ross cam-and-lever box (manual, or the weak Saginaw power box later) is vague and leaks; most good builds convert to a Saginaw power box or Borgeson unit with a new pitman arm and a hydraulic ram or quick-ratio setup. Verify the conversion is bolted through reinforced frame metal — cracked steering-box frame mounts are a known failure. Conversion cost $1,200–$2,500. Excessive on-center play or a leak at the box should be priced in.', 'Brakes. Front drums through 1975 (discs standard 1976–77) are marginal for modern traffic with big tires. Disc conversions (Wilwood/TOMS/Wild Horses, often with hydroboost) are common and desirable but must include a correct proportioning valve and sized master cylinder — symptoms of a bad job are long pedal travel, rear lockup, or no boost. Budget $1,500–$3,000 for a proper four-wheel disc/hydroboost job and inspect for fresh, correctly routed hard lines and a non-weeping booster.', "Fuel system. The original under-seat tank and sending units are a chronic problem: failing fuel gauges, cracked rubber fill hoses, weeping sender flanges, and fire risk from decades-old rubber lines under the cab. This listing's June 2026 sender and gauge replacement is exactly the typical item. A rear-tank relocation plus new lines and a properly rated in-tank pump for EFI is $800–$2,500; on EFI conversions, confirm return line, pump rating, and pressure regulator install quality.", 'Wiring and grounds. Original harnesses are brittle, the bulkhead connector and headlight/ignition switches overheat, and gauges read erratically. A complete American Autowire/Painless harness with a modern fuse box (as here) is a major plus; verify it was actually finished — look for loose splices, unfused add-ons, and LED-light or winch circuits tapped off the ignition. A proper rewire is $900–$1,500 in parts plus 20–40 hours labor.', 'Cooling. The stock radiator and shroudless fan are marginal; anything with a 302/347 stroker, big tires, and A/C or a body lift will run hot in stop-and-go or on a grade. Look for an aluminum crossflow radiator, correct shroud, and an electric fan setup with a proper relay. A 415 hp stroker in a 3,500-lb truck with 35s will also cook the transmission without an auxiliary cooler — confirm one exists.', "Drivetrain leaks and driveline angles. The Dana 20 transfer case seeps at the rear output seal and the shifter/housing gasket; twin-stick conversions can leak or pop out of gear if the detents and shift rails aren't right. Lifted trucks commonly vibrate f
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace tires — 2010 date codes are unsafe regardless of tread; a set of 33"–35" Toyo/BFG plus mount, balance, and alignment is $1,600–$2,400.', 'Full fluid service: engine oil, trans fluid and filter (fresh look at the rebuilt 4R70W), transfer case, both differentials, brake fluid flush, coolant.', 'Front-end inspection and retorque: radius arm bolts, track bar, drag link, tie rod ends, steering box mount, pitman arm nut; set toe and caster for the lift ($300–$800).', 'Brake system verification: bed-in, check hydroboost/master for weeping, confirm proportioning valve adjustment and parking brake function ($200–$600).', 'Chase leaks and finish-work items typical of a fresh build: fabricated engine mount inspection, exhaust hanger/clearance, fuel line routing and clamps, EFI fuel pressure
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Driveline vibration resolution if any remains: pinion angle shims, carrier bearing, or re-balance of the rear shaft ($400–$1,200).', 'Dana 20 rear output seal and shifter housing reseal; front axle knuckle/hub seal service ($600–$1,500).', 'EFI/ignition tuning and drivability sorting on the Sniper (idle, cold start, timing curve) plus possible distributor or coil work ($400–$1,000).', 'Seat, top, and weatherseal work: soft-top fit, windshield seam leak, door seals, and possible hardtop acquisition or refresh ($500–$3,000).', 'Cosmetic touch-in of documented chips/scratches on the tailgate and rear bumper corner; underbody cavity wax/rust-proofing given coastal Carmel air ($800–$2,000).', 'Gearing/final-drive reassessment if the truck feels under-geared on 35s, or a rear axle service if w
profiles.market_notes: Value is driven first by structure and documentation, then by build quality and taste: a rust-free, receipt-backed truck from a known builder (Icon, Gateway, Velocity, Kincer, TOMS/Wild Horses parts done well) sells far above a nice-looking backyard build. Uncut, original-spec 1966–68 examples — especially roadsters, Sports, and 1971–75 4-speed/V8 wagons with a Marti Report — command originality money, while tastefully executed restomods with fuel injection, four-wheel discs, power steering, and a modern overdrive automatic trade in a wide $45,000–$120,000 band. Color matters (factory-correct Brittany Blue, Wimbledon White, Boxwood Green read better than trendy repaints), as does a matching hardtop plus soft top; a color change away from the Marti-documented original costs some money with purists. Odometer readings are irrelevant; 'documented restoration with invoices in the gallery' is worth real dollars, and undocumented 415 hp claims are worth a discount.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a freshly restored early Bronco needs a first-year sorting budget: 50-year-old rubber and hardware (tires, seals, hoses, body mounts, weatherstrip) and the inevitable punch-list of a recent build — leaks, fuel and wiring finish work, driveline angles, and brake/steering bedding. Assume everything not on a receipt is original and due, and add coastal rust-prevention (cavity wax, underbody treatment) immediately given Carmel's salt air.

profiles.label: Ford Bronco Raptor (6th-gen U725, 2022-present)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel-based buyer, the Bronco Raptor is a high-capability, fun daily and weekend truck for Highway 1, Big Sur fire roads, and Sierra or desert trips. It is wide at roughly 86 inches, heavy at about 5,700 lb, runs on premium fuel, and returns roughly 14-16 mpg. Raptor buyers often jump, tune, and accessorize these trucks, so the main risks are off-road abuse and California emissions legality, not age. The ideal example is a stock or easily returned-to-stock truck with a clean underbody, dealer-documented service, and a clean module-level scan.
profiles.weak_points: ['Off-road and jump abuse is the defining risk on this model. Inspect frame horns, front shock towers, upper and lower control arm mounts, rear lower control arm and track-bar brackets, and the rear lower shock mounts for kinks, cracked paint, cracked welds, or fresh undercoating hiding repairs. Bent frames or brackets can mean $3,000-15,000+ in repairs or a structural write-off. Look for underbody photos and any body-shop or frame-repair records.', 'Engine tuning and California emissions. The 3.0L EcoBoost (Nano) twin-turbo V6 is robust stock, but many trucks carry tunes such as Ford Performance ProCal or aftermarket calibrations, and throttle controllers. In California, any calibration or emissions-related part without a CARB Executive Order fails the smog visual or functional check, which can block registration. A CA BAR referee can also flag a non-stock calibration ID. Ask for written proof that the truck has been flashed back to the Ford stock calibration, plus a dealer or scan-tool readout of the PCM calibration ID. Also confirm whether the truck is 50-state emissions certified.', 'Turbo system on the 3.0L. Look for wastegate rattle, oil or coolant seepage at turbo feed and return lines, and boost leaks at charge-pipe couplers, which can pop off under a tune. Charge-air-cooler condensation can cause stumble or misfire under boost in humid coastal air. Replacing one turbo typically costs $2,500-4,500 installed, both $5,000-8,000. Look for boost or misfire DTC history and any turbo or intercooler warranty claims.', 'Timing chain and cam phasers on higher-mileage or tuned 3.0 engines. Listen for a 1-3 second rattle at cold start or a cam correlation code (P0016-P0019). The dual port and direct injection limits intake-valve carbon. A catch can or air-oil separator, as on many modified trucks, suggests the owner saw oil in the intake tract. Timing chain and phaser work runs $3,000-5,500. Ask for oil-change records showing roughly 5,000-mile or shorter intervals with the correct 5W-30 spec.', '10R80 10-speed automatic. Watch for harsh 1-2 or 2-3 shifts, flare or clunk on 3-4 and 5-6, coast-down bumps, and torque-converter shudder. Many cases are fixed by TSB reflash and adaptive relearn, but valve-body or internal faults happen. A valve body costs $1,500-2,500; a rebuild or replacement $5,000-8,000. Look for TCM update and TSB records and any fluid service. Towing or desert use should trigger a fluid change by about 60,000 miles.', "Transfer case and 4x4 system. The 2-speed electronic transfer case has 4A, 4H, and 4L modes. Check for slow or failed mode changes, 'Service 4x4' messages, shift-motor or encoder faults, and grinding into 4L. Fluid is often neglected after water crossings. A transfer case replacement is $3,500-5,500. Look for transfer case fluid service records, especially after deep water or sand.", 'Locking front and rear differentials. Check the electric locker actuators and wiring for faults and lockers that fail to engage or disengage. Also check for pinion and axle seal leaks and water contamination (milky gear oil) after crossings. Diff rebuilds run $2,000-4,000 per axle. Look for a gear-oil change after any wading and inspect the axle tubes and housings for straightness.', 'FOX Live Valve 3.1 internal-bypass dampers. Watch for shock body leaks, damaged reservoirs or hoses, Live Valve solenoid or harness DTCs, and a harsh or uneven ride. They are expensive: about $1,500-2,500 per corner at the dealer, or $500-900 per corner for a FOX rebuild where available. Look for a scan of the suspension module and photos of each shock body.', 'Front IFS wear items, accelerated by 37-inch tires and worse with 38s. Check tie rod ends and inner tie rods for bending or play, ball joints, control arm bushings, front CV axles and boots (rock-torn boots fling grease), and wheel bearings. CV axles cost $700-1,400 each, tie rods and ball joints $800-2,000, and a full front-end refresh $2,500-4,000. Oversized tires also stress th
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full module-level scan with FORScan or Ford FDRS (PCM, TCM, transfer case, ABS, suspension/Live Valve, locker, body), then clear and re-verify any codes', 'If tuned: dealer reflash to the stock Ford calibration, removal of non-CARB throttle controllers and emissions-related parts, and a California smog check before registration', 'Baseline fluids if records are thin: engine oil and filter, and inspection of coolant level and condition', 'Gear oil check or change in the front and rear differentials and transfer case if there is any history of water crossings', '12V battery and charging system test; verify that aftermarket lighting and compressor wiring is properly fused and switched', 'Alignment, plus speedometer recalibration if tire size differs from stock', 'Complete any open recalls o
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Spark plugs: about 60,000 miles stock, or every 30,000-40,000 miles if the truck was tuned or towed', '10R80 transmission fluid and filter service if approaching 60,000 miles or used for towing or desert driving', 'Front and rear differential and transfer case fluid service (severe-duty interval)', 'Front and rear brake pads and rotors (roughly $900-1,800 per axle)', 'Replacement set of 37-inch tires if tread is low or date codes are 4+ years old ($1,800-2,600)', 'Front-end wear items as needed: tie rod ends, ball joints, CV boots or axles', 'Allowance for a FOX Live Valve shock rebuild or replacement if any are leaking or faulted', 'Hardtop, door, and tailgate seal adjustment or replacement to cure leaks or wind noise', 'Coolant system pressure test, plus attention to any turbo coolant
profiles.market_notes: Mileage and condition drive price most, with low-mileage stock trucks commanding a clear premium. Factory options matter mainly through the Lux Package. Colors like Code Orange, Shadow Black, and Eruption Green have a following. Heavy modification usually lowers value to mainstream buyers, especially tunes, oversized tires, lifts, and dense lighting. Trucks titled in or registerable in California with no tune history are worth more to a California buyer. Complete dealer service records, clean underbody photos, and remaining powertrain warranty also lift value.
profiles.catchup_notes: These trucks are young, so catch-up work is driven by use rather than age: deferred fluid changes after water or desert trips, front-end and CV wear from big tires, and battery and seal issues. Budget for a full fluid baseline, an alignment, and reversal of any tune or emissions-related modifications. Expect to reserve for tires and brakes sooner than on a typical SUV.

profiles.label: Ford F-150 (13th gen P552, 2015–2020, incl. 2017–2020 Raptor)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, a 13th-gen F-150 is a practical daily driver and utility truck for coastal Carmel, the Highway 1 corridor, hauling, and occasional towing or beach and trail access. It is not a project. The target is a stock, documented 2018–2020 truck with the 5.0 Coyote or 3.5 EcoBoost and the 10R80 10-speed, whose maintenance can be traced through Ford dealer or independent records. Heavily modified builds are outside this profile and should be treated as non-conforming no matter how well built they are. That includes long-travel prerunners, supercharged or tuned trucks, cages, fuel cells, and swapped axles like the reference listing. Lifts and tunes without a CARB EO can also create California smog, registration, insurance, and parts-support problems. Powertrain choice, transmission behavior, and evidence of off-road or tow abuse matter far more than cosmetics on this aluminum-bodied truck.
profiles.weak_points: ["10R80 10-speed automatic (2017 3.5 EcoBoost, all 2018–2020 except the 3.3 V6): harsh or clunky 1-2, 2-3 and 3-2 shifts, delayed engagement, gear hunting, and torque-converter shudder are common complaints. Ford addressed many cases with PCM/TCM reflashes and adaptive relearns. Some trucks needed valve body, clutch pack, or full transmission replacement, at $4,500–$7,500 out of warranty. Look for dealer records of TSB reflashes and transmission repairs, and a fluid change (Mercon ULV) by roughly 60k. Ford's 150k interval is optimistic for towing.", '6R80 6-speed (2015–2017 non-EcoBoost 3.5, 2.7 and 5.0 trucks): generally robust. Watch for harsh engagement, solenoid body or TCM faults, and torque-converter shudder. Solenoid or valve body repairs run $800–$2,000, and a rebuild runs $3,500–$5,000. Look for fluid service records by 60–80k.', "5.0L Coyote, Gen 3 (2018–2020, port plus direct injection): excessive oil consumption is widely reported. Some engines show piston, ring, or cylinder-wall scuffing with a persistent tick on cold start. Ford handled some cases with oil consumption tests and short blocks or long blocks, at roughly $8,000–$13,000 out of warranty. Look for a dealer oil consumption test record and consistent oil changes at 5,000–7,500 miles. Note any 'engine replaced' entry, as in the example listing, and find out why.", '5.0L Coyote, Gen 2 (2015–2017): stronger reputation, but some engines burn oil and develop exhaust manifold or valvetrain tick. Expect occasional water pump weep around 80–120k ($600–$1,000) and minor oil leaks at the timing cover or rear main.', '3.5L EcoBoost, Gen 2 (2017–2020): cam phaser (VCT) rattle lasting 1–3 seconds on cold start is the hallmark failure, often accompanied by timing chain stretch codes (P0016–P0019). Ford issued TSBs and revised phasers. Phasers, chains and guides run $2,500–$4,500. Gen 1 (2015–2016) adds intercooler condensation stumble under load and timing chain stretch. Look for records of phaser or timing replacement with the revised parts, plus synthetic oil changes at 5,000-mile intervals.', "3.5L EcoBoost internal water pump: the pump is driven by the timing chain inside the engine. When it fails, coolant can leak into the oil. Watch for coolant loss with no external leak, milky oil, or a sweet smell. Replacement runs $1,500–$3,000 and is often combined with timing work. Look for coolant level history and any 'coolant loss' visit notes.", 'EcoBoost turbos and ignition (3.5 and 2.7): turbo wastegate rattle, turbo coolant and oil line seepage, and boost leaks at intercooler couplers. Expect misfires from worn plugs past about 40–60k and occasional coil failures. A single turbo runs $1,800–$3,500. Look for records of plug changes on the 40–60k cadence.', '2.7L EcoBoost: the composite oil pan leaks at its seal or cracks, especially on 2015–2017 trucks, at $500–$1,000 to replace. Gen 2 (2018+) also has some cam phaser complaints. Check the underside for fresh oil and look for a pan replacement receipt.', '3.0L Power Stroke diesel (2018–2020, low volume): there are reports of oil pump failure leading to catastrophic engine damage. It also carries expensive EGR, DPF and SCR emissions hardware, with sensors and DEF components at $500–$3,000 and an engine at $12,000+. In California, emissions-system integrity is non-negotiable. Avoid this engine unless records are complete and the emissions system is untouched.', 'Front 4x4 IWE (integrated wheel end) vacuum system: grinding or clicking from the front hubs in 2WD is caused by a leaking vacuum line, check valve, or solenoid, and wears the hub internals. The fix is $150–$800, or $800–$1,500 if hubs and bearings are needed. 4x4 transfer case encoder motor faults also occur.', 'Aluminum body and collision quality: the 2015+ aluminum cab and bed resist rust. However, poor collision repairs, mismatched panels, and galvanic corrosion where steel fasteners meet aluminum (door bottoms, tailgate, hood edges) are concerns. Salt fog on
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter with a Motorcraft or equivalent spec synthetic, brake fluid flush, and front and rear differential plus transfer case fluid (4x4).', 'Transmission drain-and-fill with Mercon ULV (10R80) or Mercon LV (6R80) if there is no record within 60k, then an adaptive relearn or confirmation that the latest TCM calibration is installed.', 'Close all open recalls and check for applicable TSBs or CSPs at a Ford dealer. Have the dealer update PCM, TCM and SYNC software.', 'Engine and cabin air filters. Test the battery and charging system, since F-150 BMS behavior makes weak batteries cause odd electrical faults.', 'Spark plugs on EcoBoost engines if past about 40–60k miles without a record.', 'Tire age and date-code check, alignment, and inspection of front-e
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Monitor oil consumption on a 5.0 Gen 3 and track quarts per 1,000 miles. Start a dealer consumption test early if usage exceeds about 1 qt per 3,000 miles.', 'EcoBoost cam phaser or timing chain service if the cold-start rattle or VCT codes appear.', 'Brake pads and rotors. Heavy trucks and Highway 1 grades eat front brakes.', 'HVAC blend door actuator, SYNC 3 screen or APIM, or running board motor replacement as symptoms appear.', 'Front wheel bearings, hubs, ball joints, or tie rod ends on higher-mileage 4x4 trucks.', 'Shocks or struts on trucks with 70k+ miles. On a Raptor, a Fox shock rebuild.', 'Underbody corrosion treatment of the frame, brake lines and fasteners for a coastal-garaged truck.']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven by cab and bed, drivetrain, engine, and trim. The most liquid configurations are the SuperCrew 5.5-ft bed 4x4 with the 5.0 or 3.5 EcoBoost, with Lariat and above (King Ranch, Platinum, Limited) commanding strong premiums, and FX4 and Max Tow adding value. 2018–2020 refresh trucks with the 10-speed bring more than 2015–2017 trucks, and the Raptor (2017–2020) is a separate, higher market where unmodified, unabused examples with documented shock service are worth a clear premium. Mileage breaks matter around 60k (end of powertrain warranty), 100k and 150k, and clean single-owner, no-tow, dealer-serviced records add real money. Lifted, tuned, or heavily built trucks like long-travel prerunners trade in a niche market. They are often hard to register or insure in California and are poor value for a buyer who wants a stock daily driver.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2018–2020 truck is now 5–7 years old and past the 5-yr/60k powertrain warranty. Many have never had transmission, differential, transfer case, or brake fluid service and are approaching their first Motorcraft Orange coolant interval, while EcoBoost trucks often need plugs. Budget $1,200–$2,500 to bring fluids, filters, plugs, battery, and tires current, plus coastal underbody corrosion protection for a Carmel-based truck.

profiles.label: Ford F-250 Super Duty (1st gen, 1999–2007; pre-refresh 1999–2004 & refresh 2005–2007)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the truck is a working tool: towing, hauling, camper-shell trips, and occasional dirt roads. It is not a commuter or a collectible, and it is large and thirsty for Carmel's narrow streets and tight parking (V10 trucks get roughly 10-13 mpg). Engine choice drives risk more than anything else. The 7.3L Power Stroke (1999–2003) is the prized durable option, the 6.8L V10 and 5.4L gas engines are simpler but have known spark-plug and exhaust-stud issues, and the 6.0L diesel (2003.5–2007) should only be bought with receipts showing it was properly repaired. A documented, rust-free, unmodified one- or two-owner California truck with a tight front end and healthy transmission is worth paying for. The camper shells, tires, and intakes these trucks usually wear matter far less.
profiles.weak_points:
['Spark plug ejection on the 2-valve 6.8L V10 and 5.4L V8 (1999–2004). The aluminum heads have only a few threads holding each plug, and a plug can blow out, usually at 60k–120k miles or after a past plug change done at the wrong torque. Symptoms are a sudden loud ticking or popping and a misfire on one cylinder, often with a melted coil boot. A thread insert repair (TimeSert or Calvan type) costs about $300–$1,500 per hole if it can be done in the truck, and $2,500–$5,000+ if a head must come off. Look for plug-change records with the shop name, any prior insert repairs, and a coil that looks newer than its neighbors.', 'Two-piece spark plugs on the 3-valve V10 and 5.4L (2005–2007). The factory plugs seize and snap during removal, so the first plug change on an untouched truck can cost $600–$1,500+ at a shop that has the extraction tool. Ask whether the plugs were changed, by whom, and whether any broke.', 'Broken exhaust manifold studs and cracked manifolds on the V10 and 5.4L, both generations. The sign is a ticking on cold start that fades as the engine warms, worst at the rear cylinders. Expect $800–$2,500 for stud extraction, gaskets, and sometimes manifolds; rusted studs on coastal trucks cost more.', '4R100 4-speed automatic (gas trucks and the 7.3L diesel, 1999–2004). It runs hot when towing heavy, especially in overdrive. Watch for slipping on the 3-4 shift, overdrive band wear, a shudder from the torque converter clutch, and dark or burnt fluid. A rebuild is about $3,000–$4,500. Look for fluid and filter service every 30k–50k miles and an auxiliary cooler. Towing in overdrive with no service records is a red flag.', '5R110W TorqShift 5-speed (6.0L diesel from 2003.5 and V10 from 2005). It is generally stronger, but it can shift harshly and the torque converter can fail on tuned or neglected trucks. A rebuild is about $4,000–$5,500. Check for fluid service records.', '7.3L Power Stroke (1999–2003). The core engine is durable, but these parts fail with age:
- Camshaft position sensor: causes stalling or a no-start. It is cheap, but a spare should be carried.
- Injector O-rings and individual injectors: $300–$500 each.
- Under-valve-cover harness and glow plugs: cause hard cold starts.
- Exhaust up-pipe leaks.
- Fuel bowl heater leaks.
- Injector driver module.

Get records for oil changes every 5k miles and a recent idle/load scan. A blow-by test is worth doing above 200k miles.', "6.0L Power Stroke (2003.5–2007). Known failures are head gaskets (the root cause is stretched head bolts), EGR cooler ruptures, oil cooler clogging, injector control module (FICM) voltage drop, injector stiction, and high-pressure oil leaks. A full 'bulletproofing' with head studs, an upgraded EGR cooler, and an upgraded oil cooler costs about $8,000–$14,000. Without receipts for that work, treat a 6.0L as a large risk. A rising coolant level in the overflow bottle, white exhaust smoke, or coolant temperature diverging from oil temperature by more than 15°F under load are bad signs.", "Front axle, steering, and suspension wear. 1999–2004 4x4 F-250s use a leaf-spring Dana 50 or 60; 2005–2007 use a coil-spring Dana 60 with a track bar.
- Ball joints, tie-rod ends, the drag link, and the steering box (leaks or play) wear out. These parts have grease fittings and last if they were greased.
- Wandering, or 'death wobble' on 2005+ trucks with a worn track bar or oversized tires.
- Ball joints run about $600–$1,200; full steering linkage $500–$1,000; a steering box $500–$900.
- Look for grease entries in the service log and an alignment printout.", 'Front hub bearings and the vacuum-actuated auto-locking hubs. Cracked vacuum lines or failed hub seals cause no 4WD engagement, grinding, or hubs that will not lock. Hub bearing assemblies cost about $400–$900 per side installed. Test 4WD in both auto and locked positions on a loose surface.', "Rust, made worse by Carmel's coastal salt air.
- Cab corners and rocker panels.
- Bed wheel arc

- 2-valve engines: if there is no recent record, change plugs carefully with anti-seize and

profiles.market_notes: ['Powertrain drives price. Clean 7.3L Power Stroke trucks bring a large premium, and manual-transmission diesels (ZF6) more still. V10 trucks sit in the middle. 5.4L trucks are cheapest. 6.0L trucks are discounted unless head studs and the EGR and oil coolers are documented as done.', 'Body and trim also matter. Crew Cab and 4x4 sell for more than SuperCab, 2WD, or regular cab, and Lariat, King Ranch, FX4, and Harley-Davidson trims sell for more than XL or XLT.', 'Condition and history set the rest. Rusty, lifted, tuned, or undocumented trucks trade far lower.', 'Accident history, aftermarket wheels and tires, and intakes slightly depress value for a buyer seeking an unmodified truck. Camper shells add little.']
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 18-25-year-old example needs a full fluid baseline and front-end grease, often for the first time in years. It will likely also need tires, belts, hoses, and plugs. Coastal or towing trucks usually add rear brake calipers, brake lines, exhaust studs, and front-end joints. Budget roughly $2,000–$4,500 of catch-up beyond the purchase price for a gas truck, and more for a diesel needing injector or cooler work.

profiles.label: Ford Focus ST (Mk3, 2013–2018 North America)
profiles.framing: The Mk3 Focus ST is a practical, manual-only hot hatch with a 252 hp 2.0L EcoBoost direct-injection turbo engine. For a Carmel buyer it is a fun daily driver for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the 68 that can still haul groceries and gear. The main risk is ownership history, not the basic design. This platform has a large tuning culture (Cobb Accessport, downpipes, intakes), and hard launches punish the clutch, dual-mass flywheel, engine mounts and pistons. A documented, never-tuned, smog-legal example is worth a real premium, because California smog visual checks fail cars with non-CARB downpipes or intakes.
profiles.weak_points: ["Tuning history and cracked pistons: The 2.0 EcoBoost is reliable when stock. Tuned cars, especially aggressive off-the-shelf or e-tune maps, have a known history of cracked ring lands and pistons. Symptoms are a persistent single-cylinder misfire (P0301–P0304), low compression on one cylinder and oil consumption. The only real fix is an engine replacement or rebuild, roughly $5,000–$9,000. Ask directly about any Accessport, Livernois or other tune and whether it was returned to stock. A 'returned to stock' car may still carry piston damage, so require a compression or leak-down test regardless.", 'Turbo wastegate rattle and turbo health: The BorgWarner K03-family turbo commonly develops wastegate actuator or bushing wear. You hear a metallic rattle at idle, on light throttle or when coasting off throttle. It ranges from a $100–$300 band-aid (wastegate clip or spring) to a $1,800–$3,000 turbo replacement. Check for blue smoke, shaft play and oil in the charge pipes. Boost leaks are also common: the plastic charge-pipe coupler on the throttle body can crack or pop off, giving limp mode and a big loss of power.', 'Clutch, concentric slave cylinder and dual-mass flywheel: The ST uses a DMF with a concentric slave cylinder inside the bellhousing. Original clutches commonly last 60k–100k miles, much less if the car was launched hard. Watch for a high or sticky pedal, slipping in 4th–6th under boost, chatter on take-off, or a pedal that stays on the floor (slave failure). A full clutch, DMF and slave job runs about $1,600–$2,800 at an independent shop. Also verify that any clutch or pressure-plate recall applicable to the VIN has been completed.', "MMT6 6-speed manual gearbox: Notchy or grinding 2nd and 3rd synchros are common on hard-driven cars. Bearing whine and worn shifter-cable bushings or shifter-base bushings (sloppy, vague shifts) also occur. Bushings cost $100–$300. A used or rebuilt transmission is $2,500–$4,500. Many owners install short shifters and stiffer bushings, which is a modification flag. Look for gear-oil change records, because the factory 'lifetime' fill benefits from a change around 60k–80k miles.", "Engine and transmission mounts: The rear torque mount ('dog bone' or RMM) and passenger engine mount soften with age. That produces clunks on throttle tip-in and lift, wheel hop and excess shifter movement. Expect $200–$600 parts and labor for OEM replacements. Aftermarket polyurethane RMMs and mount inserts are very common on these cars and signal an enthusiast-modified history.", 'Direct-injection carbon buildup: Intake valves coke up with no port-injection wash. Symptoms by 60k–100k miles are rough cold idle, hesitation and misfire codes, worse with short trips and poor PCV health. A walnut-blast cleaning costs about $400–$800. Ask whether it has been done, and whether a catch can was fitted (another mod flag, but benign).', "Spark plugs and coil packs: The ST is sensitive to plug gap. Ford's interval is commonly cited around 60k miles, and many owners do it at 30k–40k. Worn plugs cause misfire under boost and can damage coils. Plugs run about $150–$300; coils about $250–$500 for a set. Look for receipts with Motorcraft plugs at the correct gap. Colder or one-step plugs indicate a tune history.", 'Cooling system: The plastic coolant degas (expansion) bottle cracks at the seams and the cap can fail, causing slow coolant loss and a sweet smell. That is about $150–$350. Water pump and thermostat housing leaks appear at 80k–120k miles, about $500–$1,000. On a turbo GDI engine, any overheating history is a serious red flag.', 'EVAP canister purge valve and fuel system: The purge valve sticks open on 2.0 GDI Focus models. Symptoms are hard starting or a rough idle right after refueling, EVAP codes (P0455/P0456/P0171) and sometimes a deformed fuel tank. The valve is about $100–$250. Neglected cases have needed a fuel tank, $800+. Also watch for low-pressure fuel pump or fuel pump driver module faults (stalling, lon
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter with Ford-spec 5W-30 (WSS-M2C946-A or equivalent), brake fluid flush, and inspect or replace coolant if the history is unknown.', 'Transmission (MMT6) gear oil change with the correct Ford spec fluid if there is no record.', 'Spark plugs at Ford gap if more than 30k–40k miles or no record, plus a coil inspection.', 'Engine air filter and cabin filter.', 'Inspect and fix the charge-pipe coupler, intercooler hoses and degas bottle. Tighten or replace the wastegate clip if it rattles.', 'Run a Ford-capable scan (FORScan or a dealer IDS) for stored and pending codes, module faults and calibration ID; confirm the car is on the stock calibration.', 'Check all recalls and campaigns by VIN at Ford/NHTSA (door latch, any clutch or pressure-plate campaign
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Intake valve walnut-blast cleaning if over 60k–80k miles with no record or with rough cold idle.', 'Rear torque mount and/or passenger engine mount replacement with OEM parts if there are clunks or excess shifter movement.', 'Front lower control arm bushings, end links and strut mounts as the car approaches 80k–100k miles.', "Front and rear brake pads and rotors, given the car's weight bias and hill driving.", 'Clutch, DMF and concentric slave cylinder set aside if over 70k–90k miles or showing early slip or chatter.', 'Water pump and thermostat housing inspection, replacing proactively near 100k miles if there is any weep.', 'Liftgate harness repair and door latch replacement if any intermittent faults appear.', 'Battery (often original or near end of life on 7+ year cars) and battery m
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by originality: a never-tuned, stock-exhaust, smog-legal car with service records commands 10–25% over a modified one, especially in California. 2016–2018 cars carry a premium for SYNC 3 and the 2015+ facelift. ST3 trim adds leather Recaros, navigation and HID lights and is the most desirable; ST1 cloth cars are cheapest. Mileage bands matter (under 50k strongest, 50k–90k mainstream, over 100k discounted unless the clutch, DMF and mounts are done), and Performance Blue, Tangerine Scream and Race Red sell faster than black, white or silver. As of this writing, typical clean 2015–2018 private-party asks run roughly $13k–$20k; verify against current comps before relying on that band.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2015–2018 ST at 60k–90k miles is usually due for plugs, transmission fluid, a brake fluid flush and an intake-valve cleaning. Plan for one or more of the following: engine mounts, front suspension bushings, a degas bottle, and the first clutch/DMF job. Budget $1,500–$3,000 in year-one catch-up on an unmodified car with partial records, and more if a previous tune or hard launching is suspected.

profiles.label: Ford GT (2005–2006, first generation)
profiles.framing: The 2005–2006 GT is a roughly 4,000-unit, manual-only, mid-engine supercar. Its running gear is mostly Ford, but its chassis, transaxle and body parts are low-volume and scarce. For a Carmel buyer who wants to actually drive it, the priorities are documented maintenance by a GT-experienced shop, an intact twin-disc clutch and Ricardo transaxle, no structural or aluminum-panel collision history, and a stock calibration that will pass a California smog visual and functional check. Every example carries collector-level purchase prices, so a weak or tuned car costs far more in lost value and remediation than it saves at purchase.
profiles.weak_points: ['Twin-disc clutch: Clutch life ranges from about 15k to 45k miles depending on launches and traffic use, and replacement requires dropping the transaxle. Expect roughly $7k–$14k at a specialist. Symptoms include slip under boost in 3rd–4th gear, a high or variable engagement point, chatter from a standstill, and judder when hot. Ask for a dated clutch receipt with mileage. Without one, have a specialist assess slip and engagement, and treat any car over 25k miles with no record as clutch-due.', 'Ricardo 6-speed transaxle: The unit is strong but low-volume. Cold 1st/2nd crunch, worn synchros and bearing whine show up on hard-driven or high-mile cars. Rebuilds run about $15k–$30k with long parts lead times. The transaxle cooler lines and hoses are a known leak and replacement item (about $800–$2,000). Look for fluid-change history and cooler-line replacement, and check for wet residue at the cooler lines and the bellhousing.', 'Lysholm 2300 twin-screw supercharger and drive: Watch for bearing or rotor noise, a worn coupler/nosecone, and oil seepage. The drive belt, tensioner and idler pulleys also wear. Belt and pulley service is roughly $500–$1,500, and a blower rebuild about $4k–$8k. A smaller pulley or tune (common on these cars) raises boost and stress on the blower, clutch and transaxle. Listen for whine changes and rattles at idle, and confirm the stock pulley diameter is fitted.', 'Air-to-water intercooler circuit: The intercooler pump, its relay and the front heat-exchanger plumbing can fail. The usual signs are heat-soak, timing pull and power loss on warm days. Pumps are inexpensive (about $300–$900 installed), but a failed pump on a tuned car risks detonation. Verify the pump runs at key-on or with the engine running.', 'Dry-sump 5.4 DOHC oiling: Oil level must be checked hot, at idle, on the remote tank dipstick. Overfilling pushes oil into the breather and intake, and a mis-serviced car can starve or smoke. Generic quick-lube shops get this wrong. Look for oil changes logged by GT-familiar shops roughly every 3k–5k miles or annually, with the correct capacity noted. Oil residue in the intake tract or at the PCV/breather is a red flag.', 'Crank position sensor and connector pigtail: This is a known cause of intermittent stalling, no-start and stumbling. Sensor and pigtail replacement runs about $500–$1,500. Look for a dated replacement record, or plan for it.', 'Fuel system and gauges: The twin in-tank pumps sit in the center-tunnel tank, so they are labor-heavy to replace (about $2k–$5k). The individual analog gauges, especially the fuel gauge, are known to fail, at roughly $500–$2,000 per gauge installed with scarce supply. Test every gauge, compare fuel level to trip miles, and check for long-crank hot-start behavior.', 'Front suspension control arms and rear toe links: The aluminum front control arms should be inspected for cracks, ball-joint play and any open service actions. Some owners swap to billet aftermarket arms, which are not stock and may need reversal. Rear tie-rod/toe-link ends and engine/transaxle mounts wear at about 30k–40k miles or 15+ years, roughly $1.5k–$4k together. Run a VIN check with Ford/NHTSA for open recalls.', 'Cooling system: The front radiator is fed by long underfloor coolant lines. Air pockets after improper bleeding, debris damage to the radiator and A/C condenser, and aging hoses cause overheating and coolant loss. A coolant flush with the correct bleed procedure every 4–5 years is the minimum. Check the radiator fins and the overflow level when cold.', 'Aluminum spaceframe and body panels: Collision repair requires aluminum-certified procedures, and front and rear clamshells, doors and other panels are scarce and very expensive ($20k–$50k+ for major panels). Hidden structural repair destroys value. Use a non-ferrous-capable paint meter across all panels. Inspect the spaceframe welds, the underbody, the front splitter and frunk floor, and the rear diffuser for crunch damage.', 'R

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch replacement if the PPI shows slip, a high engagement point or no record past about 25k miles ($7,000–$14,000)', 'Crank position sensor and pigtail if not documented ($500–$1,500)', 'Transaxle cooler lines and hoses if original or seeping ($800–$2,000)', 'Engine and transaxle mounts plus rear toe-link/tie-rod ends on 30k+ mile cars ($1,500–$4,000)', 'Supercharger belt, tensioner and idler pulleys ($500–$1,500)', 'Brake rotors and pads if the cross-drilled rotors show cracking ($1,500–$3,000 per axle)', 'Failed gauge replacement, especially the fuel gauge ($500–$2,000 each)', 'A/C compressor or blend-door repair if weak ($1,500–$3,500)']
profiles.market_notes: Mileage band, ownership count and originality drive price most. Sub-5k-mile cars and four-option cars (McIntosh stereo, BBS forged wheels, painted calipers, painted stripes) sit at the top. Driver-grade 25k–50k-mile cars trade at a meaningful discount but are still in collector territory. Heritage Edition (Gulf livery) cars and desirable colors such as Mark IV Red, Midnight Blue and Tungsten carry premiums, while documented celebrity or press provenance adds auction heat. Tunes, pulleys, twin-turbo conversions, non-original wheels and any collision or aluminum-panel repair history lower value with purist buyers, and complete records, window stickers and the original build book support price.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most GTs were driven lightly and stored, so a typical example needs age-driven catch-up regardless of miles. That means tires, battery, all fluids including a properly bled coolant system, gas struts, rubber mounts, toe links, and often the crank sensor pigtail and transaxle cooler lines. Budget about $5k–$12k for a well-kept car, and more if the clutch is undocumented or modifications must be reversed for California registration.

profiles.label: Ford Mustang GT (S197 II, 2011–2014 Coyote 5.0)
profiles.framing: This is a manual (ideally) naturally aspirated 412–420 hp Coyote V8 driver with a solid rear axle. It is cheap to buy, simple to service, and the engine is robust in stock form. For a Carmel buyer, three things matter most: whether the car is California smog-legal as delivered (intakes, tunes, and exhausts are near-universal on these), how healthy the MT-82 manual is, and whether the car has had hard launches or accident repair. Note that 2010 GTs share the S197 II body but use the 4.6L 3V and a Tremec TR-3650 or 5R55S, so evaluate those separately.
profiles.weak_points: ["Getrag MT-82 6-speed manual (all 2011–2014 GTs, Boss included). This is the generation's signature weakness. Known symptoms are notchy or high-effort 1-2 and 2-3 shifts when cold, 3rd and 5th gear lockout or grinding during high-rpm shifts, synchro wear, and 'money shifts' on cars that were launched or tracked. Ford issued several TSBs covering fluid changes and shifter and bushing revisions. Some units were replaced under warranty, and records of that are a positive sign. A used replacement transmission installed runs $2,500–4,000, and a rebuild or new unit $4,000–6,000. Look for dealer warranty transmission repair records and receipts showing a fluid change to the TSB fluid (Motorcraft MERCON LV per the TSB era).", 'Clutch, concentric slave cylinder (CSC), and pedal hang. The internal CSC leaks or fails, and the clutch pedal can stick to the floor or return slowly after high-rpm shifts. That pedal behavior is usually caused by old or aerated fluid, since the clutch shares the brake master cylinder reservoir. CSC replacement requires removing the transmission, so it is usually done together with a clutch: $1,500–2,500 for clutch, flywheel, and CSC at an independent shop. Ask for clutch replacement receipts, which should show OEM vs. aftermarket parts and whether the stock dual-mass flywheel was changed to a single-mass unit. Also confirm brake/clutch fluid service history.', "6R80 6-speed automatic (if equipped). It is generally durable, but it can develop harsh or flared 2-3 and 3-4 shifts, torque converter shudder, and valve body or solenoid faults. Ford called the fluid 'lifetime,' so most units have never been serviced. Expect $250–400 for a fluid exchange, $1,200–2,000 for a valve body or solenoid pack, and $3,500–5,000 for a rebuild. Ask for fluid service records and any TCM reflash.", '8.8-inch rear axle with Traction-Lok LSD. The carbon-disc clutches chatter on tight low-speed turns if the fluid is old or lacks the Ford-spec friction modifier. Pinion and axle-shaft seals weep, and launched cars develop whine or clunk on throttle transitions. A fluid service with friction modifier is $150–250, seals run $250–500 per side, and a carrier or gear rebuild is $1,500–2,800. Look for differential fluid service receipts, especially on cars with the 3.55 or 3.73 gear option.', "Coyote Gen 1 engine wear points. The engine is very durable stock, but there are a few known issues. The familiar 'Coyote tick' (an injector or lifter cadence) is usually benign, but loud knocking under load is not. The powdered-metal oil pump gears can fail on boosted or over-revved engines. The engine can also suffer valvetrain damage from a missed downshift. Minor oil seeps from the timing cover and valve covers are common. On cars over 90,000 miles, ask for spark plug records (the 100,000-mile item). Also ask for oil-change receipts using 5W-20, and for any oil pump or engine replacement records.", 'Cooling system. The water pump weeps at the weep hole or at the timing cover seal. The plastic degas bottle cracks, heater hoses and the thermostat housing age out, and the coolant (Motorcraft Orange) is past its age interval on nearly every example. A water pump job is $500–900, the degas bottle $150–250, and a coolant service $150–200. Check for pink or orange crust at the front of the engine and ask for coolant service records.', "Electronic throttle body and reduced-power 'wrench light' faults. Intermittent limp mode was seen on some cars and was sometimes addressed by Ford service actions or reflashes. Replacing the throttle body costs $350–600. Look for a dealer service history showing throttle body or PCM updates, and scan for stored P2xxx throttle codes.", 'Solid-axle suspension wear by 60,000–100,000 miles or 10+ years. Common items are the rear upper (third-link) control arm bushing, rear lower control arm bushings, and Panhard bar bushings, plus front strut mounts, lower control arm bushings, and sway bar end links. Symptoms are clunks over b

profiles.market_notes: Boss 302 and Boss 302 Laguna Seca models are a separate, collector-priced tier and should not be compared to regular GTs. Among GTs, manual cars bring more than automatics. The 2013–14 refresh (420 hp, HIDs, LED tails) and the Track Pack, Brembo, California Special, and Premium trims add value. Low-mileage, documented, unmodified cars with a clean title command a meaningful premium. Modified cars, especially those with tunes or non-CARB parts, trade at a discount in California because of smog risk and abuse suspicion. Salvage and rebuilt titles, repaints, and evidence of launching or drifting hurt values sharply. Colors such as Grabber Blue, Gotta Have It Green, Race Red, and School Bus Yellow draw some extra interest, while black and silver are plentiful.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 2011–2014 examples are now 10–15 years old. Brake/clutch fluid, MT-82 or 6R80 fluid, differential fluid, and coolant have usually never been changed, regardless of low mileage. Expect to refresh tires by age, the battery, and the rubber suspension bushings, especially the third link, and to sort out any non-CARB modifications before a California smog check.

profiles.label: Ford Mustang Shelby GT500 (S550, 2020–2022)
profiles.framing: The S550 GT500 is a 760-hp, supercharged, DCT-only weekend car. In Carmel it will see cool, damp mornings, Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, and maybe the occasional Laguna Seca track day. It is not a daily commuter, and the stock Cup 2 tires on CFTP cars are poorly suited to cold, wet local roads. Every GT500 of this generation has the Tremec 7-speed dual-clutch, so the lack of a manual is not a defect. What matters most is a stock, never-tuned powertrain with clean DCT history, undamaged carbon-fiber parts and front-end heat exchangers, and correctly handled time-based maintenance on what are often low-mile, stored cars. Confirm remaining powertrain warranty (5yr/60k from the in-service date) for each car. On 2021–2022 cars it can be a real asset.
profiles.weak_points: ["Tremec TR-9070 7-speed DCT. This is the single biggest risk on the car. Owners report clunky or harsh low-speed and reverse engagement, shudder when creeping in traffic, 'Transmission Fault/Service Now' warnings, clutch-slip codes, and some outright transmission replacements. Ford addressed many of these with TCM software updates. Ask for dealer records of TCM reflashes, any clutch or transmission replacement, and a current scan. An out-of-warranty transmission replacement runs roughly $15k–$25k. Cars used for launch control, drag runs, or tuning are at the highest risk.", "DCT fluid and filter. Ford's normal-use interval is long. Many specialists recommend roughly 30–40k miles, or after every few track weekends, because the dual clutches shed material into the fluid. Expect about $500–$900 at a dealer that has the correct fluid and fill procedure. Unknown history on a tracked car is a negotiating point.", "Engine calibration tampering. GT500s are among the most commonly tuned cars on the market: pulley swaps, aftermarket PCM/TCM flashes, E85 conversions. A 'returned to stock' car may still carry a flash history Ford can detect, which can jeopardize powertrain warranty claims. Insist on a dealer FDRS scan confirming factory calibrations. Check for non-stock supercharger pulleys, injectors, or fuel-system parts.", 'Predator 5.2L supercharged V8 and its intercooler (low-temperature) cooling loop. The engine itself has a good record when stock. Watch the separate intercooler circuit: its coolant level, the electric pump, and leaks at the heat exchanger and lines. A weak pump or low coolant causes high intake temperatures and power pull. Pump replacement is about $400–$900. Also listen at cold start for misfires or ticking. Coil and plug issues are modest jobs ($400–$900) but show up sooner on tuned or tracked cars. CA 91-octane fuel works but costs some timing versus the 93 the car is tuned for.', 'Front-end heat exchanger stack. The car runs multiple radiators and coolers behind a low front opening. Stone and curb damage, bent fins, and leaks are common on driven cars. Individual exchangers run about $600–$2,000 installed, and an impact that damages several plus the splitter can reach $4k–$7k. Inspect from underneath with the undertray in view.', 'Carbon-fiber wheels (CFTP and some option packages). The clearcoat chips easily, and curb strikes can cause delamination or cracks that are not cosmetic. Replacements run roughly $3,500–$5,000+ per wheel. Ford specifies particular lug nuts and torque, and wrong hardware or impact-gun abuse damages the lug seats. Inspect inner and outer barrels and spokes in good light.', 'Carbon-fiber aero on CFTP cars: the GT4-style rear wing, front splitter, and wickers. Scrapes from driveways and parking blocks are common. Wing or splitter replacement is about $2k–$6k+, and many owners hide damage with vinyl or touch-up.', 'Brembo brakes, with 6-piston fronts on 16.5-inch (420mm) steel rotors. These are excellent but expensive to service. A front rotor and pad set runs roughly $1,800–$2,800, and a full four-corner job $3k–$4.5k. Track use cracks rotors and cooks fluid. Low-mile stored cars often have overdue brake fluid (2–3 year interval) and rust-ridged rotors from sitting.', 'Tires. CFTP cars came on Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires (305/30R20 front, 315/30R20 rear); other cars on Pilot Sport 4S. Cup 2s wear fast and have poor grip below about 50°F and in the wet, which is a real safety issue on foggy coastal roads. A set costs roughly $2,000–$2,800 installed. Tires older than about 5–6 years should be replaced regardless of tread. Flat-spotting on stored cars is common.', "MagneRide magnetorheological dampers. Dampers can leak or fail, causing 'Check Suspension' messages, a harsh or floaty ride, or oil residue on the strut body. Each damper is about $900–$1,500 installed. Track-driven and high-mile cars are most at risk.", 'Torsen rear differential and half-shafts. Repeated launch-control use,

profiles.market_notes: Factory spec drives price most. The Carbon Fiber Track Pack (carbon wheels, wing, Cup 2s, Recaros, rear-seat delete) typically adds roughly $15k–$30k over a base car with the Handling or Technology packages. The 2022 Heritage Edition and its stripe and color combos carry a further premium, as do strong colors like Twister Orange, Grabber Lime, and Velocity Blue. Under about 1,000 miles is the collector band. Clean 5k–25k-mile drivers trade meaningfully lower and are the right target for this buyer. Tuned or 'returned to stock' cars, Shelby American–modified cars (often voiding Ford warranty), and cars with DCT replacement history without records sell at notable discounts. Remaining factory powertrain warranty and documented TCM updates add real value.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most examples are 3–5 years old with low miles, so the catch-up work is driven by age, not wear. Expect brake fluid, battery, and coolant checks, aging or flat-spotted tires (especially Cup 2s), and any outstanding TCM/PCM updates or recalls. Cars that sat for long periods should get a full fluid baseline and a DCT relearn before any spirited driving.

profiles.label: Honda Acty Truck, 2nd generation (HA1/HA2 550cc, HA3/HA4 660cc E07A)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 2nd-gen Acty is a low-speed utility toy: garden and yard hauling, beach gear, Carmel Valley back roads, and narrow village streets where a full-size truck is a nuisance. It is not a freeway vehicle. It tops out around 55-60 mph and struggles on grades like Carmel Hill on Hwy 1. What matters is a straight, rust-free frame and cab, a healthy cooling system and timing belt, and above all a confirmed path to California registration. Coastal and Okinawa-sourced trucks, repaints and bedliner-coated bodies deserve extra suspicion, because they often hide corrosion.
profiles.weak_points: ["California registration risk is the first gate, not a mechanical one. California has no 25-year emissions exemption, so a 1976-or-newer gray-market import must get through DMV verification and smog/BAR referee scrutiny. Some kei trucks have been refused or later had registrations revoked. A Florida 'Exempt' or other out-of-state title does not guarantee a California plate. Get import paperwork (export certificate, CBP 7501, HS-7, EPA 3520-1) that matches the frame number (e.g. HA4-xxxxxxx), and confirm feasibility with the DMV/BAR before bidding. Worst case is an unregistrable truck worth a fraction of the purchase price.", 'Frame and body rust is the main mechanical killer. Snow-country trucks were salted, and Okinawa or coastal trucks live in salt air. Check the frame rails (especially under the cab and around the rear spring hangers), crossmembers, cab corners, floor pans, door bottoms, rocker seams, the bed floor and drop-side hinges. Bedliner or textured full-body coatings often conceal rot. Patching cab corners and floors runs roughly $800-2,500. A rotted frame usually makes the truck scrap or a $3,000+ project.', 'The cooling system is the classic Acty weak spot. The radiator sits at the front, the engine sits midship under the bed, and long steel coolant pipes and rubber hoses run underneath. The pipes rust through, hoses crack, and air pockets after any service cause overheating unless the system is bled properly through its bleed screws. Overheating leads to E07A head gasket failure, roughly $1,200-2,200 at a kei-savvy shop. Look for receipts for radiator, hoses, coolant service and pipe replacement. Watch for a gauge creeping on hills and for sweet smell or residue under the cab.', 'The E07A timing belt, tensioner and water pump are due every ~100,000 km or 10 years. On a 25+ year-old import with no records, assume the belt is original or of unknown age. Belt failure strands the truck and can cause engine damage, so treat it as non-optional. Expect roughly $500-1,000 parts and labor, more if access through the bed hatch is rusted. Ask for a dated receipt or a belt sticker with the kilometer reading.', 'Valve adjustment (screw-and-locknut) is due about every 40,000 km and is commonly neglected. Symptoms are ticking, rough idle and hard hot starts. It is cheap, about $150-300, but a tight exhaust valve left too long burns. Also expect oil leaks from the valve cover gasket, cam and crank seals and distributor O-ring. These drip onto the midship exhaust and can smell or smoke.', 'Fuel system and carburetion vary by year and trim; verify whether the truck is carbureted or PGM-FI. Carbureted trucks suffer varnish from sitting during export, cracked vacuum lines and choke faults, leading to hesitation and poor cold starts. A carb rebuild or cleaning runs about $200-500. Steel fuel tanks and lines can rust internally on coastal trucks, and a contaminated tank or pump means sputtering under load.', 'Clutch and gearbox: the 5-speed works hard because the truck is always near full throttle. Common faults are worn clutches (slipping on hills when loaded), stretched or binding clutch cables, sloppy shift linkage bushings, and worn 2nd/3rd synchros that grind on fast shifts. A clutch job is roughly $800-1,500. A used transmission swap is $1,000-2,000 plus sourcing time from Japan.', 'On the 4WD driveline (HA4), confirm what the truck actually has. Many use a viscous-coupling full-time system; others are part-time, and some trims have a rear diff lock or an extra-low first gear. Viscous units stiffen with age, causing binding, tire scrub and crow-hopping in tight parking-lot turns. Diff-lock actuators and cables seize from disuse. Front CV boots split; a CV axle runs about $200-450 per side installed. Differentials often have never had fresh gear oil.', 'Brakes are front disc and rear drum, and age-related failures are typical. Rear wheel cylinders weep, drum hardware rusts, rubber brake hoses crack, and brake fluid is often dec
