profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch disc, pressure plate and cable if slipping or high engagement shows up under load', 'Front CV boots or axles and wheel bearings (especially if spacers or oversized wheels were fitted)', 'Shocks and struts, spring shackle bushings, tie-rod ends', 'Radiator replacement or recore and remaining coolant hoses if original', 'Carburetor rebuild (carbureted trucks) or fuel pump and injector service (FI trucks)', 'Exhaust section replacement (midship system rusts)', 'A/C leak repair, recharge or R134a conversion', 'Engine mounts and valve cover gasket or oil leak cleanup', 'Spot rust repair on cab corners, floors or bed before it spreads']
profiles.market_notes: 4WD, a manual gearbox, working A/C, a rust-free frame and documented kilometers carry the most value. Dump-bed or scissor-lift variants and stock, unmodified condition add further premium. Clean stock 4WD examples generally trade around $5,000-10,000, and online auctions can spike higher on hype. Heavy modifications (lifts, big wheels, bedliner repaints, novelty upholstery) are polarizing. For a documented-originals buyer they are a negative and a reversion cost. Title state matters enormously: a truck already registered in California, or with a clear CA-registrable paper trail, is worth meaningfully more to this buyer than an out-of-state 'exempt' or off-road-titled truck.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 25-30 year-old import arrives with unknown service history, decades-old fluids, aged rubber (hoses, belts, brake hoses, bushings, CV boots) and fuel varnish from export storage. Budget roughly $1,500-3,000 for a baseline refresh (timing belt, fluids, brakes, cooling, tires) before treating it as a reliable local runabout. Undo any unsafe modifications as part of that work.

profiles.label: Honda Beat (PP1, 1991–1996)
profiles.framing: The Beat is a right-hand-drive, mid-engine 656cc kei roadster that revs to about 8,500 rpm. For a Carmel buyer it is a low-speed joy machine for Carmel Valley Road, Highway 68 and the backroads, not a commuter. It is slow (~63 hp) and very small in Highway 1 traffic, with no meaningful crash structure by modern standards. The decisive issues are a clean California registration path, rust-free structure (made worse by coastal salt air), and verifiable mileage via Japanese export paperwork. Engine health, cooling-system integrity and soft-top condition come right behind.
profiles.weak_points:
['California registration is the first and biggest risk. Federal 25-year exemptions do not exempt a 1976+ non-US-certified car from CARB/BAR smog requirements. Out-of-state titles (VA, ME, MT etc.) on cars sitting in California are a common workaround, not a solution. Some owners have reached a BAR referee and registered successfully, others have not, and outcomes are inconsistent. Get written confirmation of the path (DMV verification plus BAR referee appointment feasibility) before bidding. Converting an unregistrable car is costly, if possible at all.', "Body rust is the car-killer: rear wheel arches, sills and side-skirt seams, floor pans, rear subframe and suspension mounting areas, door bottoms, the spare-tire well under the front lid, and around the fuel filler. Japanese snow-region cars and cars stored outdoors near the coast suffer badly. Repainted cars ('repainted prior to import') can hide filler. Expect $1,500–$6,000+ for proper structural repair. Demand clear underbody photos or a lift inspection.", 'The long coolant pipes run under the floor from the front radiator to the mid engine. They corrode externally, and their hoses and joints weep. A failure leads to sudden overheating and risks the head gasket. Pipe and hose replacement runs $500–$1,500. Look for crusty pipes, green or white residue, and a coolant level that drops. Also check the front radiator and electric fan operation in traffic.', 'Timing belt and water pump service on the E07A is due every 100,000 km (~62k mi) or about 10 years, whichever comes first. The belt-driven water pump must be replaced at the same time. Expect $600–$1,200 at an indie familiar with kei Hondas. An engine-bay sticker alone is weak evidence, so ask for a receipt or parts invoice. An unknown history means doing it immediately.', 'Engine wear on high-mileage, hard-revved E07As shows up as several symptoms:
- Worn valve stem seals cause blue smoke on cold start or after idling.
- Rings and bore wear show as oil consumption.
- Valve cover and distributor O-ring leaks are common.

A compression test (healthy cylinders read roughly even) and a leak-down test are essential. A rebuild runs $4,000–$7,000. A used imported E07A swap runs $1,500–$3,500 plus labor.', "The PGM-FI ECU's electrolytic capacitors leak with age, a common early-'90s Honda failure. Symptoms include rough or hunting idle, intermittent stalling, a check-engine light, and no-start. Leaked electrolyte can eat the circuit board. A mail-in or local recap costs $150–$400; a board damaged beyond repair means a scarce replacement ECU. Ask whether it has been recapped and inspect the board if accessible.", 'The MTREC individual throttle bodies and idle air control can stick or drift, causing high or erratic idle and flat spots. Vacuum hoses and intake boots crack with age. The distributor (igniter/coil) and an aging fuel pump cause intermittent misfires or no-start. Read OBD-I blink codes from the ECU.', 'The clutch and 5-speed transaxle wear at high mileage. Watch for clutch slip in higher gears. Synchro wear (especially 2nd/3rd) shows as grinding on quick shifts. Worn shift cable and linkage bushings, typical of a mid-engine layout, make the gear lever vague and sloppy. A clutch job runs about $1,000–$1,800; a transaxle rebuild costs more, and parts are mostly Japan-sourced.', 'The soft top and its drains are trouble points. Look for torn fabric, a hazed or cracked rear screen, and failed seals. Clogged body drains let water into the cabin and onto the floor pans, feeding rust and electrical gremlins. A replacement top costs roughly $600–$1,500 plus install. Check for damp carpet, musty smell and staining under the seats.', 'Suspension and brakes are aging items:
- The four-wheel MacPherson struts, top mounts and control-arm bushings are often original and tired, which shows as clunks and wandering.
- The four-wheel discs commonly have sticking rear calipers.
- The parking brake is integrated into the rear caliper

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch replacement if slipping or high-engaging at 100k+ miles', 'Shift cable and linkage bushing refresh to tighten the gear change', 'Strut, top mount and bushing refresh; four-wheel alignment', 'Underfloor coolant pipe replacement if externally corroded', 'Valve cover and distributor O-ring reseal; valve stem seals if smoking on startup', 'Soft top or rear screen replacement if torn, hazed or leaking', 'A/C diagnosis, repair or R134a conversion (optional)', 'Window regulator or motor service; driver seat bolster repair', 'Fuel pump and filter if original and showing signs of weakness', 'Rust repair on arches and sills found during the first underbody inspection']
profiles.market_notes:
US prices typically run about $5k–$12k. Rough or modified cars sit at the low end, and very clean, documented, original examples push into the low-to-mid teens. Special editions command a premium:
- Version F in Aztec Green Pearl
- Version C in Captiva Blue Pearl
- Version Z with aero parts and special colors

Festival Red, Carnival Yellow and Blade Silver are the common standard colors. What moves value most:
- Verified mileage via the export certificate
- Rust-free structure
- Original paint
- Intact Zebra interior
- Factory wheels and steering wheel
- A clean title already registrable in the buyer's state

Aftermarket wheels, MOMO wheels and aftermarket head units are common and slightly negative to the originality-minded. A cheap no-reserve bid on a car with an out-of-state title often reflects registration uncertainty and deferred work.
profiles.catchup_notes:
A typical import has 30+ year-old rubber throughout and has never had a full US-side baseline service. Assume the following need replacing on arrival:
- Coolant hoses
- Vacuum lines
- Bushings
- Brake hydraulics
- Top seals
- ECU capacitors

Plan roughly $2,500–$5,000 in catch-up work beyond the purchase price. Coastal Carmel storage makes immediate underbody rust treatment and covered parking part of that baseline.

profiles.label: Honda CR-V (1st gen RD1, 1997-2001)
profiles.framing: A first-gen CR-V is a simple, durable, Civic-based compact utility. Here it serves as a practical coastal daily for Carmel and an easy-to-wrench beach and Big Sur hauler. It is not an off-roader: Real Time 4WD is a reactive rear-pump system with no low range. Condition matters more than mileage, specifically rust, oil consumption, timing belt history and rear-diff fluid care. A documented, unmodified, rust-free manual 4WD example is the target, and it must pass California smog without an expensive CARB-compliant catalytic converter.
profiles.weak_points: ["Timing belt is an interference-engine wear item. The B20B (1997-98, 126 hp) and B20Z (1999-2001, 146 hp) are both interference designs. Honda's interval is 105k miles or about 7 years, and on these cars age is usually the deciding factor. A snapped belt bends valves, and the repair often exceeds the car's value. Do the water pump, tensioner, cam and crank seals, and drive belts at the same time, for about $700-1,200. Ask for a dated receipt with the odometer reading. A sticker on the belt cover alone is not enough.", 'B20 oil consumption is a known trait. Stuck or worn low-tension oil control rings can burn a quart every 500-1,500 miles. Symptoms are blue smoke on cold start or after idling, oily or fouled plugs, and a sooty tailpipe. Ring and rebuild work runs $2,500-4,500, or about $2,500-3,500 for a used engine swap. Watch the cold-start video for smoke. Ask how often the owner adds oil. Ask for a compression test, and a leak-down test if compression is borderline.', 'Real Time 4WD rear differential depends on its fluid. The dual-pump rear diff needs genuine Honda Dual Pump Fluid (DPSF / DPF II) changed roughly every 30k miles or 3 years. Neglected or wrong fluid causes groaning, shudder or binding on tight low-speed turns such as parking lots and U-turns. A fluid change is $80-150 and often cures it. A worn clutch pack or failed pump runs $600-1,500 used, or more for a rebuild. Mismatched tire sizes or wear between axles also stresses the system. Ask for diff fluid receipts.', 'The 4-speed automatic (only transmission in 1997; optional thereafter) is more robust than later Honda automatics but not immune. Look for flare between 2-3 or 3-4, harsh engagement, and torque-converter lockup shudder. These issues are often worse with non-Honda ATF; it should be Z1, now superseded by DW-1. A used unit installed costs $1,500-2,500 and a rebuild $2,500-3,500. Look for regular drain-and-fill records, and check that the ATF is red rather than brown or burnt-smelling.', 'On the 5-speed manual (1998+ in the US, the desirable spec), check for 2nd and 3rd gear synchro grind when shifted quickly, especially if non-Honda gear oil was used. Honda MTF is correct. Also check for a high or slipping clutch engagement and leaks at the clutch master or slave cylinder. A clutch job runs $900-1,400. Synchro repair means a transmission rebuild, $1,500-2,500, or a used unit.', 'Rust is the main killer of these cars. Check the rear wheel arches and quarter-panel lips, rocker panels behind the plastic cladding, rear subframe and trailing-arm mounts, spare-tire carrier and swing gate lower edge, and floor pan seams. Coastal Carmel fog and salt air keep working on any existing rust. Washington, Northeast and Midwest cars may have seen road salt. Structural rust at the trailing-arm or subframe mounts is a walk-away. Get underbody photos or a lift inspection.', 'The swing-out rear door and its hinges sag over time from the weight of the full-size spare. The result is a rubbing latch, hard closing, rattles, and water leaks into the cargo floor well. Hinge pins and bushings or an adjustment run $100-400. Look for water staining or rust under the cargo picnic table and in the spare well.', 'Ignition distributor problems are common. The igniter or ignition coil inside the Hitachi/TEC distributor fails with heat, causing a hot no-start or stalling. The distributor shaft O-ring leaks oil onto the block. Cap and rotor wear out. A remanufactured distributor is $150-400 in parts. Worn plug wires and cap cause misfires that can fail a California smog test.', "The PGM-FI main relay is a classic Honda hot no-start. Its solder joints crack, so the engine cranks but won't start on hot days, then starts after cooling. Resoldering is cheap and a new relay is $40-100. It is worth carrying a spare.", 'Idle and emissions control parts age out. Watch for a fast-idle thermo valve or IAC valve causing high or hunting idle, a clogged EGR passage on the B20Z, aging upstream and
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Timing belt service if there is no dated receipt within about 5 years or 90k miles: belt, water pump, tensioner, seals and accessory belts ($700-1,200)', 'Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, Honda MTF or DW-1 ATF drain-and-fill (x2-3 for automatics), Honda Dual Pump Fluid II in the rear diff, Honda Type 2 coolant, DOT 3 brake fluid, and power steering fluid ($300-500)', 'Valve lash adjustment on the screw-type rocker valvetrain, with a new valve cover gasket if it is seeping ($150-350)', 'Ignition tune-up: NGK plugs, distributor cap and rotor, plug wires; inspect the distributor O-ring for leaks ($150-350)', 'Tires if they are older than about 6 years by date code. Fit a matched set of four to protect the Real Time 4WD system ($500-800)', 'Inspect and adjust the rear drum brakes
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Engine and transmission mounts, especially the rear and passenger-side hydraulic mounts ($300-700)', 'Front and rear suspension bushings, sway bar links, and possibly struts and shocks ($800-2,500)', 'CV axles or boots if they are torn or clicking ($200-500 per side)', 'A/C service: compressor clutch gap, O-rings, recharge; compressor or condenser if failing ($200-1,400)', 'Radiator replacement if the tanks are seeping, plus heater and radiator hoses ($300-600)', 'Distributor replacement (igniter or coil) or main relay resolder or replacement if there is any heat-related stalling ($100-400)', 'Upstream and downstream O2 sensors or a CARB-compliant catalytic converter if smog readings are marginal ($200-2,000)', 'Rear window regulators or motors and glass run channel cleaning and lubricat
profiles.market_notes: Prices for clean examples have risen sharply. Documented low-mileage manual 4WD cars now reach $10k-15k+ at enthusiast auctions, while average automatics with 150k+ miles trade around $3k-7k. Value is driven by the 5-speed manual, 4WD, a rust-free underbody, originality (paint, steelies or factory alloys, no lift or aftermarket wheels), mileage under about 100k, and a recent timing belt receipt. The EX adds alloys and ABS, and the 2001 SE adds leather and body-color trim. Desirable colors include Tahitian Green, Supermarine Blue, Clover Green and Taffeta White. Single-owner documented cars carry a meaningful premium over unknown-history examples.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most surviving RD1s are 25+ years old and due for a rubber refresh regardless of mileage: timing belt, hoses, mounts, bushings, CV boots and tires. Many also need a full fluid reset with Honda-specific fluids. Budget about $1,500-3,500 to bring a typical undocumented example to a reliable baseline, and more if rust repair or a CARB-compliant catalytic converter is needed.

profiles.label: Honda Civic Si (10th gen, FC1 sedan / FC3 coupe, 2017-2020)
profiles.framing: The 10th-gen Si is a manual-only, turbocharged, front-drive compact with a helical limited-slip differential and adaptive dampers. It is an affordable, efficient enthusiast daily that suits Carmel's twisty coastal roads and Highway 1. The buyer is paying for a stock, un-tuned, unabused example. This platform is heavily modified and often driven hard by young owners, so the drivetrain's history and proof of a stock ECU matter more than cosmetics. The 2020 refresh adds standard Honda Sensing, LED headlights, a roughly 6% shorter final drive and an optional summer-tire HPT package, which makes it the most desirable year to own.
profiles.weak_points: ['Tuning and modification history is the biggest risk on this car. Hondata FlashPro and KTuner flashes, downpipes, intakes, blow-off valves and lowering are extremely common, and a car can be returned to stock before sale. A tune can stress the clutch, the dual-mass flywheel and the 2nd/3rd synchros. Look for a Honda dealer software and calibration check. Signs of past mods include aftermarket clamp marks on the intercooler piping, a non-OEM charge pipe, pinch-weld damage from jacks, or a reflash note in dealer records.', 'The 6MT has well-documented 2nd and 3rd gear grind or crunch, especially on fast upshifts at high rpm and when the gearbox is cold. This is a synchro wear issue that hard driving and abuse accelerate. Fresh Honda MTF often helps. A synchro or transmission rebuild runs $2,500-4,500, or more for a replacement unit. Look for MTF change receipts using genuine Honda MTF.', 'The clutch and dual-mass flywheel (DMF) wear out. Clutches can be worn by 60-90k miles on hard-driven cars. Watch for a high engagement point, slip in 4th to 6th under boost, and rattle or chatter at idle or on takeoff from a worn DMF. Clutch plus DMF costs $1,800-2,800 at an independent shop. Many owners swap to a single-mass flywheel and aftermarket clutch, which is a modification flag for this buyer.', 'Rev hang, the clutch delay valve and the throttle calibration make shifts feel slow and notchy. This is a design trait rather than a failure, but a removed CDV, aftermarket shifter bushings or a short shifter all indicate an enthusiast owner. Confirm whether the clutch hydraulics are stock.', "The L15B7 1.5T is direct-injected and can suffer oil dilution, where fuel ends up in the oil. This is mostly seen in cold climates and short-trip use, and Carmel's mild climate reduces the risk. Signs are a rising dipstick level and a fuel smell on the oil. Look for 0W-20 changes at 5,000-7,500 miles rather than stretched maintenance-minder intervals, and confirm any software update or TSB was done.", 'Direct injection also causes carbon buildup on the intake valves by 70-100k miles. Symptoms are rough cold idle, light misfires and a loss of crispness. Walnut blasting costs $400-800. Spark plugs are often due around 60-100k miles under boost, at $200-350.', 'Boost leaks come from the OEM plastic charge pipe and intercooler couplers, which can crack or pop off, especially on tuned cars. Symptoms are a hiss, low boost, a check-engine light and a limp mode. OEM pipe and couplers cost $150-500. Also listen for wastegate rattle on decel or at idle, which can require an actuator or turbo replacement at $1,200-2,500.', 'Engine and transmission mounts wear, especially the passenger hydraulic mount and the rear torque mount. Symptoms are clunks on throttle tip-in, vibration at idle in gear and wheel hop. Replacement costs $250-700. Aftermarket stiffer inserts are a common mod.', 'A/C condensers and compressors fail on the 10th-gen Civic. Rock damage and leaks were widespread on 2016-2019 cars and led to Honda warranty extensions; 2020 is less affected. Check vent temperature. A condenser costs $600-1,200 and a compressor $1,200-2,000. Ask for records showing any condenser replacement.', 'The adaptive dampers can leak or trigger damper-system warnings, especially if the car was lowered on springs or fitted with coilovers. OEM dampers cost roughly $300-600 per corner installed. Look for a damper warning light, oil on the strut bodies, or a car sitting low.', 'Front and rear brakes, the electronic parking brake and the 235/40R18 tires wear quickly. Summer tires on the HPT package and on 2017-2019 cars wear fastest and suffer on cold roads. Pads and rotors cost $400-900 for all four corners, and a set of tires $700-1,100. Check for curb rash and bent wheels, since the low-profile 18-inch wheels bend easily on rough roads.', 'Electronics and the interior have known niggles. The Display Audio head unit can freeze or reboot, Bluetooth and CarPlay can drop, and the bac
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Engine oil and filter (0W-20 full synthetic), and check the dipstick for a fuel smell and an overfull level', 'Manual transmission fluid change with genuine Honda MTF, unless there is a recent receipt', 'Brake fluid flush (3-year interval) and inspection of pads and rotors on all four corners', 'Engine and cabin air filters', 'Tire replacement if the tires are near 4/32 or past 5 years old, plus a four-wheel alignment to check for lowered or bent suspension', 'Spark plugs if there is no record by around 60k miles (turbo engine)', 'Dealer VIN recall and TSB check, including an ECU software status check', 'A/C performance check, plus condenser inspection for rock damage and leaks']
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch and dual-mass flywheel replacement if engagement is high or there is idle rattle ($1,800-2,800)', 'Engine mount and rear torque mount replacement ($250-700)', 'Intake valve carbon cleaning (walnut blast) if there is rough idle or misfires near 80-100k miles ($400-800)', 'Coolant service (Honda Type 2) per the maintenance minder', 'Rear brake pads and rotors and an electronic parking brake service', 'OEM charge pipe or intercooler coupler replacement if boost leaks appear', 'A/C condenser or compressor replacement on 2017-2019 cars if output degrades', 'Wiper, battery and 12V system checks (the original battery is often weak by year 4-5)']
profiles.market_notes: Unmodified, un-tuned, one-owner cars with dealer service records command a clear premium, and documented stock examples are increasingly scarce. 2020 refresh cars, especially the HPT summer-tire spec, bring the most. Rallye Red, Blazing Orange, Energy Green (2017-18) and Sonic Gray sell faster than black or white. Coupe and sedan are close in value, with the coupe slightly ahead in some markets. Mileage bands matter: under 40k is premium, 50-80k is the mainstream value zone, and over 90k cars are discounted for clutch, synchro and carbon risk. Any evidence of a tune, an aftermarket intake or exhaust, lowering, or a salvage title cuts value sharply and is a walk-away for this buyer.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2017-2020 Si at 60-80k miles is due for MTF, brake fluid, plugs, tires and possibly a coolant service. The original clutch, DMF and engine mounts are near the end of their life on cars driven hard. Budget $1,000-1,500 in first-year catch-up on a well-kept stock car, and much more if the clutch, synchros or tune history are questionable.

profiles.label: Honda Civic Type R (EK9)
profiles.framing: The EK9 is the purest expression of the B-series VTEC formula: ~1,060 kg, a hand-ported 8,400-rpm B16B, a helical LSD, a seam-welded shell, and a 5-speed with the best shift feel Honda ever built. For a Carmel-based driver it is a weekend Highway 1 / Laureles Grade toy that can also do a grocery run, not a daily commuter — no airbag-era safety margin, RHD on US roads, and grey-market parts logistics. What matters most for this buyer is that the car is a genuine, unbutchered EK9 (correct VIN prefix, correct chassis, matching-spec engine) with an honest Japanese auction sheet and a clean, documented US import; cosmetics and bolt-on mods matter far less than shell integrity, theft/VIN history, and whether the engine has been thrashed or swapped. Because these are now 25+ year old imports, the realistic goal is a sorted, documented driver, not a museum piece — but a car with a fabricated chassis story or hidden structural repair is worth far less than the bid suggests.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Identity and import legitimacy: real EK9s carry an EK9-1xxxxxx VIN and a B16B with '00' cylinder-head casting and a specific engine number range. Cloned EK4/EK3/EG shells wearing EK9 badges and B16A engines are a persistent problem, as are stolen/recovered Japanese cars and 'VIN-swapped' shells. Demand the Japanese export certificate (deregistration/'matsusho' document), the auction sheet, the US Customs HS-7/EPA 3520-1 and DOT HS-7 25-year exemption paperwork, the bill of lading, and the US title — and verify the chassis-plate VIN against the paperwork and the stamped firewall/strut-tower number. A wrong or restamped VIN is a walk-away, not a discount.

2) Front-end structural repair: EK9s in Japan were raced and crashed. Replaced radiator core support, replaced hood, aftermarket bumper and non-OEM fenders (exactly the pattern in this listing) usually mean a front hit. Check frame-rail creases behind the bumper beam, seam-sealer disturbance at the rail-to-apron welds, overspray in the engine bay, and mismatched panel gaps. Also confirm the EK9-specific factory seam welding along the strut towers and floor seams is intact — a shell repaired by a Japanese body shop with a donor front clip is common. Proper frame straightening plus OEM panels is $3,000–$8,000; a car already 'repaired' badly is a permanent value hit of $3k–$6k.

3) Rust: JDM cars from snow-belt or coastal Japan rust at the rear wheel-arch lips, the rear quarter behind the arch, the rear subframe/trailing-arm mounting points, the front strut tower tops, the battery tray and fuel-filler neck area, and the rear beam pockets under the spare tire well. Undercoating/'Wax-oyl' sprayed by an importer is often hiding pitting. Budget $1,500–$5,000 for proper arch/quarter repair; structural rust at the rear suspension mounts is a dealbreaker.

4) B16B timing belt, water pump and tensioner: 90k-mile/7-year interval, and an interference engine. A B-pillar sticker or Japanese shaken record is only weak evidence. Want a receipt with belt, tensioner, idler, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance-shaft-free (B16B has no balance shafts) done together — $700–$1,200 at an independent Honda specialist. A snapped belt is an $3,500–$6,000 rebuild.

5) VTEC and valvetrain wear at 90k+ miles: sticking VTEC spool valve / clogged screen causing a P1259 or no upper-cam engagement, noisy exhaust-side rocker, and worn valve guides on cars run hard with long oil intervals. Valve lash must be set every 30k; ticking at idle is normal Honda, harshness plus smoke on overrun is not. Leakdown on all four cylinders is mandatory — healthy is under 8%. A tired B16B that won't pull cleanly to 8,400 rpm means either a top-end refresh ($2,500–$4,000) or an honest rebuild ($5,000–$8,000).

6) Distributor and ignition: OEM TD-series distributor leaks oil from the O-ring into the cap, the internal ignition coil and igniter fail with heat, and the crank/cyl-position sensors inside the distributor cause intermittent no-starts and high-rpm misfires. A genuine Honda distributor is now $400–$700; rebuild kits and no-name units are a common cheap fix that fails again.

7) Engine oil leaks and seals: valve cover gasket and spark plug tube seals, distributor O-ring, oil pan gasket, front and rear main seals, and the VTEC solenoid gasket. On a 25-year-old car expect at least two of these. Individually cheap ($150–$500 each), collectively a $1,000 day.

8) S4C transmission and helical LSD: 3rd- and 5th-gear synchro wear (crunch on fast 2-3 upshifts), and on abused cars worn LSD gears or a whining final drive. Clutch life on a hard-driven EK9 is 50k–80k miles; clutch, pressure plate, release bearing and resurfaced flywheel is $900–$1,500. A rebuilt S4C with LSD is $2,500–$4,500, and a correct EK9 LSD transaxle is getting scarce — a car with an EK4/EG swap transaxle loses the LSD and real value.

9) Suspension and bushings: almost every EK9 has been on coilovers (Tein, Buddy Club, etc.) for decades. Expect blow
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (Honda MTF in the transaxle, correct 10W-30/0W-40, coolant, brake fluid flush); timing belt/water pump/tensioner unless a verifiable receipt with parts and date exists; compression and leakdown-driven decisions; replace valve cover gasket, plug tube seals and distributor O-ring; new OEM-spec plugs, wires, cap and rotor (or full distributor if it leaks or misfires); set valve lash; four matching correct-size tires (185/60R14 or 195/55R15 depending on wheel) — the listing's mismatched 185/65 and 195/55 pairs must all be replaced immediately; full alignment after correcting ride height; brake pads/rotors and caliper slide service; wheel bearings if humming; A/C diagnosis and repair or a decision to live without it; sort or remove any hack alarm/immobilizer wiring. Realistic
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and transmission fluid/synchro assessment, likely clutch job; replacement of tired coilovers with a known damper set plus new top mounts, ball joints, tie rods, and front/rear bushings; radiator, hoses and thermostat if original; fuel pump and filter on a car that sat; exhaust system returned to a quieter, hanger-correct setup; Recaro bolster repair or retrim; replacement of broken climate vents and cracked mirror housing with OEM-used JDM parts; sourcing and fitting the correct EK9 front lip, fenders and hood if the front-end repair was done with non-OEM panels; rust remediation at rear arches and undercarriage with a proper cavity wax treatment for coastal Carmel air. Expect $3,000–$7,000 depending on how much of the front-end and suspension story needs undoing.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by authenticity and chassis honesty: a documented, accident-free, low-kilometer EK9 with the Japanese auction sheet, export certificate, and clean US title trades far above a repaired or clone car. Championship White is the iconic and most valuable color and typically commands a 15–25% premium over Flamenco Black Pearl, Sunlight Yellow (99/00 facelift), and Milano Red; the 1999–2000 facelift with the optional A/C and audio package is slightly preferred as a usable car. Originality of the drivetrain (matching B16B and the LSD-equipped S4C transaxle), intact factory seam welds, unmolested engine bay, and the presence of original Recaros, wheels, wheel, shift knob and front lip move money meaningfully; heavy mods, missing trim, mismatched tires and dead A/C are discounts but also leverage. Under ~$15k in 2024–25 usually signals a repaired shell, unverifiable history, or a dealer flip of a fresh import with no PPI — good, honest examples sit in the $25k–$45k range and exceptional low-km cars go higher.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any 25-year-old JDM import as needing a full deferred-maintenance reset: timing belt/water pump, all seals and gaskets, every rubber hose and bushing, fuel pump and filter, brake and clutch hydraulics, and a complete fluid change regardless of what the seller claims. Coilovers and exhaust fitted a decade ago in Japan are consumables that are almost certainly finished. Budget $4,000–$7,000 in the first year purely to bring a driver-grade EK9 back to a known, safe baseline before spending anything on cosmetics.

profiles.label: Honda Prelude Type-SH (5th gen BB6, 1997–2001)
profiles.framing: The BB6 Type-SH is a manual-only, high-revving H22A4 VTEC coupe with Honda's Active Torque Transfer System (ATTS). ATTS overdrives the outside front wheel to kill understeer, which makes it one of the best-handling front-drive cars of its era. For a Carmel buyer who wants a fun, reliable driver on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, the car stands or falls on three things: an ATTS system that still works, a healthy oil-tight engine with documented timing belt service, and an unmodified, non-abused chassis. The ATTS hardware and Type-SH transaxle are scarce, and Preludes were heavily modified and thrashed. Documented, stock, original-ATTS examples are the ones worth buying.
profiles.weak_points: ['ATTS unit and controls: The planetary/clutch-pack ATTS unit on the transaxle output has its own fluid fill, separate from the gearbox MTF, and that service is frequently neglected. Symptoms include a flashing or steady ATTS light, binding or hopping in tight parking-lot turns, whine or groan under cornering load, and clunks. Failures also come from the linear solenoids, the yaw/lateral-G sensors and the ATTS control unit. Many ATTS-specific parts are discontinued. A used unit or transaxle runs about $1,000–2,500, and installed fixes run about $2,000–4,000. Some owners pull the fuse to hide the light, so confirm the ATTS light illuminates at key-on and then goes out. Ask for ATTS fluid change receipts.', 'Type-SH 5-speed transaxle: Synchros wear, especially 2nd and 3rd. Expect grinding on fast or cold shifts, popping out of gear and bearing whine at high mileage, often accelerated by redline abuse. The SH gearbox is not a simple swap with base-Prelude units. A rebuild or used SH box costs about $1,500–3,500. Look for MTF change records using Honda MTF.', "H22A4 oil consumption: The FRM cylinder liners and ring wear lead to oil burning past 150k, or earlier after overheating or neglect. FRM bores cannot be honed or bored conventionally, so a worn block usually means a replacement engine at about $3,000–5,000 installed. Watch for blue smoke on startup or after long decel, oily spark plug wells or plugs, and frequent top-ups. Get the owner's consumption history, plus a compression or leak-down test.", 'Timing belt service: The interference engine uses a timing belt plus a separate balancer-shaft belt, with tensioner and water pump. The interval is about 105k miles or 7 years. A broken belt bends valves, at roughly $2,500–4,500. The full job with water pump, balancer belt, tensioner and seals costs about $900–1,500. Demand a dated receipt with mileage that lists both belts.', 'Valve clearance: The screw-and-locknut adjusters on the H22 need periodic valve adjustment. Tight exhaust valves cause rough idle, misfires and eventually burnt valves. Loud ticking means loose clearances. An adjustment with a valve cover gasket costs about $250–450. Look for adjustment records, ideally every 30–60k by enthusiast practice.', 'Distributor and ignition: The internal igniter and coil fail, causing intermittent stalling, a hot no-start or misfires. The distributor shaft O-ring also leaks oil. A new or reman distributor or igniter costs about $200–600.', 'PGM-FI main relay: Cracked solder joints cause a no-start in heat or after the car sits in the sun, and the fuel pump fails to prime. The repair is cheap, about $50–150, but it is often misdiagnosed. Listen for the 2-second fuel pump prime at key-on.', 'Common oil leaks: Look at the VTEC solenoid/spool valve gasket and screen, valve cover and plug-tube seals, distributor O-ring, oil pressure switch, cam/crank seals and rear main. Oil on the exhaust manifold, or on the clutch causing slip, is the concern. Individual reseals run about $100–600.', 'EGR and emissions: EGR passages and ports carbon up, triggering P0401. Aging catalytic converters trigger P0420. Both matter for California smog. EGR port cleaning costs about $150–400. A CARB-legal cat costs about $800–1,500.', 'Double-wishbone suspension wear: Look at front compliance and lower arm bushings, upper control arm ball joints (the joint is integral, so the whole arm is replaced), rear trailing arm and toe/compensator arm bushings, and tired shocks. Symptoms are wander, clunks, inside-edge tire wear and poor ATTS feel. A full refresh costs about $800–2,000.', 'Engine and transmission mounts: The rear and passenger-side mounts collapse or tear, especially on manuals that were launched hard. Symptoms are a clunk on throttle on/off, heavy shift-lever movement and vibration. Expect about $300–700.', 'Clutch hydraulics and clutch: The master and slave cylinders weep, and the clutch slips or has a high engagement point. A clutch with flywheel cos
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil, Honda MTF in the transaxle, ATTS unit fluid (Honda ATF), coolant (Honda Type 2), brake and clutch fluid, and power steering fluid ($300–500).', 'Replace tires older than about 6 years (any with date codes from 2018 or earlier are aged out) and get a four-wheel alignment ($700–1,100).', 'Valve clearance adjustment and valve cover gasket if undocumented in the last 30–60k ($250–450).', 'Spark plugs, distributor cap and rotor, and a cabin filter if undocumented ($150–300).', 'Timing belt, balancer belt and water pump job if there is no receipt within about 105k miles or 7 years ($900–1,500).', 'Clean the sunroof drains, and inspect and replace wiper blades and bulbs ($50–150).']
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Suspension bushing and ball-joint refresh plus shocks as wear is found ($800–2,000).', 'Engine and transmission mount replacement ($300–700).', 'Oil leak reseal: VTEC solenoid gasket, distributor O-ring, oil pressure switch ($150–600).', 'Distributor or igniter replacement if intermittent stalling appears ($200–600).', 'Clutch master or slave cylinder replacement ($200–500).', 'Brake pads, rotors and a brake fluid flush ($400–800).', 'EGR port cleaning or catalytic converter ahead of a California smog check if codes are present ($150–1,500).', 'A/C recharge and leak check, or compressor work ($150–1,200; low priority in the Carmel climate).']
profiles.market_notes: The Type-SH is manual-only and brings a premium over base Preludes, with a further premium for 1999–2001 cars (200 hp, refresh). Price is driven most by originality (stock ECU, intake, suspension and wheels), a functioning ATTS, single or long-term ownership with receipts, and accident-free history. Sub-100k documented cars can reach roughly $15k–25k+ at enthusiast auctions. Driver-grade 150k–200k+ cars typically trade in the $6k–12k band. Desirable colors include Premium White Pearl, Electron Blue Pearl and Milano Red. Carfax accident entries, aftermarket parts, ATTS lights and smoking engines discount heavily.
profiles.catchup_notes: At 25+ years old, most BB6 Type-SH cars need a rubber-and-fluids catch-up even with good records: suspension bushings, mounts, coolant hoses, radiator, and aged tires. Expect ATTS and MTF fluid changes, a valve adjustment, and fixes for small oil leaks around the distributor and VTEC solenoid. Budget $1,500–3,000 in the first year beyond any ATTS or transaxle surprises.

profiles.label: Hummer H3T (2009–2010, incl. Alpha V8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the H3T is a driver-grade midsize 4x4 pickup for Highway 1, Big Sur fire roads, beach access, and hauling gear. It is not an appreciating asset, whatever sellers claim. The Alpha's 5.3L V8 (LH8) is the powertrain to have; the 5-cylinder trucks are slower and carry their own cylinder-head and valve concerns. What matters most is a rust-free frame and brake lines, a transmission that shifts cleanly, a working full-time 4WD system, and a clean path to California smog and registration. Expect roughly 13–15 mpg, poor rearward visibility, and tight parking in Carmel village.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Frame, rockers and underbody corrosion: the H3T rides on a GMT355-derived chassis shared with the Colorado and Canyon. Trucks from salt states (NC, the Midwest, the Northeast) often show scaling on frame rails, crossmembers, spring hangers and rear shackle mounts, and rust in the rocker panels below the doors where mud packs in. Surface scale is normal. Flaking, perforation or patched rails are walk-away items, because frame repair can run from $1,500 to well past the truck's value. Ask for high-resolution underbody photos taken after a pressure wash. Any listing that admits 'corrosion on underbody components' needs an in-person or lift inspection.

2) Steel brake and fuel lines: GM's uncoated steel lines rust along the frame rail and above the fuel tank, and failure is sudden. Full brake line replacement costs about $600–1,500. Fuel lines and tank straps add $300–900.

3) 4-speed automatic behind the V8: this is a heavy-duty 4L60-E-family Hydra-Matic. Past 120k miles, typical failures are the 3-4 clutch pack, the sun shell, and torque-converter shudder. Watch for flare or slip on the 2-3 or 3-4 shift when hot, delayed engagement, or harsh 1-2 shifts. Many trucks never had a fluid service. A rebuild or reman unit costs about $2,800–4,500 installed. Look for fluid-and-filter receipts and check that the fluid is not dark or burnt-smelling.

4) Full-time 4WD transfer case: this is a 2-speed BorgWarner unit with a center differential. Adventure-package trucks have the 4:1 low range and lockers, and the seller says this example has neither. Failure modes are a 'Service 4WD' message, selector switch or encoder faults, fluid leaks, and a chain stretch clunk. Many owners never change the fluid. Repairs run about $300–700 for an encoder or switch and $1,500–3,000 for a case rebuild or replacement.

5) Front IFS (torsion bars): watch the lower ball joints, upper control arm ball joints (integrated into the arm), tie-rod ends, front hub bearings, and CV boots. These trucks are heavy, and ball joints are a known wear item past 100k. Fresh ball joint boots, as on the example truck, usually mean the joints themselves are original. Ball joints and arms run about $600–1,500. Hub bearings are about $250–500 per side, and CV axles about $250–500 each.

6) Front differential and rear axle: expect leaks at the front diff output seals and vent, and at the rear axle shaft seals and pinion seal. Rear wheel bearings hum or roar at speed. Diff services are often skipped. Seals and bearings run about $200–800 per axle; gear damage from a run-dry diff is $1,500+.

7) LH8 5.3L V8 (Gen IV aluminum block, no AFM in this application): it is generally durable, but has a few common faults. The oil pressure sensor and its screen leak or fail, giving an erratic or zero gauge reading; this costs about $150–400. Exhaust manifold bolts break, causing a cold-start tick (about $400–1,200). The rear main seal and oil pan gasket seep (about $800–1,800 if the transmission must come out). Knock sensors sit under the intake (about $400–800). Confirm the eighth VIN digit is 'L' for the LH8.

8) Cooling system: the water pump weeps at the weep hole, the radiator's plastic end tanks crack, and Dex-Cool sludges if neglected. A water pump and thermostat run about $400–800, and a radiator about $400–700. Overheating on an aluminum V8 risks head gaskets.

9) Instrument cluster stepper motors: this is a common GMT355-era failure. The speedometer, tach, fuel or temp needles stick, read wrong, or drop dead. Cluster repair or rebuild costs about $150–500. Verify all gauges sweep and track.

10) Sunroof drains and water intrusion: clogged or disconnected sunroof drains are a well-known H3 problem. Signs are a stained headliner, wet front footwells, a musty smell, and corroded under-seat connectors and floor pans. Drain clearing costs about $100–300; a headliner, carpet and electrical cleanup can reach $500–2,000.

11) HVAC and accessories: watch for blend door or mode door actuat

profiles.market_notes: The Alpha V8 commands a clear premium over 5-cylinder H3Ts. Adventure-package trucks, with the 4:1 low range and electronic lockers, sit at the top of the driver market alongside very-low-mile examples. Mileage and rust drive price most. Clean, rust-free southwestern or West Coast trucks under ~90k miles can bring two to three times what a 140k+ mile salt-state truck brings. Documented transmission and driveline service, an unmodified spec, and bright original colors (such as Solar Flare Metallic) help modestly. Treat seller claims of guaranteed appreciation as sales talk. Value the truck as a used midsize 4x4 with a parts-sharing GM drivetrain and some orphan-brand trim and body parts.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2009–2010 H3T at 120–150k miles has original driveline fluids, original lower ball joints and hub bearings, and some degree of underbody corrosion. Budget roughly $1,500–3,500 in the first year to service the transmission, transfer case and differentials, refresh the front end, and treat or replace rusty brake lines. Salt-state trucks bought for California use deserve a one-time underbody cleanup and rust-proofing.

profiles.label: Infiniti FX50 (S51, 2009-2013)
profiles.framing: The S51 FX50 is a 390-hp V8 performance crossover built on Nissan's FM platform. For a Carmel driver it is a comfortable, quick, all-weather daily and weekend car that is at home on Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and occasional Tahoe runs. It has real cargo utility but is not an off-roader, and expect roughly 14-17 mpg on premium fuel. The core drivetrain is robust. The risks are in the aging interior materials, the complex chassis electronics (especially on Sport-package cars), and a 7-speed automatic that Nissan called 'lifetime fill'. Prioritize documented fluid service and a clean full-module scan over trim level.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Dashboard bubbling and delamination: the soft-touch upper dash on S51 FX (and related G/M/EX interiors of the era) is well known for bubbling, lifting, and turning sticky, typically around the defroster area, above the center screen, and above the glovebox. Heat and UV make it worse, and it shows up at any mileage by year 8-10. Look for repairs or patching (as seen in the example listing's comments), dash covers hiding damage, and any record of an Infiniti goodwill or extended-coverage replacement. A proper dash panel replacement runs roughly $1,500-3,500 installed; a professional reskin runs $600-1,200.

2) Electronic steering column lock (ESCL): the Nissan/Infiniti ESCL of this era can fail to disengage, causing a no-start condition with a steering-lock warning, often intermittent at first. Nissan issued service campaigns and bulletins for this family of cars. Ask for campaign completion or an ESCL replacement or reprogramming record. Out-of-pocket cost is roughly $400-1,200.

3) 7-speed automatic (Jatco JR710E/RE7R01A): marketed as lifetime fill, but fluid degraded past 60-80k miles can bring harsh 2-3 or 3-4 shifts, flare on upshift, delayed engagement, or torque-converter shudder. Valve body or solenoid faults also occur. Look for Matic S (or approved equivalent) drain-and-fills with receipts every 30-60k. Valve body work runs $1,200-2,500; a rebuild or replacement runs $4,000-7,000.

4) VK50VE V8 oil leaks: the engine is often misprinted in listings as 'VQ50VE' and is the VK-family V8. It is generally durable. Common age items are valve cover gaskets and spark-plug tube seals, which leak oil into the plug wells and cause misfires, plus seepage at the timing chain cover and oil cooler. Valve cover gaskets run $700-1,400 per pair with labor. Timing cover resealing is $1,500+.

5) VVEL, timing chain, and exhaust manifold: the VVEL (variable valve event and lift) system on the intake side can throw control-shaft sensor or actuator codes (P1090-P1093-type families). Chain rattle or guide wear can appear on engines run on long oil-change intervals. Exhaust manifold ticking from cracks or gasket leaks, a known VK-family trait, is worth listening for cold. VVEL actuator or controller work runs $800-2,000; exhaust manifolds run $800-2,000 per side.

6) Rear Active Steer (RAS), Sport-package cars: the rear-steer actuator and its control module can fail or leak, setting a warning light and making rear-end handling feel odd. The actuator runs $1,500-3,000 installed; used units are an option.

7) Continuous Damping Control (CDC) adaptive dampers, Sport package: the electronically adjustable shocks leak or fault with age and are expensive, roughly $600-1,200 per corner OEM. Some owners convert to passive dampers, which the buyer should treat as a modification.

8) ATTESA E-TS AWD transfer case and differentials: the electronically controlled transfer clutch and the front and rear diffs are frequently never serviced. Watch for AWD warning lights, binding in tight parking-lot turns, or whine. Fluid services are cheap ($150-400). A transfer case or diff replacement runs $1,500-3,500.

9) Front suspension wear: this is a heavy car, and the standard 21-inch wheels make it harder on parts. Front lower control arm compliance bushings, rear upper arms, and sway-bar links wear by 60-90k, causing clunks, brake shimmy, and uneven tire wear. Arms and bushings run $600-1,500 plus an alignment.

10) Wheels and tires: 265/45R21 tires cost $1,200-2,000 per set, and the rims bend and curb easily. Check tire date codes, since low-mileage cars often have 8+ year-old tires. Straightening or refinishing a wheel runs $150-300.

11) Brakes: this 4,300-lb car goes through pads and rotors fairly quickly and can develop pulsation from warped or overheated rotors. Expect $600-1,200 per axle for OEM-quality parts.

12) HID and AFS adaptive headlights: xenon bulbs, ballasts, and the swivel motors in the adaptive front lighting system (AFS) fail with age. Lens

profiles.market_notes: The FX50 was produced in small numbers and carries a meaningful premium over FX35/FX37 examples. Low-mileage, one-owner, documented cars sit at the top of the market, roughly $20-25k in 2026 (the example sold at $23,500 with 41k miles). Typical 80-120k-mile cars trade far lower. Technology and Deluxe Touring equipment adds value, and Sport-package cars (CDC, RAS, sport seats) appeal to enthusiasts but carry higher repair exposure. 2012-2013 refresh cars are marginally preferred. Dash condition, documented transmission service, and a clean scan move price more than color. Black Obsidian and dark interiors are common; lighter interiors show dash and wear issues more visibly.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 2009-2013 FX50s treated the transmission, transfer case, and differential fluids as lifetime-fill and are due for driveline fluid catch-up, plus coolant, brake fluid, and aged tires, even at low miles. At 13-17 years old, expect to address rubber bushings, valve cover and plug tube seals, HID components, and dash material condition within the first year. Budget about $1,500-3,000 of catch-up on a typical example beyond the risk reserve.

profiles.label: Infiniti G37 (V36: Coupe, Sedan & Convertible, 2008-2013)
profiles.framing: The V36 G37 is a front-mid-engine, rear-drive Nissan FM-platform car with the 330 hp VQ37VHR. For this buyer it is a usable, comfortable sports-GT daily driver, and the Sport 6MT coupe is a cheap substitute for a 370Z with a back seat and a nicer cabin. What matters is the health of the VQ37VHR, especially oil pressure, the VVEL system, and the timing-cover oil gallery. On manual cars, the clutch hydraulics matter, and every example needs bushings and aged rubber sorted. For a Carmel buyer, the car must also pass California smog and registration as an out-of-state vehicle, so any aftermarket intake or exhaust must either carry a CARB EO or be returned to stock before purchase or immediately after.
profiles.weak_points: ['VQ37VHR oil gallery gasket: a small gasket in an oil passage behind the front timing cover can harden and leak internally. The result is low oil pressure at hot idle, VTC/VVEL-related codes (P0011/P0021, P1090-series), rattle or ticking on hot restarts, and eventually chain or cam-phaser wear. It is most common past about 60k miles or 10+ years, but age alone can trigger it on low-mile cars. The repair requires pulling the front timing cover; plan on $2,000-$3,800 at an independent shop, more if chains or guides are done at the same time. Ask for oil pressure readings or a receipt showing the gasket was replaced.', 'VVEL (variable valve event and lift) faults: the actuator motors, VVEL control module, and control-shaft position sensors can fail. Symptoms are a check-engine light (P1090/P1091/P1092/P1093, P1088), rough or limp running, and reduced power. Costs run about $800-$2,000 per bank for actuators. A stored or pending VVEL code is a negotiation item; intermittent codes after battery work are sometimes benign, but they need diagnosis.', 'Valve cover gaskets and spark plug tube seals: these weep with age, so expect oil on the cover edges and in the plug wells. Ignition coils then fail with misfire codes (P0300-P0306). Gaskets cost about $500-$900 including intake plenum removal, and coils about $300-$700 for a set. Plugs are a 105k-mile item but should be checked on any old car.', 'Timing cover, front crank seal, oil pan, and rear main seepage: low-use cars can leak more because the seals dry out. Seepage at the timing cover may also point toward the gallery gasket job. Look underneath for wetness on the upper and lower pans and at the bellhousing.', '6MT clutch hydraulics: on the CD009-based 6-speed, the concentric slave cylinder (CSC) is inside the bellhousing. Its fluid sits near the exhaust and can overheat, so the clutch pedal sticks or stays down after high-rpm shifts or hard driving. The fixes are an updated clutch line, a damper-delete line, and fresh high-boiling-point fluid. A failed CSC means transmission removal: $1,200-$1,800, or about $2,000-$3,200 if the clutch and dual-mass flywheel are done at the same time, which is usually wise.', 'CD009 6MT synchros and shift feel: early units can grind going into 3rd and 2nd when cold or on fast shifts, and shift effort is notchy. Transmission fluid service helps; synchro rebuilds run about $2,000-$3,500. Drive it cold and hot, with both fast and slow shifts.', 'Automatic transmissions: 2008 coupes use a 5-speed (RE5R05A); 2009 and later cars use a 7-speed (RE7R01A). Watch for harsh or late shifts, flare on the 2-3 or 3-4 upshift, and valve-body or solenoid issues. Fluid should be changed at 60k miles or less; a valve body or solenoids cost $800-$2,000. Ask for fluid service records.', "Electronic steering column lock (ESCL): the lock can fail, causing a 'steering lock malfunction' or no-start/no-unlock condition, and it can strand the car. The fix is about $400-$1,200 depending on the part revision and dealer programming. Check the VIN for open campaigns or recalls, and cycle the start/stop button repeatedly during the PPI.", 'Front suspension bushings: the compression (tension) rod bushings and lower control arm bushings crack, causing clunks over bumps, braking shimmy, and inner tire wear. The front upper control arms and rear upper arms also wear. Expect $500-$1,500 for bushings or arms plus an alignment. 19-inch Sport cars show the wear sooner.', 'Sport package brakes (Akebono 4-piston front, 2-piston rear) are excellent but expensive to maintain. Pads and rotors cost $900-$1,600 for all four corners with OEM-grade parts. Check for rotor lip, warping, or pulsation, and for caliper seals on low-use cars.', '4WAS (four-wheel active steer) on some Sport-package automatic cars: the rear steering actuator and its sensors can fail, causing a warning light. Used or rebuilt actuators are $800-$2,000 installed. Confirm whether the car has 4WAS and that it shows no warnin

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Valve cover gaskets and plug tube seals if weeping, plus coil replacement if misfires appear', 'Front compression rod and lower control arm bushings or arms, with alignment', 'Brake pads and rotors depending on condition, plus caliper service on long-stored cars', 'Manual transmission fluid and rear differential (VLSD) fluid change, or automatic fluid service', 'Updated clutch line or CSC refresh if the pedal sticks after spirited driving', 'Oil gallery gasket replacement if the oil pressure test or codes indicate it', 'Window regulator or index recalibration, and sunroof drain cleaning', 'Headlight ballast or bulb replacement or lens restoration as needed']
profiles.market_notes: The 6-speed manual coupe with the Sport package (19-inch wheels, Akebono brakes, viscous LSD, sport seats) is the most desirable configuration, with IPL cars at the top. Automatic sedans and AWD G37x cars trade at a steep discount. Documented one-owner, low-mileage examples with records draw a meaningful premium, especially on auction platforms. Modifications generally reduce value and California saleability, while included factory parts partly offset that. Proof that the oil gallery gasket, clutch, and bushing work has been done adds real value; a clean but undocumented 100k+ mile car should be priced as if those jobs are due. Ordinary drivers trade far below pristine low-mile 6MT coupes.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most V36 G37s are now 13-18 years old, so treat any car without records as due for coolant, brake/clutch fluid, transmission and diff fluids, a battery, tires, and front bushings. That is roughly $1,500-$3,000 of catch-up work before any big items. Very low-mileage cars still need this age-based work and should be screened carefully for the oil gallery gasket and dried-out seals. Cars headed for California registration also need smog-legal intake and exhaust.

profiles.label: International Harvester Scout II (incl. Traveler, Terra, SSII)
profiles.framing: This is a hand-built-feeling, body-on-frame 1970s 4x4 that the buyer will drive on the Monterey Peninsula, Carmel Valley Road, and the occasional beach/fire-road run — not a garage queen and not a stock-market substitute. What matters most is metal: a Scout II is essentially a rust-and-documentation purchase wrapped around a very simple, very rebuildable drivetrain. Mechanicals (304/345 V8, TF727 or T-19, Dana 20, Dana 44s) are cheap and well-supported by the aftermarket; a rotten rear quarter, floor, or frame rail is what turns a $29k truck into a $50k truck. Because coastal California air is hard on these, a Scout that has lived near the ocean without proper undercarriage care should be judged more harshly than mileage or cosmetics would suggest.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rear quarter panels and the rear 'kick-up' area behind the rear wheels are the classic Scout II rot zone — the inner/outer quarter sandwich and the rear wheelhouse trap mud and never dry out. Any car described as having 'some typical Scout rust' should be assumed to have this. Proper cut-and-weld repair with quality reproduction panels runs $3,000–$8,000 per side once paint blending is included; bondo-and-fiberglass patches are common and disqualifying at this price point.", 'Floor pans, footwells, and the seat-belt/seat-mount reinforcements rust from the top down (leaking windshield gasket, cowl vent, and door seals) and from the bottom up. Pull the carpet or mats; look for fresh undercoating or seam sealer hiding perforation. Floor pan replacement $1,500–$3,500.', 'Frame: the boxed rails are usually decent but rot at the rear spring hangers, the rear crossmember, and where the body mounts perch. Body mount bushings (12 points) collapse and let the tub shift, causing door-gap and hood-alignment weirdness. New mount kit $150–$400 in parts, a full day of labor; frame rail section repair $2,000–$5,000 and a value cliff.', 'Tailgate, rear hatch/glass frame, and the tailgate lower channel rot from the inside out; drain holes plug. A good used or repro tailgate is $600–$1,500 and often needs paint.', 'Windshield frame, cowl, and A-pillar corners: the windshield surround rusts under the gasket and leaks into the cowl and kick panels. Repair means glass out and welding — $1,500–$3,000 with glass and paint.', "Engines: the IH 304/345/392 V8s are torquey and durable but low-compression and thirsty (10–13 mpg). Common issues are cracked exhaust manifolds, hardened valve stem seals (blue smoke on startup), rear main seepage, and timing chain stretch past ~90k. Parts supply is aftermarket-dependent (IH Parts America, Super Scout Specialists, Scout Light Line); a full rebuild is $5,000–$8,000. Ask for a compression/leakdown record, not just 'runs great'.", 'Fuel system: the original Holley 2210/2300-series two-barrel is finicky and often replaced with a Motorcraft 2100 or Edelbrock. Original dual side-mounted fuel tanks rust, sending units fail, and the selector valve and steel lines corrode — expect $600–$1,500 to sort tanks, lines, pump, and sender. Sniff for gas smell in the cabin and under the rear.', "Cooling: 304 + TF727 combinations run hot in traffic; original radiators, fan clutches, and rotted heater cores are common. 'New radiator' is a good sign but confirm the fan clutch, shroud (often missing), water pump, and hoses were done as a system — $600–$1,200 for the rest.", 'Electrical: 40+ year old harnesses go brittle behind the dash and at the bulkhead/engine bay connectors; ammeter-based charging circuits, headlight switch, and turn-signal switch are common failure points and a real fire risk. Look for a documented harness replacement or at minimum clean, non-crispy, non-Scotch-locked wiring. Full harness $1,500–$3,000 installed. Points/Prestolite ignition is usually (and sensibly) converted to Pertronix or HEI.', 'Steering: Saginaw box wear, worn steering shaft rag joint, sagging Pitman/idler geometry and worn tie rod/drag link ends give the famous Scout wander. A rebuilt box plus full linkage rebuild is $1,200–$2,500 and transforms the truck. Also check the steering column mount and the frame-side box mounting area for cracks.', 'Brakes: front discs from 1974-on, drums prior; master cylinders, rubber flex lines, rear wheel cylinders, and the vacuum booster all age out. Sticky rear drums and a long pedal are typical. Full system refresh $1,200–$2,500. Confirm the parking brake actually works.', 'Drivetrain: the Chrysler TF727 automatic and T-19/T-428 four-speeds are stout; the Dana 20 transfer case leaks from the rear seal and gets sloppy shift detents. Dana 44 front (closed knuckle on early, later units too) and Dana 44/Dana 60 rear are strong, but front axle U-joints, knuckle seals, and wheel bearings are frequently overdue
profiles.immediate_repairs: Assume a full fluid and filter service (engine, TF727 with pan drop and filter, Dana 20, both diffs, brake fluid flush), all rubber brake flex lines plus a master cylinder, a carb rebuild or Motorcraft 2100 swap with fresh fuel filter and rubber lines, ignition tune (cap/rotor/wires/plugs or a Pertronix/HEI conversion), full steering linkage inspection with tie rod ends and rag joint as needed, new door/window/tailgate weatherstrip and a windshield gasket reseal, body mount bushing replacement, and battery/charging cleanup including the ammeter circuit. Budget $2,500–$5,000 at an independent shop, less if you do it yourself.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Expect a Saginaw steering box rebuild and possibly a steering shaft, front axle U-joints and knuckle/wheel bearing service, a cooling system round-out (water pump, fan clutch, shroud, heater core), exhaust from the manifolds back including cracked manifold repair, fuel tank and sender work, seat foam and interior trim, and localized rust repair on the rear quarters/floor once you know how deep the 'typical Scout rust' really goes. $4,000–$9,000 is realistic; a proper quarter-panel and floor job alone can eat all of it.
profiles.market_notes: Values are driven almost entirely by metal quality, documentation, and how honest the presentation is: a rust-free Arizona/California truck with the original line-setting ticket and receipts can be double a rusty one with identical mileage. Traveler and Terra long-wheelbase bodies and SSII/Rallye trim carry premiums, as do factory 345/392 V8s, four-speed manuals, factory A/C, and desirable two-tone paint; automatics are normal and not a penalty on a truck like this. Mileage matters far less than a documented engine/trans rebuild and evidence of professional rust repair. At $29k the market expects either a solid, well-documented driver or a truck with clearly disclosed and quantified rust — 'some typical Scout rust' with no photos is a price-negotiation lever, not a description.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 45-year-old Scout II that has not had a documented recommissioning needs the full age-related sweep regardless of mileage: all rubber (brake lines, fuel lines, coolant hoses, weatherstrip, body mounts, suspension bushings), the wiring harness assessed for brittleness, and every fluid changed. Assume $3,000–$6,000 of catch-up in year one on a good example, and treat any 'some typical rust' language as an open-ended line item until you have seen it on a lift.

profiles.label: Jaguar E-Type / XKE Series 2 (1969-1971, 4.2L six)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, a Series 2 E-Type is a weekend and fair-weather car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the Monterey events. It should be driven and maintained, not trailered. The Series 2 is the most usable E-Type, with a better cooling system, better brakes, a full-synchro gearbox and more comfortable seats. US cars carry Stromberg carbs and emissions equipment that cost them some power. Structural soundness (sills, floors, front frame, rear suspension mounts) matters far more than paint. A tired but honest, unrestored or well-documented car is a better driver buy than a shiny car with unknown metalwork under fresh paint.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural rust in the monocoque is the number-one risk. The E-Type tub gets much of its strength from the inner, outer and center sills, floor pans and transverse crossmembers. Check the castellated sill seams, the floor-to-sill joints, the footwells under the carpet and the seat-pan crossmember. Doors that sag, or door gaps that change when you jack the car, mean structural rot. Proper sill and floor work runs about $15k-40k+. A full tub restoration runs $60k-120k+. Ask for lift photos and any metalwork receipts with photos taken during the work. Fresh undercoating or new carpet over the sills is a yellow flag.', 'Rear structure: the radius-arm mounting points on the rear floor crossmember, the rear inner and outer wheel arches, the boot floor and spare-wheel well, and the rear valance. Rot at the radius-arm mounts is a safety issue, because the rear suspension locates there. Repairs run roughly $3k-12k depending on extent. California cars are usually better, but coastal fog cars and East Coast transplants can be bad.', "Bonnet (hood) and front frame: the huge one-piece forward-tilting bonnet rusts along its lower edges, the side valances, the headlight areas and the bonnet hinge/subframe. A replacement bonnet plus fit and paint costs about $10k-20k. The engine and front suspension hang on a bolted tubular steel front frame attached to the bulkhead ('picture frame'). Check it for kinks from accidents or bad jacking, cracks near the mounts, rust inside the tubes and loose or wrong bolts. Frame repair or replacement with alignment runs about $5k-12k.", 'Bulkhead, footwells and A-posts rust from windshield, scuttle and soft-top leaks and from heater-box drainage. Pull the carpets and check the footwells, the inner A-post bottoms and the battery tray area (battery acid). Paint bubbling at the base of the windshield pillars is a warning sign. Repairs run $3k-10k+.', "4.2L XK twin-cam six: an S2 engine number should carry the 7R prefix (suffix -8 or -9 indicates compression). The engine is durable if cared for, but look for low oil pressure (healthy is about 40 psi at 3,000 rpm hot, and should not drop near zero at hot idle), worn top and bottom timing chains (rattle at idle; the top chain is adjusted via a snail-cam tensioner), out-of-spec bucket-and-shim valve clearances, and head-gasket failure from past overheating. Corrosion in the aluminum head's water passages and seized head studs can turn a simple head-gasket job into an $8k-15k job. A full engine rebuild runs about $20k-35k. Rear crank (rope-type) seal leaks are near-universal. A slow drip is acceptable, but a steady leak means engine-out work. Get compression or leakdown numbers and a hot oil-pressure reading.", 'Cooling: the S2 has a larger crossflow radiator, twin electric fans and an enlarged nose intake, but these cars still overheat in traffic and on hot Carmel Valley days if the radiator is silted, the fan thermoswitch or relay has failed, or the water pump is weak. Check hoses, the header tank and the heater valve. Sustained overheating leads to head-gasket and head damage. Budget $800-2,500 to sort a tired system with a recored radiator, water pump, hoses, thermostat and fan switch.', 'US-spec fuel and emissions: US S2 cars use twin Zenith-Stromberg 175CD carbs with emissions plumbing. Diaphragms crack, the throttle linkage wears, and the cross-over/emissions hardware is often half-removed. Many cars have been converted to triple SUs, which counts as a modification for this buyer. Also check for fuel-tank sediment and rust, perished rubber fuel lines (a fire risk), and electric fuel pump failure. Carb rebuild and sync runs $600-1,500. A tank and line refresh runs $800-2,000.', "Gearbox and clutch: the S2 manual is Jaguar's own all-synchromesh 4-speed. Watch for worn synchros (2nd especially), jumping out of gear and bearing whine. Clutch replacement requires removing the engine and gearbox, so it costs roughly $4k-7k. Clutch master and slave cylinders leak and
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter, gearbox oil, limited-slip-correct diff oil, coolant flush, and brake/clutch fluid flush (about $400-900)', 'Tires if older than about 8-10 years, including the spare; correct-size radials balanced for wire wheels (about $900-1,800)', 'Brake hydraulic safety inspection: flex hoses, front caliper seals, servo function, and working handbrake (about $500-2,000, excluding inboard rear work)', 'Fuel system safety: replace rubber fuel lines and filter, inspect the tank and pump, rebuild or sync the Stromberg carbs as needed (about $500-2,000)', 'Cooling system baseline: pressure test, check fan thermoswitch and relays, hoses, thermostat, and verify the radiator is flowing (about $300-1,500)', 'Ignition tune: points, condenser, plugs, leads, distributor
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['IRS drop for inboard brake pads/discs/calipers, handbrake calipers, diff output seals, U-joints and cage mounts if records are absent or seals are weeping (about $2,500-6,000)', 'Clutch master/slave cylinder replacement and hydraulic hose (about $400-1,000)', 'Front suspension refresh: ball joints, wishbone bushes, rack mounts and gaiters, wheel bearings (about $1,500-4,000)', 'Timing chain adjustment, or chain/tensioner replacement if noisy (about $500 for adjustment, $3,000-6,000+ if the head must come off)', 'Soft top, frame adjustment and weatherstrip replacement to stop leaks that rot the floors (about $1,500-4,000)', 'Exhaust system replacement with a correct-style system (about $1,200-2,500)', 'Radiator recore and water pump if cooling margins are marginal (about $800-2,000)', 'Re
profiles.market_notes: Body style drives value most. Roadsters (OTS) bring the most, then Fixed Head Coupes, with 2+2s well behind. Series 2 cars trade below Series 1 and 1.5, but driver-quality S2 roadsters still commonly trade roughly $60k-110k, with top restorations higher. Treat these figures as rough mid-2020s bands to be checked against current sales, not fixed values. Matching numbers (chassis, engine, gearbox and body, ideally confirmed by a Jaguar Heritage certificate), documented rust-free structure, quality of past metalwork, a manual gearbox and desirable original colors all move price up. Converted carbs, non-original engines, poor restorations, and A/C or 2+2 bodies move it down. A low opening bid on a no-records survivor usually reflects uncertainty about structure and mechanicals, which the buyer must resolve with a PPI.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical unrestored or old-restoration S2 needs a full rubber, fuel-line, hydraulic and cooling refresh, often $5k-12k, before it is a trustworthy Highway 1 driver. Many also need an IRS drop for neglected inboard brakes and seals. Treat any car without documented recent structural inspection as a possible metalwork project, and keep the reserve intact until a lift inspection confirms otherwise.

profiles.label: Jaguar F-Type V6 (X152, 2014–2020, 3.0 Supercharged incl. S / P380)
profiles.framing: A supercharged V6 grand-touring sports car that suits Highway 1 and Carmel Valley roads. It is louder and more theatrical than a Cayman and costs less to buy. Ownership cost is driven less by the engine's core durability than by age-related plastics, coolant parts, electronics and expensive brakes and tires. For a documented, unmodified driver, the job is to find a car whose cooling system, leaks, electronics and underbody have been inspected and recorded, and to remember that a low-mileage, older car still has age-related problems.
profiles.weak_points: ['Coolant system plastics on the AJ126 3.0 supercharged V6 are the biggest age-related risk, and they age by years more than by miles. The concerns are the plastic coolant crossover/outlet pipes in the engine valley under the supercharger, the rear-of-engine pipes, the thermostat housing, quick-connect fittings and the expansion tank. Symptoms include a sweet coolant smell, white crust on top of the block or around the supercharger, slow coolant loss and an overheating warning. Any pipe in the valley requires removing the supercharger, typically $1,500–$3,500 at an independent and more at a dealer. Look for receipts showing pipes replaced with updated parts, ideally aluminum-upgraded or latest-revision OEM, and for coolant pressure-test results.', 'Water pump: the pump fails or weeps at the weep hole, commonly between 50k and 90k miles or 7–10 years. Signs are dried coolant trails below the pump, bearing noise and temperature fluctuation. Repair runs $900–$1,800, often done with the thermostat. Ask for records, or budget for it on cars older than 8 years regardless of mileage.', "Supercharger drive: the Eaton TVS supercharger's coupler/isolator wears and causes a rattle or diesel-like clatter at idle, especially warm. The repair is $600–$1,500 with the supercharger out, so it is smart to combine it with any valley coolant work. The supercharger bypass valve or actuator can also cause boost-related faults and P-codes.", 'Oil leaks: cam cover gaskets, the oil filter housing/oil cooler gasket, the front timing cover and the oil pan perimeter all seep with age. The cam covers also carry the integrated PCV/breather. A failed PCV diaphragm causes a whistle or hiss, a rough idle, lean codes (P0171/P0174) and high crankcase pressure, and the fix is usually a cam cover replacement. Typical cost is $700–$2,000 depending on which side and how many covers. Look for wetness at the gasket lines under the engine cover and on the undertray.', "ZF 8HP automatic (8HP45/8HP70 family): the plastic mechatronic connector sleeve/adapter commonly leaks transmission fluid. The part is cheap but the job runs $250–$500 including the fluid top-up. The transmission is marketed as 'lifetime fill', but a fluid and pan/filter service at about 60–80k miles or 8–10 years ($500–$900) is good practice. Harsh 2–3 or 3–2 shifts and slow engagement call for a software check and a fluid level check.", 'AWD driveline (2016+ AWD cars): leaks at the transfer case and front differential seals, and fluids that are rarely serviced. A clunk on tight low-speed turns can indicate driveline wind-up or a transfer-case issue. Fluid service is about $300–$600. A transfer case replacement is a $3,000+ event.', 'Adaptive Dynamics dampers (standard on S): units weep oil, and fault messages can come from the damper or its wiring. Each damper costs $700–$1,400 installed. Front lower control arm and rear knuckle bushings crack with age, showing as clunks, tramlining or uneven tire wear. Arms run $400–$900 per side.', 'Brakes: Super Performance Braking (380mm front / 376mm rear iron, red or black calipers) works very well, but rotors and pads run roughly $1,200–$2,200 per axle at an independent. The optional carbon-ceramic system costs $10,000+ to replace, so verify rotor condition and wear indicators on CCB cars. Brake fluid that is older than 2–3 years needs replacing whatever the mileage.', 'Tires: staggered 19 or 20-inch Pirelli P Zero or similar performance tires wear quickly and cost $1,400–$2,200 a set. On low-mileage cars the original tires are often 6–9+ years old by date code, hardened and possibly flat-spotted. They are unsafe for spirited driving and should be replaced regardless of tread depth.', 'Electrical and body hardware: the deployable flush door handles fail through the motor, microswitch or a frozen mechanism, at $400–$1,200 per side. Faults also show up in the deployable rear spoiler motor, the switchable active-exhaust valve actuators (stuck flap, rattle) and the
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace tires if date codes are older than about 6 years, regardless of tread depth.', 'Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, brake fluid flush, and coolant inspection and pressure test, with a coolant flush if age is unknown.', 'Load-test the 12V battery and charging system, and replace the battery if it is weak or older than 4–5 years.', 'Run an all-module scan, clear and verify faults, and complete any open recalls and software updates at a Jaguar dealer.', 'Inspect the valley and rear-of-engine coolant pipes, thermostat housing and water pump for crust or weeping, and repair any active seep before it fails on the road.', 'Check for a leak at the transmission mechatronic connector sleeve, and replace the sleeve if wet.', 'Test the deployable door handles, rear spoiler and active
profiles.repairs_12mo: ["Preventive replacement of the coolant crossover/valley pipes and thermostat housing if records don't show it, ideally combined with supercharger coupler replacement while the supercharger is off.", 'Water pump replacement on cars older than 8 years without records.', 'Cam cover gasket or cam cover replacement for oil seepage or PCV breather failure.', 'Transmission fluid service, plus transfer case and front differential fluids on AWD cars.', 'Brake pads and possibly rotors on Super Performance or standard systems, depending on measurement.', 'Front lower control arm or bushing replacement if clunks or uneven wear appear.', 'Door handle mechanism or motor repair as the handles age.', 'Adaptive damper replacement if one starts weeping.', 'Clean and re-seal hatch, roof or convertible drain
profiles.market_notes: Price hierarchy runs base 340hp V6 < S/R-Dynamic 380hp V6 < V8 R < SVR, and coupes generally hold value slightly better than convertibles. The rare 2016–2017 six-speed manual (RWD V6 only) carries a meaningful premium, but the ZF 8-speed automatic is the normal configuration, so an automatic is not a value penalty here. Very low mileage, full service history, a window sticker, desirable options (Super Performance Braking, Premium/Vision packs, panoramic roof, Meridian, carbon-ceramics) and colors other than gray or white support higher prices. Known coolant-pipe work done, clean underbody condition and California or dry-state history add confidence. Salt-state underbody corrosion, sparse records, aftermarket exhaust or tunes, and stored module faults push prices down.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even very low-mileage examples are now 5–11 years old. Plan on new tires, a battery, a brake fluid flush and coolant service, plus close attention to the plastic coolant pipes and water pump, which age by years rather than miles. A typical catch-up bill runs $2,000–$4,000. It rises to $5,000–$7,000 if valley coolant pipes or the supercharger coupler need doing, or if salt-belt hardware must be replaced.
