profiles.label: Lexus LC 500 / LC 500h (first generation, 2018–2026), incl. Inspiration Series and limited editions
profiles.framing: The LC 500 is a heavy (about 4,300 lb), beautifully built grand tourer with a naturally aspirated 2UR-GSE V8. For a Carmel driver it is an ideal Highway 1, Big Sur and Carmel Valley Road car with Toyota-grade durability, not a track tool or an investment play. The drivetrain is the least of the worries. What matters is the cosmetic and consumable liabilities of a low, wide car: matte or premium paint, 21-inch forged wheels on run-flats, carbon roof, and big brakes. Software and recall status, storage history, and warranty in-service date also matter on near-new examples. Automatic is the only transmission offered (10AT on the V8, multi-stage hybrid on the 500h), so it is not a mark against any listing.
profiles.weak_points: ['Aisin 10-speed automatic (LC 500): 2018–2020 cars are known for busy shifting, hunting on light throttle, and low-speed 1-2/2-3 clunks or flare. Lexus issued ECU/TCM reflashes, and 2021+ cars received revised calibration. Mechanical failures are rare but not zero, and an out-of-warranty valve body or unit replacement runs roughly $6,000–12,000. Look for dealer records showing transmission software updates and any shift-quality complaints with their resolution.', 'Run-flat tires on staggered 20- or 21-inch wheels (21-inch is 245/40RF21 front, 275/35RF21 rear): the tires are expensive ($2,000–3,000 per set), wear the rears quickly (often 10–15k miles), and degrade with age even on low-mile cars. There is no spare. Check DOT date codes; anything over about 6 years old or with uneven inner-edge wear should be budgeted for replacement, along with an alignment.', '21-inch forged wheels (Inspiration Series, Performance Package and many limited editions): they curb-rash easily and can bend on potholes, which causes vibration at 60–75 mph. Refinishing runs $250–450 per wheel, and an OEM forged replacement can exceed $1,500–2,500 each. Inspect barrels and lips, not just faces.', 'Matte paint (Smoke Matte Gray on the 2026 Inspiration Series; some other limited colors): it cannot be polished, compounded or spot-repaired. Any scratch or chip-correction means a full-panel repaint at a qualified shop ($3,000–7,000+ per panel, harder to match on flake matte). PPF must be a matte/stealth film. Installer quality matters: look for knife cuts at panel edges, contamination or dust trapped under the film, lifting edges, and gloss patches. Get the PPF invoice showing the film type, and inspect in direct sunlight.', 'Carbon-fiber roof (Performance Package, Inspiration Series): the CFRP clearcoat can haze or yellow with sun exposure and is essentially non-repairable short of replacement, which is a five-figure job. Glass-roof cars should be checked for seal condition and water ingress at the headliner.', 'Lexus Dynamic Handling active rear steering (where equipped): failures are uncommon, but an actuator or control fault brings a warning light and a $3,000–5,000+ repair plus a specialized alignment. Scan for stored codes and confirm there is no off-center steering wheel or crabbing after any alignment work.', 'Active rear spoiler (Performance-type cars): the motor or actuator can fail or get stuck. It is testable via the manual button, and a repair runs roughly $1,500–3,000.', 'Adaptive Variable Suspension dampers: these can weep or fail at higher mileage (typically 50k+), causing clunks, a floaty ride or AVS warnings. Expect $900–1,500 per corner installed. Inspect the shock bodies for oil misting.', 'Large brakes (6-piston front, 4-piston rear): pads and rotors are costly. A dealer pad-and-rotor job runs $1,500–2,500 per axle. Brake fluid is often neglected on low-use cars, and squeal is a common complaint. Check rotor lip and thickness, plus fluid service date (every 3 years).', '12V battery and storage issues: the trunk-mounted 12V battery drains during long storage, and low voltage causes random warning lights, telematics faults and no-start. An AGM replacement runs $300–500. Cars that sit, as many LCs do, may also show flat-spotted tires and stale fluids.', '2UR-GSE V8: very durable. At roughly 80–120k miles, expect the typical Toyota V8 water pump weep (pink crust at the timing cover) and valve cover or cam-cover seepage. Water pump service runs about $1,200–2,000. Low-mile cars mostly need storage-related care rather than repairs.', 'Recalls and campaigns: 2018–2020 LC models were included in the Denso low-pressure fuel pump recall (stalling or no-start risk), and there have been other software and electrical campaigns. Verify completion by VIN on every car. 2018–2020 cars also use the Remote Touch touchpad interface; later years added touchscreen and phone-integration updates. Confirm all infotainment, camera, HUD and Mark Levinson function
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Verify all open recalls and campaigns by VIN and schedule completion (fuel pump on 2018–2020)', 'Engine oil and filter service (0W-20 full synthetic) unless just documented', 'Load-test the 12V battery and replace it if weak or original on a 5+ year old car; fit a battery maintainer if the car will sit', 'Check DOT dates and replace run-flat tires if aged out, flat-spotted or worn on the inside edges; four-wheel alignment afterward', 'Brake fluid flush if more than 3 years old or undocumented', 'Full module scan (Techstream-level) and clearing of stale codes; dealer software updates for transmission and infotainment if not already applied', 'Near-new examples: inspect PPF edges and matte paint condition, confirm first complimentary service status, and address any installer defects throug
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Rear tires, or a full set, on driven examples ($2,000–3,000 for 21-inch run-flats)', 'Brake pads and possibly rotors on cars over 30k miles ($1,500–2,500 per axle at dealer)', 'Wheel refinishing for curb rash ($250–450 per wheel)', 'Cabin and engine air filters, wiper inserts', "Transmission fluid exchange and limited-slip differential fluid service around 60k miles despite 'lifetime' fill claims", 'Adaptive damper replacement if weeping on higher-mile cars ($900–1,500 per corner)', 'Coolant and water pump inspection or service on 80k+ mile cars; spark plugs due around 120k', 'Matte-safe detailing and PPF maintenance; recurring cost for matte cars']
profiles.market_notes: LC 500 V8 cars command a large premium over the LC 500h, and coupes and convertibles trade closely, with limited editions on either bringing the most money. Inspiration Series, Structural Blue and other numbered or limited editions carry strong premiums. That premium has grown as production winds down, so final-year (2025–2026) near-new examples can trade near or above original MSRP while early 2018–2019 cars sell far lower. 2021+ cars (revised suspension and transmission calibration, weight reduction, updated infotainment) are preferred over 2018–2020. Performance Package content (carbon roof, rear steer, active wing) adds value. Clean single-owner dealer records, original or well-documented paint, quality matte-appropriate PPF, and sub-15k mileage move price most; curbed wheels, aged tires or any paintwork on matte cars are significant deductions.
profiles.catchup_notes: Typical 2018–2020 cars are now 6–8 years old and often low-use. Expect aged-out original run-flats, a tired 12V battery, brake fluid never changed, and possibly missing transmission or infotainment software updates and open recall work. Near-new examples (2024–2026) need little beyond storage-related checks and PPF/paint verification, but confirm the warranty in-service date and complimentary maintenance status at purchase.

profiles.label: Lexus LS 460 (XF40, 2007-2017)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LS 460 is a quiet, very durable full-size cruiser for Highway 1, Highway 68 and Bay Area or Los Angeles runs. Its 1UR-FSE V8 and AA80E 8-speed routinely pass 200k miles when maintained. Engine longevity is not the risk. The money goes into the heavy, complex chassis and comfort systems: front suspension arms, air suspension on equipped cars, the electronically controlled brake system, and many luxury actuators. Collision history, records and a full Lexus-level scan matter more than mileage. A documented, accident-free, rust-free West Coast car is worth a real premium over a cheap example with a vague history.
profiles.weak_points: ['Front suspension arms and bushings are the signature LS 460 wear item. Upper control arms and the front lower No.1/No.2 arm bushings crack and tear, often starting around 60-90k miles or 10+ years regardless of mileage. Symptoms are clunks over driveways, wandering at highway speed, shimmy under braking, and inner or outer tire wear. Look for receipts naming specific arms. A full front arm refresh with alignment runs about $1,200-2,000 with quality aftermarket parts and $2,500-4,000 with OEM parts at a dealer.', "Air suspension is standard on LS 460L models and the 2010-2012 Sport package, and was available on some other trims. Coil-spring cars avoid it. Air struts leak at the bellows with age (10+ years), causing the car to sit low on one corner after parking, 'Check Air Suspension' messages, and an overworked compressor that then fails. Expect about $700-1,500 per corner aftermarket or $1,500-2,500 per corner OEM installed, and about $600-1,200 for a compressor. Ask for records and check ride height after an overnight sit.", 'The electronically controlled brake system uses a brake actuator and booster/pump with an accumulator. It can fail with a pump that runs repeatedly or for a long time, a buzzing noise, a soft or inconsistent pedal, and brake/ABS/VSC warnings. Repair costs about $2,000-4,500 depending on parts source. Brake fluid neglect makes it worse, so look for brake fluid flushes every 2-3 years. A Techstream-level scan of the brake module is the only reliable screen.', 'Front brake rotors warp or show uneven pad deposits, producing a steering-wheel shake at 50-70 mph braking. It is very common on these heavy cars. Pads and rotors cost about $600-1,200 per axle. Rule out worn front control arm bushings before blaming the rotors, because the two symptoms overlap.', "The AA80E 8-speed was marketed as 'lifetime fill.' Neglected units show harsh 2-3 or downshift engagements, flare, hunting, or torque converter shudder at light throttle. Drain-and-fill with Toyota WS fluid is about $250-500 per service, and two or three cycles are often needed to refresh it. A replacement or rebuilt transmission runs $4,500-7,500. Records of any ATF service before 100k miles are a plus.", 'The 1UR-FSE water pump weeps or fails, usually somewhere between 80k and 130k miles. Look for pink crust around the pump and timing cover, a sweet smell, and a coolant level that drops slowly. Pump plus thermostat costs about $800-1,500. Toyota SLLC coolant should be changed at 100k/10 years and then every 50k miles. Ask for coolant service records.', 'Engine oil leaks show up at the timing chain cover, valve covers and cam housing seals on higher-mileage or older cars. Valve cover gaskets cost about $500-1,000. A timing cover reseal is a large job at about $1,800-3,500, so price it in if the PPI finds active seepage. On 2007-2008 cars, confirm the valve spring recall was completed.', 'Engine and transmission mounts are hydraulic and leak with age. The symptom is vibration felt in the seat and steering wheel at idle in Drive, plus a clunk on shifts. Replacement is about $400-1,200 depending on which mounts.', 'Adaptive (AFS) HID headlights can lose the swivel/leveling motor, ballast or bulb, and older lenses haze and collect moisture. Watch for an AFS OFF light flashing at startup and uneven or misaimed beams. Repairs range from about $150-400 for bulbs and ballasts to $800-2,000+ per complete headlight assembly.', 'The comfort and convenience actuators are numerous and expensive to fix individually. Soft-close door and trunk closer motors fail at about $300-800 each. Also test the power rear sunshade, ventilated and heated seat fans and elements, the power tilt/telescope column, and memory functions. Test every button. Rear-seat climate and massage packages on L models add more failure points.', 'AWD models (LS 460 AWD and LS 460L AWD, 2008+) add a front differential, transfer case and front CV axles. Torn front CV boots and neglected transfer-case

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Spark plugs at about 120k miles, or if the interval is undocumented (about $400-800)', 'Water pump and thermostat if there is weeping, or preemptively around 100k+ miles', 'Front rotors and pads if a braking shimmy persists after suspension work', 'Air strut or compressor replacement on air-suspension cars showing slow leak-down', 'Engine and transmission mounts if there is vibration at idle in Drive', 'Valve cover gaskets or other oil leak repairs found at the PPI', 'AFS headlight motor, ballast or lens restoration', 'Soft-close door or trunk actuators, seat ventilation fans and other comfort-feature repairs', 'A second ATF drain-and-fill if the first fluid came out dark', 'Rear upper control arms and sway bar links if worn']
profiles.market_notes: The 2013-2017 facelift (spindle grille, updated interior, F Sport) commands a clear premium. Earlier 2007-2012 cars are the value play, commonly about $7k-15k depending on mileage and history. Clean titles with no reported accidents, California or other rust-free history, one or two owners with dealer records, and sub-100k miles bring the strongest money. Accident history, especially a towed or 'disabling' front hit, and salt-state corrosion should take a meaningful discount. L long-wheelbase and Sport/air-suspension cars carry extra air-suspension risk, while RWD coil-spring cars are the simplest and cheapest to own. The Mark Levinson audio, Comfort and Executive packages add appeal but also more parts that can fail.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-15 year old LS 460 has been oil-changed but not much else. Expect to catch up brake fluid, ATF, coolant and AWD fluids, plus a front suspension arm refresh and alignment, for roughly $2,000-4,000 total at an independent shop. Air-suspension cars and anything with prior front-end collision repair should be budgeted at the high end or above.

profiles.label: Lexus LX 470 (J100, 1998–2007)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LX 470 is the long-haul family/adventure truck: a 100-Series Land Cruiser with a bulletproof 2UZ-FE V8, full-time 4WD with a locking center diff, and enough leather and sound deadening to make Highway 1 and I-5 runs painless. Bought right, it is a 300k-mile vehicle; bought wrong, it is a rusty AHC-warning-light money pit with a $1,500 starter job hiding under the intake. What matters most here is a documented maintenance trail (timing belt/water pump, fluids, front axle service), a genuinely clean underbody, and an honest answer on the hydraulic suspension — either working and serviced, or converted with receipts and quality parts. Coastal Carmel salt air makes a rust-free California/Southwest history worth real money over a Northeast truck with a 'protected' frame.
profiles.weak_points: 1) AHC/TEMS hydraulic suspension is the defining risk. The nitrogen accumulators ('globes') lose charge by 100–150k miles, giving a harsh ride, slow raise/lower, and eventually an AHC warning light; globes run ~$150–250 each (four) plus labor, height control cylinders, the pump/accumulator assembly, and the height sensors add up fast — a full factory refresh is commonly $2,500–4,500. AHC fluid should be flushed every ~60k with Toyota AHC fluid; look for flush receipts and for the truck to cycle Low→N→High smoothly with pressure readings within spec (Techstream). Many trucks, like the example, have been 'AHC deleted' to conventional coils/shocks (OME, Dobinsons, Slee brackets) — that is an accepted and often preferable fix, but demand parts receipts, correct front spring rate, proper rear conversion hardware, and confirmation the dash lights/controls were addressed; a cheap delete with worn-out donor springs rides badly and sags. 2) Timing belt on the 2UZ-FE is due every 90k miles/9 years — always replaced with water pump, idler/tensioner bearings, thermostat, cam/crank seals and drive belts; $900–1,600 at an independent. A 2006 with a 2022/92k belt is on the clock by date, not miles, so budget it again around 2031 or sooner. 3) Starter is buried under the intake manifold: the part is ~$300 but labor makes it a $1,200–1,900 job; slow/clicking cranks or a hot-start hesitation means plan it, and do the intake-area hoses, PCV, and knock sensors while it is open. 4) Front axle service is the classic neglected item — birfield/CV joints, inner axle seals, knuckle wiper seals and wheel bearing repack; symptoms are grease slung on the inside of the wheels, gear-oil weeping from the knuckle, or a clicking on full-lock turns; a proper both-sides knuckle rebuild is $1,200–2,200. 5) Steering: power steering pump and high-pressure hose leaks, and on AHC trucks the pump also feeds the suspension, so a weeping pump is a two-system problem; sector shaft/box play and worn idler arm bushing cause the wandering 'Land Cruiser vagueness' — box, idler arm, and drag link/tie rod ends together are $1,000–2,000. 6) Suspension bushings and lower ball joints: original ball joints at 150k+ are a genuine safety item (use Toyota/555, not cheap aftermarket); upper/lower control arm bushings and sway bar bushings clunk from 120k. 7) Rust: rear frame section above the spring perches/rear crossmember, frame rails near the leaf-less coil mounts, rear quarter inner arches, hatch lower edge and tailgate seam, brake and fuel lines, and the rear bumper mounts — Northeast/Midwest trucks need the frame probed with a pick, not just photographed; a 'Woolwax/Fluid Film applied' note is good hygiene but can also mask scale. 8) Cooling and leaks: original radiator end tanks crack and the OEM radiator seeps at 120–180k ($500–800 installed); valve cover gaskets, oil cooler lines, front and rear main seals, and the oil pan (RTV, not gasket) commonly weep by 150k. 9) HVAC: rear heater lines corrode, blend-door/servo actuators fail causing one-side-cold, and the heater core is a dash-out job ($1,200–2,000); check both front and rear A/C blow cold and that the rear unit actually works. 10) Electronics: Mark Levinson amplifier and the 6-disc changer fail, the factory nav/display screen pixelates or goes dark, and the aging head unit is a $600–1,500 problem to solve properly (many owners fit a modern unit, which affects the 'unmodified' box but not the truck's integrity). 11) Interior wear items: sagging headliner, cracked dash top on sun-belt trucks, driver seat bolster and steering wheel leather wear, power antenna failures, and third-row latch/strap breakage; also door-lock actuators and the sliding-glass moonroof drains. 12) Driveline: rear driveshaft double-cardan and slip yoke wear causing vibration at 45–65 mph, propeller shaft flange bolt fretting (Toyota TSB), and differential/transfer case breather hoses; ATF (A343F on pre-'05, A750F on '05–'07) should have drain-and-fil
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid reset: engine oil, transfer case, front/rear differentials, transmission drain-and-fill, brake fluid, coolant if not pink/recent, and AHC fluid flush if still hydraulic. Replace the battery and terminals if age unknown, all four wipers, cabin/engine air filters, serpentine belt if undated. Expect a front-end refresh: lower ball joints, idler arm bushing, tie rod ends and an alignment if steering is vague ($800–1,600). Tires are commonly date-expired even with tread left — budget $1,000–1,400 for a set of 275/65R18 all-terrains. Fix any active AHC/VSC light, and address the usual minor leaks (valve covers, oil pan RTV weep) plus a rear main inspection. On a Northeast truck: dry-ice or needle-gun the frame, neutralize, prime, and re-cavity-wax before the first coastal winter ($800
profiles.repairs_12mo: Timing belt/water pump service if the current one is over ~7 years old regardless of mileage ($900–1,600). Starter replacement done proactively with intake off if cranking is at all lazy ($1,200–1,900). Front axle knuckle rebuild with birfields, inner seals and bearing repack if grease slinging or knuckle weeping ($1,200–2,200). Radiator and upper/lower hoses if original. AHC globes (all four) plus pump/height sensor attention if the truck is still hydraulic and rides harshly ($1,500–3,000), or a proper coil conversion with quality springs/shocks if going that route ($2,000–3,500 installed). Rear driveshaft double-cardan rebuild or replacement for highway vibration, control arm and sway bar bushings, blower/blend actuator work, headliner re-stretch, and a decent audio/nav solution if the M
profiles.market_notes: The 2003–2007 facelift trucks carry a clear premium, and 2005–2007 most of all for the VVT-i 4.7, 5-speed automatic, and updated interior/nav; a clean 2006 with sub-100k miles, two owners, and full records is the top of the market. Documented service (timing belt with water pump, AHC flushes or a receipted quality conversion, front axle service) moves price more than cosmetics, and a genuinely rust-free Western truck is worth $3,000–6,000 over an equivalent-mile salt-belt example. AHC that works and has been maintained appeals to purists; a well-executed delete is neutral-to-positive for most buyers and removes the biggest liability, while a broken AHC with lights on knocks thousands off. Third row, Mark Levinson, and locking center diff are expected on later trucks; conservative colors, tan/ivory interiors in good shape, and stock 18s help, while lifts, big tires, and bumpers narrow the buyer pool.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any J100 as 18–28 years old first and low-mileage second: rubber, hoses, belts, bushings, tires, and the AHC/power steering fluid circuits age out on the calendar even at 97k miles. A typical honest example needs $3,000–6,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year — fluids everywhere, front-end wear parts, a timing belt reset by date, cooling system refresh, and frame/underbody cleanup and cavity waxing if it spent time in the salt belt.

profiles.label: Lexus LX 570 (J200, 2008–2021)
profiles.framing: The J200 LX 570 is a Land Cruiser 200 with a luxury interior and hydraulic AHC/AVS suspension. For a Carmel buyer it is a long-lived, comfortable, capable daily driver and road-trip truck that can pass 300k miles if maintained. The 3UR-FE V8 and the transmission are rarely the problem. The expensive surprises come from the hydraulic systems (AHC suspension and the brake booster), secondary air injection on earlier trucks, and the lifts, wheels and overland builds many owners bolt on. Favor stock-height trucks with working, serviced AHC and real receipts over 'built' trucks priced as if the mods add value.
profiles.weak_points: ["AHC (Active Height Control) hydraulic suspension. The four wheel spheres ('globes'), the pump-side accumulator, the AHC shock/strut bodies, and the height sensors age out from roughly 100–150k miles or 12+ years. Symptoms include a harsh or bouncy ride, slow or uneven height changes, a flashing height indicator, sagging overnight, and wet shock bodies. Budget $1,500–2,800 for spheres plus accumulator at an independent shop, and $3,500–7,000+ for AHC shocks and a full refresh. A coil conversion (OME, Dobinsons and similar) costs $2,500–4,500 but is a modification. Ask for AHC fluid flush and sphere pressure-test receipts.", 'Lifted AHC trucks. These are raised with height-sensor link adjusters, torsion-bar re-indexing, or spacers, as in the example listing. The lift changes CV and upper-control-arm angles and alignment, and it confuses headlight leveling. It accelerates CV boot tears, ball joint wear and inner axle wear. Ask for the lift receipt, the exact method used, and a post-lift alignment printout. Returning a truck to stock costs about $300–1,500 depending on method.', 'Secondary Air Injection (SAI) pumps and switching valves on 3UR-FE trucks, mainly 2008 to early-2010s. Water intrusion and carbon cause the pump or valves to fail, setting P2440, P2442, P2444, P0418 and related codes. The truck may go into limp mode and will fail California smog. Expect $1,200–3,500 depending on whether one or both valves plus the pump are replaced. Some years had extended Toyota coverage, now long expired. Ask for replacement records or a clean scan with SAI readiness complete.', 'Hydraulic brake booster pump and accumulator (not a vacuum booster). Symptoms are the pump running or buzzing excessively, brake/ABS/VSC warning lights, and a hard pedal after sitting. The pump-and-motor assembly or accumulator costs about $1,500–3,000 installed. Brake fluid must be replaced on schedule; old fluid shortens booster life.', '3UR-FE water pump and thermostat. Weeping at the pump weep hole leaves pink or white crust on the timing cover and a slow coolant loss, typically 90–150k miles. Replacement runs $700–1,500 with the thermostat and Toyota SLLC coolant. Ask for water pump receipts on any truck past about 120k.', 'Cam tower, timing cover and valve cover seepage on the 3UR-FE. A slow oil seep at the cam tower seams, with oil on the heads or a burning smell, is common with age. A cam tower reseal is a $1,500–3,000 labor-heavy job; valve cover gaskets run about $500–900. Seepage is usually monitor-only unless oil is dripping onto the exhaust.', 'Radiator and cooling system aging. The plastic tanks crack, and the radiator carries an integrated transmission cooler circuit. Budget $700–1,400 for a radiator, hoses and a coolant service. An overheating event on a heavy V8 truck is a deal-breaker without records.', "Transmission service neglect. Toyota calls the fluid 'lifetime' (6-speed AB60E 2008–2015; 8-speed AA80E 2016–2021). Neglect shows up as harsh 2–3 or 3–4 shifts, torque converter shudder at 40–50 mph, and a delayed engagement into gear. A drain-and-fill with WS fluid every 60k costs $200–400. A rebuild or replacement is $4,000–7,000. Rare, but towing history matters.", 'Front suspension wear. Upper control arm bushings and ball joints, lower ball joints, tie rod ends, and front wheel hub bearings wear out on these 6,000-lb trucks, especially on oversize all-terrain tires. Expect clunks over bumps, humming at speed, and uneven tire wear. Control arms cost $600–1,200 per pair installed; hub bearings run $400–800 per side.', 'Front CV axles and boots, plus front differential and transfer case seals. Look for torn boots slinging grease, clicking on full lock, and weeping pinion or axle seals. Lifted trucks are much worse. CV axles run $300–700 per side; seals run $250–600 each.', 'Spark plugs and ignition coils. Plugs are on a 120k interval and are labor-heavy on the V8. A misfire over 150k often means the original plugs were never done. Plugs co

profiles.market_notes: The 2016–2021 facelift (8-speed, updated interior and safety tech) commands a large premium over 2013–2015 spindle-grille trucks, which in turn sell above the cheapest 2008–2012 examples. Under 150k miles with dealer or specialist records sells at a premium. Trucks at 180k+ trade at a steep discount even though the drivetrain can go much further, which makes documented high-mile trucks the value play. Verified AHC health and SAI records move price meaningfully. Lifts, aftermarket wheels, racks and sliders are often priced up by sellers but should be discounted by a stock-preferring buyer. Clean black, white pearl and dark gray colors, Luxury or rear-entertainment packages, and the 2019–2021 Inspiration or Sport trims help resale.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 12–16-year-old, 150k+ LX 570 needs a fluids reset (transmission, diffs, transfer case, AHC, brake, coolant), plugs, and a water pump if these are undocumented. Expect roughly $2,000–4,000 in catch-up before addressing AHC or brake booster health. Lifted or overland-built examples usually add alignment, CV and suspension-joint work, or a return to stock height.

profiles.label: Lexus LX450 (80-Series / FZJ80, 1996–1997)
profiles.framing: The LX450 is a Lexus-trimmed 80-Series Land Cruiser with the 1FZ-FE 4.5L inline-six, A442F four-speed automatic, and full-time 4WD with a center diff lock. US LX450s were not offered with the factory front and rear lockers available on the Land Cruiser. For a Carmel driver it makes sense as a durable, comfortable utility truck for Highway 1, Big Sur, beach access, and Sierra snow trips, as long as the buyer accepts roughly 12–14 mpg and 1990s braking. The money is in documented cooling, head gasket, and front axle work, a rust-free body, and a stock or reversibly modified chassis that still passes a California smog check. Heavily built overland trucks like the example listing need extra scrutiny for lift geometry and emissions legality, and the accident history, refinished panels, and recent in-frame rebuild all need verification.
profiles.weak_points: ['Head gasket (1FZ-FE): Most common at 200k+ miles or after any overheating. The rear of the head near the firewall is the usual failure area. Symptoms are slow coolant loss with no visible leak, white exhaust smoke, combustion gas in the coolant, and an overheat on long grades or when towing. An independent shop charges roughly $3,000–5,000 in California, including head machining, valve job, and gaskets. Ask for receipts naming the machine shop and the head bolt torque procedure. A truck with a documented head gasket job done with OEM gaskets is worth a premium.', 'Cooling system: The original-style radiators have plastic tanks that crack. The firewall heater control valve is a notorious leak point, and the fan clutch and water pump weep with age. Budget $600–1,500 for radiator, hoses, fan clutch, and thermostat. A 1FZ that has run hot is a head gasket candidate, so look for receipts with dates and brand names. OEM or Koyo/Denso parts are preferred.', 'Rear heater and rear A/C lines: These steel and rubber lines run under the body to the rear heater and A/C. They rot or chafe and dump coolant or refrigerant without obvious warning. Many trucks have the rear heater bypassed. A bypass is acceptable, but it should be disclosed. Repair runs $300–800. Ask whether the lines were replaced or bypassed, and inspect them on a lift.', 'Front axle knuckles and Birfield joints: Expect trunnion (knuckle) bearings, wheel bearings, and wiper seals to need a full rebuild every 100–150k miles. Signs are grease or gear oil weeping from the knuckle ball, play in the knuckle, front-end shimmy, and Birfield (CV) clicking on tight turns. A full front axle service runs roughly $1,800–3,500 for both sides, more if Birfields or spindles are needed. This is one of the most important records to find.', 'Steering box, pump, and hoses: Leaks from the steering box sector shaft seal and the pump are common, along with excess on-center play. A worn box combined with worn tie rods, drag link, and steering damper produces vague tracking and shimmy. Hoses cost $200–500. A rebuilt box installed runs about $800–1,500.', "Driveshafts and the '80-series clunk': A dry front or rear driveshaft slip yoke causes a clunk on takeoff or when shifting into gear, and worn U-joints vibrate. The fix is often just grease every 3–5k miles, but a truck that clunks with no grease history may also have worn U-joints or a worn double-cardan joint, roughly $300–900 per shaft.", 'A442F transmission and HF2A transfer case: Both are robust but not immortal past 250k miles, especially after towing, lifts with bigger tires, or neglected fluid. Watch for delayed engagement, a soft or flaring 3–4 shift, shudder, or burnt-smelling fluid. A rebuild runs about $3,500–5,500. The center diff lock vacuum actuator and indicator can stick or fail to engage or release, typically $300–800 to repair. Ask for fluid change intervals.', 'Starter solenoid contacts: The starter is buried under the intake manifold, and its solenoid contacts wear out. The symptom is a single click and no crank, often intermittent and worse when hot. The contacts kit is cheap, but labor is $800–1,500 as a standalone job because the intake must come off. A smart owner does it alongside a head gasket job, so ask whether it was.', 'Valve adjustment and ignition: The 1FZ-FE uses shim-under-bucket valves due for adjustment about every 60k miles, and it is often skipped. Tight valves lead to burnt valves and rough idle. An adjustment runs about $600–1,000. Distributor cap and rotor, plug wires, and the distributor O-ring (an oil leak) are routine wear items.', 'Oil leaks and exhaust manifold: Valve cover gasket, oil filter housing and oil cooler lines, front crank seal, and rear main seal leaks are common, as is oil pan seepage. The cast exhaust manifold can crack and its studs break, producing a ticking noise on cold start; repair runs $800–1,800. Note that the factory oil pressure gauge and sender are notoriously erratic. Verify

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front axle knuckle service (trunnion bearings, wheel bearings, seals, Birfield inspection) if not documented within ~100k miles', 'Steering box reseal or replacement, power steering pump, and tie rod, drag link, and damper refresh', 'Suspension bushing refresh (radius arms, trailing arms, panhard) and shocks; coils if sagging', 'Starter solenoid contacts, ideally combined with any intake-off work', 'Valve cover gasket, oil cooler line, and distributor O-ring leak repairs', 'Exhaust manifold stud or crack repair if ticking is present', 'A/C service; possible compressor, expansion valve, or rear A/C repair', 'Rear axle full-floater hub service and axle seals', 'Rust treatment and undercoating appropriate to coastal Carmel conditions']
profiles.market_notes: LX450s generally trade at or slightly below equivalent Land Cruisers because they lack factory lockers, though clean, stock, low-mileage examples now command strong prices. Price is driven by documented head gasket, cooling, and front axle work, a rust-free Western or Southern history, and an unmodified or tastefully modified chassis. Clean-Carfax trucks under ~150k miles bring a large premium over 200k+ trucks. Heavily built overland trucks sell to a different buyer pool, and an accident history, refinished panels, or a recent in-frame rebuild without strong receipts should discount meaningfully.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 25+ year-old LX450 needs a cooling system refresh, a full fluid baseline, front axle knuckle service, steering and suspension bushing work, and attention to rear heater lines and sunroof drains. Plan $3,000–6,000 of catch-up even on a good truck. Trucks with an undocumented head gasket or a warm-running history should be priced as if a head gasket job is coming.

profiles.label: Lexus RX 350 (AL10, 3rd generation)
profiles.framing: This is the low-drama family/utility slot in the garage: a 2GR-powered, port-or-D4S V6 crossover with a properly engineered automatic, a quiet cabin, and a parts and service network that reaches everywhere. For a Carmel-based buyer it is a Highway 1 / Salinas run-around and airport hauler that should never be the reason a weekend gets cancelled. Nothing about it is engaging, so the entire buying case rests on documentation, condition, and price relative to a market that stubbornly refuses to depreciate. Note that US-market 2010–2015 cars are the true AL10 with the 2GR-FE and U660E/U760E; 2016 is the AL20 redesign with the 2GR-FKS and 8-speed — mechanically similar in spirit but a different platform, so verify which car you are actually looking at.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing-cover and cam-tower oil seepage on the 2GR-FE is the signature 100k+ issue: the RTV-sealed front cover weeps down the back of the block and onto the subframe, often mistaken for a rear main leak. Diagnosis is easy from below with a light; repair is engine-out-of-the-way labor at roughly $1,800–3,000 at an independent. Ask for photos of a clean underside or a documented reseal. 2) Water pump failure/weeping around 80k–130k, usually announced by pink crust at the weep hole or a faint coolant smell; $500–900 including the belt. 3) The VVT-i oil supply line failure that killed early 2GR engines was addressed by recall/updated hard line on earlier cars, but on any 2GR verify the metal line is present and dry — a burst line dumps oil in seconds and destroys the engine. 4) U660E/U760E 6-speed: Lexus calls the WS fluid 'lifetime,' which it is not. Neglected units develop a 1-2 shift flare, torque-converter shudder at light throttle 35–50 mph, or a delayed engagement clunk. Drain-and-fills every 60k are cheap insurance; a car at 120k with zero fluid history is a $3,500–5,000 gamble. 2013+ F Sport uses the 8-speed U880E, which is fine but has its own valve-body software updates. 5) Melting/sticky and cracking dashboards on 2010–2013 cars, especially sun-belt and coastal-sun examples — Lexus ran a warranty extension that has now expired; replacement is $1,400–2,500. Check the top pad and the passenger airbag seam. 6) HVAC blend-door and mode actuators tick or knock behind the dash and cause split hot/cold; $250–600 each depending on access. 7) Remote Touch mouse controller and the 8-inch nav screen: sticky/erratic cursor, ghost touches, screen delamination or DVD/HDD nav drive failure. New OEM units are $900–1,800; many owners live with it or fit an aftermarket head unit (a modification this buyer should be wary of, as it often means hacked wiring). 8) Power liftgate struts and the electric lift actuator/motor fail around 100k — the gate drops, beeps, or refuses to latch; struts are cheap, the actuator is $600–1,000. 9) Suspension: front lower control arm bushings, sway bar end links, and strut mounts produce a clunk over Carmel Valley pavement joints by 100k–120k; struts and mounts all around run $1,200–2,000. Rear wheel bearings hum from ~120k, $400–600 each. 10) Hydraulic engine and transmission mounts collapse and cause a diesel-like idle shake in Drive; front mount $350–650 installed. 11) Spark plugs are a 120k service and the rear bank requires intake plenum removal — budget $450–700, not $120. 12) A/C condenser stone damage and slow leaks are common on freeway cars; condenser plus recharge $700–1,100. Also check for the compressor clutch rattle at idle. 13) AWD models: the transfer case and rear diff fluids are almost never changed, and the driveshaft center support bearing rumbles at 40–60 mph on higher-mileage cars. 14) Sunroof drains clog with coastal pine needles and Monterey litter, soaking the A-pillar trim and headliner — pull the trim and look for water staining, plus check the spare well for standing water.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: transmission WS drain-and-fill (repeat in 500 miles if the old fluid is dark), coolant if past 10 years, brake fluid flush, transfer case and rear diff on AWD. Four new tires if the DOT codes are over six years old regardless of tread (very common on low-mile Lexus SUVs), plus an alignment. New 12V battery if undated or over four years, cabin and engine air filters, wiper blades, and a sunroof-drain flush. Expect to fix at least one HVAC actuator tick or a pair of liftgate struts. Budget $1,500–2,800.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not documented; timing-cover reseal if seepage is dripping rather than weeping; spark plugs and coil inspection at 120k; front strut assemblies and sway bar links if it clunks; engine and transmission mounts if it shakes at idle in Drive; a rear wheel bearing; brake pads and rotors all around; possibly a dash pad replacement on a 2010–2013 sun-baked car. Budget $2,000–4,000.
profiles.market_notes: RX 350s trade on records and mileage bands more than on spec — a one-owner car with a full Lexus dealer history and under 90k will command a real premium over an identical 120k trade-in. AWD carries a modest premium nationally but matters little on the Monterey Peninsula, so FWD is the value play; Navigation/Premium/Luxury packages, ventilated seats, blind-spot monitor, and the 2013+ F Sport add appeal, while the F Sport's stiffer ride and 19s add nothing for this mission. Neutral colors (Nebula Gray, Starfire Pearl, silver) with tan or black leather sell fastest; a clean, unmodified California car with no rust, no accidents, and a factory head unit is worth paying up for because the whole point of this vehicle is not thinking about it.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-15 year old RX arrives with 'lifetime' fluids that were never changed, original coolant, aging suspension bushings, and six-to-eight-year-old tires on a low-mile example. Plan on a full fluids-and-rubber reset in the first month — trans, coolant, brake fluid, diff/transfer case, tires, battery, belt — then treat water pump, spark plugs, and struts as scheduled 12-month items rather than surprises.

profiles.label: Lexus RX350 (XU30, 2007–2009)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the XU30 RX350 is a quiet, comfortable, low-drama daily and road-trip vehicle for Highway 1, foggy wet coastal winters, and the occasional Sierra run. The 2GR-FE V6 and U151E five-speed can easily pass 200k miles when fluids have been changed, so the purchase decision rests on documented maintenance and on the cost of predictable age items: dash, steering rack, suspension bushings, headlights, and electronics. AWD is useful but not essential on the coast. A clean FWD car with records beats a neglected AWD one. Treat every listed 'cosmetic' flaw as a line item with a price.
profiles.weak_points: ["VVT-i oil cooler line (2GR-FE): early 2GR engines used a line with a rubber hose section feeding the intake cam phasers. It can split suddenly, dump the engine oil in seconds, and destroy the engine. Lexus ran a limited service campaign to replace it with an all-metal line. Look for a dealer campaign record, or a photo or inspection confirming the all-metal line on the right/rear of the engine near the timing cover. If it hasn't been done, the parts and labor are a few hundred dollars. Skipping it risks a $5,000–8,000+ engine replacement. This is the single most important item on the car.", 'Power steering rack and hoses: rack seal leaks, typically from 80–150k miles or 12+ years, show up as wet boots, ATF-type fluid on the subframe, groaning at full lock, or a dropping reservoir level. A replacement rack costs roughly $1,200–2,200 installed. The pressure and return hoses also weep. A recently replaced rack with a receipt is a real positive.', "Dashboard cracking: the 2004–2009 RX dash pad cracks and shrinks from UV and heat, usually starting near the defrost vents and passenger airbag seam. Lexus's dashboard extended-coverage program has largely expired. A full dash replacement runs about $1,500–2,500 at an independent shop. The alternatives are a molded overlay cover or a filler kit. An airbag-area crack can matter for inspection and resale.", 'Water pump (2GR-FE, belt-driven): weep-hole seepage and pink or white coolant crust on the pump body are common at 80–130k miles or with age. Replacement runs about $500–900, with a coolant service at the same time. Look for records of Toyota/Lexus SLLC pink coolant. The first service is due at 100k miles or 10 years, then every 50k miles or 5 years.', "U151E five-speed automatic: Toyota called the WS fluid 'lifetime', so many cars have never had it changed. Symptoms are harsh 2–3 or 3–4 shifts, flare on upshift, delayed engagement into Drive/Reverse, and torque converter shudder at light throttle around 40–50 mph. Preferred maintenance is repeated drain-and-fills with Toyota WS fluid. A machine 'flush' on a high-mileage neglected unit can sometimes trigger problems. Valve body or solenoid work costs about $800–1,500. A reman transmission costs about $3,500–5,000.", 'AWD driveline (AWD models): the transfer/PTU and rear differential use gear oil that is often never changed. PTU output seal and vent leaks are common. Neglected PTUs can overheat, whine, or bind, and rebuild or replacement runs about $1,500–3,000. Also check the propeller shaft center support bearing, the rear diff mount bushings, and the CV boots. Ask for records of transfer and rear diff fluid changes.', 'Front suspension: the front lower control arm bushings (especially the rear horizontal bushing) crack and cause clunks, wandering, and uneven tire wear. Struts and mounts cost about $800–1,500 per axle pair if they are original and soft. An alignment is needed afterward.', 'Air suspension (Height Control / Adaptive Variable Suspension, optional on Premium-equipped cars): air springs crack with age, and the compressor or height sensors fail. Symptoms are sagging overnight, a height-control warning light, or the compressor running constantly. Expect about $400–800 per air spring and $800–1,500 for a compressor. Coil conversion kits count as a modification. Verify which suspension the car has and test raising and lowering it.', 'Headlights with AFS: the swiveling Adaptive Front Lighting System motors and sensors fail, flashing the AFS light at startup. Housings fog or take on moisture as seals age. HID ballasts and igniters can fail at $200–500 each. A new OE headlamp assembly can cost $800–1,500+ each. Moisture inside the housing usually means seal failure, not a simple fix.', 'Navigation, display, and backup camera: the touchscreen can develop dead zones, the display can dim or fail, and the backup

profiles.market_notes: The RX350 (2GR-FE, 2007–2009) brings more than the earlier RX330. Low miles (under 80k), one-family ownership, a window sticker, and continuous service records produce the strongest results, especially on enthusiast auction sites. AWD, Premium Plus, Navigation, Mark Levinson, and the 2008–2009 Pebble Beach Edition add value. A badly cracked dash, failed air suspension, foggy headlights, or electronics faults are used to negotiate down roughly by their repair cost. Neutral colors (white, silver, black, smoky granite) with ivory or black leather are the norm. Clean, documented, low-mile examples generally trade high-single-digit to mid-teens thousands, while high-mile cars with no records sell well below that.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2007–2009 RX350 is 15+ years old, and rubber has aged regardless of mileage. Expect catch-up on all fluids (ATF, transfer/diff, coolant, brake), tires by date code, suspension bushings, and possibly PS hoses and the water pump. Budget roughly $1,500–3,500 for this catch-up on a documented car. Add more for dash, headlights, or air suspension if those are faulty.

profiles.label: Lincoln Mark VII (1984–1992, Fox platform)
profiles.framing: The Mark VII is a comfortable, affordable American personal-luxury coupe built on Ford's Fox platform. The 5.0 V8, 8.8 rear axle and much of the chassis share parts with the Fox Mustang, so the drivetrain is cheap and easy to source. The real cost and risk sit in the Lincoln-specific systems: the four-corner air suspension, the Teves Mk II integrated ABS/power-brake unit, the digital cluster and EATC climate control, and dozens of power accessories. Every Mark VII uses the AOD 4-speed automatic, and all U.S. examples are 25+ years old. For a Carmel-based driver, prioritize a 1988–1992 car with the 225 hp HO engine, solid rust-free structure, safe and functional brakes, and an engine that will pass California smog with no check-engine light. Avoid the 1984–85 BMW turbo-diesel variant unless you have a specialist.
profiles.weak_points:
["Air suspension (four air springs, under-hood compressor, three height sensors, solenoid valves, trunk-mounted module and on/off switch). Rubber springs dry-rot after 20–30 years. Symptoms: the car sags overnight, the compressor runs constantly or overheats, and the 'Check Suspension' warning lights up. Air springs cost about $250–500 each and a compressor $300–500; a full refresh runs $1,500–2,500. Coil conversion kits (Suncore, Arnott) cost $400–900 plus labor. If converted, ask for the receipt and kit brand, confirm the module was properly disabled, and check that ride height is level and not jacked up.", 'Teves Mk II integrated ABS (1985–92): the master cylinder, hydraulic booster, electric pump, nitrogen accumulator and valve body are one unit, and power assist comes from that system. A failing accumulator or pump means frequent pump cycling, a hard or high pedal, and amber ABS plus red BRAKE lights. Worst case is substantially reduced braking assist, so treat this as a safety system, not a nuisance light. New parts are largely NLA. A remanufactured unit runs $900–2,000 installed, an aftermarket accumulator $150–350, and a conversion to a conventional vacuum booster/master cylinder $800–1,500. Look for records of accumulator or pump replacement and correct brake fluid flushes using the pump-bleed procedure.', 'AOD 4-speed automatic: everything depends on correct throttle-valve (TV) cable adjustment. A misadjusted or broken cable starves line pressure and burns the overdrive band and intermediate/direct clutches. Symptoms: soft or slipping 3-4 shift, late or flared upshifts, no overdrive, delayed engagement, burnt dark fluid. A rebuild costs $2,000–3,500, more for an AODE/4R70W swap. Look for rebuild receipts, fluid/filter changes, and evidence the TV cable was set with a pressure gauge or proper gauge tool.', '5.0 V8 (EEC-IV). Early cars (1984–85) have a lower-output 5.0; 1986–87 LSC and all 1988–92 cars have the 225 hp HO sequential-injected engine. Known issues include:
- The distributor-mounted TFI ignition module fails when hot, causing stalling or a hot no-start ($60–200; a remote-mount kit is the cure).
- Idle air bypass valve, TPS, EGR and vacuum leaks cause hunting idle.
- Aging injectors and connectors, and brittle vacuum lines.
Request a KOEO/KOER self-test code readout.', 'Fluid leaks and cooling on the 5.0: rear main seal, upper/lower intake and plenum gaskets, timing cover, oil pan and valve cover gaskets. Water pumps weep, and plastic-tank radiators crack. Heater core leaks show up as a sweet smell, fogged glass or a wet passenger floor, and replacement means dash-out labor of $900–1,500. Ask for coolant service, radiator and water pump replacement records.', "Rust on the Fox structure: rear wheel arches and quarter panels, rockers, trunk floor and spare-tire well, lower doors, and front torque boxes and frame rails. The areas around the windshield and rear window gaskets and clogged moonroof drains are also known rot points. Florida and coastal cars can hide corrosion under clean paint, and Carmel's marine air will keep working on any rust you buy. Structural repair can exceed the car's value.", 'Digital instrument cluster (Base/Bill Blass; LSC uses analog gauges from 1986) and message center. Vacuum-fluorescent displays dim, flicker or go dark, and solder joints crack. Specialist rebuilds run $300–700. Also expect EATC automatic climate faults (blend door, servo, sensor, control head) at $200–900.', 'Power accessories: seat track motors and drive cables (fore/aft failure is very common), door lock actuators, mirror motors, window motors and regulators, power antenna, and the illuminated keyless entry/keypad where equipped. Individually these cost $100–400, but they add up fast; budget $500–1,500 to sort a neglected car. Corroded grounds and connectors cause many intermittent faults.', "A/C: originally R-12, and many cars have been converted to R-134a with mixed results. The FX-15 compressor can fail a

profiles.market_notes: The LSC (especially the 1988–92 225 hp cars and the rare 1992 LSC SE) commands the strongest prices, with the Bill Blass close behind and base and Versace models generally lower. 1990–92 cars with the revised dash and driver airbag are the most usable. Typical driver-quality examples trade around $5,000–10,000, while documented, rust-free cars under about 60k miles with working original air suspension and ABS can reach $15,000–25,000. Records showing ABS, transmission and air-suspension work add real value. Non-functional luxury electronics, aftermarket modifications, rust and hidden structural repair push prices down sharply.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical Mark VII will need rubber and fluid catch-up: hoses, belts, bushings, seals, brake fluid, transmission fluid and tires, regardless of mileage. Expect to spend $1,500–4,000 bringing a driver-quality example to dependable condition, more if the ABS, air suspension or transmission need attention. California smog compliance and coastal rust prevention should be addressed immediately after purchase.

profiles.label: MG MGC Roadster & GT (1967–1969)
profiles.framing: The MGC is an MGB body with a heavy 2.9L seven-main-bearing C-Series straight-six, torsion-bar front suspension, 15-inch wheels and a long-legged overdrive gearbox. It is a relaxed grand tourer, not a sharp sports car: it suits Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road at a steady pace and is noticeably nose-heavy in tight corners. For a Carmel driver who wants documented, unmodified cars, the deciding factors are structural rust (coastal salt air will not slow it down), whether the MGC-specific mechanicals were rebuilt and invoiced, and whether the engine and body match the Heritage certificate. Pre-1976 cars are smog-exempt in California, so the main registration hurdles are VIN verification and any title or odometer brands.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Structural rust. The MGB-derived monocoque rots at the inner and outer sills (castle sections and center membrane), floor pans, front and rear jacking points, A-post bases, door bottoms, lower front fenders, rear arches and dog-legs, and trunk floor. Check under the rear seat area too: the twin 6V battery cradles behind the seats and the heel board rot from acid and trapped water. Correct three-piece sill and floor replacement runs about $8k–25k+ before paint. A bubbled sill on an MGC is never minor. Ask for underside photos taken on a lift, and for receipts naming which panels were replaced, by whom, and with or without jigging.

2) MGC-specific front structure. The unique front crossmember, torsion-bar reaction mounts and inner fender structure carry the suspension loads. They are harder to source and repair than MGB parts. Look for cracking, rust or crude welding around the torsion-bar rear anchor points under the floor and at the crossmember ends. Structural repairs here run $3k–8k.

3) Torsion-bar front suspension and steering. Expect sag (uneven or low ride height), worn lower-arm and torsion-bar bushes, worn telescopic dampers, and wear in the vertical link and swivel bushes. The MGC-specific rack wears and leaks through split bellows. Tie rods and rack mounts loosen. Symptoms are wander, clunks and heavy, vague steering. A full front-end refresh costs about $1.5k–3.5k. Ride-height adjustment needs proper re-indexing, not just cranking the adjusters.

4) C-Series engine wear and oil leaks. The rope rear main seal leaks chronically, as do the pushrod-tube side covers, rocker cover and timing cover. The duplex timing chain and tensioner wear and rattle. Valve guides and rocker shafts wear, and the heavy cast-iron engine runs warm. Oil pressure should be roughly 50–70 psi hot at cruise; persistent pressure below about 20 psi hot at idle points to bearing wear. A proper rebuild with machine work costs about $8k–15k. Ask for machine-shop invoices showing bore size, crank grind and new cam/followers, plus a compression test.

5) Cooling margin. The radiator sits far forward under the bulged bonnet, and the six-cylinder engine heat-soaks the bay. Look for overheating in traffic, head-gasket seepage, a tired water pump, a sticking heater valve and corroded core plugs. Aluminum radiators and electric fans are common non-original fixes. Note them as modifications, and check whether the originals come with the car. Cooling work runs about $600–2k; a head gasket with skim, about $1.5k–3k.

6) Carburetion and US emissions. Twin SU HS6 carbs suffer worn throttle spindles (air leaks, uneven idle) and need correct needles and damper oil. 1968–69 US cars came with an air-injection pump, gulp valve and anti-run-on equipment, often removed or partly disconnected. California does not require it on a smog-exempt car, but its absence affects originality. A carb rebuild with new spindles and bushes runs about $700–1.5k.

7) Gearbox and overdrive. The all-synchro 4-speed suffers worn synchros (crunching 2nd/3rd), noisy laygear bearings and jumping out of gear. The Laycock overdrive (3rd and 4th only) fails through a faulty solenoid, inhibitor switch or relay, or low oil pressure from a dirty filter and sludged pump. Symptoms are slow or no engagement, or slipping. A box rebuild costs about $2.5k–4.5k; overdrive repair, about $500 for electrical to $1.5k–2.5k for a rebuild. Ask for rebuild receipts and confirm the gearbox number. The rare Borg-Warner 35 automatic needs its own scrutiny.

8) Rear axle. The Salisbury-type axle leaks from the pinion seal and half-shaft seals, and worn bearings cause whine. MGC ratios are unique, which matters if someone swapped in an MGB axle. Rear leaf springs sag, and lever-arm rear dampers leak. Expect about $800–3k depending on whether gears are needed.

9) Brakes. Front discs and calipers are larger than the MGB's, with a vacuum servo. US cars have dual-circuit hydraulics with a pressure-differential warni
profiles.immediate_repairs: Expect these in the first 30 days: replace all fluids (engine oil with a zinc-rich classic oil, gearbox/overdrive oil, axle oil, brake and clutch fluid, coolant); replace tires if older than about 6 years and check the wire wheels and hub splines; rebuild or replace the brake failure warning switch and fix any servo or caliper drag; inspect and replace aged brake and fuel hoses; tune ignition (points, condenser, timing) and balance the SU carbs; clean and correct earth straps; and fix fluid leaks severe enough to reach the exhaust. Budget about $1,500–4,000 on a sorted car, and more if the brakes or tires are original-era.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Over the next 12 months, expect: a front suspension bush and damper refresh with ride-height correction; rear damper refills or replacement; a new rope rear main seal or conversion to a modern seal during any clutch work; overdrive solenoid or switch sorting; cooling system parts (hoses, thermostat, water pump, possibly radiator recore); SU fuel pump replacement or electronic conversion; harness and switch repairs; and rust treatment before small rust spots spread. Budget about $3,000–8,000 depending on how complete the previous restoration really was.
profiles.market_notes: Roadsters generally command more than GTs, and fully documented, numbers-matching cars with a BMIHT certificate, original color, factory overdrive and original wire wheels bring strong premiums. Automatic cars, cars with non-original engines or MGB conversions, branded titles (TMU, mechanical limits) and heavily modified examples trade at clear discounts. Rust history and the quality of the bodywork matter more than odometer reading, which is often unknown or irrelevant on a five-digit 1960s car. Invoiced restorations by known MG specialists move prices up meaningfully over unverified claims.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most MGCs on the market have had partial restorations of varying quality. Assume aged rubber (hoses, bushes, seals), tired Lucas wiring and some hidden rust unless invoices and photos prove otherwise. Budget for a full suspension, brake and fluid refresh, plus ongoing rustproofing, given Carmel's salt air.

profiles.label: MINI Cooper S (F56 Hardtop, 2014-2024, incl. F55 4-Door / F57 Convertible siblings)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer the F56 Cooper S is a fun, economical, easy-to-park daily driver that suits Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and tight village parking. It is much more robust than the R56 that came before it, because the BMW-derived B46/B48 2.0T engine fixed the old timing-chain and carbon problems. It is still a German small car with plastic cooling parts, wear-prone suspension bushings and, on 2019+ automatics, a dual-clutch gearbox that rewards documented care. What matters most is consistent oil-service history, a dry cooling system, a smooth-behaving transmission, and knowing exactly where the car sits relative to the 4-year/50,000-mile factory warranty.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Cooling-system plastics on the B46/B48. The thermostat housing and coolant outlet flange, the expansion tank and its hoses, and the turbo coolant feed/return lines commonly weep from roughly 40-90k miles or 5+ years. Symptoms include a sweet smell, pink/blue crust around the front of the block or turbo, a low-coolant warning, or a slowly dropping reservoir. Repairs run about $400-1,200 depending on the part. Look for receipts naming the thermostat housing or coolant lines, and inspect under the car for dried residue.

2) Valve cover with integrated PCV, plus oil pan and oil filter housing gaskets. Oil seepage onto the exhaust side or the subframe becomes common past about 60-80k miles. A failing PCV diaphragm can cause a rough idle, whistling, or lean codes. Valve cover replacement is about $700-1,300; oil pan gasket about $500-900, since the subframe has to be dropped on some cars.

3) 7-speed Getrag dual-clutch automatic (7DCT300, Cooper S from mid-2018/MY2019 through 2024). Known issues are low-speed hesitation, judder when creeping or reversing up driveways, harsh 1-2 shifts, and occasional mechatronic faults with 'transmission malfunction / drive moderately' warnings. Many symptoms are cured by software updates. Fluid is marketed as long-life, but specialists recommend a fluid/filter service around 40-60k miles ($400-700). A mechatronic unit runs about $2,500-4,500; a replacement transmission about $6,000-9,000. Ask for dealer software-update and fluid-service records, and note whether the work was done under warranty.

4) Aisin 6-speed automatic (2014-2018). It is generally durable but never serviced from the factory. Watch for flare or harsh shifts and delayed engagement when warm. A drain-and-fill around 60k miles costs about $350-600. A valve body or replacement unit is a $2,500-5,000+ risk on neglected cars.

5) 6-speed manual clutch and dual-mass flywheel. On aggressively driven or turbo-tuned cars, expect clutch slip, DMF rattle at idle, or chatter by about 60-100k miles. Clutch plus DMF runs about $1,800-2,800. The slave cylinder and lines occasionally leak.

6) Engine and transmission mounts. The upper passenger-side hydraulic mount and the lower torque (dogbone) mount wear from about 50k miles. Symptoms are idle vibration felt in the steering wheel and seats (worse in Drive), and a clunk on throttle tip-in or shifts. Repair runs about $300-800.

7) Front suspension bushings and links. Front control arm and thrust arm bushings, sway-bar end links, and strut top mounts produce clunks over driveway lips, wandering, and uneven inner-edge tire wear past about 50-80k miles. Repair runs about $500-1,400. Lowered or stiffly modified cars wear these faster.

8) Run-flat tires and wheels. Most F56s left the factory on run-flats with no spare. They ride harshly and cost about $900-1,400 a set for 17-18 inch sizes. Many owners switch to conventional tires and add an inflator kit. Check DOT date codes, matching brands, and curb rash or bends on 17-18 inch alloys.

9) Direct-injection carbon buildup and ignition. The B48 is far better than the R56 N14/N18, but intake-valve deposits can still cause a slightly rough cold idle or misfire codes past about 70-100k miles. Walnut blasting runs about $500-900; plugs and coils about $350-700 (plugs due around 60k miles).

10) Turbo and wastegate. A rattle from the electronic wastegate actuator on cold start or at lift-off, or boost-related fault codes, is uncommon but possible. Turbocharger replacement runs about $2,500-3,800. Oil-change discipline is the best predictor of turbo health.

11) Moonroof drains and seals. Clogged front or rear drain tubes dump water into the headliner, A-pillar, or footwells. Carmel's fog and tree debris (pine needles, cypress) make this more likely. Rattles and wind noise from the panoramic roof are also common. Check the headliner and carpets for stains and a musty smell. Clearing the drains is cheap; water-damaged modules are not.

profiles.market_notes: The 6-speed manual carries a clear premium with enthusiasts and is getting scarcer as the generation ages out. Among automatics, the 2014-2018 Aisin 6AT is viewed as more durable, while the 2019+ 7-speed DCT is quicker but more scrutinized. Upper trims and packages raise value: Iconic and Signature Plus with heads-up display, Harman Kardon, adaptive LED lights, and Comfort Access, as is the 2022+ LCI2 refresh with the digital cluster and updated styling. One-owner cars with complete MINI dealer service printouts, remaining factory warranty or CPO coverage, and stock tuning sell faster and for more. Cars past 60-70k miles, or past warranty with no DCT/cooling records, should be priced to absorb $1,500-3,000 of catch-up work.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 4-7 year old F56 near 50-70k miles is often due for brake fluid, spark plugs, a battery, tires (frequently aged or mismatched run-flats) and front brakes. It often needs a first transmission fluid service as well. Cooling-system plastics, mounts and front bushings commonly need attention in the same window. For cars at or past 50k miles, budget $1,500-3,000 for catch-up on an otherwise healthy example. Get the work done before the factory warranty expires where possible.

profiles.label: MINI Cooper S John Cooper Works GP (R53 GP1, 2006)
profiles.framing: The GP1 is the most focused R53: a two-seat, Bertone-finished, factory-JCW-tuned supercharged hatch with a mechanical LSD, stiffer and lower suspension, and unique wheels and aero. For a Carmel driver it suits Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and Laureles Grade, and Tritec/R53 running gear is cheap and well understood. GP-only pieces are scarce, though, and a 20-year-old example lives or dies on the supercharger, gearbox, power-steering pump, rubber, and rust history. A documented, unmodified, accident-light car is worth paying up for. A tired, modified, salt-state car is a parts-hunting project dressed up as a bargain.
profiles.weak_points: ["Supercharger (Eaton M45, JCW-spec on the GP): the sealed nose oil is effectively a wear item. Without service, bearings and coupler wear between roughly 60k and 100k miles. Symptoms are a louder or rattly whine at idle, a 'marbles' rattle that changes when the clutch is pressed, and lost boost. An oil service is cheap. A rebuild or exchange unit runs about $600–$1,500 installed. Ask for a dated rebuild invoice that names the shop or rebuilder and the parts replaced, not just 'rebuilt.' Aftermarket reduction pulleys add boost and speed up supercharger wear.", 'Crankshaft harmonic damper (crank pulley): the factory rubber-bonded damper delaminates with age. The outer ring wobbles or walks off, which leads to belt shredding, vibration, and possible damage to the crank snout or timing cover. This is a must-check on any example over about 10 years or 80k miles. An OEM or ATI replacement plus labor runs about $350–$900. Record the part brand and date, and note that an ATI damper usually comes paired with a reduction pulley.', 'Electro-hydraulic power steering (EHPS) pump: the pump sits low behind the front bumper, and its small cooling fan fails or clogs. The pump then overheats, and steering goes heavy or intermittent, often after hot or slow driving. A failed pump costs about $800–$1,600 for a reman unit installed. A preventive fan replacement or retrofit is about $100–$250. Look for receipts for the fan or pump, and inspect for fluid leaks and a crusty, corroded harness at the pump.', "Getrag 6-speed gearbox with mechanical LSD: R53 boxes are known for input and output shaft bearing whine, which is worst on overrun or at steady cruise and changes with load. Expect occasional 2nd/3rd synchro crunch on high-mileage or hard-driven cars. A rebuild or used replacement runs about $2,500–$5,000, and a correct LSD-equipped unit costs more and is harder to find. This is a manual with no serviceable filter, so a 'transmission filter replaced' claim points to sloppy records.", "Clutch and flywheel: the GP's extra torque plus enthusiast use wears clutches. Many R53s also get single-mass flywheel conversions, which add chatter and gear rattle. Check for slip in 4th–5th at low rpm under full load, a high engagement point, judder, and slave cylinder or hose leaks. A clutch with a flywheel runs about $1,300–$2,800. Ask for the clutch replacement mileage and the brand of clutch and flywheel.", "Cooling system plastics: the water pump has a plastic impeller, and the plastic thermostat housing, coolant expansion tank, and hoses all crack or weep with age. Overheating on the Tritec risks the head gasket and warping. A water pump, thermostat housing, and tank refresh runs about $500–$1,000. The radiator fan and its resistor or control module also fail, which shows up as rising temps in traffic; budget about $250–$600 for that. Look for coolant crust at the housing on the driver's side of the head and under the reservoir.", 'Tritec oil leaks: common sources are the oil filter housing gasket, valve cover gasket, oil pan gasket, rear main seal, and supercharger and manifold gaskets. Leaking oil fouls belts and soaks engine mounts. Typical leak repairs run $200–$800 each, and a rear main seal is best done alongside a clutch job. Wet undersides plus fresh gasket receipts can mean either a sorted car or one still chasing leaks.', "Engine and transmission mounts: the upper passenger-side hydromount and the lower 'dog bone' torque arm mount wear. Symptoms are clunks on throttle tip-in and lift, excessive engine rock, and vibration at idle. Expect about $300–$800 for a full set. Stiffer aftermarket mounts add cabin vibration.", 'Front control arm rear (thrust) bushings, strut mounts, and sway bar links: these produce clunks, vague turn-in, steering wheel shimmy under braking, and uneven tire wear. Arms or Powerflex-type bushings plus an alignment run about $400–$1,000. Adjustable or aftermarket arms should come with a recent alignment sheet.', 'Rear subfram
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, coolant flush with correct BMW/MINI coolant, brake fluid flush, and manual transmission fluid change using MINI-approved MTF. Add a supercharger oil service if there is no record within about 50k miles.', 'Inspect the crank harmonic damper for rubber cracking or ring wobble, and replace it if it is original or undocumented. Replace the serpentine belt and tensioner if they are aged or noisy.', 'Check the EHPS pump cooling fan and clean the pump area. Replace or retrofit the fan preventively if it is original.', 'Replace worn engine mounts, particularly the upper passenger-side mount and the lower dog bone, if there is clunking or excessive rock.', 'Tires: replace any tires over 6 years old or mismatched. Decide on run-flats versus non-run-flats
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front control arm rear bushings, sway bar links and bushings, and strut mounts as clunks develop.', 'Rear trailing arm bushings and a rear suspension squeak diagnosis (shocks, mounts, and bushings).', 'Reseal the oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets if not recently done. Investigate pan and rear main seal leaks.', 'Preventive water pump and thermostat housing replacement if not documented in the last 5 years or 60k miles. Check the radiator fan and its resistor or control module.', 'Window regulator replacement as cables fail. Headliner re-cover if sagging (about $300–$600).', 'Brake service: pads, rotors, and a check of caliper slide and seal condition. Replace any aged rubber brake hoses.', 'Clutch replacement if engagement is high, slip appears, or the clutch is undocumented pas
profiles.market_notes: Only about 415 GP1s were sold in the U.S., and all came in Thunder Blue Metallic with a silver roof and red mirrors, so color does not move price. Condition, originality, mileage, and history do. Unmodified examples command the strongest prices, especially those with intact original suspension, unbent GP wheels, the carbon wing, aero, Recaros, the rear brace, the numbered plaque, the window sticker, and continuous records. Low-mileage clean-Carfax cars bring clear premiums. High-mileage (100k+), modified, accident-reported, or salt-state cars with rust or a replaced subframe trade at a steep discount. Some of these sell for well under typical GP values, but they often need $3k–$8k of sorting, and their originality may be hard to recover.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2006 GP needs a 20-year rubber-and-plastics catch-up: the crank damper, engine mounts, suspension bushings, coolant plastics, belts, and hoses, plus supercharger oil and gearbox fluid if undocumented. Budget roughly $2,000–$5,000 beyond purchase for a 'running and driving' example to make it reliable. Cars from salt states should also get an underbody rust reckoning before any money goes into refinement.
