profiles.label: MINI John Cooper Works Roadster (R59, 2012–2015)
profiles.framing: The R59 JCW Roadster is a small, light, turbocharged two-seat convertible with a six-speed manual. That makes it an ideal top-down car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the Laureles Grade, and practical enough to drive daily. For this buyer, value comes from mechanical honesty rather than rarity. The things that matter are short-interval oil history, a quiet timing chain on a cold start, a dry engine bay and footwells, and a stock ECU. The N18 engine is far better than the earlier N14, but it is still a direct-injected BMW-era turbo four that punishes neglect and long factory service intervals. Coastal fog and marine air make soft-top drainage, mildew and rubber seals more relevant here than in a dry climate.
profiles.weak_points: ["Timing chain, guides and tensioner (N18B16). The N18's revised tensioner and chain are much better than the N14's, but stretch still happens on cars that followed MINI's 10–15k-mile service intervals. The symptom is a 1–3 second rattle on a cold start, sometimes followed by cam-timing codes (2A82/2A87 family). A full chain, guides, tensioner and sprocket kit runs roughly $1,500–2,800 at an independent shop. Look for oil changes at 5,000–7,500 miles or annually, and any record of a chain or tensioner job. A cold-start video recorded after the car sat overnight is good evidence.", 'Intake valve carbon buildup from direct injection. Expect it at 40–70k miles, or sooner on cars used mostly for short trips. Symptoms are a rough cold idle, hesitation, and misfire codes that persist after new plugs and coils. Walnut blasting costs about $450–900. Look for a walnut-blast receipt on cars over about 50k miles, or plan for one.', 'Oil filter housing gasket leak. The filter housing sits above the accessory belt. A leak soaks the belt, which can delaminate, jump off and get pulled behind the crank pulley into the front main seal. That turns a $250–500 gasket job into $1,000+ or worse. Look for oily residue down the front of the block and a swollen or frayed belt. A record of a housing gasket and belt replacement is a plus.', 'Other oil leaks. Valve cover gasket, vacuum pump gasket, oil pan gasket (replaced on the example car), and turbo oil feed and return line seals all leak on these engines. Valve cover and vacuum pump jobs run $300–700. An oil pan gasket is $500–900 because the subframe has to be lowered. A burning-oil smell after a drive and drips on the exhaust are the tells.', 'Cooling system. The mechanical water pump, the plastic thermostat housing, the coolant expansion tank and the hose junctions weep with age. Symptoms are a sweet smell, pink or blue crust around the housing at the front of the engine, and a slowly dropping reservoir level. Water pump plus thermostat costs about $700–1,300. Any 10+ year-old car without a record of these parts should be treated as due.', 'Turbocharger. Watch for wastegate actuator and rod bushing rattle (a metallic buzz at idle or tip-out), shaft play, and oil coking in the feed line on cars run on long oil intervals. Smoke, whistle, low-boost or overboost faults point to trouble. Fixing the wastegate linkage is $300–700; a replacement turbo is $2,500–4,000 installed. Look for boost and fault data on a scan and a clean, oil-free intercooler pipe.', 'High-pressure fuel pump and injectors. Failures are less common on the N18 than on the N14 but still occur. Symptoms are a long crank, limp mode, and fuel-pressure codes (29E0/29E1-type). An HPFP runs $800–1,500, and a leaking injector or its seals add $300–600 per cylinder. Ask whether software updates or campaigns were applied.', 'Clutch, dual-mass flywheel and hydraulics. On a JCW driven hard, the clutch can be done anywhere from 40k to 90k miles. The DMF may chatter or rattle at idle in neutral, and the clutch slave or master cylinder can fail. A clutch with flywheel costs about $1,800–3,000. Signs of wear are a high engagement point, slip in 3rd or 4th under boost, and judder pulling away on a hill. Look for clutch receipts and check whether the original DMF has been swapped for a single-mass unit (a modification).', 'Getrag six-speed manual (GS6-55BG). It is generally robust, but expect worn shift-cable bushings (vague, sloppy shifter, $150–400) and second- or third-gear synchro crunch on abused cars. Bearing whine is also possible. MINI calls the fluid lifetime fill, so a fluid change is usually overdue. Look for a fluid-change receipt and a test drive that includes quick shifts once the car is warm.', 'Soft top, drains and water intrusion. The R59 top is manually latched, with optional power assist on some cars. The weak points are the canvas, the rear window, the seals around the frameless door glass, and the body drains that clog with debr
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Oil and filter service with BMW LL-01 approved oil, plus a new oil filter housing gasket if it shows any seepage. Reset the service interval to 5,000–7,500 miles.', 'Inspect the accessory belt and replace it if it is oil-contaminated, cracked or of unknown age.', 'Flush the brake fluid, which also serves the clutch hydraulics on this car.', 'Replace the spark plugs if there is no record within 30k miles. Scan for misfire counts and swap any weak coil.', 'Clear and flush the soft-top body drains. Clean and treat the canvas and seals, and dry out any damp carpet or trunk padding.', 'Replace tires older than about 6 years regardless of tread.', 'Return aftermarket intakes or bolt-ons to stock if present and the original parts are available. Confirm the ECU is on factory software.', 'Top up
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Walnut-blast the intake valves if over about 50k miles with no record, or if cold-idle misfires persist.', 'Replace the timing chain, guides and tensioner if there is any cold-start rattle or cam-correlation fault, or proactively on high-mileage cars with no chain history.', 'Replace the water pump and thermostat housing on an original-part 10+ year-old car, combined with a coolant flush.', "Change the manual transmission fluid, which is usually never done under the 'lifetime' spec, and refresh the shift-cable bushings if the shifter is vague.", 'Replace front control arm rear bushings and strut mounts if there are clunks or tramlining.', 'Address valve cover, vacuum pump or turbo oil line leaks found at the PPI.', 'Budget for a clutch and flywheel if engagement is high or there is slip
profiles.market_notes: The JCW manual commands a clear premium over the Cooper S Roadster, and the automatic JCW and base Cooper trade noticeably lower. Final-year 2014–2015 cars and low-mileage examples (under 30k) sit at the top of the market, and auction heat can push exceptional ones past $30k. Typical clean driver-quality JCWs trade well below that, so don't anchor on outlier results like the example's $31,750. Price is moved most by comprehensive short-interval service records, a stock or reversible condition (intakes, tunes, exhaust and lowered suspension discount the car for this buyer), the condition of the top and interior, and desirable options or colors such as Chili Red or the JCW contrast scheme. A high owner count, like six on a 24k-mile car, warrants scrutiny of how consistently it was maintained.
profiles.catchup_notes: Every R59 is now 10+ years old, and many low-mileage cars aged on MINI's long condition-based service intervals. Assume rubber and plastic parts are due unless documented. That means the oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets, the accessory belt, coolant hoses and thermostat housing, and soft-top seals. Fluids sold as 'lifetime' (transmission, coolant) and the brake/clutch fluid are probably also overdue. Plan roughly $1,500–3,000 of catch-up on a typical example, even one with low mileage.

profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (NA, 1990–1997)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the NA Miata is a cheap-to-own, top-down Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road car — a 2,200-lb, 116–133 hp roadster whose whole appeal is steering feel, shifter quality and the ability to drive it hard at legal-ish speeds. It is not a hauler and not an investment; the right car is a rust-free, documented, largely stock West Coast example where the timing belt, cooling system and soft top are already sorted. Because purchase price is low relative to the cost of fixing a bad one, condition and documentation matter far more than mileage or a rare color. A tidy 80k-mile car with receipts beats a 45k-mile survivor with an unknown belt history every time.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt: the 1.6L (B6ZE) and 1.8L (BP) are interference-risk on the 1.8 and generally considered non-interference on the 1.6, but either way the belt, tensioner, water pump and front seals are a 60k-mile/7-year item. Most NAs on the market are overdue. Expect $600–$1,200 done properly with pump and seals; demand a dated receipt, not 'seller says it was done.' 2) Crank nose / crank keyway failure — the 'crank wobble' or short-nose crank issue on 1.6L cars (and some early 1.8s) where the pulley bolt loosens, chews the keyway and destroys the crank snout. Symptoms: wandering timing mark, clunk at idle, wobbling pulley. A trashed crank means engine-out, $2,500–$5,000. Ask whether the pulley bolt was re-torqued to spec (roughly 80–100 lb-ft plus) at the last belt job. 3) Rust — rear wheel arches, rocker panels, front frame rails behind the fenders, floor pans, and especially the rear frame rail near the differential mount and the battery tray corner. Northeast/Midwest cars are frequently structurally rotten under fresh paint. A California car should be clean; still check the rockers and the seam under the rear of the doors. 4) Soft top and rain leaks: original vinyl/cloth tops are 25+ years old, plastic rear windows craze and crack, and zippers fail. Patched tears (as in the example listing) mean a top is due: $400–$900 for a quality cloth top with glass window installed. Leaks track to clogged drain tubes behind the seats — water pools in the floor pans and rots them and the ECU area. 5) Cooling system: 30-year-old radiators (plastic end tanks), brittle hoses, failing thermostats and radiator caps. Overheating on a hot day is common and these engines are tolerant but not immortal. Budget $300–$600 for radiator, hoses, cap, thermostat. 6) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, front crank seal, cam seals, and rear main. The 'oil leak noted' in this listing is typical — valve cover $150, front seals with the timing belt job, rear main $600–$900 with trans out. 7) Suspension bushings and shocks: original bushings are shot at this age; sloppy rear subframe, worn ball joints, torn CV/axle boots, and dead OEM dampers. A full refresh with decent dampers and bushings runs $900–$2,000. 8) Differential and drivetrain: PPF bushings, worn differential mount, leaking diff and transmission seals, and the notorious 5th-gear/2nd-gear synchro wear on high-mile boxes. A crunchy 2nd gear cold is a warning; a rebuilt or used trans is $800–$1,800 installed. Also check the clutch slave cylinder (very common leak, $80 part) and master. 9) Electrics: pop-up headlight motors and linkage (slow or one-eye-up), failing window regulators/motors, worn ignition switch, aged main relay, cracked crank angle sensor O-ring leaking oil, and corroded grounds. Individually cheap, collectively annoying. 10) Interior degradation: sun-baked dashboards crack at the defroster vents, seat bolsters split (especially tan leather on Special Edition/M Edition cars), door card vinyl delaminates, and the plastic rear window scuffs. Dash cap or replacement $200–$600. 11) Brakes and fuel system: seized rear caliper slide pins and parking brake mechanisms, rusty hard lines on non-West-Coast cars, and original fuel pumps/filters that are well past service. 12) Modifications: many NAs have been autocrossed, lowered on cheap coilovers, or fitted with turbo kits. Aftermarket exhaust (as here) may not be CARB-legal for California registration; sway bars and roll bars are benign but raise the question of track use. Look for evidence of an untracked life. 13) Airbag/SRS and the 1990–93 short-nose crank plus 1.6L's smaller brakes are worth noting; 1994+ 1.8L cars gained more power, larger brakes and a stiffer chassis, but also the 1994–95 OBD-I/1996+ OBD-II split which affects California smog testing ease.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt/water pump/tensioner and front seals with a properly torqued crank pulley bolt if no dated receipt exists ($700–$1,200); full fluid service (engine oil, coolant flush, brake fluid, gear oil, diff oil, $300–$500); clutch slave cylinder and a look at the master ($150–$300); clean the soft-top drain tubes and reseal/replace the top if patched ($400–$900); radiator cap, thermostat and hoses if age-unknown ($200–$400); four fresh tires if the current set is over six years old regardless of tread ($500–$800); alignment after any suspension work ($120); fix the noted oil leak, usually valve cover gasket and front seals ($150–$400); new battery and a check of all grounds.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Shock/strut and bushing refresh including rear subframe, control arm and PPF bushings ($900–$2,000); rear main or transmission seal if a leak develops ($600–$900); clutch if it's original and slipping ($800–$1,200 with rear main done at the same time); pop-up headlight motor or linkage repair ($150–$400); window regulator/motor ($150–$300 per side); dash cap or dash replacement if cracked ($200–$600); seat re-bolstering or covers on leather cars ($400–$1,200); brake caliper rebuild/slide pin service and rotors/pads ($400–$700); possible fuel pump, CAS O-ring and ignition refresh (cap, rotor, wires, plugs, $200–$400); catalyst/exhaust restoration to CARB-legal configuration if California smog is a concern ($400–$1,200).
profiles.market_notes: NA prices are driven by rust-free bodies, dated timing belt receipts, originality, and color/trim rarity far more than mileage — clean drivers sit in the $8k–$15k band, sorted 1.8L R-package or low-mile survivors reach $18k–$30k+, and museum-grade 1990 launch cars or pristine BRG Special Editions can exceed that. The 1991 British Racing Green Special Edition (tan leather, Nardi wood, LSD, ~4,000 built) carries a modest premium over a base 1.6, but modifications, a patched top, a noted oil leak and only partial records pull it back toward driver money — which is exactly why the example car landed near $11k. Automatics, non-LSD cars, aftermarket body kits, turbo builds and anything with rocker/rail rust trade at a steep discount. In coastal California, smog-legality of the exhaust and a clean CA title in the seller's name are real value items.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-plus-year-old car needs a deferred-maintenance sweep regardless of mileage: all rubber (belts, hoses, bushings, seals), all fluids, tires by date code, the soft top and its drains, and the cooling system. Budget $2,000–$3,500 in the first year on a clean California example just to bring the consumables current, plus a contingency for a crank/timing surprise on a car with no belt receipt.

profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (NB, 1999-2005, incl. NB1/NB2 and Mazdaspeed)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the NB is a lightweight, analog, top-down driver for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the Laguna Seca area. It is cheap to run when sorted. Condition and history matter far more than badges. The main risk is structural rust, especially on cars from the salt belt or the East Coast, followed by deferred rubber, cooling and timing-belt maintenance on 20-25 year old cars. Favor a documented, unmodified manual car with rust-free rails and a known timing-belt date over low miles alone. Coastal fog makes a good top, working drains and ideally a hardtop worth paying for.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural rust is the number-one NB killer. Look first at the front frame rails where they meet the rocker just behind the front wheels, then the rockers and sills ahead of the rear wheels, the rear wheel-arch lips and the rear subframe mounts. Salt-state cars (this example is from PA) can look fine on top and be rotten underneath. Rail repair runs $1,500-4,000+ and can total the car. Require lift photos of both rails and sills; fresh undercoating or rocker covers over the rails is a red flag.', 'Soft-top drain holes behind the seats clog with debris. Water then backs into the rocker cavities and footwells, causing rust from the inside and damp, mildewed carpet. Check that both drains are clear, carpets and pads are dry, and the cabin has no musty smell. Clearing the drains is free; rust repair from neglected drains is not.', 'The timing belt is due every 60k miles or about 5-7 years, regardless of mileage on a low-use car. The BP 1.8 is generally treated as non-interference in stock form, but a failed belt still strands you. Do the water pump, thermostat, cam and crank seals, and tensioner/idler at the same time. Expect $700-1,200 at an independent shop. Ask for a dated receipt with mileage; without one, budget it immediately.', 'Cooling-system aging is common. The OEM plastic-tank radiator cracks at the seams, the coolant expansion tank yellows and cracks, and hoses and heater hoses go soft. A radiator plus hoses runs $350-800. Look for crusty coolant at the tank seams, low or brown coolant, and temperature creep in traffic.', 'Oil leaks are routine. Expect seepage from the valve cover gasket (including the spark-plug-well seals), the dipstick tube O-ring, and the cam angle sensor (CAS) O-ring at the back of the head. The CAS leak can foul the sensor and cause misfires. Each fix is roughly $100-350. A rear main seal leak shows at the bellhousing drip point and costs $700-1,200 if done with a clutch. Oil in the plug wells points to the valve cover seals.', 'Ignition parts wear out. The coil packs (wasted-spark) crack and cause misfires, especially when hot or damp. Old plug wires leak spark in coastal fog. Coils plus wires and plugs run $200-500.', 'Idle problems are common. A dirty or failing idle air control valve, vacuum leaks from brittle intake hoses, or a sticky throttle body can cause high or hunting idle or stalling. On 2001+ NB2 VVT cars, the oil control valve and VVT system dislike neglected oil changes. Usually $100-400 to sort.', 'Clutch hydraulics and clutch wear: the slave and master cylinders weep or fail, and the clutch can slip at high mileage. Check the throwout bearing for noise and the pivot for wear. A clutch job with seals runs $900-1,600. Check for a soft or high engagement point and for slip in 4th/5th under load.', 'Transmission and driveline: on 5-speeds, look for 2nd/3rd synchro grind (worse when cold) and old gear oil. profiles.market_notes: Clean, rust-free, unmodified manual cars with records command a premium. Sub-60k-mile examples like the $15,800 example sale show the market rising for top-condition cars, while tired, modified or rusty cars still trade in the $4,000-8,000 range. Prices move most with structural condition and documentation (timing belt and recent service), manual vs. automatic (automatics are heavily discounted), and an included factory hardtop (roughly $1,000-2,000). Special editions (1999 10th Anniversary, SE, Shinsen, Club Spec) and the 2004-2005 Mazdaspeed carry extra value when stock. Desirable colors such as Emerald Mica, Evolution Orange, Crystal Blue and Titanium Gray help. NB2 (2001+) cars bring a little more for VVT and the refreshed interior, but NB1 (1999-2000) is not a meaningful penalty for a driver.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most NBs are now 20-26 years old, so even low-mileage cars usually need a rubber and fluid catch-up: timing belt by age, coolant hoses, expansion tank, radiator, valve cover/CAS seals, clutch hydraulics, tires and bushings. Plan $1,500-3,500 to bring a typical unsorted example to dependable driver status. Structural rust is the one problem that money may not sensibly fix.

profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (NC1, NC2 & NC3, 2006-2015)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer the NC is a cheap, durable, and comfortable roadster for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and Laguna Seca weekends. It is roomier and more refined than the NA/NB, and much less money than an ND. The engine and drivetrain are robust. Condition is driven by cooling-system plastics, roof and drain health, suspension wear, and abuse or modification history. In California, an unmodified, smog-legal, documented car beats a tuned one at almost any price difference, because non-CARB intake, exhaust, or ECU tunes will fail the smog visual or functional check. Return-to-stock adds cost and hassle.
profiles.weak_points: ['Coolant expansion tank: the plastic reservoir yellows, goes brittle, and cracks or weeps at the seam, usually from 8-12 years of age regardless of mileage. Left alone it can dump coolant and overheat the aluminum MZR 2.0 (LF) engine, risking a head gasket or warped head. The part is $60-150 and installation is $150-300. Look for a receipt showing replacement, or a clear, non-yellowed tank with no crusty residue at the seam or cap.', 'Radiator: the plastic end tanks crack and seep with age, often 80k+ miles or 10+ years. The original radiator on an early NC1 is now a due item. Replacement runs $350-700. Look for pink or green crust on the tank seams and a cooling-system service record (Mazda FL22 coolant changed roughly every 5 years or 50k).', 'Soft-top drains and seals: two drain tubes behind the seats clog with debris, and water then backs up into the floor pans and footwells. Soaked carpet, mildew, corroded seat-track bolts, and electrical gremlins follow. The vinyl or cloth top wears at fold points and the rear seam; a replacement is $900-2,000 installed. Look for dry carpet and pad underneath, clear drains (pour water and watch it exit behind the front wheels), and an intact rear glass seal.', 'Power Retractable Hard Top (PRHT): roof motor, microswitches, latch adjustment, and weatherstrip faults cause slow, stalled, or incomplete cycles. Water leaks at the header or quarter seals are common. Drain tubes clog the same way as on the soft top. Diagnosis and repair runs $400-2,500 depending on motor versus switch versus seal work. Ask for a video of several full open/close cycles, and confirm no warning chimes or flashing lamp. Treat aftermarket top controllers (such as Mods4cars SmartTOP) as something to verify.', '6-speed manual synchros: early 6MT cars, especially 2006-2008, are known for 2nd/3rd gear grind or notchiness, worst when cold or on fast shifts. Shift quality often improves with a fluid change (Mazda or Redline MT-90 type). A true synchro failure means a rebuild or used transmission at $1,800-3,500. Check for transmission fluid change records and test fast 2-3 shifts at operating temperature. The 5-speed (base/SV/Sport) is very durable.', 'Clutch hydraulics and clutch wear: the slave cylinder weeps (wetness at the bellhousing) and the master can soften. Hard-driven or autocrossed cars wear the clutch early, around 60-90k. A clutch with flywheel resurface runs $1,200-2,000, and a slave $200-400. Look for high engagement or slip in 5th/6th under load, a soft pedal, and receipts for clutch fluid flushes.', 'Rear wheel bearings/hubs and rear suspension: rear hubs hum or grind, typically at 50-100k or sooner on lowered cars. Expect $300-600 per side; the example listing already shows a rear hub and spindle replacement at 49k. Also check the lower control arm bushings, front lower ball joints, and sway bar end links, which clunk over bumps. Bushing and arm work can run $600-1,500.', 'Rear differential and seals: pinion and axle seals weep, and diff fluid is often never changed. Fluid service is $100-200; seals run $250-500. Cars with a limited-slip diff (Sport/Club/GT 6MT and most PRHT manuals) should not chatter or clunk on tight turns. Check for wet residue at the pinion and a fluid change record.', 'Engine leaks and ignition: the MZR LF is durable, but the valve cover gasket and spark plug tube seals leak with age, causing an oil smell and misfires ($200-450). Spark plugs are due around 75k ($150-300), and coils can fail one at a time ($80-150 each). The 2009+ NC2 engine has a forged crank and a 7,200 rpm redline. NC1 (2006-2008) has a lower redline and a slightly different intake and cam spec, but neither engine has systemic internal failures. Look for oil change records at 5-7.5k intervals and listen for timing chain rattle on cold start at high mileage.', 'Evap and check-engine issues: purge solenoid and evap leak codes (P0441/P0455/P0456) and occasional O2 sensor codes are common, typically $100-400. profiles.market_notes: NC3 (2013-2015) facelift cars and late NC2 (2009-2012) command the most money; 2006-2008 NC1 cars are cheapest. Manual transmissions, the PRHT, Club and Grand Touring trims, and the limited-slip diff add value. Low-production specials (2015 25th Anniversary, Special Editions) carry a real premium. Clean, unmodified, documented sub-60k-mile cars bring roughly $13-20k in 2024-2026 for NC3 manuals. Higher mileage or modified cars trade around $7-12k. Modifications, especially tunes and lowered suspension, usually reduce value and smog-ability in California. Single-owner records, recent cooling-system service, and a dry, rust-free underbody move price more than color.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most NCs are now 10-20 years old, so plastic cooling parts (expansion tank, radiator), rubber seals, roof drains and weatherstrips, and bushings are due regardless of mileage. profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (ND1 2016-2018 & ND2 2019+, soft top and RF)
profiles.framing: The ND is a light, simple, reliable roadster. For a Carmel buyer it suits Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the coast loops, and it can also do daily errands. Mechanical risk is low compared with most sports cars, so the purchase depends on driveline health (especially early 6MT gearboxes), soft-top and RF roof condition, and proof the car was maintained by time and not just by mileage. A documented, unmodified, manual example with clean cabin and no water history is the target. ND2 (2019+, 181 hp, 7,500 rpm redline) is the better engine if the budget allows.
profiles.weak_points: 1) The 6-speed manual on early ND1 cars, mainly 2016 and early-2017 builds, had a higher rate of failures. These showed up as grinding or popping out of gear, 2nd and 3rd synchro problems, and some outright internal failures, often on cars that saw track days or hard launches. Mazda revised the internals during production. A failed gearbox costs $3,500-6,500 outside warranty. Ask for warranty transmission-replacement records and check the build date on the door jamb. Some cold-weather notchiness into 2nd is normal and is often improved by a fluid change; grinding when warm is not normal. 2) Clutch and hydraulics: clutch life varies with use, often 60-100k miles, sooner on autocross or track cars. Replacement is $1,200-2,000. Check for slipping in 4th-6th under load, a high engagement point, and pedal squeaks. 3) Soft-top drains and water ingress: two drains sit behind the seats and clog with leaves and pine needles. Water then backs up into the cabin and footwells and can reach floor-mounted electrical connectors. Look for damp carpet underlay, musty smell, fogging and corrosion on seat-rail bolts. 4) Soft-top fabric wear: the top can rub through where it folds and contacts the body at the rear corners and along the header. Replacement is $1,500-2,500 installed. Seam and header-seal leaks also occur. 5) RF retractable roof: rattles, creaks, wind noise, and slow or interrupted cycling from sensor, motor or alignment issues. Diagnosis and repair at a dealer can run $500-3,000+. Cycle the roof several times and look for water tracks at the targa seals. 6) Mazda Connect infotainment on 2016-2018 cars: the touchscreen delaminates and 'ghost touches', and the CMU can freeze or reboot. A screen is $150-700 depending on DIY vs dealer; a CMU is $800-1,500. Firmware updates fix many software complaints, and CarPlay/Android Auto retrofit kits exist. 7) Paint and body: Mazda paint, especially Soul Red, chips easily on the nose, hood leading edge and behind the front wheels. The aluminum hood, trunk and front fenders dent easily and cost more to repair. Check for respray, PPF and curb-rashed wheels. 8) Oil leaks: watch for seepage at the valve cover gasket, timing-cover and front-crank seal areas, and the rear diff pinion and output seals. These are usually $200-800 repairs but they reveal neglect. Some ND2 owners report rear main seal weeps. 9) SkyActiv-G water pump: weeping at the pump weep hole or coolant crust is common from roughly 60-100k miles. Repair is $500-900. 10) Suspension noises: creaks and clunks from sway-bar end links and bushings, front lower control arm bushings, and rear subframe and toe-link areas. Club Bilstein dampers can leak with age, at $800-1,600 per pair installed. Low-mileage cars often still have factory alignment, which is commonly slightly out. 11) Age items on low-mileage garage queens: brake fluid is due every 3 years, yet many sparingly driven cars have never had it changed. Expect old tires (check DOT dates even when 'new' is claimed), stale fuel, and sulfated batteries. The small ND battery dies quickly when the car sits. 12) Abuse indicators: autocross or track use (number decals, worn tire shoulders, brake-pad residue, hard-launch clutch wear) and removed-then-restored modifications such as exhaust, intake, tune or lowering springs. 13) Recalls and TSBs: ND years have had campaigns covering items such as software and component updates. Confirm by VIN that all are closed.

ND2 (2019+) cars command roughly $3-5k more than comparable ND1 cars for the 181 hp engine. Manual transmissions are preferred and sell faster; automatics trade at a discount in this segment. profiles.label: Mazda RX-7 (FD3S; US-market 1993–1995, JDM through 2002)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the FD is a weekend and back-road enthusiast car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laguna Seca days. It is not a commuter. The car will reward attention and punish neglect. Purchase price matters less than three things: the documented health of the 13B-REW rotary, the state of the heat-cooked sequential-turbo plumbing, and whether the car can pass a California smog check (visual, functional and tailpipe) in its current configuration. A stock, documented, US-market manual car with a recent rotary-specific compression test is the target. Modified, automatic, or JDM-import cars carry engine, registration and resale penalties that rarely make sense for a Carmel-based driver.
profiles.weak_points: ['Apex seal and engine wear: a stock 13B-REW commonly needs a rebuild somewhere between 60k and 100k miles. Overheating, lean running, low oil or detonation can kill one much sooner. The only meaningful health check is a rotary-specific compression test that shows all three faces per rotor, normalized to 250 rpm and taken fully warm. Mazda service guidance is roughly 120 psi standard and about 85 psi minimum, and faces should be balanced within about 15 psi. One low face (for example 67 psi against 105–110 on the others) points to a failing apex seal, corner seal or side seal, not a minor quirk. Rebuild cost is about $5k–$8k for a stock reman and $8k–$14k+ for a respected-shop build with turbo work. Get the shop name, date, mileage and seal type on the receipt.', "Cooling system: the plastic air separation tank (AST) and the filler neck crack with age. The stock radiator's plastic end tanks also fail. A single overheat can warp rotor housings or blow coolant seals, which shows up as white sweet-smelling smoke, coolant loss, or bubbles in the filler. Look for receipts for an aluminum AST, the radiator, the thermostat and hoses. Many owners fit aftermarket radiators and lower fan-switch temperatures, which is acceptable if documented. Repair is $800–$2,000 for a cooling refresh and a full engine rebuild if overheating damaged the seals.", 'Sequential twin-turbo control: there are about 80 feet of vacuum and pressure hoses, several solenoids, and the charge control, wastegate and turbo-precontrol actuators. Heat makes the rubber brittle and leaks follow. Symptoms are a flat spot or hesitation at the roughly 4,500 rpm primary-to-secondary transition, boost spiking, or no secondary at all. Repair is $600–$1,500 for a silicone hose and solenoid refresh. Turbo rebuilds are $2,500–$5,000 for the pair. Ask for a dated hose-replacement receipt or recent photos.', 'Fuel system fire risk: the fuel injector hoses, fuel rail hoses and pulsation damper hoses harden and crack. Underhood temperatures and 25+ year old rubber have caused documented FD engine fires. Inspect for any fuel smell, wetness or staining around the rails. A full fuel-hose replacement runs $400–$1,000. Without a dated receipt or a visual check showing fresh hoses, assume it has not been done.', 'Engine wiring harness and connectors: the main engine harness insulation goes brittle and cracks from heat, causing intermittent misfire, sensor faults and idle problems. Repair is about $800–$2,000 for a new or repaired harness, more if a reproduction is sourced.', 'ECU capacitors: the original surface-mount electrolytic capacitors leak and can corrode the board. Symptoms are erratic idle, boost faults or no-start. A recap costs $200–$400 if caught early and much more if traces are damaged. Ask whether the ECU has been recapped or replaced, and with what.', 'Oil metering pump (OMP) and premix: the rotary injects oil into the combustion chambers. Removing the OMP or air pump (common on modified cars) shifts lubrication duty to the owner, who must premix fuel, and creates smog failures in California. An OMP replacement is $400–$900.', 'Ignition: the coil packs, igniter and the four plugs (leading and trailing) degrade, and weak spark hurts starting and flooding resistance. Expect $300–$800 for plugs, wires and coils.', "Pre-catalytic converter and emissions equipment: the stock pre-cat can break down. Many owners delete it with a 'cat-less downpipe', and that is an automatic California smog visual failure without a CARB EO. Restoring stock-type emissions equipment can cost $1,000–$3,000. Treat the absence of a pre-cat, air pump or EGR as a registration and cost problem in Carmel, not a performance plus.", 'Drivetrain: the 5-speed manual can develop 2nd and 3rd gear synchro crunch at high mileage. Clutch replacement is $1,200–$2,000 including the flywheel inspection. The 4-speed automatic is reliable but saps performance and hurts resale. Mushy differential mount, motor mount and tr
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Engine oil and filter change with fresh fluids: coolant flush, brake fluid, transmission fluid and differential fluid', 'Inspect and likely replace fuel injector and fuel rail hoses to remove fire risk', 'Inspect and refresh vacuum and pressure hoses in the sequential-turbo control system; check solenoid operation', 'Replace spark plugs (all four) and inspect coils and wires', 'Check the cooling system thoroughly: AST, radiator, hoses, thermostat, fan operation; replace any cracked or aged plastic parts', 'Replace tires if older than about 6 years and reset alignment', 'Battery test or replacement and full electrical check: headlights, pop-ups, gauges, Bose system', 'Confirm smog-check readiness for California (visual, functional, tailpipe); restore any missing emissions components if re

profiles.market_notes: The biggest price driver is a documented, stock, US-market manual car with a recent rotary-specific compression test. Those cars bring roughly 1.5–2.5× the price of modified or automatic examples. R1 and R2 trims, the 1995 cars, low miles and desirable colors (Montego Blue, Competition Yellow, Vintage Red, Chaste White) command premiums, while Touring and PEP cars sit in the middle. Automatic transmissions, cat-less downpipes, emissions deletes, engine swaps, undocumented rebuilds and weak compression faces cause steep discounts. A respected-shop rebuild with receipts and fresh compression numbers can add value to a high-mile car.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most FDs are 30+ years old and need a deferred-maintenance sweep: vacuum and fuel hoses, cooling-system plastics, the engine harness, ECU capacitors and rubber bushings and mounts. Budget $3,000–$6,000 for this work even on a healthy engine. Cars that sat for long periods may also have stuck seals, dried fuel components and degraded A/C, which raises both short-term cost and engine-health risk.

profiles.label: Mazda Rotary Pickup (REPU, 1974-1977)
profiles.framing: The REPU is the only rotary-powered pickup ever series-produced, sold only in North America, and roughly 15,000 were built with very few survivors that are not rusty, swapped, or both. For this buyer it is a weekend-and-errands novelty truck with real collector standing, not a load hauler: the 13B makes its case with a 7,000-rpm tach and a howl no small truck has any business making. What matters is a healthy (or honestly documented) rotary, a solid cab/bed/frame, and the survival of the REPU-only sheetmetal and trim that cannot be bought at any price. Engine swaps (13B-REW, 20B, LS) are common and can be well executed, but they change the car from 'documented original' to 'someone's build' and, in California, create a real registration problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Apex seals and rotor housing wear are the defining risk. A tired 13B shows hard hot restarts, blue smoke on startup, low and uneven cranking compression, and a rough idle that smooths above 3,000 rpm. Insist on a rotary-specific compression test (Mazda-style tester reading all three faces per rotor at cranking speed, ideally at operating temperature): each face should be roughly 85-100 psi corrected with no more than about 10-15 psi spread between faces on the same rotor. A proper period 13B rebuild with new seals, re-nitrided or replacement housings, bearings and a rebuilt carb runs $6,000-10,000 today; a 20B or 13B-REW rebuild is $15,000-25,000 with parts that come from wrecked JDM cars.', 'Coolant seals and O-rings between the housings fail with any overheating event. Symptoms are unexplained coolant loss with no external leak, steam or sweet smell at the tailpipe, bubbles/pressure in the overflow, and a hot-start no-start. There is no head-gasket shortcut: it is a full teardown, so this failure is effectively the same cost as a rebuild. Ask for a cooling-system pressure test and a chemical block test for combustion gases in the coolant.', 'Cooling capacity was marginal when new and worse at 50 years old. Original copper/brass radiators are silted, the fan clutch is usually dead, and the thermostat and water pump housing are commonly corroded or cracked. Most healthy survivors have an aluminum radiator and electric fan; a stock-appearing truck with an unrecorded radiator history should be assumed to need a recore ($400-800) or aluminum replacement plus hoses and thermostat ($600-1,200 installed).', 'The thermal reactor exhaust system (a heat-shielded manifold that burned unburnt fuel to meet 1970s emissions) is a known fire and heat-soak hazard. Originals crack, glow red, cook the wiring and firewall insulation, and are effectively unobtainable ($2,000-4,000 if one surfaces). Most trucks have a header and a straight exhaust; that is a functional improvement but an originality loss, and any reactor-delete should be checked for heat shielding, brake line routing, and fuel line proximity.', "The Nikki four-barrel carburetor is the REPU-specific fuel-system weak point: dried accelerator pumps, worn secondary linkage, plugged idle circuits, a seized choke, and a hot-soak percolation problem that mimics flooding. Rebuild kits are scarce ($400-1,200 for a competent rebuild) and many trucks run Holley/Weber or EFI conversions. Ask what carb is fitted and whether idle/part-throttle air-fuel has actually been checked, not just 'it runs'.", "Oil metering pump (OMP) status is the single cheapest question with the biggest consequence. If the OMP has been blocked off or disconnected, the engine MUST be premixed (roughly 2-4 oz of two-stroke or 10W30 per gallon) at every fill, forever. Ask directly for the premix routine and receipts for oil; a blocked OMP plus a seller who says 'you don't need to premix' is an apex-seal timebomb. A functioning OMP should be verified for flow at the injection lines.", 'Rust is the usual reason a REPU is not worth saving. Check cab corners, the lower rear cab panel and rear window channel (the 1977 bumped-out window in particular traps water), floor pans under the rubber/carpet, the seat riser and cab mounts, the inner and outer bedsides behind the REPU-only flares, the front fender bottoms, the battery box on the right bedside (acid rot), and the frame rails at the rear spring hangers and above the axle. Cab corner and floor repair with correct fabrication is $3,000-8,000 in bodywork, and there are no reproduction REPU panels.', "REPU-only trim is unobtainium: the eggcrate grille, fender flares, round taillights, 'Rotary Pickup/Rotary Engine' badging and tailgate lettering, the rotary-specific instrument cluster with 7,000-rpm tach, the bumpers, and the 1977 rear-window glass. Missing or damaged pieces can cost thousands on the collector market or stall a project indefinitely. Photograph and inventory e
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including a coolant flush with correct rotary-safe coolant; new thermostat, hoses, and cap; complete brake hydraulic refresh (flex lines, wheel cylinders or caliper seals, master, fluid); replace all rubber fuel line with SAE 30R9 and check the tank and sender; tires almost always need replacing on date code alone even with good tread; ignition tune (plugs, wires, points/condenser or coil check, timing set with a light on both leading and trailing); establish and document a premix routine if the OMP is blocked; belts, battery, and a full lighting/grounds sweep; leak-check the radiator and lower housing and plan an aluminum radiator/electric fan if the truck runs hot in traffic; seat belts and steering-play assessment before it is driven on Highway 1. Budget $3,000-6,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main/front cover seals if the engine is out for anything; four-speed second-gear synchro or a documented five-speed conversion; leaf springs, shackle bushings, shocks, and U-joints; steering box and drag-link refresh; exhaust fabrication or heat shielding done properly; carburetor rebuild or a documented tune of whatever induction is fitted; localized rust repair at cab corners, bedsides, and battery box before it spreads; radiator recore; wiring harness repairs where heat has cooked the insulation; and a compression retest at the 12-month mark to trend seal health. Budget $4,000-9,000 on a good truck, far more if the engine has to come out.
profiles.market_notes: Condition and originality drive REPU money far more than mileage, which is unverifiable on a five-digit odometer and largely irrelevant on a rebuilt rotary. Rust-free Southwest/California survivors with complete REPU-only trim, original 13B, correct gauges, and a documented history are the top of the market; well-executed 20B/13B-REW builds with named builders and standalone tunes can match or exceed that number with a narrower buyer pool and no smog path in CA. Long-bed 1977 cars with the bumped-out rear window have their own following as the final-year variant. Discounts come fast for rust, missing grille/flares/taillights/badges, non-rotary swaps (LS), automatic conversions, and 'ran when parked' engines; expect roughly $20,000-30,000 for a driver, $35,000-55,000 for an excellent original or a strong documented build, and $60,000+ only for concours-grade originals.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume everything rubber and every fluid is due regardless of what the seller says: fuel hose, brake hydraulics, coolant, radiator, hoses, bushings, and tires on date code alone. A 50-year-old low-production Japanese truck also needs a wiring and grounds sweep and a fuel-tank inspection before it is trusted on a mountain road, and any rotary with unknown seal history should be priced with a rebuild reserve set aside from day one.

profiles.label: McLaren 750S (Coupe & Spider, 2024–2026)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 750S Spider is a usable, warranty-backed supercar for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and occasional longer runs, not an appreciating asset. Expect steep depreciation, high consumable costs and dealer-dependent servicing (McLaren dealers are in the Bay Area and Southern California). The 7-speed SSG dual-clutch is the only transmission, so automatic is not a negative here. What matters most is remaining factory warranty and its transfer, eligibility for McLaren Extended Warranty, an honest damage history on the carbon tub and nose, a stock ECU, and a clean bill of health from the hydraulic suspension, nose-lift and roof systems.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Hydraulic suspension (Proactive Chassis Control III, carried over and retuned from the 720S). It uses interlinked hydraulic dampers, accumulators and lines rather than anti-roll bars. On 720S cars, accumulator and line seepage, pressure-sensor faults and 'Suspension Fault' warnings appeared from about 3–6 years old. The 750S is too new for a track record, but expect the same system risk. Repair runs roughly $3k–8k for an accumulator or line and $10k–20k for multiple dampers or a pump out of warranty. Ask for dealer records of any suspension fault codes or campaign work.

2) Front axle nose-lift system. It shares hydraulics with the suspension and gets cycled constantly on steep Carmel driveways. Seal leaks, slow lift and fault messages are common on the 720S family. Typical cost is $2k–6k. Verify it lifts and lowers repeatedly on the test drive.

3) Low-clearance damage to the front splitter, undertray, radiators and carbon tub (MonoCage II). Scrapes on the splitter and undertray are routine. Cracked undertrays run $2k–5k. Side radiators and condensers collect road debris and can be holed by stones, at $3k–7k per side. Any impact near the tub or crash structures is a major-value event. Get lift photos of the entire underside and confirm a clean Carfax/AutoCheck. Note that PPF and ceramic coating can hide repaint.

4) Retractable hardtop and electrochromic glass roof (Spider only). On the 720S Spider, roof faults were often triggered by low 12V voltage, microswitch or position-sensor faults, or blocked drains causing water ingress into the cabin and electronics. Electrochromic panel failure (patchy tint, delamination, cracks) can run $8k–15k+. Cycle the roof several times. Also check the drains and carpets for water marks, which matters with coastal fog and rain.

5) Dihedral doors. Watch for weak gas struts, soft-close or latch actuator faults, frameless glass not dropping or indexing (leading to wind noise or leaks), and torn door seals. Typical cost is $1k–4k per door issue. Open, close and lock both doors many times.

6) 12V electrical sensitivity. McLarens throw cascading warnings (roof, doors, infotainment, transmission) when battery voltage sags, and low-use cars often sit. Ask whether a McLaren-approved battery conditioner was used. A battery replacement is a few hundred to about $1k. A history of repeated 'random' faults may be voltage-related or a real module issue, and only a dealer MDS scan separates the two.

7) Infotainment, driver display and electronics. The 750S updated the 720S-era IRIS system and added a new display, but early cars can still show screen freezes, CarPlay drops, camera and park-assist faults, and the folding driver display misbehaving. Most fixes are dealer software updates, though module replacement can reach $3k–8k. Confirm all software campaigns and recalls are done by VIN.

8) Carbon ceramic brakes. CCM rotors last long on the street but are very expensive: roughly $8k–14k per axle for rotors, and $1.5k–3k for pads. Track use with overheating leads to oxidation and chipping. Inspect the rotor edges and surfaces and get the measured wear figures.

9) SSG 7-speed dual-clutch transmission. It is generally robust, but abuse from repeated launches, track sessions or an ECU tune accelerates clutch wear. Watch for jerky low-speed engagement, warning messages or limp mode. Clutch work runs about $8k–15k and a gearbox replacement $30k+ out of warranty. A dealer MDS readout of clutch wear and adaptation values is the evidence to get.

10) M840T 4.0L twin-turbo V8 (evolved from the 720S). It is robust when stock, but it is a very common tuning target. ECU tunes and aftermarket downpipes or exhausts void the warranty and stress the gearbox. On older M840T cars, coolant line or hose seepage, wastegate actuator rattle and occasional coil or plug misfires have been seen. Most items cost $1k–5k, and turbo replacement is $10k+. Confirm the stock software version via a dealer scan.

11) Tires. They are Pi
profiles.immediate_repairs: Expect: replace mismatched or aged tires as a matched set (check date codes; anything over about 3 years old or mixed should go), at $2.5k–4k. Have a McLaren dealer do a full MDS scan, apply outstanding software updates and recall campaigns, and verify warranty transfer. Load-test the 12V battery and set up a battery conditioner at home. Do brake fluid if more than 2 years old or undocumented. Do the annual service if it is due or unknown ($1.5k–3.5k at a dealer). Clean the roof drains and radiator intakes. Correct any nose-lift or roof-fault codes under warranty while coverage is still active.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Within 12 months, expect: the next annual dealer service ($1.5k–3.5k), with cabin and air filters. Brake fluid on its 2-year cycle. Another tire set if the car is driven 6–8k miles ($2.5k–4k). PPF touch-up or replacement on the nose and rocker leading edges ($1k–3k). Windshield or stone-chip repair. Wheel curb-rash refinishing on the forged Vortex wheels ($300–600 per wheel). Possible door-seal, door-strut or roof-sensor adjustments, ideally while still under factory warranty. Budget for an extended-warranty purchase or inspection as the factory 3-year term approaches expiry.
profiles.market_notes: Values fall steeply from MSRP, and spec matters less than history and warranty. Spiders carry a modest premium over coupes. Remaining factory warranty plus McLaren Extended Warranty eligibility moves price meaningfully. Desirable MSO paints, carbon exterior packs, Vortex or lightweight forged wheels, B&W audio, nose lift and 360 cameras support pricing; heavy options rarely recover their sticker. Low-mileage bands (under 5k) command more than 10k+ cars. Damage history, an ECU tune, aftermarket exhaust or lowering cut values sharply. Lease-encumbered or limited-edition (Le Mans, 3-7-59) cars need extra title and provenance diligence.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 2024 example is young, so catch-up is mostly maintenance and paperwork rather than wear. Bring the annual service and brake fluid current, replace aged or mismatched tires, apply all dealer software updates and recalls, and refresh the 12V battery if the car sat. Clean the roof drains and radiator intakes before coastal winter weather, and use the remaining factory warranty to fix any suspension, roof, door or electronics faults before it expires.

profiles.label: Mercedes-AMG C63 / C63 S Cabriolet (W205/A205, 2017–2021)
profiles.framing: This is a four-seat, top-down V8 grand tourer for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and weekend runs. It works as a real daily, but its running costs are those of a German twin-turbo V8 convertible, not a C300. What matters most: (1) a healthy M177 with no tune, catless parts, or exhaust-valve gadgets, because it has to pass California smog; (2) a soft top that cycles cleanly and keeps water out; (3) a transmission that shifts smoothly when cold and in traffic; and (4) a paper trail from a Mercedes dealer or AMG specialist. The 2017–2018 cars use the 7-speed MCT. The 2019–2021 facelift moved to the 9-speed MCT and updated the interior and electronics. C63 S cars add the electronic LSD, dynamic engine mounts, and more power.
profiles.weak_points: ["Soft-top system (A205-specific). The top is electro-hydraulic, with a pump and reservoir in the trunk well, multiple hydraulic rams, and many Hall/microswitch sensors. Look for: slow or jerky operation, a top that stops partway with a 'top not locked' or 'operation not possible' message, weeping fluid at the rams or the pump, a tonneau cover or rear flap that doesn't fully seat, and side windows that don't index up and down correctly. Repair bands: reseal or replace a single ram, $1,200–$2,500. Pump, fault-chased wiring, or a top control module, $1,500–$4,000. Replacing the full fabric top, $4,000–$7,000. Records to look for: dealer invoices for top repairs or software updates. Ask for video of several full open/close cycles.", 'Water intrusion. Clogged top and cowl drains, plus aging seals at the A-pillar and side windows, let water into the trunk well and footwells. Water there can reach the top hydraulics, the SAM/control modules, and the wiring under the carpet. The result is intermittent electrical gremlins that are expensive to trace, often $500 to well over $2,000. Coastal fog and parking outdoors make it worse. Look for: water stains, musty odor, corrosion on trunk-well connectors, and a damp spare-wheel or battery area.', 'Cold-start and low-speed drivability of the 7-speed AMG Speedshift MCT (2017–2018). This is a planetary automatic that uses a wet start clutch instead of a torque converter. Common faults: shudder or harsh engagement from a stop, clunky 2-1 downshifts, flares, and conductor-plate or TCU faults. Repair bands: software update, $200–$500. Conductor plate or valve body, $1,800–$3,500. Clutch or transmission rebuild, $6,000–$10,000. The 9-speed MCT in 2019+ cars is generally regarded as better but is not immune. Records to look for: fluid and filter changes roughly every 40–60k miles. Many cars have never had one.', 'M177 engine mounts. These are hydraulic mounts, and the C63 S uses active dynamic mounts. With age and heat from the hot-V layout they collapse or leak. Symptoms: vibration at idle in Drive, a clunk on throttle tip-in or when shifting into Drive, and possibly mount fault messages on S models. Expect this around 50–80k miles or 6+ years. Cost: $1,200–$2,500 for a pair, more for dynamic mounts at a dealer.', 'Hot-V turbo plumbing leaks. The turbos sit inside the V. Oil feed and return lines, coolant lines, and their O-rings and crush washers seep with heat cycling. Look for: burning smell after a hard drive, oil or coolant residue in the valley or on the rear of the block, and low coolant with no external drip. Cost: $1,500–$3,500 because the intake and plenum must come off. Turbo replacement is uncommon but runs $6,000–$9,000 for a pair. Wastegate-actuator rattle on cold start also appears on some cars.', 'Charge-air-cooler (low-temperature) circuit. The electric auxiliary coolant pump for the intercoolers can fail, as can the low-temp radiator or its hoses. Symptoms: heat-soak power loss, limp mode, and charge-air-temperature codes. Cost: $400–$1,200. Look for: a dry, undamaged low-temp radiator up front, and a pump that runs (audible) after key-on.', 'Cooling system age. Plastic coolant pipes and quick-connects, the thermostat housing, and the expansion tank become brittle with heat, and leaks or cracks are common at 6–8+ years. Cost: $300–$1,500 depending on access. Coolant itself is a long-life fluid, but it is age-due at 8–10 years.', 'Ignition. Spark plugs and coils are stressed by high boost. Misfires under load, a flashing CEL at wide-open throttle, or rough running when cold usually mean overdue plugs or a failing coil. Plugs: $500–$900. Coils: $150–$250 each plus labor. Check the service record for plug replacement. At 60k+ miles with no receipt, assume they are due.', 'Front suspension bushings. W205 front control arms and tension-strut (thrust-arm) bushings crack, especially on AMG cars with sticky tires. Symptoms: clunk over driveway lips, wander under braking, and uneven inner
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full Xentry/STAR scan of all modules (engine, transmission, top control, SAM, restraints, ESP/eLSD), with a check of TCU/ECU flash history for non-MB software', 'Engine oil and filter (MB 229.5 0W-40) if the last service is unknown or 6+ months old; reset the service clock', 'Brake fluid flush if not documented within 2 years', 'Test the main and auxiliary batteries and replace any that are weak; this alone often clears top and stop/start faults', 'Clear and test all top and cowl drains; inspect and treat the trunk well and footwells for water; recondition the soft top fabric (clean, fabric treatment) given coastal fog and outdoor parking', 'Spark plugs if past ~60k miles with no receipt', 'Address any active coolant or oil seep found at inspection before it worsens: turbo lines, coolant
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Transmission fluid and filter service (MCT 7- or 9-speed) if not done in the last ~40k miles', 'Rear differential fluid (and eLSD check on C63 S)', 'Front control arm / tension-strut bushings if a clunk or uneven tire wear appears', 'Engine mounts if idle vibration in Drive or tip-in clunk is present', 'Brake pads and rotors on at least one axle at typical mileage', 'Rear tires (and possibly a full set) given staggered wear rates', 'Coolant exchange if 8+ years old or not documented; replace brittle coolant hoses or connectors found during service', 'Cabin and engine air filters; wiper and seal conditioning for the top']
profiles.market_notes: Sorted from biggest price effect to smallest: 1. C63 S versus C63 (the S commands a clear premium). 2. Facelift 2019–2021 cars (9-speed MCT, newer interior and electronics) are worth meaningfully more than 2017–2018 cars. 3. Mileage bands: sub-30k, 30–60k, and 60k+, with values stepping down noticeably past 60–70k. 4. Desirable options: designo paint, the Premium 3 package, carbon packages, the AMG Performance Exhaust, the Night package, and red or burmester-type interior upgrades. Polarizing color combos can narrow the bidder pool even when the spec is strong. Documented dealer or specialist service, proof of a clean top, unmodified software and exhaust, and a clean California smog history all support price. Tuned or EVM-equipped cars, cars with water-intrusion history, and cars with top faults trade at steep discounts.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2017–2018 car at 60–80k miles is now 7–9 years old. Expect batteries, spark plugs, a transmission service, diff fluid, and possibly coolant to be due, along with age-related plastic coolant fittings and front bushings. Many cars also need engine mounts and some soft-top attention around this point. Budget $3,000–$6,000 of catch-up on a decent example beyond tires and brakes.

profiles.label: Mercedes-AMG G63 (W465, 2025+)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel driver this is a near-new, warranty-backed luxury 4x4 used for Highway 1, Peninsula errands, and the occasional dirt road, not an investment. The W465 has only been in the field since 2024, so long-term failure data is thin. The real risks on a 2025-2026 example are paperwork and provenance rather than wear: remaining factory warranty, open campaigns, California certification for an out-of-state car under 7,500 miles, hidden transport or cosmetic repairs, and title or lien status. Because second-year depreciation from sticker is steep, buy on verified condition and warranty runway, not on option count.
profiles.weak_points: ['Limited field history caveat: the W465 G63 carries over the M177 4.0L hot-V twin-turbo V8 and much of the W463A chassis. Expect the W463A/M177 pattern failures below to carry over, plus first-generation teething on the new systems. Get a Mercedes dealer VIN printout showing every warranty claim, recall, and software campaign. Early-production cars routinely receive module reflashes and component campaigns.', "48V mild-hybrid system, new to the G63 on W465: integrated starter-generator, 48V battery, and DC/DC converter. Symptoms include 48V or 'drive with care' warnings, start-stop unavailable, hard or slow restarts, and charging faults. Long storage on a 12V tender alone does not guarantee 48V battery health. Under warranty this is a dealer fix. Out of warranty, ISG, 48V battery, or converter replacement runs roughly $3,000-8,000. Ask for a scan showing 48V state of health and no stored hybrid-system codes.", 'M177 hot-V turbo oil feed/return and coolant lines: on W463A G63s, seepage at turbo line seals and crossover fittings shows up from roughly 20-60k miles, often as burning-oil smell or residue in the valley. Line and seal work out of warranty is about $2,000-5,000. Replacing both turbos at a dealer is about $10,000-18,000. Look for any warranty line items mentioning turbo or oil lines.', 'Cooling system: the low-temperature intercooler circuit with electric auxiliary coolant pumps and many plastic quick-connect fittings is a known M177 leak and failure area. Symptoms are coolant-level warnings, reduced power, and pink crust on fittings. Aux pumps cost about $800-1,500 each. Chased leaks can reach $2,000+.', 'Camshaft adjuster solenoids and valve cover/cam magnet seals (M177): oil can wick into connectors, causing cam timing codes and rough running. The fix is about $500-1,500. Check for oil in connector pigtails and valve-cover edge seepage during the PPI.', 'AMG active engine mounts: failure shows as idle vibration, clunk on shifts or launch, and mount fault codes. A pair costs about $1,500-3,000 installed.', 'Suspension: W463A adaptive dampers were known to weep and knock, at roughly $1,500-3,500 per corner at a dealer. Where AMG Active Ride Control (hydraulic roll stabilization) is fitted, a hydraulic leak or pump fault is a low-frequency but high-cost item, plausibly $5,000-10,000+ out of warranty. Check for ride-control warnings, fluid at damper bodies or lines, and uneven ride height.', 'AMG Speedshift 9G (9-speed with wet start clutch): reported issues include harsh 2-3 or downshift clunks, low-speed shudder from the start clutch, and shift-quality complaints usually addressed by TCU software. Out-of-warranty conductor plate or valve body work costs about $3,000-6,000. Fluid and filter service runs around $600-900 at a dealer, typically around 40-60k miles.', 'Transfer case and three locking differentials: lockers and low range that are never exercised can develop actuator or engagement faults. Front and rear diff lock actuators cost about $1,000-3,000 each. The transfer case is expensive if it fails. Any car showing heavy off-road use or towing (rock rash on skid plates, scarred hitch) deserves scrutiny of axle seals and CV boots.', 'Electronics and software: the dual 12.3-inch MBUX screens, transparent-bonnet and 360 cameras, Burmester 3D audio, keyless entry, driver assists, and the many modules on a 2024-introduced platform are prone to glitches and campaign reflashes. A weak 12V battery after storage commonly produces phantom fault codes. Out-of-warranty module or camera replacement runs about $800-3,000 each.', 'Body, paint, and water: the flat front, hood corners, and fender flares chip heavily on Highway 1. Obsidian Black and other dark paints swirl easily. Coastal fog and salt air accelerate pitting of chips. The heavy side-hinged tailgate with spare carrier can sag or rattle. Watch for sunroof drain clogs, door seal wind noise, and transport damage hidden under PPF or repaint. Get paint-meter readings o
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Run the VIN at a Mercedes dealer: complete all open recalls, service campaigns, and software updates, and print the warranty claim history.', 'Do the A-service if due by time (one year from in-service date) or mileage: oil, filter, and inspection, about $500-900 at a dealer.', 'Test the 12V battery and check 48V system status after storage; replace the 12V battery if weak, about $400-700.', 'Check tires for storage flat-spotting, pressures, and date codes; do an alignment check after transport, about $200-300.', 'Transfer the Mercedes me account and connected services; verify both keys, and any fingerprint profiles are reset.', 'Optional but sensible for Highway 1: front-end PPF on hood, fenders, mirrors, and flares, about $2,000-3,500, before chips start.']
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['B-service at the next interval, about $1,000-1,800 at a dealer.', 'Brake fluid flush at the 2-year mark from in-service date, about $200-300.', 'Possible tire replacement depending on mileage and driving style, about $2,000-3,000 for 22-inch.', 'Possible front pads/rotors on a hard-driven example, about $2,000-3,500.', 'Cabin and air filters and wiper blades.', 'Wheel curb-rash refinishing.', 'Decide on an extended or certified warranty before the factory 4yr/50k coverage expires, priced against the risk reserve.']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by remaining factory warranty (in-service date) and mileage band: under 5k, 5-15k, and 15k+ trade noticeably differently. Next come color and MANUFAKTUR paint or interior, then AMG Night and Performance packages and wheel choice. Year-one depreciation from sticker is steep: options worth $20k+ on the window sticker recover only a fraction at resale, as the example's roughly $155k bid against a $220k sticker shows. A clean Carfax with no repaint, no wrap concealing damage, full dealer service history, and California certification command a premium for a CA buyer. Aftermarket wheels, tint, wraps, or exhaust work hurt value and complicate warranty claims.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 2025-2026 example needs little mechanical catch-up. The work is administrative and time-based: open campaigns and software, the A-service by time, 12V/48V battery health after storage, and brake fluid at 2 years. Budget the post-warranty reserve now, because turbo, cooling, 48V, and ride-control failures become out-of-pocket at 4 years or 50k miles.

profiles.label: Mercedes-Benz GLS-Class (X166 facelift, 2017–2019: GLS 450 / GLS 550 / AMG GLS 63)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel-based buyer, the X166 GLS is a comfortable, quiet, seven-seat highway and family hauler. It suits Highway 1 and Bay Area runs, Tahoe trips, and light towing. It is a depreciation bargain because the cost of keeping it running is high: the 2,400–2,600 kg body rides on Airmatic air suspension, and the GLS 550 adds the complex M278 twin-turbo V8. The right car is one with documented A/B services, a healthy air suspension that holds height overnight, and a clean full-module scan. Budget for consumables like 21-inch tires and big brakes as a matter of course. The GLS 450's twin-turbo V6 (M276) is the lower-cost-of-ownership choice. The 550 trades running cost for effortless torque.
profiles.weak_points: ["Airmatic air suspension is the number-one cost center, and failures typically start between 50k miles and 6 years of age. The front air struts are the most common failure. Each is a combined air spring and damper unit: about $900–1,300 at an independent shop with OEM or OE-equivalent parts, $1,500–2,200 at a dealer, or $550–800 rebuilt (Arnott-type). Rear air springs are separate bags at roughly $300–600 each installed. Symptoms include a corner sagging after sitting overnight, the 'Vehicle Lowered' or 'Stop Vehicle Too Low' message, a harsh clunk over bumps, or a compressor running for long periods. Ask for the dates and part sources of any strut or spring replacement.", 'A leaking spring or strut overworks the Airmatic compressor, which then burns out. Replacement runs about $800–1,500, and the relay should be replaced at the same time. A failed valve block or leaking air lines produce similar symptoms. A compressor that cycles often or runs a long time to lift the car from Lift mode suggests a leak upstream. Airmatic fault codes stored in the suspension module are the key evidence.', 'Active Curve System (ACS), if equipped, is a hydraulic anti-roll system. It can develop leaks at its pressure lines, pump, or valve block, and the stabilizer actuators can wear. Symptoms are body roll, an ACS warning, hydraulic fluid seeping near the front subframe, or a groaning pump. Repairs range from about $1,200 for lines to $3,500–6,000 for actuators, pump, and valve block. Confirm from the VIN data card or Monroney whether the car has ACS, and inspect accordingly.', 'The M278 4.7L twin-turbo V8 (GLS 550) leaks oil at several points. Camshaft adjuster solenoids (magnets) can leak oil, which then wicks into the engine wiring harness. Solenoids cost about $150–400 each, and an oil-soaked harness section can add $600–1,500. Valve and timing cover gaskets, the oil filter housing and oil cooler seals, and the crankcase breather lines are other common leak sources. Look for wet oil at the front cover and at the solenoid connectors, and ask whether solenoids were replaced under recall or campaign work.', 'M278 turbocharger oil and coolant feed lines can weep, and wastegate actuators can rattle. A turbo replacement is labor-intensive at about $3,500–7,000 per side. Signs of trouble include blue smoke on startup, oil in the charge pipes, a whistle or wastegate rattle at tip-in, and boost-deviation or limp-mode codes. Healthy turbos are far more likely with oil changes on time or early at 10k miles or less, not the maximum Flexible Service interval.', 'The charge-air (intercooler) low-temperature coolant circuit is a known M278 weak spot. Its auxiliary electric pump fails at about $400–800 installed, and the low-temp radiator can be damaged. Symptoms are a loss of power in heat or on long Grapevine-type grades, plus intake-temperature codes. The main water pump and the electronically controlled thermostat also leak or stick around 60–100k miles, at roughly $700–1,500 for either. Look for pink or white crust on the coolant hoses and under the front of the engine.', 'The 9G-Tronic (725.0) automatic, used in 2017+ cars, can develop several faults. These include harsh 2–3 or 3–2 shifts, a delayed reverse engagement, shudder at light throttle (torque converter), and failures of the conductor plate or integrated TCU at about $1,500–3,000. A fluid-and-filter service runs about $450–800 and is commonly recommended around 60k miles, despite the long official interval. Ask whether it has been done, and verify current software and adaptations with a scan.', "4MATIC transfer case and front differential: watch for a whine or grind under load, binding in tight parking-lot turns, or a '4MATIC inoperative' message. Front axle seals and the front differential can also leak. A transfer case replacement runs about $2,500–4,500, so ask whether the fluid has ever been changed. Hitch-equipped cars that towed heavily put extra load on the transfer case, transmission,
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Complete any overdue B service, including oil and filter, cabin/combination filter, engine air filters, brake fluid flush, and a reset via Xentry or a capable scan tool (about $450–900).', 'Replace spark plugs if not documented. The M278 V8 plugs and coil inspection run about $400–700. On a 2018, plugs are likely due by age.', 'Get a full-module scan and clear the fault codes, then address any Airmatic, ACS, 9G, or ADAS faults found.', 'Run an overnight ride-height check and an Airmatic leak test (soapy water on the struts, bags, and lines). Replace any leaking front strut or rear bag before it takes out the compressor.', 'Clean the sunroof drains and confirm the cabin floors are dry.', 'Have the main and auxiliary batteries load-tested, and replace and register them if they are weak.',
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Replace one or both front Airmatic struts and/or the rear air springs (about $1,000–3,500 depending on how many and on OEM vs. rebuilt). Replace the compressor relay preventively.', 'Do a 9G-Tronic fluid and filter service if it is undocumented (about $450–800), plus a transfer case and front differential fluid service.', 'Do a brake pad and rotor service on at least one axle (about $600–1,200 per axle).', 'Fix camshaft solenoid or front cover oil leaks, and replace the crankcase breather lines.', 'Replace the charge-air cooler auxiliary pump, thermostat, or water pump if they show seepage or test weak.', 'Replace front control arm or thrust arm bushings and/or engine and transmission mounts if clunks or vibration appear.', 'Do the next A service, plus a new set of 21-inch tires if the c
profiles.market_notes: The X166 GLS depreciates steeply. Private-party and auction prices for 2018 GLS 550s with roughly 40–60k miles often land in the high teens to low/mid $20ks, with dealer retail higher. Prices move up with documented dealer or specialist service, a remaining warranty or CPO coverage, mileage under about 60k, a clean (non-accident) Carfax, and desirable options. Those options include the Driver Assistance Package, Designo paint and leather, the Night Package, 21-inch AMG wheels, ACS, and the rear-seat entertainment and premium audio packages. Any reported rear or structural damage, an overdue service warning, sagging suspension, or multiple prior listings that failed to sell knock 10–25% off. The GLS 450 V6 sells for less but is cheaper to own, and the AMG GLS 63 commands a premium with even higher running costs.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2018 GLS 550 at 40–60k miles is reaching the age where Airmatic struts and bags, 9G and transfer case fluids, spark plugs, brake fluid, batteries and M278 oil seals all come due at once. Expect $2,000–4,500 of catch-up in the first year even on a good example, more if a B service has been skipped or the suspension is already sagging.
