profiles.label: Porsche 911 Carrera / Carrera S Cabriolet (997.1, M97 engine)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, a 997.1 Carrera S Cabriolet is a top-down coastal driver: Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and weekend runs, not a garage queen or an appreciating asset. The car is fundamentally robust, but it carries one dominant risk: the M97 3.8 engine's bore scoring, with the IMS bearing as a smaller secondary risk. Either can turn a $35k purchase into a $55k+ one, so engine evidence (borescope, DME over-rev report, oil analysis) matters far more than cosmetics or color. The cabriolet adds a hydraulic top, drains, and water-intrusion risks that coupe-centric 997 advice skips over.
profiles.weak_points: ['Bore scoring (M97 3.8, the headline risk). The Alusil/Lokasil cylinders can score, most often on the cylinder 4-6 bank, and the 3.8 S engines are affected more than the 3.6. Symptoms are a cold-start tick or piston slap, oil consumption above roughly 1 qt per 1,500 mi, and one bank of tailpipes noticeably sootier than the other. Many cars have no symptoms until it is advanced. It can appear at any mileage, but it is commonly found from about 50k to 90k mi and on cars driven mostly in short cold trips. The only real test is a borescope by a 911 specialist, ideally with photos of all six bores, plus an oil analysis. The fix is an engine rebuild with new liners (Nikasil/LN-type) or a replacement engine, typically $18k-$30k+.', 'IMS bearing. MY2006-2008 cars use the larger single-row intermediate shaft bearing, which cannot be serviced without splitting the case. Its failure rate is low (well under the 996 rate, roughly 1% range), but failure is catastrophic, typically $15k-$30k for an engine. Some early MY2005 engines carry the smaller, retrofittable bearing, so the engine number matters. You cannot prevent it on late engines, only monitor it. Look for receipts showing oil and filter changes every 5k mi or annually, filter cut-open inspections free of metal, and no ferrous debris on the drain plug.', "DME over-rev report and cam deviation. On manual cars a money-shift (a missed downshift) can bend valves or damage the valvetrain. A Durametric/PIWIS scan shows over-rev ranges 1-6 with ignition counts. Range 1-2 hits are normal. Recent range 3+ hits, and any range 4-6, are red flags. The same scan should record VarioCam camshaft deviation values for both banks. Large or unequal deviation suggests chain, tensioner, or timing issues. Insist on the actual printout, not a verbal 'it's fine.'", 'Rear main seal (RMS) and engine oil leaks. A RMS weep at the engine/transaxle junction is common, as are leaks from the cam cover gaskets, spark plug tube seals, and oil filler or breather lines. A minor weep is a monitor-and-fix-with-clutch item. Fixing the RMS alone costs about $1.5k-$2.5k because the transaxle comes out, but it adds only a few hundred dollars during a clutch job.', 'Cooling system. The front-mounted radiators and A/C condensers sit behind open bumper ducts and trap leaves and debris. They then corrode, and coastal salt air speeds this up. Replacement runs about $1.5k-$2.5k for the radiator pair and $1k-$2k for the condensers. The water pump typically weeps or fails between 50k and 80k mi or around 10 years. It is about $800-$1,500 with the thermostat and must be done proactively, because overheating the M97 accelerates bore and head problems. The coolant expansion tank can crack and seep at the seams ($300-$600). Look for receipts showing a water pump, a coolant flush, and a bumper-off radiator cleaning.', 'Air-oil separator (AOS). Failure shows as a big cloud of white or blue smoke on startup (especially after left-side lean or hard cornering), a rough or hunting idle, oil in the intake, and high crankcase vacuum. It is about $700-$1,200. If a car smokes heavily at startup, distinguish AOS failure from bore scoring before buying.', 'Clutch and dual-mass flywheel (manual cars). Clutch life is 40k-90k mi depending on use. A DMF rattle at idle that disappears when the clutch is depressed, or chatter on take-off, means replacement soon. Clutch plus DMF runs about $3.5k-$5k and should always be paired with a RMS seal and IMS inspection where possible. The clutch slave cylinder can leak. Worn shifter cable bushings give a vague, sloppy shift ($200-$500).', 'Convertible top hydraulics. The top is driven by hydraulic rams and a pump. Ram seals eventually leak fluid onto the headliner, top fabric, or tonneau. A slow or jerky top, an incomplete latch, or a top fault on the dash points to rams, the pump, microswitches, or the top control module. A ram rebuild runs about $1k-$2.5k, and a complete top fabric replacement is about $2.5k-
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Oil and filter change with the filter cut open and inspected for metal, plus an oil analysis (Blackstone or similar) to set a baseline for wear metals and coolant/fuel contamination.', 'Brake fluid flush (2-year interval) and inspection of rotors for drill-hole cracks.', 'Remove the front bumper to clean and inspect the radiators and A/C condensers, and replace them if fins are crumbling or leaking. This is especially important for a coastal California car.', 'Clear convertible top and cowl drains, then cycle the top several times while checking for hydraulic fluid weeps at the rams and correct latching.', 'Replace spark plugs, and inspect or replace coils, if there is no record within 4 years or 40k-60k mi.', 'Replace engine air filters and the cabin filter. Service the battery or repla
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Water pump and thermostat replacement if there is no documentation, especially at 50k+ mi or around 10+ years.', 'Clutch, dual-mass flywheel, slave cylinder, and RMS together if the clutch is near the end of its life or the DMF rattles.', 'Engine and transmission mounts, front control arm bushings, and sway bar end links.', 'PASM damper replacement if leaking or tired.', 'Air-oil separator if startup smoke or idle issues develop.', 'Convertible top hydraulic ram rebuild or reseal if weeping, plus top fabric repair or replacement if shrinking or separating.', 'Coolant expansion tank replacement if seams are seeping.', 'Shifter cable bushings and any window regulator failures.']
profiles.market_notes: Transmission is the biggest lever. Six-speed manual cars command a clear premium over Tiptronic, and coupes generally out-trade cabriolets at equal condition. Carrera S over base, and desirable or rare colors (Malachite Green, Speed Yellow, Cobalt, paint-to-sample) over silver, black, or gray, add real money, as do Sport Chrono, X51, or PCCB. Engine evidence also moves price. A clean recent borescope, a clean over-rev report, and a thick service file are worth thousands, while any accident history on Carfax, more than 3-4 owners, or no engine inspection pushes values down. Mileage under about 50k carries a premium, while past 90k-100k prices soften sharply unless the engine has been rebuilt with documentation. 997.2 cars (2009+ DFI engines without the IMS bearing) sit a tier above in price.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 997.1 cab is now 15-20 years old and has often been driven sparingly, so plan on catching up deferred items: water pump and thermostat, coolant, plugs and coils, a radiator and condenser clean-out or replacement, mounts and bushings, and top hydraulic resealing. Budget roughly $3k-$7k in year one beyond the purchase price for a car with average records. In Carmel's mild, damp coastal climate, let the engine reach full temperature on every drive rather than making short foggy hops, which also helps bore longevity.

profiles.label: Porsche 911 Carrera T (992.1)
profiles.framing: The 992.1 Carrera T is the lightest, most driver-focused non-GT 992. It uses the base 3.0L twin-turbo 9A2 Evo engine but adds a standard mechanical LSD, lowered PASM Sport, sports exhaust, thinner glass and reduced sound deadening, and most US cars carry the 7-speed manual. For a Carmel driver it suits Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laureles Grade, and it is reliable enough to use daily. The main risks are abuse history (over-revs, clutch wear, track use), cosmetic and debris damage on the low nose, and the time and money a car needs as it leaves the 4-year/50k factory warranty. The best purchases are documented, PPF'd, warranty-tracked cars with a clean over-rev report and no aftermarket wheel or suspension changes.
profiles.weak_points: ['Mechanical over-revs (manual cars especially): a missed downshift (e.g., 5th into 2nd) can overspeed the 9A2 Evo even though the rev limiter prevents fuel-driven over-revs. The DME logs over-rev events by range. Ranges 1-2 with low counts are normal. Hits in ranges 3-6 point to possible valvetrain or bottom-end stress, and Porsche may refuse warranty or CPO coverage. Require a PIWIS over-rev printout, with ignition-cycle hours, before purchase. Any high-range events are a walk-away or deep-discount situation.', 'Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on the 7-speed manual: a gently driven car often reaches 40-60k+ miles, but hard launches, track days and city use can wear it out by 15-25k. Symptoms include a high or late engagement point, slipping in 4th-6th under boost, judder on take-off, and DMF chatter or rattle at idle that changes when the clutch is pressed. A clutch with DMF typically costs $4,000-6,500 at a dealer or $3,000-4,500 at an independent. Clutch wear is not covered by warranty.', '7-speed manual shift quality: some cars develop notchy or vague shifts, or a sticking 7th-gear lockout (7th is only selectable from 5th or 6th, which is normal). Shift cable adjustment is cheap; internal synchro wear from abuse is not, and a transmission costs $8,000-15,000+. Test every gear cold and hot, including the 2-3 and 3-4 shifts at higher rpm. For PDK cars, look for smooth low-speed creep and no clunks. PDK fluid service runs roughly $600-1,000 at about 60k or 6 years.', "Front axle lift system (very common option): the hydraulic pump, lines and lift struts can leak or throw 'lift system fault' messages, and the GPS-memorized lift points can stop working. Repair runs about $1,500-4,500 depending on whether it is a pump, valve block or strut. This system matters in Carmel, with steep driveways and dips. Cycle it several times and inspect the front struts for wet hydraulic fluid.", 'PASM Sport dampers and optional rear-axle steering: the lowered T dampers can weep or leak, especially on cars driven on poor roads or tracked. Expect about $1,500-2,500 per corner installed. If the car has rear-axle steering, the actuators can fault or leak at $3,000-5,000+ per side. Scan for chassis codes, look for oily dampers, and listen for clunks on broken pavement.', 'Low nose, front radiators and condensers: the T sits about 10mm lower than a base Carrera, and the radiators in the front corner intakes collect road debris, rocks and leaves. Punctured or crushed radiators or AC condensers cost about $800-2,000 per side. The front lip, splitter and bumper underside scrape easily. Inspect through the intakes with a light, look for coolant residue, and check whether the car has aftermarket mesh guards.', "Bodywork hidden under PPF, ceramic coating and wraps: many T's carry full-front PPF, which can conceal refinished bumpers, PDR, or respray lines and orange-peel mismatch. A clean Carfax does not rule out paintwork. Use a paint-thickness meter on every panel (readings work through PPF with an offset). Get invoices for any refinish and confirm no structural or airbag events.", 'Lightweight glass and ADAS calibration: the T uses thinner, T-specific rear and rear-quarter glass that costs more and has longer lead times than standard glass. Windshield replacement is common on low-nose cars. A new windshield must be OEM or OE-equivalent with the correct acoustic layer, rain sensor and camera bracket, and the front camera (lane assist, sign recognition) must be calibrated, about $1,800-3,000 total. Ask for the glass invoice and check for ADAS faults.', "Electronics and 12V system: the 992 is very sensitive to battery voltage. A weak battery or long storage causes random warnings, infotainment glitches, flush door handles that won't deploy, and rear spoiler or parking-brake faults. Batteries cost about $400-1,800 depending on type. If an aftermarket charger lead is fitted, confirm it is correctly fused and suits the battery type, especially lithium. Check PCM
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace tires if date codes are 3+ years old or tread is below about 4/32 rear; a staggered N-rated set runs about $1,800-2,600.', 'Flush brake fluid if there is no record within the last 2 years ($200-350).', 'Do an oil and filter service if no Porsche-spec oil change is documented in the past 12 months or 5k miles ($250-450).', 'Remove aftermarket wheel spacers or chargers and other bolt-ons, reinstall the factory lug bolts and parts, then do a 4-wheel alignment ($300-600).', 'Load-test the battery and charging system, and replace the battery if weak ($400-1,800 depending on type).', 'Have a Porsche dealer complete open recalls or campaigns and PCM/DME software updates (normally no charge).', 'Clean leaf and debris buildup from the front radiator intakes and inspect radiators and conde
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Intermediate maintenance (oil, filters, inspection) per the 2-year/20k schedule: about $500-1,000 at a dealer, less at an independent.', '4-year/40k maintenance once the car reaches 4 years, with spark plugs, engine and cabin air filters, and a full inspection: about $1,500-2,500.', 'Brake pads and possibly rotors on cars driven hard: $1,500-2,800 per axle.', 'Front axle lift or PASM damper repair if weeping is found once out of warranty: $1,500-4,500.', 'Decide whether to buy an extended or CPO warranty before factory coverage lapses: $4,000-7,000.', 'PPF repair or replacement on the nose and rocker panels from rock chips: $800-2,500.', 'Second tire set (rears only) if driven enthusiastically: $900-1,300.']
profiles.market_notes: The 7-speed manual carries a clear premium over PDK, often $5k-15k. Low miles (<10k), clean Carfax, full PPF and remaining factory warranty or CPO eligibility all push price up. Desirable options include front axle lift, rear-axle steering, 18-way seats, Surround View and special colors (GT Silver, Shark Blue, Python Green, Paint-to-Sample). Sport Chrono, PASM Sport, sports exhaust and the mechanical LSD are standard on the T, so 'options' totals often double-count them. Disclosed paintwork, aftermarket spacers or bolt-ons, high over-rev counts and missing dealer records all pull price down. The arrival of the 992.2 T, which kept the manual, softens values for average 992.1 examples.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 2023-2024 T is young, so catch-up work is mainly time-based: tires older than about 4 years, brake fluid every 2 years, the 4-year spark plug and filter service, and battery health after storage. The bigger issue is timing: confirm how much of the 4-year/50k factory warranty remains, and have the dealer clear all campaigns and log any lift, damper or electrical faults before coverage ends.

profiles.label: Porsche 911 G-Series (1974–1989: 2.7, SC, Carrera 3.2, 930 Turbo)
profiles.framing: For this Carmel buyer, a G-Series 911 is an analog, air-cooled, manual driver's car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the occasional Car Week outing. It is not a garage queen. Value and risk live in the engine you cannot see and the rust you cannot see, so documented engine work, by whom, and when, plus a clean underside, matter far more than paint or cosmetics. Sub-era matters a great deal. 1974–77 2.7 magnesium-case cars carry the most engine risk, the SC is the robust middle, the 1987–89 Carrera 3.2 with G50 is the easiest daily, and the 930 is a much costlier ownership proposition. 1975-and-earlier cars are California smog-exempt; 1976+ cars are not, which matters for originality and for any engine swap.
profiles.weak_points: ["2.7L magnesium crankcase (1974–77, including the US 1974–75 Carrera): the softer magnesium case lets head studs pull out of their threads, and the case halves distort and fret. This is worst on 1975 California and 1976–77 US cars with thermal reactors that run hot and lean. Symptoms are oil weeping at the cylinder base, compression or leakdown loss, ticking at the head, and an oil temperature gauge that runs high. A proper fix means engine-out work: case savers or Time-Serts, often a line bore, and a top end, typically $20k–$40k with a good builder. Look for builder invoices that explicitly mention case stud repair, line boring, and the tensioner upgrade. 'Rebuilt' with no itemized invoice should be treated as unrebuilt.", 'Head studs (Dilavar, roughly 1977–1989): the lower-row Dilavar studs corrode and snap, a well-known SC weakness that is less common on the 3.2. A broken stud causes cylinder sealing loss, exhaust leaks or ticking, and leakdown loss. A PPI tech can see broken studs with a mirror or borescope behind the heat exchangers. A replacement program is engine-out, about $6k–$12k alone, more with top-end work. Look for receipts naming steel replacement studs or ARP/Supertec studs.', "Timing chain tensioners and guide ramps (1974–83 non-pressure-fed tensioners): the original tensioners can leak down and collapse, the chain jumps, and the valves hit the pistons, which means a full rebuild at $20k+. Brittle plastic chain ramps also break. The fix is the 'Carrera' pressure-fed tensioner retrofit with new ramps and idlers, about $1,500–$3,500 if done during other engine work. Pressure-fed tensioners were standard on the 1984–89 3.2. Ask for invoices or photos showing the oil feed lines at the cam towers. Chain rattle at cold start is the warning sign.", 'Valve guides and top-end wear: at 80k–120k miles, worn guides cause blue smoke on startup or overrun, plus oil consumption above about 1 qt per 1,000 miles and fouled plugs. This is common on SCs and 3.2s with long intervals between valve adjustments. A top end with guides and valve job runs $8k–$15k. Ask for leakdown numbers, compression numbers, and valve adjustment records, which are due every 15k miles or annually.', 'Oil leaks and oil-cooler plumbing: expect weeps from cam tower and valve cover gaskets, chain housing covers, oil return tubes, the rear main seal, and the 3.2 oil pressure sender. Valve cover gaskets are a $400–$900 job; a cam tower reseal is engine-out, about $3k–$6k. The steel lines running forward to the front fender oil cooler rust and can burst, especially in coastal climates, and the thermostat can stick. Lines plus cooler run $1k–$2.5k. A dripping 911 is normal. A wet case at the cylinder bases or a dripping lower case is not.', 'CIS / K-Jetronic fuel injection (1974–83): common faults are hot-start and warm-start problems, a failing warm-up regulator, fuel accumulator and check valve, sticking fuel distributor, leaking cold-start valve, injector seal leaks, and on the SC an airbox split from intake backfire, partly mitigated by a pop-off valve. Aged rubber fuel hoses in the engine bay are a genuine engine-fire risk on these cars. Typical spend is $500–$3,000; replace fuel lines regardless. On the 1984–89 3.2 Motronic, the DME relay is the classic no-start item; it is a cheap part, so carry a spare.', "Rust (critical for 1974–75 and any coastal car): 1976+ bodies are hot-dip galvanized, while 1974–75 cars are only partially protected. Check the front trunk battery boxes and pan, the front suspension pan, the 'kidney bowls' at the rocker/A-pillar junction, longitudinals and floors under the carpet, rear torsion tube ends and spring plates, the rear shock towers, windshield and rear window corners, door bottoms, and the Targa bar and seals. Quality repair runs $5k for spot work to $30k+ for structural work. Coastal fog in Carmel accelerates it on a poorly stored car.", '915 manual transmission (1974–86): expect worn 2nd and 3rd synchros (grinding
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Oil and filter service with high-ZDDP 20W-50 air-cooled oil; check oil level properly (hot, idling, on level ground) and note consumption', 'Replace all rubber fuel hoses in the engine bay and tunnel, and inspect CIS seals, injector o-rings and the cold-start valve (fire-risk item)', 'Brake fluid flush, inspect and replace brake hoses, verify caliper function', 'Transmission fluid change with GL-4-safe oil (Swepco 201 or equivalent for 915; correct spec for G50)', 'Valve adjustment and plugs if not documented within 15k miles or 1–2 years', 'Tires if older than ~6 years regardless of tread (date codes)', 'Alternator/fan belt, battery, ground straps, and charging system check', 'Shift coupler and shifter bushing refresh if shift is vague', 'Inspect oil cooler lines, thermostat and fender
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Valve cover and chain cover gasket reseal; address oil return tube leaks', 'Suspension and steering bushings, shocks, tie rod ends, ball joints, then alignment and corner balance', 'CV joint and boot service if not documented', 'Clutch, pedal cluster bushings and clutch cable/arm (or hydraulic slave and master on G50) as needed', 'Heat exchanger, muffler and heater flap/cable repair', 'CIS components: warm-up regulator, accumulator, check valve; SC airbox and pop-off valve', 'Sunroof cables and drain service; window regulators; door and window seals', 'Rust treatment of any found bubbles, plus cavity wax and drain clearing given coastal storage', 'Chain tensioner and guide ramp upgrade if pre-1984 and not documented (best combined with other engine work)']
profiles.market_notes: Price rises by sub-era: 1974–77 2.7 cars sit at the bottom because of engine reputation, unless they are US Carreras or desirable colors. The SC is the value middle, the 1987–89 G50 3.2 carries a clear premium, and the 930, Speedster, Club Sport and factory Turbo Look cars carry large premiums. Coupes outsell Targas and Cabriolets, and period 'signal' colors (Lime/Signal Green, Continental Orange, Guards Red, Grand Prix White on clean cars) with a matching-numbers engine, COA or Kardex, and continuous records drive top money. Non-original engines, backdates and RS-look conversions are typically discounted 15–30% by collectors, but a documented builder engine in a solid, rust-free body is often the smarter buy for a driver. Mileage matters less than documented engine and transmission work. A 70k-mile car with an itemized top end and stud work beats a 40k-mile car with no history.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most G-Series cars have sat for long stretches, so expect a $3k–$10k catch-up even on a 'sorted' car. Typical items are fuel lines and CIS seals, brake hoses and calipers, fluids, shift bushings, tires, and 40-year-old suspension rubber, followed within a year or two by an oil-leak reseal. Unless an itemized invoice proves otherwise, assume a pre-1984 engine still needs the tensioner upgrade, and assume a 1974–77 2.7 has not had its case and head studs addressed.

profiles.label: Porsche 911T Longhood (LWB, 1969–1973)
profiles.framing: The 911T is the entry-level long-wheelbase longhood. Its lower-strung engine is tractable and cheaper to keep than an E or S, which makes it a sensible way into an early 911 you can actually drive on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road. For a buyer who wants a documented, unmodified driver, the car is only as good as its structure, its numbers-verified provenance and the honesty of its engine and rust history. Heavily modified restomods and backdates, like the example 3.5L MoTeC S/T-style build with an SC-sourced 915, are a different product: they fall outside this buyer's preference and should not be valued against original-spec cars.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Structural rust is the number one value killer. Porsche did not fully galvanize bodies until 1976, so check the front suspension pan and the dual-battery boxes, which suffer acid and water damage. Also check the front torsion-bar tube and pan seams, the longitudinals and kidney bowls, the floor pans, the jack points, rockers and door bottoms, the rear torsion tube, the rear shock towers, the dogleg and the headlight buckets. Repair bands run about $3–8k for battery boxes or a front pan section, $8–25k for longitudinals and floors, and $40k+ for full structural restoration. Coastal Carmel air makes garage storage and post-purchase rustproofing matter. Ask for restoration or lift photos and receipts naming the panels replaced (OEM vs. repro).

2) Provenance and numbers. Value hinges on chassis, engine and transmission numbers matching the Porsche Certificate of Authenticity or Kardex. Many 'T' cars carry later replacement engines (2.4/2.7/3.0/3.2) or 915 gearboxes from SCs. Some cars sold as longhoods are backdated 1974–89 bodies. Verify the front-trunk VIN stamp, the door-jamb and dash plates, and the engine case stamping, and look for re-stamping or grind marks.

3) Engine wear in the magnesium-case flat-six (2.0 for 1969, 2.2 for 1970–71, 2.4 for 1972–73). Worn valve guides cause blue smoke on startup and overrun. Watch for low or uneven compression and leak-down, and for cracked heads between the valve seats. Case main-bearing bore distortion and pulled case threads are less common than on the 2.7 but do occur. A correct top-end runs about $12–20k; a full rebuild by an air-cooled specialist runs $25–40k+. Ask for rebuild receipts with the machine shop, parts list, rebuild date and miles since. A rebuild without paperwork should be treated as unknown.

4) Timing chain tensioners. The original sealed, non-oil-fed hydraulic tensioners lose fluid and collapse. A skipped chain means valve-to-piston contact and an engine rebuild. Look for proof of the Carrera pressure-fed tensioner conversion (done during a top-end, about $1.5–3k) or at least tensioner safety collars, plus fresh chain ramps and idler arm bushings. Listen for chain rattle at cold start.

5) Oil leaks. Common sources are the cam tower and valve cover gaskets (magnesium lower covers warp), rocker shaft seals, the chain-housing covers, oil return tubes and the oil thermostat. A dry-sump engine leaking onto hot heat exchangers is a fire and smell issue. Reseals run about $1.5–5k depending on engine-out needs. Note that 1972 has a unique oil tank ahead of the right rear wheel with an external filler flap. That tank and its lines rust and leak, and a cracked or dented flap area signals prior impact.

6) Fuel system and fire risk. Fuel delivery varies by year and market:
- 1969 T: Weber 40IDT carburetors
- 1970–71 T: Zenith 40TIN carburetors
- 1972 ROW T: Zenith carburetors
- 1972 and early-1973 US T: Bosch mechanical fuel injection (MFI)
- Late-1973 US T: K-Jetronic CIS

MFI pump rebuilds run $3–6k, and the system needs a specialist to set up. Zenith carbs are finicky, with a $1–2k rebuild and sync. Old rubber fuel lines in the engine bay are the classic 911 fire cause, about $300–800 to replace. Also check for a rusty fuel tank and for sediment.

7) Ignition and electrical. The original Bosch capacitive-discharge (CDI) box fails with age, causing misfire or no-start, and often gets swapped for an MSD or similar (about $300–900). The twin 12V batteries in the front corners need matched replacement and clean boxes. Check the fuse panel, ground straps and alternator/regulator, and expect age-hardened, brittle wiring insulation. Aftermarket wiring hacks are a red flag.

8) Heat exchangers and heater. The original steel heat exchangers rust through, sending exhaust and carbon monoxide into the cabin, and the heater control boxes and flaps seize. Replacement exchangers run about $1–2k for Dansk-quality or $3–4k for stainless SSI-type units, plus install. Many cars run with
profiles.immediate_repairs:
Expect the following in the first 30 days:
- Full fluid service: dry-sump oil and filter (about 10–11 qt of ZDDP 20W-50, checked hot and running), transmission gear oil, and a brake fluid flush.
- Valve adjustment and ignition tune (points/CDI check, timing), plus carb sync or MFI/CIS setup.
- Replace all rubber fuel lines in the engine bay and front trunk if they are not documented within about 5 years.
- Replace brake rubber hoses if aged.
- New tires if over about 6 years old, regardless of tread.
- Battery pair and terminals, fan belt, and an engine-bay fire extinguisher.
- Fix any active oil leaks that drip onto the heat exchangers.
- Budget roughly $2–5k on a car with decent records, more for a stored or neglected example.
profiles.repairs_12mo:
Over the next 12 months, likely items include:
- Cam tower, valve cover and rocker shaft reseals ($1.5–5k).
- Chain tensioner upgrade or safety collars if not documented.
- CDI box replacement.
- Front strut inserts, rear shocks and suspension bushings, with corner balance and alignment ($2.5–6k).
- Caliper rebuilds and master cylinder.
- Heat exchanger and heater box replacement if rusted ($1.5–5k).
- Shift bushings and coupler refresh.
- Possibly a clutch or synchro work ($2–7k).
- Small rust repairs found once the car is on a lift, such as battery boxes or door bottoms.
- Plan $5–15k for a typical driver-quality example.
profiles.market_notes: Within the T range, 1972–73 2.4-liter cars usually command a premium, with the one-year-only 1972 oil-flap cars attracting their own collector interest, over the 1969–71 2.0/2.2 cars. Coupes generally out-sell Targas, and Sportomatic cars sell at a discount. The E and especially the S sit well above the T. Numbers-matching cars confirmed by a COA, factory paint-to-sample or desirable period colors (Signal Orange, Light Ivory, Gulf/Albert Blue, greens) and documented, rust-free histories bring strong premiums, often 15–30% over non-matching cars. Mileage matters little given the unverifiable odometers, while records, structure and originality matter enormously. Restomods and backdates like the example listing trade in a separate, build-quality-driven market that can exceed original-car prices but is not comparable for this buyer.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 50-year-old 911Ts carry deferred rubber, seal and suspension work even when they present well: fuel and brake hoses, leaking cam towers, tired struts and bushings, and a seized heater system. Budget for a full baseline service and a one-year sorting pass by an air-cooled specialist. California exempts 1975-and-older cars from biennial smog checks, which keeps original-spec cars easy to register locally, but stored or out-of-state cars often hide rust and stale-fuel damage that only shows up on a lift.

profiles.label: Porsche 928 S4 / GT (1987–1991, 32-valve 5.0L)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 928 S4 is a comfortable, fast V8 grand tourer for Highway 1 and Bay Area weekend runs. It is not a garage queen or an appreciation play. These cars reward deferred-maintenance catch-up already done and punish it when it isn't. The paperwork trail on the timing belt, fuel and coolant hoses in the engine valley, and electrical health matters more than the paint. Being in California adds one gate other buyers may skip: a 1987 car must pass a biennial smog check with all of its emissions equipment present. A car with its air pump removed is a registration problem, not a curiosity. Automatics are the majority of production and are fine for a GT role, though 5-speeds and GTs carry a large premium.
profiles.weak_points:
["Timing belt system: the 32-valve 5.0 is an interference engine, so a belt or tensioner failure bends valves and can turn a $16k car into a $15k–25k head job. Specialists replace the belt, tensioner, rollers and water pump every 4–5 years or roughly 45–60k miles regardless of mileage, and re-check belt tension after the first few hundred to 1,000 miles. A full job at a 928 specialist runs about $2,500–4,500, more if the cam gears or tensioner pivot are worn. Get a dated invoice listing every part and the shop that did it. A seller saying 'belt done' without paper should be treated as not done.", 'Crankshaft thrust bearing failure, mainly on 1987–1991 automatics: pressure from the torque converter or flexplate pushes the crank forward and wipes out the thrust bearing. Often the cause is a mis-set flexplate clamp bolt after past transmission or torque tube work. Ignored, it ends in a destroyed block or crank and an engine rebuild of $15k–30k. The only real evidence is a crank end-play measurement, taken with a dial indicator while prying the crank fore and aft. Readings approaching the factory wear limit (about 0.4 mm) are a walk-away. On 5-speed cars the risk is much lower, but the measurement is still cheap insurance.', 'Clutch and drivetrain on manual cars: the 5-speed uses a twin-plate clutch at the engine end of the torque tube. Replacement means dropping the transaxle and torque tube, typically $3,500–6,000 at a specialist. Watch for slip in 4th/5th under load, judder on take-off, a high engagement point, and a leaking clutch slave or master cylinder or perished clutch hydraulic hose. Clutch receipts with a mileage are valuable.', 'Torque tube bearings: the central driveshaft runs on bearings inside the torque tube. Worn bearings or deteriorated bearing inserts cause a droning rumble or whir that changes with engine speed, not road speed, and is often worst around 2,000–3,000 rpm. A rebuild is about $1,500–3,000 and is usually best done together with a clutch job.', 'Engine valley fuel and coolant hoses: the rubber fuel lines, injector hoses and fuel damper hoses under the intake manifold are 35+ years old on unrefreshed cars. A leak drips fuel onto a hot engine, which is a real fire risk. The same intake-off job also covers coolant hoses, knock sensors and intake gaskets. A complete valley refresh runs about $2,500–5,000. Raw fuel smell after a hot shutdown is a red flag. Ask for a receipt that explicitly lists fuel lines and injector hoses.', 'Electrical system and central electric (CE) panel: the fuse/relay panel sits in the passenger footwell. Clogged cowl drains, a failed windshield seal or blocked sunroof drains flood the footwell and corrode the panel and its connectors. Common symptoms:
- dead central locking, seat heaters, washer pump or hatch release
- erratic gauges
- parasitic battery drain

The battery sits in the rear, so tray corrosion and poor engine and body grounds are common. Cleaning and repinning is a few hundred dollars. A water-damaged panel or harness can run $1,500–4,000 and many hours of diagnosis.', 'Power steering rack and pump: rack seal leaks and cold-start groan or moan at full lock are very common. Pump, lines and reservoir often get replaced first without curing the noise. A rack reseal or rebuilt rack installed costs about $1,200–2,500. Check for fluid on the rack boots and crossmember. Note whether the noise disappears once warm, which suggests internal seal wear.', 'Cooling system: the radiator has plastic end tanks and integrated engine-oil and transmission-fluid coolers. Old radiators crack, and internal cooler leaks can cross-contaminate oil, coolant and ATF. The expansion tank and its cap also crack, and overheating on an all-aluminum Alusil-bore V8 is expensive. A radiator and hoses refresh is about $1,000–2,500. Look at both coolant and oil for milkiness or oil film.', 'Oil leaks: cam cover (valve cover) gaskets weep on most cars, about $600–1,200 to reseal. Cam seals, oil pa
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter, transaxle gear oil (or ATF on automatics), brake and clutch fluid flush, power steering fluid, and coolant with the correct coolant type.', 'Timing belt, tensioner, rollers and water pump if there is no dated receipt within about 4–5 years, or a tension check if done recently.', 'Engine valley fuel line and injector hose replacement if not documented, combined with coolant hoses and knock sensors while the intake is off.', 'Clean the cowl, windshield and sunroof drains. Inspect and clean the CE panel, battery tray and main ground points.', 'Restore any removed emissions equipment and pass a California smog check before or immediately after registration.', 'Replace tires older than about 6 years. Inspect accessory belts, radiator and expansion ta
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Power steering rack reseal or replacement if it groans or leaks.', 'Cam cover gasket and cam seal reseal.', 'Front control arm bushings and ball joints, rear axle bushings, and shocks.', 'Radiator replacement if original or showing tank cracks or cooler cross-contamination.', 'A/C system conversion or recharge, plus climate control and heater valve repairs.', 'Clutch and torque tube bearings on 5-speeds showing slip or drone; bearings only on automatics if noisy.', 'Electrical gremlin chase: central locking, seat heaters, hatch release, washer pump, gauges.', 'Dashboard recover and odometer gear repair if desired; ABS sensor and PSD service on 1990–1991 cars.']
profiles.market_notes:
Transmission and model are the biggest levers. A 5-speed S4 commands a large premium over an automatic, and the manual-only GT (1989–1991, 326 hp) sits above both. A thick, dated service history is worth more than paint or wheels. A documented belt and valley refresh can add several thousand dollars. Rough current pricing:
- Tired automatics trade in the low-to-mid teens.
- Sorted automatics run roughly $25k–40k.
- Good 5-speeds run $40k–80k+.

Unmodified cars with original 16-inch wheels, factory radio and intact emissions equipment sell better than cars on Panamera or Cayenne wheels with aftermarket audio. Unknown or reset mileage from a stripped odometer gear depresses value. California-legal smog status is a real plus for a local buyer.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a typical S4 needs $5k–10k of catch-up in the first year. Expect a belt service if undocumented, a valley hose refresh, cooling system work, bushings, a steering rack reseal and electrical cleanup. That total climbs if a 5-speed also needs a clutch and torque tube bearings. Cars that already carry recent dated receipts for the belt and valley work are worth paying meaningfully more for.

profiles.label: Porsche 944 Turbo / Turbo S (951, 1986–1991)
profiles.framing: The 951 is the sharpest-driving front-engine Porsche of the era: 2.5L turbo four, rear transaxle, near-50/50 balance, and in Turbo S trim the M030 suspension, 40% limited-slip, and 928 S4 brakes that make it genuinely quick on a real road. For a Carmel-based driver this is a weekend-and-occasional-commute car that rewards mechanical sympathy and punishes deferred maintenance more than almost anything else from the 1980s. What matters is not mileage on the odometer but the last five years of receipts: belts, rollers, water pump, cooling system, torque tube, and a clean compression/leak-down. Coastal humidity and salt-air storage mean the battery box, sunroof drains, and hatch surround deserve as much attention as the engine.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt and balance-shaft belt with their rollers and tensioner: the M44/52 is an interference engine and a snapped or jumped belt bends valves and can crack the head — budget $6,000–12,000 for the repair versus $900–1,800 for the preventive service. Service interval is realistically 30,000 miles or 4 years regardless of miles; demand a dated, mileage-stamped invoice, ideally with a belt-tension-gauge reading noted. Low-mileage cars are the highest risk here because owners defer on miles, not years. 2) Water pump and thermostat housing: pumps seize or leak from the weep hole and take the timing belt with them — always replaced with belts; plastic/alloy housings and the coolant crossover corrode. 3) Cylinder head cracking between the valve seats and head-gasket failure on any car that has been overheated or run lean/overboosted — symptoms are coolant loss with no external leak, pressurized expansion tank, sweet exhaust smell. A used head plus machine work and gasket set runs $3,500–6,000. 4) Oil cooler O-rings/seals at the block leak oil into coolant or coolant into oil — look for mayonnaise on the filler cap and at the cooler seams; a straightforward $400–800 job if caught early. 5) Turbocharger: K26/6 (Turbo) or K26/8 (Turbo S) shaft play, coked oil feed line, and failing oil return gasket cause blue smoke on overrun and boost loss. Rebuilt cartridges/units run $1,500–3,000 installed; the oil feed line should be replaced any time the turbo is. 6) Boost-control system: the wastegate diaphragm, KLR cycling valve, and a web of aging rubber vacuum and boost hoses crack and cause soft boost, overboost cutout, or surge. A full silicone/rubber hose refresh and wastegate rebuild is $400–1,200. 7) Torque tube bearings and center support: a resonant droning/whirring at 2,000–3,500 rpm that changes with clutch engagement; rebuild or replacement is $1,500–3,500 because the transaxle and tube must come out. 8) Clutch: the rubber-centered disc degrades with age and the pressure plate/pilot bearing go with it; do the torque tube, rear main seal, and clutch together — $2,500–4,500 as a package. 9) Front suspension: the one-piece control arms with integral ball joints and the aging bushings produce vague steering and clunks; arms are $300–700 each plus alignment. Turbo S Koni adjustables often seize or leak and are expensive to replace or rebuild ($1,200–2,500 for a set). Rear torsion bar tube bushings and seized torsion adjusters make ride-height correction a job. 10) Brakes: Turbo S (and 1989 Turbo) use 928 S4 four-piston calipers and larger rotors — parts are pricier and some rotors are becoming scarce; seized pistons and crusty ABS lines are common on stored cars. Full four-corner refresh with rotors and rebuilt calipers is $2,000–3,500. The Bosch ABS system's sensors and the hydraulic unit can be costly and hard to source. 11) Electrical gremlins: the DME/fuel pump relay is a classic no-start, ground strap corrosion causes random faults, and the VDO instrument cluster's odometer gears strip — which is exactly why so many 944s carry 'Not Actual Mileage' or mileage-inconsistency entries. A branded NAM title is permanent and materially affects value. 12) Interior consumables: cracked dash pads ($800–2,000 to replace/recover), sagging headliner and sunroof cassette, failing window regulators and motors, disintegrating door-card and rear-hatch trim, and vacuum-operated HVAC controls that stop working when the pod diaphragms fail. 13) Air conditioning: original R12 systems either converted or dead; evaporator replacement means dash-out labor at $1,500–2,500. 14) Rust and water: bodies are galvanized so rot is not endemic, but check the battery box and the floor/frame rail under it (acid), sunroof drain exits, the rear hatch surround and hinge area, the fuel tank/torsion tube area, jack points, and the inner fenders behind the front wheels. Also inspect for aged fuel hoses under the intake and at the fuel rail — 1980s rubber plus turbo h
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service if not documented within 12 months (engine oil, transaxle, brake fluid, coolant); DME and fuel pump relay replacement plus a spare; replacement of any rubber fuel line under the intake and at the rail; rubber/vacuum and boost hose refresh with new clamps; tires if older than 6 years regardless of tread (very common on low-use 951s); battery, ground straps, and a battery-box cleanup; front-end alignment; and if belt documentation is thin or older than 4 years, an immediate timing/balance belt, roller, tensioner, water pump and thermostat service. Expect $2,500–5,000 in the first 30 days on a typical documented car and more if belts are unknown.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch, rear main seal, and torque tube bearings as a combined job if any driveline drone or clutch shudder is present; oil cooler seals and valve-cover/cam-tower gasket leaks; wastegate diaphragm and boost-control refresh; brake caliper rebuild plus rotors and stainless lines; Koni damper rebuild or replacement and rear torsion-bar bushings; motor and transaxle mounts; A/C recharge or evaporator/condenser work; window regulator and sunroof mechanism service; and cosmetic catch-up on dash, seat bolsters, and rear hatch struts. A realistic 12-month figure is $4,000–9,000 depending on what the PPI finds.
profiles.market_notes: The 1988 Turbo S (about 1,000 US cars, including the Silver Rose edition) and the 1989 Turbo that inherited S mechanicals sit well above standard 1986–1988 Turbos, and a Porsche Certificate of Authenticity confirming S equipment is effectively required to claim the premium. Documented belt/water-pump service, original paint, correct 16" Club Sport wheels, a working A/C, and unmolested boost/ECU are the value drivers; chipped/overboosted cars, cut dashes, and aftermarket turbo or intercooler swaps push buyers away. Mileage bands matter but only when the odometer is credible — a 'Not Actual Mileage' or mileage-inconsistency brand should discount a car meaningfully (commonly 15–30%) versus an equivalent clean-title example, because it is permanent and follows the car. Manual-only market; color and interior condition (especially an uncracked dash and unfaded leatherette) swing the last 10%.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-plus-year-old car needs a rubber and fluid reset regardless of mileage: every vacuum, boost, coolant, and fuel hose, belts and pump on age not miles, tires, brake fluid and flexlines, and motor mounts. Low-mileage examples are often worse in this respect than driven ones — seals dry out, fuel systems varnish, and Konis seize from sitting. Budget $3,000–6,000 of age-related catch-up in year one even on a well-presented car.

checks.label: Dated, mileage-stamped timing + balance belt, roller, tensioner, water pump invoice (within 4 yrs)
Cold compression and warm leak-down on all four cylinders, cylinder-by-cylinder numbers
Cooling-system pressure test; check for pressurized expansion tank, coolant loss, oil/coolant mixing
Oil cooler O-ring area and cam tower/valve cover for oil weeping; filler cap for emulsion
Turbo shaft axial/radial play, oil feed line condition, smoke on overrun and under boost
Full-boost pull confirming correct peak boost, no overboost cutout, no surge or fuel cut
Listen for 2,000–3,500 rpm driveline drone; clutch bite point, shudder, pedal feel
Transaxle shift quality when cold, synchro crunch into 2nd, LSD behavior on a tight low-speed turn
Battery box, floor pan and frame rail beneath it for acid corrosion and repairs
Sunroof drains, cassette operation, hatch surround/hinge area and spare well for water or rust
928 S4 caliper condition, rotor thickness/scarring, ABS light behavior and sensor function
Koni adjustables for leakage/seizure, control arm bushings and ball joints, ride height and torsion adjusters
All rubber fuel lines under the intake and at the rail for hardening, cracking, or seepage
Odometer/cluster function, evidence of cluster repair or replacement, title brand and Carfax mileage entries
Dash pad cracks, window regulators, HVAC vacuum pods, A/C outlet temperature after 10 minutes
Porsche COA vs. car: Turbo S equipment (M030, LSD, brakes, wheels), paint code and options match

critical_evidence.label: Shop invoice for timing + balance belts, rollers, tensioner, water pump and thermostat with date and odometer
Written compression and leak-down numbers per cylinder from a recent test
Explanation and paper trail for any 'Not Actual Mileage' brand or Carfax mileage inconsistency, including cluster repair records

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster (981, incl. S / GTS / Spyder)
profiles.framing: The 981 is the sweet spot of modern Boxsters: the last naturally aspirated flat-six mid-engine Porsche roadster, with electric steering that is still genuinely good, a stiff aluminum-intensive chassis, and no IMS bearing to worry about. For a Carmel-based driver this is a near-ideal Highway 1 / Laureles Grade weekend car that can also be driven daily in the region's mild climate, with the caveat that it is a two-seat convertible with two small trunks. What matters here is a documented, unmodified-or-reversible example with a full Porsche/independent service file, a healthy convertible top mechanism, and evidence the engine has never been abused or run low on oil; the 9A1 flat-six is a strong motor but a bad one is a five-figure problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Bore scoring / cylinder scuffing on the 9A1 DFI flat-six is uncommon but not extinct, and it is the single catastrophic risk. Symptoms are ticking or knocking at cold start that fades as it warms, oil consumption worse than roughly 1 qt / 1,200 miles, and a faint sooty smell. It shows up most often on hard-driven or short-tripped cars past 60-80k miles. A borescope of all six cylinders plus a DME over-rev report is the only real protection; an engine replacement or rebuild is $18,000-$28,000+.', 'Cracked cylinder heads / coolant loss on early 9A1 engines (mostly 2013-2014) present as slow, unexplained coolant level drop with no visible external leak, sometimes with a sweet smell after a hard drive. Check the expansion tank level history in service records and pressure-test the cooling system. Head or engine work is $8,000-$20,000.', 'Water pump with a composite impeller typically fails between 60k and 100k miles or roughly 8-10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump area, coolant smell, or temperature creep in traffic. Budget $1,100-$1,800 done properly with a thermostat and coolant service. On a 78k-mile 2014 with no pump record, assume it is due.', 'Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age, and the plastic coolant hard lines / hose connectors get brittle. Look for dried pink-orange crust in the engine bay and at the rear of the block. $400-$900.', 'Air-oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure causes a big puff of blue smoke at startup or after a highway pull, rough idle, and oil consumption. Typical at 70k-100k miles; $700-$1,200 installed. Frequently misdiagnosed as bore scoring, so a proper crankcase vacuum test is worth insisting on.', 'Rear main seal and, less often, the case-half seam weep oil onto the transaxle bellhousing. A light film is common; drips that require topping off mean pulling the transaxle, which is a $2,000-$3,500 job unless combined with a clutch.', 'Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch. Judder from a stop, high engagement point, or a rattle at idle that disappears with the clutch depressed means DMF. Replacement with flywheel and rear main seal while you are in there runs $3,000-$4,500. Most 981 manuals go 80k-120k miles, so a 78k car is inside the window.', 'PDK cars: the 60k-mile / 6-year mechatronic fluid and filter service is $700-$1,100 and is skipped constantly. A missing PDK service record on a 70k+ car is a real negotiating point; mechatronic unit failure is $5,000-$9,000.', 'Convertible top: the drive cables, hydraulic pump lines, tensioning bow bushings, microswitches, and the rear window seam are all wear items. Symptoms are a top that stalls mid-cycle, a warning message, or a hydraulic fluid smell/stain in the rear trunk area. Cable or hydraulic repairs run $1,200-$2,500; a full top replacement is $2,800-$4,500. Always cycle the top three or four times, fully, before buying.', "Clogged convertible-top and cowl drains flood the footwells and the area under the seats where control modules live. Look for damp carpet padding, musty smell, corroded seat rail hardware, or a car with a recent 'electrical gremlin' history. Water-damaged modules are $800-$2,500 each.", 'PASM dampers (standard on S/GTS, optional on base) start weeping and losing damping between 70k and 100k miles; you get a chassis warning or clunking over expansion joints. OEM dampers are $700-$1,300 per corner installed. Aftermarket coilovers on a listing usually mean the originals were tired.', 'A/C condensers sit in the front corners behind the radiators and collect leaves, sand, and salt; in a coastal environment they corrode and leak refrigerant, and the same debris rots the radiators. Expect $900-$1,800 to replace condensers and clean the ducting. Ask for photos of the front corner ducts with the liners out.', 'Bi-xenon / PDLS headlight units and ballasts fail with age and are expensive: $1,200-$2,200 per side for OEM. A car with recently replaced headlights (as in this example) has already eaten that cost, w
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid catch-up: engine oil with genuine filter, brake fluid flush (2-year interval, almost always overdue), coolant condition check and pressure test', 'Tires: replace non-N-spec or over-5-year-old staggered set with N-rated rubber, plus alignment ($1,600-$2,200)', 'Cooling system: water pump and thermostat if there is no record within 60k miles ($1,100-$1,800)', 'Convertible top service: lubricate mechanism, clear cowl and top drains, check hydraulic lines and rear window seam ($300-$700, more if cables are stretched)', 'Battery test/replace with proper coding if the car sat or is on its original AGM ($400-$600)', 'Exhaust: verify smog compliance for California registration; source and reinstall factory exhaust if cats were deleted ($1,200-$2,500)', 'PIWIS fault-code clear and re-s
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on a manual approaching 90-100k miles ($3,000-$4,500) or PDK mechatronic service if not documented ($700-$1,100)', 'Air-oil separator if oil consumption or startup smoke develops ($700-$1,200)', 'PASM damper replacement if weeping or if ride quality is degraded ($2,800-$4,500 for four)', 'A/C condenser replacement and front duct cleanout, typical for coastal cars ($900-$1,800)', 'Spark plugs and coils at the 4-year/40k interval ($600-$1,000)', 'Engine and transmission mounts if idle shudder is present ($600-$1,200)', 'Soft-top rear window or full top replacement if the seam is delaminating ($2,800-$4,500)', 'Suspension refresh items: control arm bushings, sway bar links, and a corner-balance alignment ($800-$1,600)']
profiles.market_notes: Transmission and engine drive the money: a 6-speed manual commands a clear premium over PDK in the enthusiast market, and Boxster S / GTS 3.4 cars trade several thousand above a 2.7 base regardless of options. Spec matters at the margins - Sport Chrono with PSE, adaptive sport seats, PASM, a non-black interior, and a genuinely interesting exterior color lift a car; base cloth-spec silver/white/black cars with 19s and no options sit. Records are worth real money on this generation: a folder showing water pump, PDK or clutch service, brake fluid history, and no accidents will beat a lower-mileage undocumented car with a damage entry. Aftermarket exhaust, non-N-spec tires, and a Carfax damage report each shave value, and mileage bands break roughly at 40k, 70k, and 100k.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-12 year old, 70-80k mile 981 needs a deferred-maintenance sweep even when it looks perfect: brake fluid, coolant, plugs and coils, AGM battery with coding, water pump if undocumented, N-spec tires, and a convertible top lubrication and drain cleanout. Coastal Monterey cars additionally want the front duct liners pulled to clean debris off the radiators and condensers before corrosion sets in. Plan $3,000-$5,000 of catch-up in the first year on top of the purchase price, separate from the clutch/DMF or PDK service that lurks in the next 20k miles.

checks.label: Borescope all six cylinders for bore scoring/scuffing

Pressure-test cooling system; inspect water pump, expansion tank, hard lines for pink crust

Manual: clutch engagement point, judder, DMF rattle. PDK: mechatronic fluid service record
Cycle convertible top 3-4 times fully; check speed, stalls, warning messages, hydraulic leaks
Lift carpet/check under seats for damp padding, corrosion, musty smell; clear top and cowl drains
Inspect all four dampers for oil weep; check for suspension fault codes and clunks
Remove front duct liners: debris, corroded A/C condensers and radiators, A/C vent temp
Identify aftermarket exhaust extent (muffler vs headers/cat delete) and CARB/EO status; confirm OEM parts included
Check 20" wheels for bends/curb rash; tire DOT dates and N-spec rating
Paint depth gauge and panel-gap check on the left/left-front Carfax damage area; airbag/structural records

Inspect cross-drilled rotors for cracks at drillings, pad thickness, brake fluid date

dealbreakers: Salvage, rebuilt, or branded title

critical_evidence.label: DME over-rev/engine-hours report and full PIWIS fault scan from a Porsche specialist
Borescope images of all six cylinders showing no scoring (a bonus when present; not having one is not held against the car, policy 1.9.2)
Video of the convertible top opening and closing fully, at speed and without stalls
Invoices/photos documenting the reported left-front damage repair and what panels were touched
Photos/description proving cats are intact and identifying the aftermarket exhaust components

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster (986, 1997–2004: 2.5 / 2.7 / S 3.2)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel-based buyer, the 986 is a light, balanced mid-engine roadster for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laguna Seca weekends. It works as an honest daily-capable fun car if bought right. The car's value lives or dies on the health of the M96 flat-six: IMS bearing status, oil-coolant integrity, over-rev history and cooling-system condition matter far more than paint or options. Coastal fog and salt air raise the stakes on radiators, condensers, top fabric and drains. California smog compliance, especially the secondary air injection system, must be verified before purchase, not assumed.
profiles.weak_points: ['IMS (intermediate shaft) bearing. This is the defining M96 risk. Most 1997–1999 and early-2000 engines use the dual-row bearing, with a failure rate of roughly 1%. Engines from about 2000/2001 through 2004 use the single-row bearing, with failure rates commonly cited in the high single digits. Confirm which bearing is fitted by engine number, not model year. Failure is sudden and usually destroys the engine: $12k–$20k for a used or rebuilt replacement installed. Preventive retrofits (LN Engineering IMS Retrofit or IMS Solution) cost about $3,000–$5,000 at an independent shop when bundled with clutch and RMS. Look for a dated receipt naming the shop, part brand and engine number. Low-mileage cars that sat for long periods are not exempt, because bearing grease degrades with age.', 'Rear main seal (RMS) and IMS cover weeping. A light oil film where the engine meets the transmission is common at any mileage, and dried-out seals on long-stored cars make it more likely. Standalone repair runs about $1,000–$1,600 because the transmission must come out. If the seal is done alongside clutch or IMS work, it costs little extra. A heavy drip, or an oily IMS flange bolt, deserves a closer look.', "Oil-coolant intermix and early 2.5 block/head defects. 1997–1999 2.5L engines saw a higher incidence of porous or cracked cylinder heads and cylinder/liner cracking, which lets oil and coolant mix. Check for oil sheen or 'mayonnaise' in the coolant expansion tank and milky residue under the oil filler cap. Persistent unexplained coolant loss is another warning. Confirmed cases usually mean engine replacement, so a clean tank and a clean cap are cheap reassurance.", 'Cylinder bore scoring. This is less common on 986 engines than on 987/996 3.4–3.8L engines, but it is documented, particularly on the S 3.2. Symptoms are ticking on one bank, oil consumption, and a sooty tailpipe on one side only. Borescope inspection costs about $300–$500. Confirmed scoring means an engine rebuild or replacement of $12k–$20k+.', 'Over-revs and cam timing. 2000+ cars with the ME7.2 DME store over-rev counts by ignition range, readable with a Durametric scanner or PIWIS. Early M5.2 cars (1997–1999) give limited or no over-rev data. Any counts in ranges 4–6 indicate mechanical over-revs from missed downshifts and are a serious concern. Camshaft deviation readings that are out of spec point to worn chain tensioner pads or guides, or stretched chains. Tensioner and guide work costs $1,500–$3,500+.', 'Cooling system. The plastic coolant expansion tank yellows and cracks at the seams or cap neck, costing $250–$500 installed. Early water pumps with plastic impellers fail at about 50k–70k miles or with age, and should be replaced with the thermostat for $500–$900. The front-corner radiators and A/C condensers trap leaves and debris and corrode from the inside out, which is worse in coastal air. Replacing these costs $800–$2,000 for both sides. Overheating is especially damaging to M96 engines.', 'Air-oil separator (AOS) failure. Symptoms are a big plume of white or blue smoke on startup, high crankcase vacuum, oil in the intake, a rough idle, and lean codes (P1128/P1130). Replacement runs about $400–$900 at an independent shop. A ruined AOS can hydrolock the engine in extreme cases, so smoke on a cold start is a red flag to investigate.', 'Ignition coils and spark plug tubes. Coils crack with heat and age, causing misfires and P030x codes. Spark plug tube O-rings leak oil into the coil wells. Coils, plugs and tube seals together cost about $400–$900. Expect replacement every 60k miles or about 8–10 years if records are absent.', 'Secondary air injection (SAI) and California smog. Carbon clogging of the SAI ports, along with failed pump or valve parts, sets P0410/P1411 and leaves readiness monitors incomplete. Either outcome can fail a California smog check. Port cleaning and valve or pump replacement costs about $500–$1,500, and more if the head passages are badly blocked.
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Oil and filter change with a cut-open filter inspection for metal and a Blackstone-style oil analysis to establish an engine-health baseline.', 'Coolant flush with Porsche-spec coolant and brake fluid flush (DOT 4) if not documented within 2 years; inspect the expansion tank cap and seams.', 'Serpentine belt, tensioner and idler pulley replacement if age is unknown.', 'Remove the front bumper corner grilles and clean debris from the radiators and A/C condensers; inspect fin and tube corrosion.', 'Clear all top, cowl and body drains; dry and treat any damp carpet.', 'Tire replacement if DOT date codes are over 6 years old, regardless of tread depth; alignment check.', 'Battery and charging system test; replace if the battery is old (986s are sensitive to low voltage).', 'Full scan with Du

profiles.market_notes: The Boxster S (2000+, 3.2L, 6-speed) commands a clear premium over the base 2.5/2.7. 2003–2004 facelift cars, with the glass rear window, glovebox and more power, bring more than the early cars. The 2004 550 Spyder Anniversary is a collector outlier priced well above other 986s. Manual transmission, documented IMS retrofit or a verified dual-row original, under-50k miles, single-owner records, and desirable colors or options all add meaningfully to value. Desirable colors include Speed Yellow, Guards Red, Arena Red and Ocean Jade; desirable options include factory hardback sport seats, sport design packages, sport exhaust, hardtop and LSD on the S. Tiptronic cars, cars over 100k miles without records, and cars with unknown IMS status trade at steep discounts; a documented retrofit is typically worth $2,000–$4,000 in price.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 986 is now 20–30 years old, so even low-mileage cars carry age debt: dried seals (RMS, plug tubes), aged coolant tank and hoses, belt and tensioner, top fabric and window, tires, and suspension bushings. Without documentation, budget $3,000–$6,000 to bring an example current. Add another $3,000–$5,000 if the IMS, clutch and RMS have never been addressed.

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster / Boxster S (987.1 & 987.2)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 987 is a mid-engine, open-top back-road car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the occasional track day — not a garage investment. It is one of the last analog, hydraulically-assisted Porsches available at commuter-car money, and a well-documented manual example is a genuinely usable daily driver with a frunk plus trunk. The entire buying decision hinges on engine provenance: 987.1 cars (2005–2008, M96/M97) carry IMS bearing and bore-scoring risk that can turn a $16k car into a $30k car overnight, while 987.2 cars (2009–2012, 9A1 DFI) eliminate both. Coastal humidity and salt air matter less than rust-belt exposure, but clogged convertible-top and cowl drains cause expensive electrical damage in any climate.
profiles.weak_points: 1) IMS bearing (2005–2008 M96/M97 only): 2005 and very early 2006 engines use the smaller single-row bearing with the highest failure rate; engines built from roughly mid-2006 through 2008 use a larger non-serviceable bearing with a lower failure rate but which cannot be retrofitted without splitting the engine. A proactive IMS retrofit (LN Engineering ceramic hybrid or IMS Solution) done with clutch and RMS runs $3,000–$4,500 and should be documented by invoice with the engine number. Absence of a retrofit is not a dealbreaker on a 2006+ car but is a $3.5k line item. 2) Bore scoring: most common on the 3.4 M97 (2007–2008 S) but present on 2.7s too; symptoms are cold-start rattle/ticking that fades, elevated oil consumption (worse than ~1 qt/1,000 mi), and a smoky start after sitting. Only a borescope through the spark plug holes proves cylinder condition — this is the single most valuable pre-purchase test. A scored engine means a $12,000–$20,000 rebuild or used-engine swap. 3) Rear main seal (RMS) weeping: nearly universal at some level; a light film is normal, active dripping onto the bellhousing means $1,500–$2,000 alone or fold it into a clutch/IMS job. 4) Air/oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure at 60k–100k miles: huge white smoke cloud at startup, rough idle, oil pulled into intake; $600–$1,200 installed. 5) Water pump with plastic impeller: typical life 60k–80k miles; impeller blades shed and clog the system, $700–$1,100. Do it with the thermostat and coolant. 6) Coolant expansion tank cracks and cap failure at 10–15 years, $700–$1,200; look for dried pink/orange crust in the engine bay and under the rear. 7) Front radiators and A/C condensers: leaves and debris pack the lower ducts, holding moisture against aluminum until the condensers corrode through — extremely common on 12–20 year old cars. Full front radiator/condenser refresh with grilles is $1,500–$2,800. 8) Convertible top: transmission cables fray and the plastic drive blocks/rollers break, the hydraulic pump and rams leak onto the trunk carpet, the microswitches and the rear window seam fail. Top mechanism work is $1,000–$2,500; a new top with window is $2,000–$3,500. 9) Blocked top and cowl drains: water backs up into the footwells and into the seat/convertible-top control modules and under-seat wiring — causes dash warnings, dead tops, and mildew. Pull the carpet edges and check for staining. 10) Suspension wear at 70k+ miles: front lower control arms (including the rear 'coffin' arm bushings), front and rear top mounts, and tie rods; a full corner refresh is $1,500–$3,000. Sagging ride height and clunks over expansion joints are the tell. 11) Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on 100k-mile manuals: $2,500–$3,500 done properly with RMS and IMS access. Judder from a stop is the DMF. 12) Variocam actuators/solenoids and chain-pad wear on M96/M97: a rattle for 1–3 seconds on cold start plus cam deviation values out of spec on a Durametric scan; actuator/solenoid work $1,200–$2,500. 13) Electrical annoyances: ignition switch failure, door lock/latch microswitches (door won't unlock, top won't operate), airbag light from the passenger seat occupancy mat ($600–$1,000 for the mat), and PCM2 unit/CD-changer failures. 14) Tiptronic (5-speed auto in 987.1) and PDK (987.2): the Tiptronic is durable but dulls the car badly and hurts resale; PDK mechatronic and clutch-pack service is expensive out of warranty ($3,000+). 987.2 DFI engines are far more robust but are known for occasional high-pressure fuel pump and injector issues and for coolant-pipe/thermostat housing seepage.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluids service (Mobil 1 0W-40 with a genuine filter, brake fluid, coolant top-up), four correct-size tires if mismatched or over 6 years old, front radiator/condenser duct cleaning and grille installation, convertible-top and cowl drain clearing, serpentine belt and tensioner if undocumented, battery if unknown age, and an alignment. Budget $1,200–$2,500. If the borescope or oil filter cut shows anything marginal, stop and renegotiate rather than repairing.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if there is no receipt in the last 60k miles, AOS if there is any startup smoke or idle hunt, coolant expansion tank on any 15+ year old car, front control arms and top mounts, a clutch/DMF plus IMS retrofit combined job on a 987.1 approaching 100k miles, convertible top transmission cables or hydraulic ram seals, and typically one electrical gremlin (ignition switch, door latch microswitch, or seat occupancy mat). Realistic 12-month spend on an unsorted 2006: $3,000–$6,000.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission is worth a clear premium over Tiptronic and is close to mandatory for resale; S models (3.2 then 3.4) carry roughly a 15–25% premium over base 2.7s, and 987.2 DFI cars command a further step up because they have no IMS and no meaningful bore-scoring reputation. Documented IMS retrofit, recent clutch, and a clean borescope report can add $2,000–$4,000 of buyer confidence on a 987.1. Color and options move money more than mileage below 100k: Guards Red, Cobalt/Aqua Blue, Speed Yellow and GT Silver with sport seats, PASM, Sport Chrono, litronics and a hardtop sell fastest, while black-on-black base cars with automatics are the soft end. Boxster Spyder and RS 60 Spyder trade in their own, much higher tier.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 15–20 year old 987.1 arrives needing rubber and plastic more than metal: coolant expansion tank, water pump, AOS, serpentine belt and tensioner, engine and top-mechanism seals, convertible-top cables and drain hoses, and front suspension bushings — plus tires and brake fluid regardless of tread and pedal feel. Assume $2,500–$4,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year even on a nicely kept car, and treat any clutch job as the right moment to bundle IMS, RMS, and flywheel work.

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster S (986, 2000-2004)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 986 Boxster S is an affordable mid-engine roadster for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laureles Grade. It is a driver, not an appreciating asset. Nearly the whole purchase decision comes down to verifiable engine health: IMS bearing status, DME over-rev history, oil filter debris and cylinder condition, because an engine failure can cost more than the car is worth. After that, prioritize a documented cooling system, a sound top that keeps out coastal fog and rain, and a clean structural history. Cosmetic wear is cheap to live with; an undocumented engine is not.
profiles.weak_points: ["Intermediate shaft (IMS) bearing. Early engines (MY2000 to roughly early MY2001) mostly used the stronger dual-row bearing. The 2002-2004 cars, including the 2003 example, use the single-row bearing, which has a meaningfully higher failure rate. The failure is often sudden: metal in the oil filter, cam deviation codes, then chain and valve destruction, and a used or rebuilt engine runs about $10,000-20,000. The fix is a retrofit, LN Engineering IMS Retrofit (ceramic hybrid) or IMS Solution (plain bearing), ideally done alongside a clutch job for about $3,000-4,500 all-in. Seller claims of 'IMS done' with no invoice should be treated as not done. Require an invoice naming the part, the mileage and the shop. A photo of the removed bearing and LN's engine-bay sticker help corroborate it.", 'Rear main seal (RMS) and IMS flange leaks at the engine-transmission junction. These are very common on the M96. A light seep is tolerable, but an active drip or oil on the clutch is not. Standalone repair is about $1,500-2,500 because the transmission must come out, so it is normally done with the clutch and IMS. Look for a recent RMS invoice and check the bellhousing seam from below.', 'Over-rev and mechanical over-rev (money shift). The DME logs ignition counts in rev ranges 1-6. Ranges 1-3 are mostly harmless (fuel cut), but significant counts in ranges 4-6 indicate a mis-shift such as 5th to 2nd. That raises the risk of bent valves, chain and guide damage, or rod bearing stress. Read it with PIWIS or Durametric, and note the total operating hours so you can judge how far back the log goes.', 'Cam timing deviation and timing chain wear. Worn chain tensioner pads and guides, or a slipped VarioCam adjuster, show up as cam deviation values outside spec, typically beyond about ±6°, or bank-to-bank mismatch. They also appear as P1341-family codes and as a rattle on cold start. Tensioner pads and guides are roughly $1,500-3,500. Cam deviation is also an early warning of IMS trouble.', "Bore scoring, cracked or slipped cylinder liners, and porous blocks. These are less common on the 986's 3.2 than on later 3.4/3.6/3.8 engines, but they are not rare at this age and mileage. Symptoms are a sooty single tailpipe on one bank, rising oil consumption (more than about 1 qt/1,000 mi), a ticking that does not go away when warm, and oil mixed into coolant from the 'D-chunk' liner crack. A borescope inspection costs about $150-300 and is the only real test. A rebuild is $12,000-20,000.", 'Air-oil separator (AOS). It fails as a cloud of white or blue smoke on cold start, a rough or hunting idle, high crankcase vacuum (oil filler cap hard to remove at idle), oil in the intake and throttle body, and lean codes (P0171/P0174). Replacement is about $400-900 in parts and labor. A badly failed AOS can hydrolock the engine with oil.', 'Cooling system. The coolant expansion tank cracks and seeps at its seams (about $400-700). The water pump impeller and bearing wear out (about $700-1,200 with thermostat, preventively every 50-60k miles or about 6 years). Bypass and heater hoses age. Coolant smell in the cabin or engine bay, pink crust on the tank, or a low reservoir are red flags. Records should show a water pump and thermostat within the last 60k miles or 6 years.', 'Front radiators, condensers and the S-specific center radiator. They sit behind front openings that trap leaves and debris, which hold moisture and corrode the fins. In salty, foggy Carmel air this accelerates. Expect AC failure and higher coolant temperatures. Condensers run about $200-400 each in parts, radiators about $300-500 each, plus about $400-800 labor. Plan on yearly cleaning with the bumper off.', 'Ignition coils and spark plug tubes. Coils crack with heat cycles and cause misfires (P0300-P0306), about $60-90 each. Leaking spark plug tube O-rings and VarioCam solenoid seals let oil into the plug wells. Check the coil boots for oil and look for a dated plug and coil invoice. Plugs are due ab

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Water pump, thermostat and coolant expansion tank if not documented within 60k miles or 6 years', 'Spark plugs and coils, plus spark plug tube and VarioCam solenoid seals if oil is in the plug wells', 'Serpentine belt, tensioner and idler pulleys', 'Front coil springs, control arms and end links, and shocks/top mounts if original or of unknown age', 'AC condensers and radiators if corroded, plus AC recharge', 'Top drive cable adjustment or replacement and fabric/rear window seam repair', 'Shifter cable bushings and transmission shift rod seal; engine/transmission mount if there is a clunk on take-off', 'Ignition switch electrical section, door handle cables and headlight lens restoration as nuisance items']
profiles.market_notes: The 6-speed manual Boxster S commands a clear premium over the 5-speed Tiptronic. The 2003-2004 facelift cars (glass rear window, glovebox, revised bumpers and lights) are preferred, and the 2004 550 Spyder 50th Anniversary sits in its own collector tier well above regular S cars. A documented IMS retrofit with recent clutch/RMS work and thorough records can add roughly $2,000-4,000, while a reported accident, undocumented engine work or rebuilt title knock values down hard. Desirable options (Sport package, LSD, 18-inch wheels, interesting colors like Speed Yellow, Guards Red or Lapis Blue) help modestly. Mileage under about 60k earns a premium but is not a proxy for IMS health, since low-use cars can be more at risk.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 20+ year-old 986 S with patchy records needs a cooling system refresh (water pump, thermostat, tank), AOS, plugs and coils, and belts. It also usually needs suspension bushings and springs, radiator/condenser cleaning or replacement, and top service, which together run roughly $3,000-6,000 before any IMS or clutch work. Budget an additional $3,000-4,500 for IMS, clutch and RMS if none is documented.
