profiles.label: Subaru Legacy 2.5GT (5th gen BM, 2010-2012 US turbo)
profiles.framing: In the US the BM Legacy 2.5GT is a rare, understated manual-only turbo AWD sedan. It ran 2010-2012 before the turbo was dropped, and it pairs WRX-class EJ255 power with a quiet, roomy midsize body. For a Carmel driver it is an all-weather sport sedan for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Big Sur. The car to buy is one that stayed stock, ran on premium fuel, and got short-interval oil changes, because the EJ255 forgives age far better than it forgives tuning, knock or oil neglect. Engine health evidence and timing-belt history matter far more than cosmetics or options.
profiles.weak_points:
1) EJ255 ringland/piston failure. Cracked ringlands on cylinders 2 and 4 are the classic turbo EJ failure. Causes include aggressive tunes, low-octane fuel, lean conditions and lugging. Symptoms are low compression on one cylinder, oil consumption, blue smoke, misfires and crankcase pressure. The fix is a short block or rebuild at $6,000-9,500. Look for a stock ECU, premium-fuel receipts and a recent compression or leakdown test.

2) Rod bearing failure. Spun #2 rod bearings come from oil starvation or degraded oil. Contributors are extended intervals, low oil level from unchecked consumption, and RTV or debris on the oil pickup screen after prior engine work. Listen for a rhythmic knock that rises with rpm and is often worse warm. Repair runs $6,000-10,000. Look for 3,000-5,000-mile synthetic oil change records and an oil analysis if available.

3) Turbo oil-feed and turbo health. Earlier EJ255s used a filter screen in the turbo oil-feed banjo bolt that could clog and starve the turbo. Many techs remove it at first service, so verify its status on this engine. Turbo wear shows as shaft play, whine or siren noise, smoke, or wastegate rattle. A replacement turbo with gaskets and lines runs $2,000-3,500.

4) Timing belt kit. Subaru's interval is about 105k miles, but at 13-16 years old every original belt is overdue on age. Original idlers and the hydraulic tensioner fail regardless of mileage. The EJ255 is an interference engine, so a failure means bent valves and $3,500+. A full kit with water pump and thermostat costs $1,200-2,000. Demand a dated receipt; without one, budget it immediately.

5) Oil leaks. Valve cover gaskets and spark-plug tube seals seep onto the exhaust and cause a burning-oil smell. Also check the cam seals, oil separator plate and rear main seal (oil at the bellhousing). The turbo EJ255 uses MLS head gaskets, so it is less prone than the NA EJ25 to external coolant weeps, but oil seepage at the head-to-block seam happens. Valve covers and tube seals cost $400-800. Oil separator plate or rear main jobs are combined with clutch work.

6) AVCS oil control valves. The valves and their screens clog from poor oil history and set P0011/P0021/P0014-type codes with rough idle. Valves are $300-700 per side installed. Treat these codes as a proxy for oil-change neglect.

7) Clutch, dual-mass flywheel and hydraulics. The 6MT uses a dual-mass flywheel that develops idle rattle and chatter. Note that the example car needed a flywheel at only about 30k miles. Slipping in 4th-6th under boost, a soft or sticky pedal, a grinding 2nd/3rd synchro and throwout-bearing whir are common complaints. Clutch plus flywheel runs $1,800-3,200. Ask whether an OEM or single-mass flywheel was used and get the receipt.

8) Electronic parking brake. The 2010+ Legacy uses an EPB with Hill Holder. The actuator, cable and controller can fault and set EPB warning lights or fail to release. Rear brake service requires the EPB service mode. Repairs run $400-1,500 depending on whether it is a cable, the actuator or the module.

9) Exhaust and emissions. Watch for cracked up-pipe or downpipe flanges, failed donut gaskets, rattling heat shields, and aging cats or O2/AF sensors (P0420, P0137). California smog compliance means a stock exhaust, intact cats and a stock or CARB-legal tune. Non-compliant parts can make the car unregisterable. Repairs run $300-2,500.

10) Suspension and driveline wear. Expect worn front lower control arm rear bushings (clunk, vague steering), rear trailing-arm and subframe bushings, front and rear hub/wheel bearings (droning hum at speed), torn CV boots, and rear diff seals. Each item runs $300-900.

11) Rust. Many survivors are Northeast and Midwest cars; the example is a NY-delivered, CT-titled car. Inspect the rear subframe, rocker pinch welds, rear wheel arches, brake and fuel lines, and exhaust hangers. Heavy subframe or line corrosion on a salt-belt car is expensive and can be a walk-away.

12) Modifications and tun

profiles.market_notes: All US 2.5GTs are 6-speed manuals, so price is driven by originality, mileage, documentation and rust history rather than transmission. Bone-stock, untuned, one- or two-owner cars with full oil-change records command large premiums. A 36k-mile documented car brought $27,000, while typical 90-160k-mile examples trade roughly $8,000-15,000 and tuned or salvage cars sell well below that. Limited trim (leather, Harman Kardon, power passenger seat) and factory nav add modestly. A documented timing belt, recent clutch and flywheel, clean West Coast history and California smog-legal status add real value. Evidence of a Cobb tune, a missing downpipe or cats, or heavy salt-belt underbody corrosion should push price down sharply.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even low-mile examples are now 13-16 years old. Expect age-driven work: a timing belt kit, all fluids including coolant and brake fluid, tires, a battery, and possibly rubber seals and bushings. Budget roughly $2,500-4,500 in catch-up unless receipts prove recent completion. Salt-belt cars also need a careful underbody assessment before any California registration and smog work.

profiles.label: Subaru WRX (VA, 2015-2021, FA20DIT)
profiles.framing: The VA WRX is a practical, all-weather, turbocharged sedan that suits Carmel's mix of Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and the occasional Sierra ski run. It is a good real-world driver, but a large share of these cars were tuned, launched, and driven hard by young owners. The single most important question is whether the engine has run stock calibration and received short-interval oil changes for its whole life. A documented, unmodified, single-owner car with a healthy FA20DIT and a sound clutch and gearbox is worth paying up for. A cheap modified car is usually a deferred engine bill. Note that the WRX STI of these years uses the older EJ257 engine and has a different risk profile, so do not mix STI listings into this profile.
profiles.weak_points:
1) FA20DIT piston and ringland failure. Cracked ringlands and low compression on one cylinder are the generation's signature catastrophic failure. They are strongly associated with aftermarket tunes (Cobb Accessport or pro-tunes), lean or knock conditions, low-speed lugging (LSPI), and poor fuel. Early 2015-2016 cars are reported somewhat more often. Symptoms are misfire codes, rough idle, blue smoke, oil consumption, and crankcase pressure. Short block or used engine runs roughly $6,000-$10,000 installed. Look for a never-tuned ECU, a compression and leakdown test, and 91+ octane fueling habits.

2) Rod bearing spin and oil starvation. This is less common than ringlands and also skews toward tuned or tracked cars and extended oil change intervals. It shows up as knock under load or a low-oil-pressure event. The fix is engine replacement in the same cost band. Ask for oil change receipts at 3,000-5,000 mile intervals, not the 6,000-7,500 the monitor allows.

3) Intake valve carbon buildup. The FA20DIT is direct-injection only, with no port injectors, so deposits accumulate from about 50,000-100,000 miles. Symptoms are cold-start stumble, misfire, and flat midrange. A walnut-blast cleaning runs roughly $500-$900. PCV and oil-catch history helps; a catch can is a modification but is benign.

4) Turbo wastegate rattle and turbo wear. A metallic rattle on decel or at low RPM from the twin-scroll turbo's wastegate actuator linkage is common. Some cases were addressed with updated parts or under warranty. Shaft play, oil in the intercooler piping, or smoke indicate turbo wear. Turbo replacement runs roughly $2,000-$3,500. Look for dealer records of wastegate repairs.

5) Clutch, throwout bearing, and hydraulics (6MT). Clutch life is heavily owner-dependent: 40,000-100,000+ miles. Launches and hard driving shorten it sharply. Watch for slipping in 4th/5th under boost, judder, throwout bearing whine with the pedal released or depressed, and a high engagement point. Many owners removed the clutch delay valve, which is a minor mod but a clue to driving style. Clutch replacement runs roughly $1,500-$2,500, plus about $400-$800 if the flywheel needs resurfacing or replacement.

6) 6-speed manual synchros and notchiness. The VA 6MT is known for notchy or crunchy 2nd and 3rd shifts, especially cold. Grinding when warm on quick shifts indicates synchro wear from hard use. A gearbox rebuild or replacement runs roughly $2,500-$5,000. A gear oil change with quality fluid can improve feel. Look for documented manual transmission fluid changes.

7) Sport Lineartronic CVT (SPT/automatic cars). The CVT is less robust under boost than the manual. Watch for shudder, whine, hesitation, or limp mode. Fluid service is often neglected because Subaru marketed it as 'lifetime'. Valve body or torque converter repairs run roughly $1,500-$3,000; replacement runs roughly $5,000-$8,000. Look for CVT fluid change records around 30,000-60,000 miles.

8) Oil leaks. Valve cover gaskets, front timing cover and cam carrier RTV seams, and turbo oil feed and return lines can seep. This is often noticed at 50,000-100,000 miles. Valve cover gaskets run about $300-$700. Timing cover reseals cost more, roughly $800-$1,500. Inspect for oil residue on the heads, turbo area, and crossmember.

9) Drivetrain bearings and differentials. Rear differential whine, wheel bearing hum (often front), and CV boot tears or axle clicks occur. These are more common on lowered or wide-wheel cars. Wheel bearings run roughly $350-$600 per corner; rear diff service or repair runs roughly $150-$2,000. Look for diff and transfer fluid change records.

10) Windshield cracking. Subaru windshields of this era crack readily from small chips. Replacement runs roughly $400-$900 on manual cars. CVT cars with EyeSight run roughly $900-$1,500 including the required EyeSight camera recalibration.

11) Infotainment and electronics. On 2018-2021 cars, the Starlink head unit can freeze, reboot, or lose the b
profiles.immediate_repairs: Engine oil and filter change with a Subaru-spec 5W-30 full synthetic, then shorten the interval to about 3,000-5,000 miles. Manual transmission gear oil, front diff (shared with the trans on the 6MT), and rear diff fluid change if not documented, roughly $250-$400 total. Brake fluid flush if older than 2-3 years. Engine and cabin air filters. Spark plugs if at or near 60,000 miles without a record, roughly $250-$450. Battery test, and replacement if original on an older car. Alignment and tire check (WRXs often show inner-edge wear). For CVT cars, a CVT fluid drain-and-fill if no record exists. Confirm all open recalls are completed at a Subaru dealer.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Intake valve carbon cleaning if the car shows cold-start roughness or misfire above about 60,000 miles, roughly $500-$900. Clutch and throwout bearing if the engagement point is high or slip appears, roughly $1,500-$2,500. Brake pads and rotors if near the wear limit, roughly $500-$900 per axle with OEM-grade parts. Valve cover gasket or other oil seep repairs, roughly $300-$1,500. Wheel bearing or CV axle replacement if hum or click develops. Coolant service with Subaru Super Coolant if no record, plus a check of the drive belt and PCV hoses. Windshield replacement if a chip spreads. Possible wastegate rattle repair.
profiles.market_notes: The biggest price movers are evidence the car is unmodified and never tuned, single-owner dealer service records, and mileage bands. Under 40,000 miles commands a strong premium; 40,000-80,000 miles is the value zone; over 100,000 miles drops sharply. 2018-2021 facelift cars, especially the final 2021 model year, bring more than 2015-2017, and Limited, Series, or packaged trims (Premium with Popular Package) add modestly. The 6-speed manual is the enthusiast default and usually holds value better than the CVT. WR Blue Pearl and Series.Gray-type colors are most liquid. Tuned or modified cars should be discounted heavily ($3,000-$6,000+) for engine risk, regardless of the quality of the parts.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 4-7 year old, 40,000-80,000 mile example usually needs a full fluid catch-up (gear and diff oils, brake fluid, coolant, CVT fluid if equipped) plus spark plugs around 60,000 miles. Expect possible intake valve carbon cleaning and attention to clutch wear and minor oil seeps. Budget roughly $800-$2,000 for catch-up on a good car, and more if the clutch is near the end of its life.

profiles.label: Subaru WRX STI (VA, 2015–2021)
profiles.framing: The VA STI is the last of the EJ257-powered, manual-only, DCCD-equipped STIs. It is a raw, loud, mechanically involving all-weather sports sedan that makes good sense on Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and the Santa Cruz Mountains. Condition depends almost entirely on how the previous owners treated it. Most examples have been tuned, launched, or tracked, and the EJ257's fragile pistons and rod bearings punish that history. For this buyer, the right car is an unmodified, stock-ECU example with documented oil changes, a compression/leakdown baseline, and a clean path through a California smog check. A tuned car is a different and much riskier purchase.

profiles.market_notes: Unmodified, stock-ECU examples with documented maintenance command a strong premium. Tuned or heavily modified cars typically trade 20–40% lower, and they are the right discount given EJ257 risk and California smog problems. The 2018+ refresh brought better Brembo brakes, a fully electronic DCCD, and an improved interior. The 2019–2021 cars added a small output bump to 310 hp versus 305 hp for 2015–2018, so these later cars bring more money. Limited editions and special trims carry a real premium. The Series.HyperBlue, Series.White, and Series.Gray are modest premiums; the 2018 Type RA and 2019 S209 are collector-tier and priced accordingly. WR Blue Pearl is the most sought-after color, under-50k miles is a meaningful price band, and documented compression/leakdown results add buyer confidence.
profiles.catchup_notes: Every 2015–2017 car has crossed the 105-month timing belt age threshold. Assume a belt and water pump job unless a dated receipt proves otherwise, along with coolant, brake fluid, and gear oil that may have aged out regardless of mileage. Expect bushings, mounts, and rubber hoses to show age on earlier cars. On any previously tuned example, add a stock reflash and smog compliance work before California registration.

profiles.label: Sunbeam Tiger Mk 1 / Mk 1A (260 V8)
profiles.framing: A Tiger is a small, light, honestly crude British roadster with a Ford small-block shoehorned into it by Shelby's shop and built by Rootes on a shoestring. For a Carmel-based owner it is a Sunday-morning Highway 1 and Laguna Seca paddock car: short-hop fun, big torque, terrible ergonomics, and genuine period charisma; it is not a road-trip car and it is not a commuter. What matters most is authenticity (Alpine-to-Tiger 'Algers' are everywhere), the structural condition of a unibody that was never engineered for 200+ lb-ft, and whether the cooling/heat-soak issues have been solved properly. A documented, TAC-authenticated car with sorted brakes, cooling and wiring is worth paying a lot more for than a shiny one with no paper.
profiles.weak_points: 1) AUTHENTICITY FIRST. Roughly a third of 'Tigers' offered for sale are converted Alpines or re-bodied/re-stamped cars. Mk 1 LHD chassis numbers run B9470001-onward (Mk 1A B9471... series), with the serial plate on the left inner fender/engine bay and a separate JAL (Jensen assembly) number; body stamps, the Panhard rod mount, the rack delete and the Burman steering box mount are all conversion tells. Absence of a Tiger Authentication Committee (TAC) certificate or a Norman Miller build-details letter is a 20-40% value haircut, and on a car with weld-in structure or fresh paint over the stampings it's a walk-away. 2) RUST, and it hides. Check the front frame rails/crossmember ahead of the radiator, inner and outer sills/rockers, floor pans under both seats, footwell toe boards, the battery area, rear spring hangers and their body-mount boxes, trunk floor and spare well, rear wheel arches and doglegs. Rootes rustproofing was nil and these live in coastal California with salt-air and top-down parking. Proper sill/floor/spring-hanger repair is $12k-35k with paint; a full body-off restoration is $80k-150k+ and will never be recovered on a Mk 1. 3) STRUCTURAL FATIGUE from V8 torque: cracking around the rear leaf-spring front hangers, Panhard rod anchor, differential snubber, and the transmission tunnel/crossmember. Look for stress cracks, added plating, and doors that won't shut squarely when the car is jacked at one corner. 4) OVERHEATING AND HEAT SOAK is the defining Tiger complaint. Stock radiator and packaging leave almost no airflow; expect 210-230F in traffic, vapor lock, a cooked footwell and a steering column that runs beside the exhaust. Sorted cars have an aluminum radiator, shroud and electric fan, header wrap or ceramic coating, insulation, and a phenolic carb spacer - budget $1,500-3,000 to do this properly if it hasn't been done. 5) STEERING: the Tiger uses a Burman worm-and-roller box (the Alpine's rack wouldn't clear the V8) with a fragile, heat-soaked column and a rag joint. Play, wander and column lash are endemic; a rebuilt box or a modern R&P conversion runs $1,200-3,500. 6) CLUTCH SLAVE/HYDRAULICS are packaged so badly that the classic Tiger job is 'pull the engine to change the slave cylinder' unless a remote or through-the-hole kit is fitted; a $60 part becomes a $1,200-2,000 job. Ask when the clutch, slave and master were last done. 7) OIL FILTER CLEARANCE: no room for a spin-on filter against the steering box, so a remote filter/adapter is near-mandatory; badly done remote lines are a known fire/oil-starvation risk - inspect hose routing and age. 8) ENGINE: almost no Tiger retains its original 260 (5-bolt bellhousing, correct block casting and engine number on the STOA/TAC paperwork). 289s and 302s are extremely common and are not a defect in a driver, but they cost real money at the top of the market. On any small-block, check for oil pressure at hot idle, rear main seepage, and whether the 289/302 firing-order camshaft issue was addressed with the correct distributor/cam combination. Rebuilds run $8k-15k. 9) DRIVELINE: the BorgWarner T-10 four-speed has weak 2nd-gear synchro and whines; rebuild $1,800-3,000, 5-speed (Tremec TKO/T5) conversions are common and improve drivability but cost originality points. Rear axle is a Salisbury 4HU (Mk 1/1A) - listen for whine and check for pinion-seal leaks and Panhard rod bushing slop. 10) BRAKES: Girling front discs/rear drums with a vacuum servo that routinely fails; steel lines corrode, and the Tiger is genuinely underbraked for its power. Full hydraulic refresh $1,500-3,000; Wilwood conversions are the usual fix. 11) FUEL SYSTEM: twin rear-fender tanks joined by a crossover hose and vent lines that rot out of sight and dump fuel into the trunk area. Old tanks, sending units and rubber are a fire risk - replacement/lining $800-2,500. Also watch for ethanol-rotted pump diaphragms and hard fuel lines routed near headers. 12) LUCAS ELECTRICS AND WIRING: 60-year-old h
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid and hose service including the fuel crossover and vent hoses; brake hydraulic inspection with likely master/slave/wheel cylinder and flex-hose replacement; cooling system verification under a 20-minute hot idle with an IR thermometer, plus fan/shroud fixes if it climbs; carburetor tune and ignition timing/dwell set with correct distributor curve; battery, grounds and charging check; steering box adjustment or rebuild and rag-joint replacement; tire date codes - almost every Tiger on the market wears 8-12 year-old rubber that must be replaced regardless of tread; wheel alignment and rear Panhard/spring bushing check. Budget $2,500-5,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch hydraulics with a remote-slave fix if not already done; T-10 synchro rebuild or accept a 5-speed; leaf springs, bushings and shocks; fuel tank cleaning/lining and new sender; exhaust/header heat management and footwell insulation; gauge and switch rebuilds and likely partial rewiring; convertible top and windshield/door seals; localized rust repair at sills, spring hangers or trunk floor discovered after purchase; differential pinion seal and axle service. Budget $5,000-12,000 depending on what the PPI finds.
profiles.market_notes: Mk 2 cars (289, 633 built, distinctive egg-crate grille) trade at roughly double a comparable Mk 1; within Mk 1/1A, TAC authentication plus documented original-type engine, a factory hardtop, and known ownership history are the biggest value levers. Correct or period colors and LAT/Shelby-era dealer options add; modified restomods - 302s, coilovers, 5-speeds, Wilwoods, non-stock wheels - drive beautifully and sell to a narrower audience, typically well under concours-original money regardless of how much was spent. Driver-quality authenticated Mk 1s generally sit in the $45k-75k band, strong restored cars $85k-130k, with no-paperwork or suspected-Alger cars much lower and hard to resell. Receipts matter more than mileage on a 60-year-old five-digit odometer.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 60-year-old car is due for everything rubber and hydraulic regardless of presentation: fuel crossover and vent hoses, brake and clutch hydraulics, coolant hoses, suspension bushings, top seals and tires by date code. Even a $200k-receipts show car needs a shakedown-and-sort budget because low post-restoration mileage means untested systems, and a Tiger's two chronic subsystems - cooling and wiring - are the ones that strand or burn cars.

profiles.label: Tesla Model X (1st gen, 2016–2021 pre-refresh)
profiles.framing: For this buyer, a first-gen Model X P100D is a quiet, roomy coastal daily driver and family hauler with absurd acceleration. It is not a toy or an investment. A 2016–2017 car is now outside Tesla's 8-year battery and drive-unit coverage. Value and risk therefore come down to three things: HV pack health, drive-unit condition, and whether the complex falcon-wing doors, air suspension and MCU are working without faults. Before committing, confirm home Level 2 charging and garage door and ceiling clearance for the falcon doors. Also verify that the software entitlements (FSD, free unlimited Supercharging, HW3) are real and will survive the ownership transfer.
profiles.weak_points: ["Falcon-wing rear doors are the signature weak point. Faults include hinge and actuator motor failures, ultrasonic proximity-sensor faults that stop doors mid-travel, door ECU faults, chafed wiring at the roof hinge, and misalignment that causes wind noise and closing errors. Watch for 'Door not closed' or 'Falcon door motion disabled' alerts. Repairs run about $800–$2,500 per side for actuators, sensors or harness, and $4,000+ for structural or hinge realignment. Ask for any Tesla service invoices on door calibration or actuator replacement.", 'Water intrusion is common. Leaks come past the falcon-wing seals and the roof glass/door glass interface, and into the rear footwells, third row and liftgate area. Wet carpets lead to musty smells, corroded connectors and phantom electrical faults. Seal, drain and cleanup work typically runs $300–$1,500, more if modules corrode. Ask for photos under the rear carpets and frunk/trunk liners, and for any leak-repair records.', "The front doors are self-presenting and powered. Door motors, latch actuators and handle-less proximity/brake-pedal close logic can fail. Symptoms are doors that won't auto-open or close, or clicking latches. Expect roughly $500–$1,500 per door.", "On the high-voltage battery, the original 2016–2017 100 kWh packs are now out of warranty. Expect 8–15% degradation by 50–80k miles. Warning signs include BMS alerts, isolation faults ('BMS_u018', 'BMS_f107'-type messages), and software-limited range or Supercharging speed. A remanufactured or new pack runs about $14,000–$25,000 installed, or $5,000–$9,000 for independent module or contactor repairs. Get a full-charge range readout plus a ScanMyTesla/TeslaFi usable-capacity reading or a Tesla battery health test, and ask about any pack replacement.", "Early S/X drive units (the large rear on the P100D, the small front) are known for bearing whine, 'milling' or grinding at low speed, and coolant leaks past the drive-unit seal causing isolation faults. A reman unit costs about $6,000–$12,000 per drive unit; independent rebuilds run $3,000–$6,000. Check service history for prior drive-unit swaps, which are common and actually reassuring on high-mileage cars.", "Air suspension: front air struts leak with age, causing overnight sag, a 'Suspension system needs service' alert or a compressor running constantly. Struts are about $1,200–$2,000 each installed and the compressor about $1,000–$1,500. Check that the car holds height after sitting overnight and that all height levels (including Very High) and auto-lower-at-speed work.", 'Front suspension on this ~5,400 lb vehicle wears hard. Front upper control arms (fore and aft links), lower control arm bushings, ball joints and rear toe links all wear, producing clunks over bumps and uneven inner tire wear. A typical full front-arm refresh is about $1,200–$2,500. 22-inch staggered wheels accelerate wear and bend or crack easily.', 'MCU1 (Tegra 3) infotainment: the original 8 GB eMMC fails, leaving a blank or rebooting screen, lost backup camera and no climate control. This was covered by NHTSA recall 21V-035 (eMMC replacement) for 2016–2018 Model X. MCU1 cars on 3G also needed an LTE modem retrofit after the 3G sunset (~$200). An optional MCU2 upgrade runs about $1,500–$2,500. Confirm recall completion and which MCU/modem is fitted.', "Several 2016 recalls need confirming by VIN. These include the parking brake gear fracture (2017, early 2016 builds) and power-steering assist motor bolt corrosion (2020). Also check the roof trim applique detachment (2020, early builds) and the 2016 third-row seatback latch. Some 2016 cars also have the early non-folding 'monopost' second-row seats, which were later revised. Missing recall work is free at Tesla but signals neglect.", "Autopilot hardware: a late-2016 P100D shipped with HW2.0. FSD-purchased cars are eligible for an HW3 computer retrofit. Repeater and B-pillar cameras fog from condensation, and ultrasonic sensors fail (each about $150
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace the 12V lead-acid battery (or upgrade to the Tesla/aftermarket lithium unit) unless documented within ~3 years: $200–$450.', 'Four-wheel alignment and tire inspection for inner-edge wear; budget tires if near limit (22-inch staggered set about $1,800–$2,500).', 'Brake fluid moisture test and flush if overdue (about every 2 years): $150–$250.', 'Replace cabin and HEPA filters; replace the A/C desiccant bag if never done: $150–$500.', 'Get a full Tesla Service visit to clear open recalls (eMMC/MCU, parking brake, power-steering bolts, roof trim) and check the alert log.', 'Falcon-door and front-door calibration, plus hinge and seal inspection and cleaning of drains: $0–$500 if only calibration is needed.', 'Buy a second key fob if only one is supplied: about $175–$250 plus pairing.
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front air strut replacement on one or both sides as leaks develop: $1,200–$4,000.', 'Front upper control arms, lower bushings and rear toe links if clunks appear: $1,200–$2,500.', 'Falcon-wing door actuator, proximity sensor or harness repair: $800–$2,500 per side.', 'Brake caliper slide and parking-brake caliper service (regen keeps pads alive but hardware corrodes in coastal air): $300–$900.', 'Ultrasonic sensor or fogged camera replacement: $150–$600 each.', 'Coolant pump or A/C compressor failure on a higher-mileage example: $400–$3,000.', 'Windshield chip repair or replacement with camera calibration: $100–$2,800.', 'Optional MCU2 upgrade for performance, streaming and longevity: $1,500–$2,500.']
profiles.market_notes: Price drivers, in rough order, are HV battery health and range, model year, and the presence of transferable FSD and free unlimited Supercharging. P100D/Ludicrous carries a modest premium over 100D/90D, but performance trims add drive-unit risk. Later cars are worth more: MCU2 became standard from about early 2018, and 2019+ 'Raven' Long Range/Performance cars bring adaptive suspension and more efficient motors. 6-seat captain's chairs are generally preferred over 7-seat. Documented drive-unit or pack replacements, HW3, MCU2, LTE and a clean alert log add real value. Accident history (aluminum structure, expensive bodywork), title brands and Tesla-revoked features hurt value heavily. Mileage matters less than battery condition, though sub-50k cars still sell at a premium.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2016–2017 example needs routine catch-up: 12V battery replacement, brake fluid flush, A/C desiccant bag and HEPA/cabin filters, and an alignment. Expect front suspension arm bushings, air struts and falcon-door seal or calibration work as the car approaches 8–10 years old. Coastal Carmel air also justifies inspecting brake hardware and underbody fasteners for corrosion.

profiles.label: Toyota 4Runner (3rd gen N180, 1996–2002)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, a 3rd-gen 4Runner is a durable, simple, body-on-frame utility vehicle for beach access, Big Sur and Sierra trips, and daily errands. The 5VZ-FE 3.4L V6 and A340 automatic routinely pass 250k miles when maintained. That means condition and documentation matter far more than the odometer. The deal-breakers are frame and underbody rust (favor West Coast trucks), coolant-contaminated transmissions, and neglected front-end safety parts like the lower ball joints. A stock, smog-clean, California-history example with timing-belt and radiator receipts is worth a meaningful premium over a cheap lifted or salt-state truck.
profiles.weak_points: ['Lower ball joints (front): The 3rd-gen front lower ball joints have a well-known separation failure mode, where the wheel folds under the truck at speed. At 100k+ miles, or with unknown history, treat them as due. Look for a receipt naming the brand: genuine Toyota/OEM Japanese joints are strongly preferred, and some cheap aftermarket units have a poor reputation. Inspect for boot tears and vertical play with the weight off the wheel. Expect $400–$800 a pair installed with alignment, more with upper ball joints.', "Radiator internal ATF cooler ('pink milkshake'): The factory and cheap aftermarket radiators can fail internally and mix coolant into the A340 transmission fluid. This destroys clutches and the torque converter. Ask for the radiator replacement date and brand; OEM/Denso is preferred. Pull the ATF dipstick: fluid should be red and clear, not pink, milky, or frothy. Coolant should show no ATF sheen. A radiator is $350–$700 installed; a contaminated transmission is a $2,500–$4,500 rebuild or replacement.", "Frame and underbody rust: Rust concentrates at the rear frame rails, rear crossmember, rear lower and upper control arm mounts, spare tire carrier, and fuel tank straps. It also attacks brake hard lines at the rear axle and the fuel and EVAP lines. Rust is rarely terminal on CA/AZ trucks but can be severe on Northeast and Midwest trucks like the Maine example. Get underbody photos and tap-test the frame. Line and strap repairs run $300–$1,200; serious frame or crossmember work can exceed the truck's value.", "Timing belt service (5VZ-FE): The interval is about 90k miles, or roughly 8–9 years by age. Proper service includes the water pump, thermostat, idler and tensioner pulleys, hydraulic tensioner, and cam/crank seals. The engine is generally regarded as non-interference, but a snapped belt still strands the truck, and a weeping water pump or seals contaminate the new belt. Expect $900–$1,500 at a shop. The example's belt was done at 110.5k and the truck is now at 199k, so it is due. An engine-bay sticker alone is weak evidence; get the receipt.", "Lean codes P0171/P0174 and vacuum leaks: These usually come from a cracked intake air boot between the MAF and throttle body, brittle vacuum and PCV hoses, intake plenum gaskets, or a dirty or failing MAF. Repairs are often cheap ($50–$400), but in California any stored or pending code or incomplete readiness monitor means a failed smog check. The example's intermittent P0171 is typical.", 'Oil leaks: The common sources are valve cover gaskets and spark-plug tube seals, which leak oil into the plug wells and cause misfires and bad coil/wire boots. Others include the rear main seal, oil pan, and cam seals (best addressed during the timing belt job). Valve covers with tube seals cost $350–$700. A rear main seal is $800–$1,500 with transmission removal, usually deferred unless dripping.', 'Exhaust manifolds: Expect broken or rusted manifold studs, cracked manifolds, and leaking gaskets. A cold-start tick that quiets as the engine warms is the classic sign. Seized studs drive the cost up: $400–$1,200 per side depending on extraction. Downstream, aged catalytic converters can set P0420/P0430. In California, replacements must be CARB-approved (EO-numbered) converters, which run $1,000–$2,500+ installed.', 'A340E/A340F 4-speed automatic: It is robust if serviced. Watch for harsh or delayed shifts, flare on the 2–3 shift, slipping, or overdrive light flashing. Most trucks never had a fluid change, so do gentle drain-and-fills rather than a power flush on high-mileage units. Shift-quality issues can also come from failing shift solenoids, TPS, or an aging ECU. Aging Denso ECUs of this era are known to develop leaking capacitors, causing erratic idle or shifting.', '4WD system, transfer case, and lockers: Setup varies by year and trim. Part-time 4WD uses the ADD front axle disconnect, which is vacuum/VSV-operated; cracked vacuum lines cause failure to engage and a flashing 4WD l
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Timing belt service with water pump, thermostat, idler and tensioner pulleys, and cam/crank seals if undocumented or past 90k miles or about 9 years ($900–$1,500)', 'Inspect front lower ball joints and replace with genuine Toyota/OEM if age or brand is unknown, plus alignment ($400–$800)', 'Replace the radiator with OEM/Denso if original or unknown, as insurance against ATF contamination ($350–$700)', 'Fluid baseline: ATF drain-and-fill (repeat 2–3x), front and rear diff and transfer case gear oil, coolant, brake fluid, and power steering fluid ($300–$600)', 'Diagnose and fix any lean codes and vacuum leaks (intake air boot, PCV and vacuum hoses, MAF cleaning) so the truck is California smog-ready ($50–$400)', 'Spark plugs, plus valve cover gaskets and plug-tube seals if oil is found in
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Exhaust manifold gaskets and studs, or cracked manifold replacement ($400–$1,200 per side)', 'CV axles or boots and inner/outer tie rods ($200–$800)', 'Steering rack or power steering pump if seeping ($500–$1,600)', 'Rear axle seals and bearings, wheel cylinders, and drum service ($400–$900 per side)', 'Front calipers and rotors if sticking or pulsing ($400–$800)', 'Rear hatch window motor or regulator ($200–$600)', 'ADD/4WD vacuum lines and VSVs, or locker actuator service ($150–$900)', 'O2 sensors and possibly a CARB-approved catalytic converter if P0420/P0430 appear ($250–$2,500)', 'Rear coil springs and shocks if sagging, plus suspension bushings ($500–$1,200)', 'Motor and transmission mounts and remaining coolant/heater hoses ($300–$800)']
profiles.market_notes: Rust-free West Coast trucks with documented timing belt and radiator service command strong premiums over salt-state or modified trucks. The example (199k miles, lifted, rusty, from Maine) sold for $5,900, which is roughly the floor for a running 4x4 Limited. Clean stock trucks under about 150k miles with records commonly trade in the low-to-high teens, and exceptional low-mile examples go well above that. The 4x4 V6 is the core of the market. Factory rear E-locker trucks, 5-speed manual 4x4s (rare, SR5/base only), Sport Editions, and 1999–2002 facelift trucks are most sought after; the Limited's leather and full-time 4WD appeal to drivers. 2WD and 4-cylinder (2.7L 3RZ) trucks sell at a clear discount, as do lifted, rusty, or salvage-titled trucks.
profiles.catchup_notes: At 25-plus years old, most trucks need a rubber-and-fluids reset: coolant and heater hoses, vacuum lines, CV boots, suspension bushings, and engine and transmission mounts. Every driveline fluid should be changed, since many have never been touched. Budget $1,500–$3,000 beyond the purchase price for a typical example to reach a reliable, smog-legal baseline, more if the timing belt or ball joints are undocumented.

profiles.label: Toyota 4Runner (5th gen, N280, 2010-2024)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 5th-gen 4Runner is a durable, body-on-frame daily driver and weekend utility vehicle. It suits Highway 1, Big Sur, beach access roads, and occasional dirt, and it is chosen because the 1GR-FE V6 and A750 5-speed automatic routinely reach 250k+ miles when serviced. Configuration matters more than how hard the engine has worked. Whether the suspension is stock (X-REAS on Limited, KDSS on some off-road trims) and whether the truck has been lifted or modified matter most. Mods often hide wear on CV axles, ball joints, and alignment, and they can be irreversible (body-mount chops). Prefer stock or near-stock trucks with fluid records over 'built' rigs. Expect to pay a premium for that, and know it is worth it.
profiles.weak_points: ['Secondary air injection (SAI/AIR) system, where equipped: the AIR pump and the two switching valves fail from moisture and carbon. Codes are P2440/P2441/P2442/P2443/P2444/P2445, and the truck may go into limp mode on some years. It matters most for trucks that mostly make short trips. Dealer repair runs roughly $1,500-3,500 if both valves and the pump are needed. Scan for current, pending, and permanent codes, confirm readiness monitors are set, and ask for any SAI repair or warranty-extension paperwork. In California a freshly cleared ECU with incomplete monitors is a red flag before smog.', 'X-REAS cross-linked shocks (standard on Limited) and KDSS (optional on Trail/TRD Off-Road Premium trims): X-REAS shocks and their center control unit/lines leak and lose damping, typically from 80-120k miles. OEM replacement is about $1,500-2,500, and many owners delete it when lifting. KDSS hydraulic cylinders, accumulator, and lines can weep or be mis-bled after lifts. Correcting KDSS is $500-2,000+. Ask exactly which system the truck left the factory with and whether it is still intact. A deleted or bodged system changes ride, stability, and resale value.', 'Front suspension wear, worse on lifted trucks: upper control arm ball joints (non-serviceable on OEM UCAs), lower ball joints, tie-rod ends, sway-bar links, and CV axle boots wear out. Spacer lifts of 2-3 inches steepen CV angles and cause torn inner/outer boots, clicking, and vibration. A typical refresh costs $600-2,000 depending on UCAs, CVs, and alignment. Look for alignment printouts and the parts brand on any lift.', "Lift and modification quality: cheap spacer/coil lifts, mismatched shocks, and incorrect panhard/track bar geometry can cause death wobble, pulling, uneven tire wear, and bump steer. A 'body mount chop' (cutting the front body mount for tire clearance) is irreversible. It must be properly plated, welded, and rust-sealed. Unsealed cuts become rust starters near salt air. Get photos of the cut area and the name of the shop that did it.", 'Frame and underbody corrosion: the 5th gen is far better than 2nd/3rd-gen Tacomas, but rear frame sections, crossmembers, spare-tire carrier hardware, brake lines, and exhaust hangers corrode on salt-belt or coastal trucks. Carmel fog and beach parking make this relevant even for CA-registered trucks. Surface scale is normal. Flaking, swelling, or holes in the frame rails or crossmembers are not. Repair can run $1,000-5,000+, or the truck may be scrap-level.', "Drivetrain fluids marketed as 'lifetime': the A750E/F transmission and the transfer case are often never serviced. At 100k+ miles, harsh 2-3 shifts, flare, or torque-converter shudder suggest neglect. Drain-and-fill intervals of 60k are reasonable. A replacement transmission is rare but costs $4,000-6,000. Look for ATF, transfer case, and front/rear differential fluid receipts, especially on any truck that has towed or done water crossings (check diff breathers).", '4WD system function: part-time trucks (SR5/Trail/TRD) use an electrically actuated transfer case and front-axle engagement. A flashing 4LO or center-diff light, slow engagement, or grinding points to the actuator or ADD/front engagement. Repair is $300-1,500. Limited trucks are full-time 4WD with a Torsen center differential and a center lock. Verify the lock engages and releases. Rear electronic lockers (Trail/TRD Off-Road/Pro) seize from disuse. Test them on loose ground, since a seized locker costs $400-1,500 to repair.', 'Cooling system: 1GR-FE water pumps commonly weep at 100-150k miles. Look for pink crust at the weep hole behind the pulley. The thermostat and coolant hoses age out too. Preventive water pump and thermostat with Toyota SLLC costs about $700-1,200. Check for coolant service records. The first change is due at 100k, then every 50k.', 'Oil seepage: 1GR-FE valve cover gaskets and spark plug tube seals start seeping at 120-180k miles, and the timing cover sometimes seeps. These are usually m

Budget roughly $500-900.', 'Engine air filter and cabin filter. Replace any oiled aftermarket intake filter, or return to an OEM airbox if the MAF is contaminated.', 'Four-wheel alignment and tire inspection. profiles.market_notes: Trim and configuration drive price. TRD Pro sits at the top, followed by TRD Off-Road and Trail (manual-locker trucks), with KDSS adding a premium. Limited sells for comfort, full-time 4WD, and X-REAS, while SR5 is the value play. 2014+ facelift trucks bring more, and 2020+ trucks add Apple CarPlay and Toyota Safety Sense with a clear price step up. Premium colors and special editions command extra money, including Lunar Rock, Army Green, Lime Rush, Voodoo Blue, Cement, the Nightshade and Trail/Venture specials, and the 40th Anniversary. Documented stock trucks under ~100k miles with fluid records sell at a significant premium over lifted or 'built' rigs, and modifications rarely return their cost. Accident history, heavy aftermarket wheel/tire/lift packages, body-mount chops, and missing service records materially discount a truck. They should push a stock-preferring buyer to bid well below clean-comparable pricing.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 100k+ mile 5th-gen has had oil changes but none of the 'lifetime' drivetrain fluids, coolant, or spark plugs. Expect $1,000-2,000 to bring it current, plus a water pump or front-end refresh if it is near 120k miles. Lifted or modified trucks usually need additional CV, ball-joint, and alignment work. Budget extra if the original suspension system (X-REAS/KDSS) has been removed or compromised.

profiles.label: Toyota 4Runner N210 (4th Gen, 2003–2009)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the N210 is a 20-year-old body-on-frame family/adventure rig that should still be a low-drama daily driver: Highway 1 commuting, Big Sur trailheads, dump runs, and the occasional Sierra snow trip. The value proposition is Toyota durability plus real 4WD hardware, so the entire decision hinges on whether THIS truck has been kept out of salt and given honest fluid service — not on trim badges. A documented, unmodified, rust-free Western or Southern-dry example at 100–180k miles is a better buy than a low-mileage Rust Belt truck at any price. Automatic is the only transmission offered and is completely normal here.
profiles.weak_points: 1) FRAME AND UNDERBODY RUST is the single generation-defining risk. Midwest/Northeast trucks rot at the rear frame rails above the axle, the rear spring/shackle hangers, the crossmember behind the transfer case, and the body mounts. Toyota's frame rust campaigns largely covered Tacoma/Tundra/Sequoia, not the 4Runner, so there is no warranty backstop. Fresh black undercoating or 'fresh paint' on the underside of an auction truck from a salt state is a red flag, not a feature — it hides scale. A rotten frame is a walk-away, not a repair. 2) 'PINK MILKSHAKE' — on 2003–2005 (and some 2006) trucks the transmission cooler lives inside the radiator; when the internal barrier fails, coolant enters the ATF and destroys the A750F 5-speed. Symptoms: pink/strawberry-milkshake ATF on the dipstick, low coolant, harsh or slipping shifts. Prevention is a radiator replacement with an external cooler ($600–1,000); the cure after contamination is a transmission ($3,500–5,500 installed). Look for a radiator replacement receipt or verify clean red ATF and clean coolant. 3) REAR AIR SUSPENSION / X-REAS. Limited models (and some V8s) used a rear height-control air system whose bags, compressor and height sensors fail; Sport Edition used X-REAS cross-linked dampers with a center transfer valve. Both are expensive ($1,200–2,500 for OEM parts) and are commonly 'fixed' by converting to conventional coilovers/shocks — a conversion is acceptable but must be documented. Sagging rear, compressor running constantly, or a bouncy/uneven ride are tells. 4) LOWER BALL JOINTS. 2003–2007 front lower ball joints are a known wear/failure item, especially with lifts or aftermarket parts; a failure drops a corner. Check for grease boot tears, clunks over bumps, and insist on Toyota/OEM-quality parts in any receipt ($400–900/side installed). 5) DASHBOARD CRACKING/STICKINESS. Very common on N210 in sun-belt cars; Toyota's extended coverage has expired. Full dash replacement runs $1,200–2,500; a cap is $250–500. Cosmetic but it moves price. 6) 1GR-FE V6 OIL SEEPAGE at the cam towers, timing cover, and front main. A weep is typical by 150k; an actual reseal means pulling the timing cover, $2,000–4,000. Look for oil film on the front of the block and drips on the skid plate. Head gaskets are NOT a chronic 1GR failure — if coolant loss is present, suspect radiator/heater lines first, but a block test is cheap insurance on any truck with unexplained coolant use. 7) 2UZ-FE V8 TIMING BELT + water pump every 90k miles / ~9 years, $900–1,600. It's a non-interference engine so a break usually won't bend valves, but a dead water pump will cook it. No belt receipt on a V8 = assume you're buying one. 8) ABS/VSC BRAKE ACTUATOR. The ABS pump/actuator assembly fails with ABS+VSC+TRAC lights and sometimes a buzzing pump; new OEM assemblies run $1,500–2,500, rebuilt units $500–900. Verify all warning lamps extinguish after start. 9) POWER REAR WINDOW (tailgate glass). The regulator/motor and its wiring harness in the hatch fail, and a leaking tailgate seal rots the lower tailgate and the rear sill from the inside. Cycle the glass up and down from both the key and the dash switch; pull the cargo mat and look for standing water. 10) REAR HATCH/QUARTER AND WHEEL-ARCH ROT even on otherwise clean trucks — check behind the rear wheels, the rocker pinch welds, and under the rear bumper cover. 11) FRONT DIFFERENTIAL ACTUATOR (ADD) on part-time 4WD trucks leaks and sticks; full-time 4WD/locking-center-diff trucks use a Torsen center diff whose locker actuator can also fail. Any 4WD system must be range-shifted 2WD-4HI-4LO and, if equipped, center-diff-locked on a test drive. 12) EXHAUST/SECONDARY ITEMS OF AGE: cracked exhaust manifold studs on high-mile V6s, tired original struts (fronts commonly leak by 120k, $800–1,400 for a full set installed), steering rack and pump seeps, brittle radiator/heater hoses, and a heater blower resistor/AC amplifier that kills fan speeds. 13) HIGH-MILE V6 WATER PU
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service if records are thin: engine oil, ATF drain-and-fill (Toyota WS, no aggressive flush), front/rear diff and transfer case gear oil, coolant (Toyota SLLC), brake fluid. Replace the radiator with an external trans cooler on any 2003–2006 without a radiator receipt. Four tires if date codes are over 6 years old regardless of tread, plus an alignment. New wiper blades, cabin/engine air filters, and likely a battery. Expect a rear tailgate glass seal or regulator fix, a dash cap or trim tidy, and correcting any minor oil/coolant seep. Budget $1,500–3,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Struts/shocks all around if not recently done ($800–1,400), lower ball joints and possibly upper control arm bushings, front brake pads/rotors, serpentine belt and idler/tensioner, water pump and thermostat on a V6 over 130k, timing belt/water pump on any V8 without documentation ($900–1,600), front cam-tower or timing-cover seepage monitoring, wheel bearings/hub if there's a growl, and exhaust hardware. If it's a Limited or Sport with air suspension or X-REAS still fitted, budget for a documented conventional conversion ($1,000–1,800). $2,000–4,000 typical.
profiles.market_notes: Rust-free provenance is worth more than mileage on this generation — a 160k California/Arizona truck with clean frame photos regularly beats a 65k Illinois truck. V6 (1GR-FE) commands a premium over the V8 for most buyers because of the timing chain and better fuel economy, though V8 fans like the smoothness; the V8/Limited's rear air suspension is a price drag unless converted. Desirable spec: 4x4 with the locking center differential (full-time 4WD), rear locker on Trail/Sport trucks, cloth over cracked leather, sunroof, and no third-row (rare and space-eating anyway). Unmodified, one/two-owner cars with a real service file and 2009 facelift trucks sit at the top; lifted, big-tire, light-bar builds and any pink-fluid transmission history sit at the bottom.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any N210 as needing a full 20-year fluid and rubber reset: all gear oils, ATF drain-and-fill with Toyota WS, coolant, brake fluid, hoses, belt, and tires by date code rather than tread. Even a 64k-mile example will have hardened bushings, aged struts, dried tailgate/door seals, and an original radiator that is living on borrowed time. Budget roughly $2,000–3,500 in the first year for catch-up work on an otherwise sound, rust-free truck.

profiles.label: Toyota Altezza / Lexus IS (XE10)
profiles.framing: This is a cheap, rear-drive, six-cylinder manual sedan bought to be driven on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not stored. The JDM AS200 with the J160 six-speed and an LSD is the interesting spec: 158hp of 1G-FE BEAMS inline-six that needs revs, in a light, well-balanced chassis with double-wishbone rear suspension. Because it is a fresh direct import with a Japanese service history that mostly does not translate, the real questions are body/underbody corrosion from Japanese winters, whether the timing belt has actually been done in the last decade, whether the J160 and clutch are healthy, and whether it can be legally titled and registered in California. Parts for JDM-only pieces (bumpers, lenses, RHD-specific trim, 1G-FE BEAMS ancillaries) are a mail-order-from-Japan exercise, so a car that is already complete and undamaged is worth far more than the bid gap suggests.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt on the 1G-FE BEAMS: rubber belt with hydraulic tensioner, nominal 100k km interval and an age limit of roughly 7-10 years regardless of distance. The sticker on this car claims service at 76k km — that is ~107k km and likely 15+ years ago. It is a non-interference-ish design in theory but the VVT-i cam gear and tensioner are the expensive parts; budget $900-1,500 for belt, tensioner, idlers, water pump, cam and crank seals, and the drive belts. Treat any car without a dated receipt as needing the job immediately. 2) VVT-i intake cam actuator: cold-start rattle/diesel-like clatter for 1-3 seconds is the classic symptom; also oil-fed, so it tolerates neglected oil poorly. Actuator ~$350-700 plus labor, usually bundled with the timing belt job. 3) Oil consumption and rear main / valve cover / cam-plug leaks: 1G-FE BEAMS at 150k+ km often uses 0.5-1qt per 1,000-1,500 miles via valve stem seals and PCV. Check the PCV valve and look for oil misting at the back of the head and the oil pan rail. Valve cover gasket $250-450; rear main with trans out $900-1,400. 4) J160 six-speed: the known weak spots are 2nd (and sometimes 3rd) synchro balk on fast cold shifts, input shaft/front bearing whine in neutral with clutch out, and a notchy 5th-6th shift when the oil is old. Toyota specified a specific 75W-90 GL-4; wrong fluid accelerates synchro wear. Rebuild or used-unit swap $1,800-3,500; a fluid change is the cheap first move. 5) Clutch hydraulics and clutch: master and slave cylinders leak with age (pedal goes soft/low engagement point creeps down), $200-450 for both. Clutch and rear main together $1,300-2,000 since the box is already out. 6) Rust from Japanese road salt: inspect rear wheel arch lips, the sills below the jacking points, the rear subframe and its mounting cradle, rear shock towers, the spare wheel well, the fuel and brake hard lines over the rear axle, and the exhaust hangers. Northern-Japan auction cars can be badly scaled underneath even with flawless paint. Any structural rear subframe or floor rot makes the car a parts donor at this price level. 7) Suspension bushings and rear geometry: at 180k km the rear upper/lower arm bushings, rear subframe bushings, front lower control arm bushings and sway bar links are typically done, producing clunks over expansion joints and a wandering rear under braking. Full bushing/shock refresh $1,600-2,800 with alignment; many components are shared with US IS300 so parts are obtainable. 8) Chronograph gauge cluster: dimming/dead cluster illumination, sticking or lazy needles, and dead LCD odometer segments are common; clusters are km-only and 180 km/h, and Japanese repair/refurb or a swap is the fix ($200-600). Verify the odometer against the auction sheet — Japanese odometer rollback exists though the Car VX/auction sheet usually catches it. 9) Climate control blend-door and servo actuators: clicking behind the dash, one-temperature-only output, and dead auto mode are typical; actuators $120-300 each plus dash disassembly. Also check the A/C — R134a systems of this age commonly need a compressor, drier and expansion valve, $900-1,600. 10) Ignition and sensors: coil-on-plug packs, crank/cam position sensors, knock sensor and the MAF drift with age and cause rough idle, hunting idle, or a P0335/P0325 code. An IACV/throttle body clean fixes most idle hunting; individual sensors $100-300 each. 11) Cooling system: original plastic-tank radiator, thermostat housing and the small hoses under the intake fail with age; a 25-year-old radiator on a tightly packaged inline-six should just be replaced ($400-700 with hoses and coolant). 12) Sunroof drains and interior water: clogged drains rot the front footwell carpet and short the under-carpet harness; check for damp padding and rust bubbles under the door sills. Power-folding mirror motors also fail ($150-300 per side). 13) JDM-specific legal and hardware items: 180 km/h speedometer and km odometer, JDM headlight beam pattern aimed
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full timing belt service with water pump, tensioner, idlers and front seals unless a dated receipt exists; complete fluid service (engine oil, J160 gear oil with correct GL-4 75W-90, LSD/diff oil, brake fluid, coolant); replace the cracked left-rear taillight lens and reseal to stop trunk water intrusion; new plugs, PCV valve, air filter and a throttle body/IACV clean; inspect and likely replace clutch master and slave cylinders; four tires if the Potenzas are date-coded older than ~6 years regardless of tread; headlight aim correction or US-pattern/left-traffic conversion for legality and for unlit Carmel Valley roads; CA DMV VIN verification plus BAR referee appointment and whatever it demands; wheel alignment; deal with any surface rust with a wash-down and underbody treatment before it
profiles.repairs_12mo: Radiator, hoses and thermostat; front and rear suspension bushings, shocks and sway bar links with alignment; clutch and rear main seal if the pedal or oil leak dictates; A/C service or compressor/drier if it blows warm; valve cover gasket and cam plug reseal; blend-door actuator(s) and cluster illumination repair; front lower ball joints and outer tie rods; exhaust hangers, rear brake calipers or rebuild kits if the rears are seized from sitting; possible J160 2nd-gear synchro work if it balks when hot; sorting or removal of the aftermarket Blaupunkt head unit wiring.
profiles.market_notes: XE10 values are driven by drivetrain and rust, not cosmetics: RS200 (3S-GE BEAMS, 210hp, six-speed, Torsen) commands a clear premium over AS200, and AS200 manual over AS200 automatic; the AS300/IS300 2JZ-GE cars sit in their own market. Fresh direct imports with a clean auction sheet, a documented timing belt, and a clean rust-free underbody sell well above generic $3-6k import money, while salt-belt Japanese cars with arch or subframe rot are effectively parts cars. Low km, unmodified interiors, working chronograph clusters, factory wheels and intact JDM lenses/bumpers add real dollars; big aftermarket wheels, non-original head units and cut-in exhausts subtract. Titling status matters — a car already on a clean US state title with import paperwork in hand is worth meaningfully more than one still in customs limbo, and a California buyer should discount for referee/registration risk.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 25-year-old Japanese-market car has had almost no preventive maintenance since its last shaken and that every rubber and plastic part is original: belts, hoses, radiator, bushings, motor/trans mounts, brake and clutch hydraulics, and all fluids. Budget a deliberate $3,000-4,500 catch-up program in the first year on top of the purchase price, plus time and shipping for JDM-only parts sourced from Japan.

profiles.label: Toyota FJ Cruiser (1st gen, 2007–2014)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel-based buyer, the FJ Cruiser is a durable body-on-frame 4x4 that is relatively simple to maintain. It suits Highway 1, Big Sur fire roads, and Sierra trips, and it should last for years with ordinary maintenance. It is not a refined daily driver: visibility is poor, real-world economy is about 15–18 mpg, and the rear doors are awkward. The 1GR-FE V6 and the drivetrain are very robust when fluids have been serviced. The real risks are underbody corrosion, cracking of the inner fender and firewall structure, off-road abuse hidden under 'stock-looking' parts, and California smog compliance for out-of-state cars. Prioritize a clean frame, a well-documented maintenance history, and an unmodified or factory-like suspension over low mileage alone.
profiles.weak_points: ['Frame and underbody corrosion: The FJ frame (shared with the Prado 120) is not part of the Tacoma frame-rot campaign, but salt-state and coastal cars still rust. Typical spots are the rear crossmember, spring and shock perches, rear frame rails above the axle, body mounts, the fuel-tank straps, and the spare/hitch area. Surface rust is normal on 15-plus-year-old trucks. Flaking, scaling, or perforation is not. Remediation of moderate rust runs $1,000–3,000 for wire-wheeling, treatment, and replacing straps and brackets. A perforated or heavily scaled frame is effectively a walk-away, since there is no Toyota buyback. Ask for dated underbody photos taken on a lift, and be suspicious of fresh undercoating that hides the metal.', 'Inner fender and firewall cracking: Especially on 2007–2009 trucks and those used off-road, the driver-side inner fender apron and firewall near the brake master cylinder and booster mount can crack. Symptoms include a soft or flexing brake pedal, or visible cracks in the sheet metal and seam sealer around the master cylinder, upper fender mounts, and hood-hinge area. A reinforcement brace (Toyota or aftermarket) is the common fix. Catching it early with a brace costs about $200–600. Welding a crack that has propagated plus re-sealing costs $800–2,000 or more. Ask for close-up photos of both inner fenders and the firewall with the battery and engine cover area visible, and for documentation of any brace installation.', '1GR-FE water pump: Weeping or failure is common at 80k–130k miles. Look for pink or crusty coolant residue behind the timing cover and pulley, or a slow coolant drop. The pump sits behind the timing cover area and is driven by the serpentine belt, so replacement with a thermostat and belt runs $600–1,100. Receipts for a pump replacement (with a date and mileage) remove one of the most likely near-term repairs.', '1GR-FE timing chain cover and valve cover leaks: Oil seepage at the timing cover seam or valve cover gaskets appears with age. Valve cover gaskets cost $300–700. A full timing cover reseal is labor-intensive at about $1,800–3,000. Distinguish a light film from active dripping onto the skid plate. A freshly degreased engine bay or skid plate on a high-mileage truck deserves a closer look.', '1GR-FE head gasket: Failure is low-frequency on this generation. It usually follows an overheat event, or shows as an external coolant seep at the rear of the cylinder heads. Repair costs $3,000–4,500. Look for unexplained coolant loss, bubbles in the overflow tank, or a sweet smell. Cooling system service records, with coolant changes at about 100k miles and then every 50k, are the best evidence of a healthy engine.', 'Secondary air injection (AI) pump and switching valve, 2010–2014 dual VVT-i trucks only: This is a known failure point that triggers P2440, P2441, P2442, or P2444 codes and limp mode or a failed smog test. Repair costs $1,200–3,000 at a dealer. Toyota issued an extended warranty on some of these, but most coverage has now expired. Get an OBD-II scan showing no stored or pending AI codes and confirm whether the AI pump was replaced under warranty.', '6-speed manual (RA61F) and clutch: The gearbox is robust, but clutch life varies widely with off-road and towing use, typically 80k–150k miles. Watch for slipping in higher gears under load, a high engagement point, throwout bearing whine that disappears when the pedal is pressed, and clutch hydraulic weeping. A clutch, flywheel, and hydraulics job runs $1,500–2,800. Manual cars use full-time 4WD with a lockable Torsen center differential. profiles.market_notes: Unmodified, rust-free trucks with documented service command a strong premium, because so many FJs were lifted, re-geared, or wheeled hard. A stock example from a West Coast or southern state is the most desirable and easiest to register. 2010–2014 trucks with the dual VVT-i 1GR (260 hp) and the final 2014 model year usually bring more, as do Trail Teams editions and popular colors such as Voodoo Blue, Iceberg, Army Green, and Cement. The 6-speed manual with full-time 4WD and the factory rear locker is a meaningful premium over the 5-speed automatic. Mileage under 100k sells for a premium, but a well-documented truck at 150k–200k is still a strong buy. Rust, damage history, and a non-CARB exhaust or emissions setup are the biggest price reducers for a California buyer.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 15-plus-year-old FJ needs a full driveline fluid baseline (differentials, transfer case, transmission), a cooling system refresh including the water pump if it has not been done, aged tires, worn shocks and front-end components, and basic rust treatment underneath. Budget about $1,500–3,500 in catch-up work beyond the purchase price for a truck with average records. Coastal Carmel ownership makes ongoing underbody rinsing and rust prevention worthwhile.

profiles.label: Toyota GR86 (ZN8, 2nd gen, 2022+)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, the ZN8 GR86 is a cheap-to-run, rear-drive, manual-first driver's car. It suits Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laguna Seca Road, and it doubles as a reasonable daily. Laguna Seca is next door, so many examples have done track days or HPDEs, and that history matters more than mileage. The things that decide a good example are an untouched ECU, no evidence of sustained high-G track abuse or underbody impacts, a clean (ideally reversible-only) modification list, and remaining Toyota factory warranty coverage.
profiles.weak_points: 1) FA24D rod-bearing and oil-starvation failures. A cluster of 2022–2023 cars, overwhelmingly tracked, spun bearings after sustained high-G cornering such as long sweepers and long track sessions. Low or overfilled oil, track tires and extended sessions raise the risk. Out-of-warranty engine replacement runs roughly $9,000–$15,000. Ask for track history, oil-change intervals (ideally 5,000 mi or less, plus a post-track change), any oil-analysis reports, and whether a baffled pan or oil cooler was fitted. Note that a fitted cooler or pan also tells you the car was driven hard. 2) ECU reflashes, typically ECUTek or similar. Flex-fuel, rev-hang or throttle maps are extremely common, and a dealer can usually detect them. A reflash can jeopardize powertrain warranty claims even after the car is flashed back, so get proof of a stock calibration. 3) Clutch and clutch delay valve (CDV). Owners complain of an inconsistent engagement point, chatter or judder, and an odd over-center or assist-spring feel. CDV removal and clutch-spring changes are common, mild modifications. A worn clutch from launches or track use costs about $1,800–$2,800 to replace. Check the engagement height and look for slip in 4th–5th at low rpm under full throttle. 4) 6-speed manual shift quality. Cold notchiness into 1st–2nd is normal. Grinding into 2nd or 3rd on quick shifts was reported on some cars. A fluid change helps somewhat ($200–$350), but persistent grinding on a warm car points to synchro wear, which is a warranty or rebuild item. 5) Torsen LSD and rear diff. Look for diff whine, clunk on take-up or wet seals, especially on tracked cars. A diff fluid service is about $120–$250. 6) Underbody and front-end contact. The low front lip, undertray, mid-pipe and the area near the rear diff scrape easily on driveways and speed bumps. Harder strikes can crack bumper mounting tabs, misalign headlights, and bend the undertray or exhaust hangers. Bumper repair or replacement plus paint is about $1,200–$2,500. Get the car on a lift and photograph everything. 7) Soft, chip-prone paint on the nose, hood and rear quarters. PPF is common. Bubbling or lifting film costs $300–$1,500 to correct, and film can hide repaint or fitment issues, so read the paint with a meter where possible. 8) Interior rattles and creaks. Common sources are the hatch and trunk area, the rear deck, B-pillar trim, the seatbelt buckle against the trim, and dash creaks in cold weather. These are mostly annoyances that can be fixed under warranty or with felt tape and butyl. 9) Infotainment. Early software had freezes, reboots, CarPlay dropouts and backup-camera lag. Confirm the latest dealer software and check function. Aftermarket wireless-CarPlay dongles are harmless but should be noted. 10) Tires and brakes age fast on performance spec cars. Premium and Performance Package cars use Michelin Pilot Sport 4 215/40R18, which costs about $1,000–$1,400 a set. Base cars use 215/45R17. Brake fluid should be changed after any track use. Look for heat-tinted rotors, uneven pad wear and glazing on Brembo-equipped cars. 11) Accident and track-car prevalence. These are frequently bought as track or autocross builds. Look for coilovers, aftermarket camber bolts, tow hooks, seat harness bars, and tire wear on the outer shoulders. Check alignment specs against factory values. Uneven panel gaps or replaced bolts on the radiator support suggest a front-end hit. 12) Normal noises that are not faults. The FA24 has D-4S port and direct injection, so heavy carbon buildup is less of a concern than on DI-only engines. Injector tick and boxer clatter at cold start are also normal. Don't mistake these for valvetrain failure, but any knock that persists warm is a stop sign.

profiles.market_notes: Manual cars carry a clear premium over the 6AT. Premium trim beats Base, and for 2026-era cars the Performance Package (Brembo brakes and SACHS dampers) adds value. Limited editions (Special Edition, Hakone, Trueno, Yuzu) and colors like Trueno Blue or Solar Shift bring modest premiums, while plain silver or black cars and automatics trade lower. Documented no-track history, a stock ECU, remaining factory warranty, and dealer or receipted oil changes move price more than small mileage differences. Tracked, tuned or heavily modified cars trade at meaningful discounts, and the Subaru BRZ twin is a direct price ceiling to cross-shop.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most ZN8s are young, so catch-up work is mainly fluids and consumables: brake fluid at about 3 years or after any track day, MT and diff fluid on hard-driven cars, and tires that age out before they wear out on low-mileage examples. Low-mileage cars that sat should also get a 12V battery test and a check for flat-spotted tires.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 100 Series (J100, US 1998–2007)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, a 100 Series is a durable, comfortable full-time-4WD wagon for Highway 1, Big Sur fire roads, beach access, and long hauls. Its value depends on whether the overdue big-ticket items are already done, not on mileage alone. The 2UZ-FE V8 and the transmissions routinely pass 300k miles. The money goes into timing-belt service, front suspension and steering, the starter buried in the valley, brakes, and age-related leaks. Documented, unlifted, rust-free examples are worth paying up for, because a neglected one can absorb $5–10k in catch-up quickly.
profiles.weak_points: ["Timing belt and water pump: due every 90k miles or 9 years. The service should include the water pump, idler pulleys, tensioner, and usually cam/crank seals and thermostat. Budget $1,000–1,900 at an independent shop. Treat the later VVT-i 2UZ-FE (2006–07 is rated 275 hp) as interference. Require a dated receipt showing mileage and the parts list; a 'belt done' claim without paper means doing it again.", 'Starter and knock sensors: both sit under the intake manifold in the engine valley. Expect a click-no-crank as starter contacts wear (often 150–250k miles), or P0325/P0330 knock-sensor codes from failed sensors or chafed sub-harness. Labor-heavy job at $1,200–2,000. Smart owners replace both together with intake gaskets and the knock-sensor sub-harness; look for that combined receipt.', 'Steering rack: leaks at the boot seals and pinion are very common past 150k. Signs are a damp rack and boots, low PS fluid, whine, and wander. An OEM or reman rack with alignment runs $1,500–2,800. Inner/outer tie rods and the PS pressure line also weep.', 'Front lower ball joints: original and some aftermarket joints can separate at high mileage, which is a wheel-collapse risk. Look for documented replacement with OEM (Toyota/Sankei 555 class) parts around 150–200k. Upper control arms and ball joints, lower control arm bushings, and the rear lateral rod/trailing arm bushings also wear. Front-end refresh costs $800–2,500 depending on scope.', 'Brakes: pre-2003 trucks are known for warped front rotors and pedal pulsation; calipers can stick on any year. 2003–2007 models use a hydraulic brake booster with an electric pump and accumulator. Pump or accumulator failure brings ABS/VSC/TRAC/brake warnings, a long-running buzz, or a hard pedal, and costs $1,500–3,500. Ask how recently brake fluid was flushed.', "Secondary air injection system (late VVT-i trucks): the air pumps and switching/air valves fail. This sets P2440/P2442/P2444-family codes and causes a California smog failure. Parts and labor run $1,000–3,000. A recent 'air valve replaced' entry is a good sign; confirm no pending codes.", 'Exhaust manifolds: cracked manifolds and broken or leaking studs cause a cold-start tick that fades as it warms. Repair is $800–2,500 depending on broken-stud extraction. Rusty studs are worse on salt-belt trucks.', 'Cooling system: the plastic-tank radiator cracks or weeps at the seams with age, at $600–1,100 installed. The rear heater hoses run under the body to the rear HVAC unit; they rot, leak coolant, and can dump it suddenly. Repair or bypass costs $200–600. Check the coolant level and look for pink crust on the hoses and frame.', 'Oil leaks: valve cover gaskets and spark plug tube seals, cam/crank seals (often missed at belt time), and the oil cooler or oil filter housing area are common. Dripping onto the exhaust smells. Plugs and coils are a $400–900 job with valve covers.', 'Rust: inspect the frame rails at the rear crossmember and spring perches, the spare-tire area, rear quarter panels and wheel arches, the liftgate lower edge, and the rocker and running-board mounts. Out-of-salt-belt examples (South, Southwest, West) are worth a premium. Coastal Carmel air will attack exposed brake lines and fasteners over time. Deep frame scale or perforation is usually walk-away.', 'Driveline: front CV boots tear and grease the suspension, at $250–700 per axle. Driveshaft U-joints and slip yokes need periodic greasing or else clunk. Front axle seals, front/rear differential seals, and the transfer-case output seals weep. Check that the center diff lock engages and releases, with the light going on and off. The A343F 4-speed (1998–02) and A750F 5-speed (2003–07) are robust, but a burnt-fluid or never-serviced history matters.', "Suspension sag and shocks: original front torsion bars settle, rear coils sag especially with a third row and roof load, and shocks fade. Expect a nose-down or rear-sag stance and a floaty ride. A quality OEM-height refresh costs $80

profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 15–25-year-old 100 Series without strong records needs a timing belt, a full fluid baseline, and front-end and steering attention. Expect $3,000–7,000 across the first year. Valley starter/knock-sensor work, the radiator and rear heater hoses, and age-related seals and bushings make up most of the rest.
