profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 200-Series (URJ200, 5.7L 3UR-FE)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 200-series is a lifetime-grade family/adventure truck: full-time 4WD, locking center diff, CRAWL control, 8,100 lb tow rating, and a 3UR-FE V8 that routinely sees 300k miles with fluids and attention. It is not a value play — it is a buy-once vehicle where the purchase price is often the smallest number in the first three years, so documented maintenance and a clean, unbypassed emissions system matter more than mileage. The 2008-2011 cars (pre-facelift, DVD nav, no Entune) are the cheap entry point but carry the generation's two most expensive known faults. In California, the smog transfer requirement makes emissions-system honesty a purchase gate, not a nice-to-have.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Secondary air injection system (2008-2011 especially): the AIS pumps, switching valves and air-injection driver fail from moisture ingestion, throwing P2440/P2442/P0418/P1441-family codes and a CEL that appears on cold starts. Toyota's ZE4 warranty enhancement (10yr/150k) has expired on a 2008. Dealer repair with both pumps and valves runs $3,000-4,500; independent with quality aftermarket parts $1,800-3,000. Bypass/delete kits and ECU tricks will fail a California smog inspection or leave incomplete readiness monitors — ask specifically whether the system is intact. 2) Cam tower / timing cover oil leaks on the 3UR-FE: Toyota reseals the cam towers under TSB; symptoms are oil weeping down the rear of the heads, oil in the valley, and drips onto the bellhousing/exhaust (burnt oil smell). Because the intake, timing cover and often the heads come off, expect $3,500-6,500. Very common at 120k-200k. 3) Starter motor lives under the intake manifold; when it fails (typically 150k-220k) it is a 6-10 hour job, $1,200-2,000. Smart owners do it preemptively with the water pump or air-pump work — look for that receipt. 4) Water pump and thermostat: whining/weeping around 100k-150k, $900-1,400 done properly with coolant and belt. 5) KDSS (Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System): hydraulic sway-bar system with cylinders and a valve body on the driver's frame rail. Look for oil film on the cylinders/lines and for the truck sitting cocked or with one front corner high; seized valves or a leaking accumulator is $1,200-2,500 and must be bled correctly. 6) Front suspension wear: upper control arm ball joints (integral, arm replaced, ~$500-800/side), lower ball joints, sway bar end links and bushings, and leaking front shocks/struts — the listed 'small leak from the front left shock' is textbook and means a pair at minimum ($600-1,400 for quality OE-spec or Bilstein/OME). 7) Brakes: the 200 is 5,800 lbs and eats pads and rotors; full four-corner pads and rotors $800-1,400. The ABS/VSC brake actuator (skid-control ECU/pump) is a known high-cost failure — a flashing VSC/ABS/brake light cluster can mean $2,000-3,500. 8) Drivetrain fluids: Toyota calls the AB60F six-speed 'lifetime' WS fluid; at 185k with no records assume a drain-and-fill service ($250-400) and budget for the possibility of a tired torque converter. Transfer case, front and rear diffs should be on a 30k cycle — no records means do all three now ($300-450). 9) Exhaust manifold/header cracks and broken manifold studs cause a cold-start tick and can mimic an air-injection code; repair $800-2,000. 10) Radiator end tanks and the intercooler-free cooling stack: plastic tank seepage and a clogged radiator around 150k+, $700-1,100. 11) Drive shaft: non-greaseable U-joints and center support bearings produce a driveline shudder at 40-60 mph; replacement shaft or rebuild $500-1,200. 12) Electronics of the 2008-2011 era: DVD-based navigation and Bluetooth are obsolete, rear-seat entertainment screens fail, the rear hatch struts sag, and the rear A/C evaporator can leak — none are fatal, but a head-unit swap is $500-1,500. 13) Frame and body rust: California cars are usually fine, but many 200s migrate from the Rockies/Midwest — inspect frame rails behind the rear wheels, the KDSS lines, brake lines and the rear crossmember. 14) Modification risk: lifted, re-geared, big-tire or 'delete' trucks are common in this platform; a lift without an OEM-correct KDSS-compatible setup causes driveline vibration and premature CV/ball joint wear.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Front shocks/struts in pairs and sway bar end links and bushings ($900-1,800 for the front end done properly); brake pads and likely rotors all around ($800-1,400); full fluid catch-up — engine oil, transmission drain-and-fill, transfer case, front and rear differentials, brake fluid flush, coolant if not documented ($700-1,100); new tires if the set is over 6 years old or mismatched ($1,200-1,700 in 285/60R18); serpentine belt, PCV valve, engine and cabin air filters, and iridium plugs if not done by 120k ($500-900 with plugs); alignment after suspension work ($150-250). If any CEL or incomplete readiness monitor exists, resolving it to pass California smog before or immediately after purchase.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump/thermostat if not documented ($900-1,400); preemptive starter replacement done concurrently with any intake-off work ($1,200-2,000 standalone, far less as an add-on); secondary air injection pumps and valves if the system is original and untouched at this age ($1,800-3,500); upper control arms/ball joints ($1,000-1,600 the pair); cam tower reseal if any weep is developing ($3,500-6,500); radiator ($700-1,100); rear hatch struts, cabin blower resistor, and assorted 15-year-old rubber — bushings, hoses, hatch and door seals ($400-900); driveline center support bearing or U-joints if a shudder appears ($500-1,200).
profiles.market_notes: There is one US trim, so price moves on mileage bands, records, rust history, and whether the air-injection and cam-tower jobs are already done with receipts — a documented sub-150k California truck with those two items addressed commands a real premium over an undocumented 185k example. 2008-2011 cars are the value tier; the 2013+ facelift and especially 2016+ (8-speed, Safety Sense, Entune) step up several thousand dollars. Neutral colors with tan or grey leather and unmolested stock suspension sell fastest to this buyer type; big lifts, aftermarket bumpers and light bars narrow the buyer pool and add hidden wear. At 185k a clean, documented example in Northern California realistically trades in the low-to-mid $20s, so anything near $26k needs receipts, not just a seller's summary of a PPI.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 15-year-old, 185k-mile 200-series should be assumed to need a full fluid reset (transmission, transfer case, both diffs, coolant, brake fluid), a front-end refresh of shocks, links and bushings, and new tires — roughly $3,000-4,500 before touching the two headline jobs. The secondary air injection system and the cam tower reseal are the budget-defining unknowns: if neither has receipts, plan for one or both within two years. Everything else on this truck is ordinary Toyota wear that rewards preemptive work, especially bundling the starter with any intake-off service.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 60 Series (FJ62, US 1988–1990)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the FJ62 is a characterful, slow, mechanically simple vintage SUV to drive on Highway 1, run to Big Sur, and use for light trail work. It is not a commuter appliance. The value lives in a rust-controlled body, a healthy original 3F-E/A440F drivetrain that passes California smog in factory configuration, and a front axle that has been properly serviced. In Carmel, smog legality is the gating issue. A 1990 needs a biennial smog check, and any engine swap must carry a BAR Referee label to be registerable. An original, documented truck is therefore worth far more to this buyer than a modified one.
profiles.weak_points: ['Rust is the number-one value killer. The usual areas are the rear quarter panels behind the rear wheels, the lower tailgate and its seams, rocker panels, rear floor pans under the cargo area and rear seat, the roof drip rails and gutters, and the lower windshield frame and cowl, where water sits under the gasket. Frames are usually sound but should be checked at the rear crossmember and spring hangers. Proper bodywork runs $3,000–$15,000+, and coastal salt air will accelerate anything already started. Get clear underbody, rocker and windshield-corner photos, and probe with a pick at inspection.', 'Front axle closed knuckles leak grease and gear oil past worn wiper seals, inner axle seals and trunnion bearings. The symptoms are a greasy inner wheel and tire, a wet knuckle ball, and a death-wobble-prone feel once the trunnion preload is gone. Birfield CV joints click on full lock when worn. A full knuckle rebuild with seals, trunnion bearings, wheel bearings and preload set runs $1,200–$2,500. Birfields add $400–$900 per side. Ask for a dated rebuild invoice.', '3F-E exhaust manifold leaks and broken studs are near-universal. You get a ticking at cold start that fades as it warms, plus soot at the head junction. The cast manifold and the intake/exhaust combo gasket warp, and the studs snap on removal. Expect $600–$1,500 depending on how many studs need extraction. Manifold cracks can also cause smog failures and false O2 readings.', '3F-E overheating and head gasket failure. The cooling system (radiator, fan clutch, water pump, thermostat, aged hoses) is marginal when neglected, and overheating leads to a blown head gasket or warped head. Watch for milky oil, bubbles in the radiator, coolant loss, and a temperature needle above center on hills or with the A/C on. A head gasket job is $2,000–$3,500, and a full engine rebuild is $6,000–$10,000. Look for radiator replacement receipts and a compression or leak-down test.', '3F-E has adjustable solid valve lash that is often neglected. Loud tapping and poor idle point to lash out of spec, and burnt exhaust valves show up on high-mileage engines. A valve adjustment with a cover gasket is about $200–$400. Low compression on one cylinder means a head job.', "The 3F-E EFI and emissions system is aging. Brittle vacuum hoses, a failing cold-start injector or thermo-time switch, a worn airflow meter, and a sticky EGR valve or modulator cause rough idle, hard hot starts, hesitation and smog failures. A clogged or tampered catalytic converter is a common smog failure, and a CARB-legal replacement cat is $500–$1,200. California's visual inspection will fail missing EGR, charcoal canister or air injection parts. Request recent smog test reports.", "The A440F 4-speed automatic has an integrated full-time transfer case. Watch for slipping, harsh or delayed 2-3 and 3-4 shifts, a flare into overdrive, and burnt fluid. The vacuum-actuated center differential lock fails through cracked vacuum lines, a bad actuator or a bad switch, so the CDL light either won't illuminate or won't release. Fluid and filter service is cheap. Vacuum lock repair is $150–$600. A rebuild is $3,000–$5,000 and needs a 60-series-savvy shop. Look for service records showing fluid changes.", 'Steering wears in the steering box, drag link, tie rod ends and power steering pump. Symptoms are excessive play, wandering and a leaking box. Steering damper and component refresh runs $400–$1,200. A box rebuild or reman unit is $600–$1,200. Worn components plus front axle trunnion wear cause death wobble after bumps at 45–60 mph.', 'Suspension and driveline age shows as sagging original leaf springs, worn spring and shackle bushings, and dry U-joints and slip yokes. Signs are clunks on takeoff and a driveline vibration. Springs and bushings are $1,000–$2,500 installed. Prop shaft U-joints are $150–$400 per shaft.', 'Brakes are typically rusty or sticky front calipers, rear drums with a seized load-sensing proportioning valve (LSPV), an
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter, A440F ATF and filter, front and rear differential gear oil, and closed-knuckle grease or oil per spec.', 'Cooling system service: flush the coolant, replace the thermostat, inspect the hoses, radiator, fan clutch and water pump, and pressure test.', 'Valve lash adjustment with a new valve cover gasket.', 'Replace brittle vacuum lines, then inspect the EGR, the charcoal canister and the CDL vacuum circuit.', 'Tune-up: distributor cap, rotor, plugs, wires, air filter and fuel filter.', 'Brake fluid flush, plus inspection of the hoses, calipers, wheel cylinders and LSPV.', 'Tire age check and replacement if more than 6 years old. Check alignment and steering play.', 'Grease the driveshaft U-joints and slip yokes, and check them for play.', 'Confirm
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front knuckle rebuild (seals, trunnion bearings, wheel bearings) if leaking or out of preload.', 'Exhaust manifold and gasket replacement with stud repair.', 'Steering refresh: tie rod ends, drag link, damper, and possibly the steering box.', 'Leaf spring and bushing refresh if sagging or clunking.', 'A/C system repair or proper R-134a conversion, and rear heater core service.', 'Catalytic converter or EGR repair if smog margins are thin.', 'Rust treatment and repair at drip rails, rockers and quarters before it spreads.', 'Power tailgate window motor or regulator, and window regulators.', 'Odometer gear repair if the odometer is inaccurate or not counting.']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by body condition and rust, then by originality and documentation. Clean, rust-free, original Western or Californian trucks bring strong premiums over driver-grade examples. Low-mileage originals with records and factory colors can approach collector money, while rusty or high-mileage drivers trade well below that. Restomods and engine swaps, including LS V8s with expensive invoices, rarely recover their build cost. They appeal to a different buyer, and in California an unreferee'd swap is a large negative for registration. Color, Power Package equipment, a working A/C and rear heater, and complete service records all add value. Clear-coat failure, interior wear and replaced or unverifiable odometers subtract.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 30+ year-old FJ62 needs deferred fluid, vacuum, cooling and front-axle service. Plan $2,500–$6,000 in catch-up work to make it reliable and smog-ready. Rust remediation and manifold or knuckle work are the most common surprises.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 70-Series (HZJ75 Troop Carrier, 1HZ Diesel)
profiles.framing: This is a gray-market, leaf-sprung, 129-hp naturally aspirated diesel work truck imported under the 25-year rule — it is a slow, loud, utterly repairable adventure platform, not a comfortable daily. For a Carmel buyer it makes sense as a weekend/overland and hauling vehicle: Highway 1 and Los Padres dirt are fine, but sustained 75 mph freeway runs to the Bay Area are punishing and a 1HZ will struggle on Highway 17 or the Grapevine. The two decisive issues are documentation (import paperwork, odometer credibility, prior life — UN/NGO/Eastern European fleet trucks are common and often hard-used) and structural rust, because everything mechanical on these is serviceable but a rotten frame or a cracked head erases the value. Unmodified is nearly impossible here; what matters is that the lift, bumper, winch and snorkel were installed competently and that nothing (especially a bolt-on turbo) has stressed the engine beyond stock.
profiles.weak_points: 1) 1HZ cylinder head cracking between the valve seats and into the prechamber is THE known failure, usually on trucks that were turbocharged without EGT management, overheated, or run on a clogged radiator; symptoms are coolant loss with no external leak, pressurized/bubbling expansion tank, white smoke on a hot restart, and a combustion-gas-positive coolant test. A replacement head with valves and gasket runs roughly $3,500–$6,000 installed; ask for a cooling-system pressure test and block/coolant gas test as a condition of sale. 2) Injectors and nozzles are due around 150,000–250,000 km — hard hot starting, rattle, hazy smoke and a 'diesel knock' that won't settle; a set of rebuilt nozzles is $600–$1,200 installed. 3) The Denso injection pump (inline on most HZ applications) leaks from the front seal and governor housing, and pump timing drifts; rebuild/reseal is $1,200–$2,500, and that leak seen near the crank pulley in listing photos is exactly what to chase. 4) Glow plugs, glow-plug harness bus bar and the glow relay/timer fail and produce 15-second cranking and clouds of white smoke below 50°F — a $250–$500 job, but a truck that's been habitually cold-cranked has also been eating starters and batteries. 5) Rust: rear wheel arches and the inner arch lip, rocker/sill bottoms, door skin bottoms, windshield frame under the seal, the battery tray, rear crossmember, rear spring hangers and the frame around the shackle mounts. Troop carriers that lived in Eastern Europe or served salted-road fleets can be sound outside and perforated at the hangers; body rust repair is $2,000–$8,000 and frame perforation at spring mounts should be treated as terminal unless professionally plated with photo documentation. 6) Front swivel hubs (knuckles): the wiper seals and inner axle seals leak, and the birfields need a repack roughly every 60,000 km. Symptoms are gear oil smeared on the backing plate and steam/grease on the knuckle ball; a proper rebuild with bearings, trunnion shims, seals and knuckle balls is $800–$1,500 per axle. 7) Steering: relay rod and idler bushings, drag link ends and the recirculating-ball box develop play; a 3-inch lift without a caster correction and a drop pitman/steering-arm fix makes it worse and can induce death wobble on leaf-sprung 75s. Box rebuild or replacement is $500–$1,200, plus $400–$900 for tie-rod and relay-rod ends. 8) Brake vacuum pump mounted on the alternator is 1HZ-specific: it seeps oil and eventually fails, giving a hard pedal and no assist. Alternator/pump unit is $450–$900. 9) Rear drum brakes with wheel cylinders that seize and weep, and a load-sensing proportioning valve that rusts solid on trucks used unladen; full rear drum service $400–$800. 10) Clutch in the H55F five-speed is heavy and often the wrong side of 200,000 km; a clutch with rear main seal and pilot bearing is $1,200–$2,000 given the transmission has to come out. Listen for input-shaft whine in neutral and grind into 2nd. 11) Cooling: original brass/copper or later plastic-tank radiators, the viscous fan clutch and the thermostat all go lazy, and a 1HZ that runs hot is a cracked head waiting to happen — radiator $400–$800, fan clutch $200–$400. 12) The auxiliary/sub fuel tank, its transfer valve, pump and sender rust internally and clog filters; a dash-mounted aftermarket aux gauge (as on this example) means the system is already non-factory. 13) Leaf packs sag under winch/bumper weight, shackle and spring-eye bushings knock, and U-bolts stretch — a full front and rear spring/bushing refresh is $800–$1,600. 14) Import-specific: HZJ75 troop carrier production overlapped the HZJ78 changeover in early 1999, so build-plate date, VIN and chassis code must match the import paperwork; six-digit km odometers roll over at 999,999 and 'low km' claims on ex-fleet trucks are frequently unverifiable.
profiles.immediate_repairs: All fluids including front/rear diff, transfer case and H55F gear oil; new fuel filter and water separator drain plus a check for tank sediment; coolant flush with a fresh thermostat and pressure test; glow plugs, bus bar and relay if cold starting is at all slow; trace and reseal the injection-pump front seal/oil leak visible at the crank-pulley area; rear drum service (wheel cylinders, shoes, adjusters) and a brake fluid flush; repack front wheel bearings and reseal the swivel hubs if any gear-oil weeping; steering-linkage tightening with a caster/alignment correction to sort the 3-inch lift; verify winch wiring, battery, and that snorkel and aftermarket lighting are fused properly; tire date codes — Wranglers on an import are often 8+ years old regardless of tread. Budget $2,500–$4,500.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Injector/nozzle set if hot-start rattle or smoke persists; injection pump reseal or rebuild; radiator and viscous fan clutch; clutch and rear main seal if pedal engagement is high or there's any slip under load; leaf spring and shackle bushing refresh with new U-bolts to settle the lift; alternator/vacuum pump assembly; exhaust and muffler (imports usually arrive with patched systems); underbody rust arrest, seam sealing and cavity wax before coastal Carmel air gets to work; possible A/C system rebuild since the retrofit/replacement compressor on these rarely cools well; sound and heat insulation and seat/seal work for livability. Budget $3,000–$6,000.
profiles.market_notes: Troop carriers (11-seat, long-wheelbase, side-window body) command a premium over HZJ75 pickups and short bodies, and clean diesel manuals with genuine low kilometers and legible import paperwork sit in the high-$20Ks to $40K+; this example stalling at $28K with unanswered questions about history and a visible engine-bay leak is exactly the market punishing missing documentation. Value drivers: verifiable chassis/km history, absence of rust and prior fleet abuse, a stock naturally aspirated drivetrain (a poorly done turbo conversion is a discount, a documented Safari/Denco-style kit with EGT gauge is neutral at best), factory-style white or Toyota-original colors, and tasteful reversible mods over heavy overland builds. Ex-UN/NGO trucks trade at a discount unless the service history is deep. California buyers should also discount for the registration and emissions hassle of a 1998–1999 diesel import versus a 1997-or-older one.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any 25-year-old import as arriving with unknown maintenance regardless of odometer: assume all fluids, cooling system, fuel filtration, glow system, brake hydraulics, tires, and rubber bushings/hoses are due within the first season. Coastal Carmel air makes underbody rust arrest and cavity waxing a first-year priority even on a truck that looks dry, and budget separately for the 1HZ's big-ticket items (head, injection pump, clutch) which tend to surface once the truck is actually driven hard rather than shuttled between auctions.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 80-Series (FZJ80 / FJ80)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 80-Series is a slow, heavy, deeply over-engineered family 4x4 that can do Carmel-to-Big-Sur duty on Monday and Alabama Hills or the Sierra on Friday, and still be fixable in a home garage twenty years from now. The car to want is a documented, mostly-stock 1993-1997 FZJ80 with the 1FZ-FE, factory front and rear lockers if possible, a legible service history on the head gasket, birfields, radiator and cooling system, and California/dry-state provenance so the frame and rear body seams are solid. Because these are all 28-35 years old with 150k-300k miles, value lives almost entirely in documentation and rust, not mileage. Modification level matters: a tasteful mild lift and bumpers are acceptable, but engine/trans swaps of unknown provenance, mileage inconsistencies, and undocumented drivetrain work should be priced as risk, not as features.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Head gasket on the 1FZ-FE: the factory gasket typically lets go somewhere between 150k and 250k miles, often as coolant loss with no external leak, combustion gases in the coolant, or overheating on grades. A proper job includes head resurfacing, ARP or new OEM head bolts (the factory bolts are torque-to-yield and stretch), new intake/exhaust gaskets and a cooling-system refresh; expect $2,500-$4,500 at a shop. Look for a dated invoice naming the head gasket, head machining, and bolt type. 2) Birfield joints and front axle service: knuckle seals weep, the moly grease and gear oil mix, and clicking/popping on full-lock turns signals worn birfs. A full front axle 'birf job' with new birfields, knuckle seals, wheel bearings, and trunnion bearings runs $1,200-$2,500; a leaking knuckle that's been ignored also wrecks wheel bearings and can contaminate the front brakes. 3) Rust: the classic spots are the rear quarters above the wheel arches, the rear hatch/tailgate lower seam, the area beneath the rear window (a known water trap on these, exactly as noted in the example listing), floor pans under the rear cargo mat, the rear crossmember and frame rails behind the rear wheels, and the third-member/skid area. Frame rust near the rear spring hangers is a structural dealbreaker. 4) Cooling system: original brass radiators crack at the plastic tanks, the fan clutch goes soft, hoses and the heater T's fail; a full refresh (radiator, clutch, hoses, thermostat, cap, flush) is $800-$1,500 and is cheap insurance against another head gasket. 5) Power steering and brake system: PS pump and gearbox seep, and the hydro-boost/brake booster accumulator ('boost accumulator') on ABS-equipped trucks fails, giving a hard pedal and an intermittent brake warning light; accumulator is roughly $400-$900 installed and the ABS pump assembly is much worse. 6) Rear main seal, oil pan gasket, and front crank seal weeps are common at 200k+; not urgent but budget $600-$1,500 if combined with other work. 7) A440F/A442F four-speed automatic: generally robust but dark, burnt fluid or a shudder in lockup means a rebuild ($2,500-$4,000). Ask for drain-and-fill records; these were often never serviced. 8) Front and rear axle/differential seals and the factory e-locker actuators: locker motors and the wiring/vacuum for the CDL and lockers fail, and the dash locker lights blink without engaging. Confirm both lockers actually engage on a lift, not just that the buttons light up. 9) Suspension bushings, radius arm bushings, panhard and sway bar bushings, and steering damper are all worn out at this age; a full bushing and shock refresh is $1,200-$2,500 and transforms the driving feel. Lifted trucks with poor geometry wander and eat tires. 10) Electrical gremlins: door lock actuators, power window regulators, sagging headliners, cracked dash tops, failing ABS sensors, dead gauge cluster lights, and the notorious A/C evaporator/expansion valve and rear A/C lines on dual-A/C trucks; an R-12-to-R134a conversion done badly cools poorly. 11) Odometer and identity risk: many 80s have had clusters swapped, engines swapped, or Carfax mileage inconsistencies. Without a provenance trail the true mileage on the chassis and drivetrain is unknowable, which is what happened on the example truck. 12) Exhaust manifold and downpipe studs on the 1FZ shear and hiss; heat shields rattle. Minor but annoying, $300-$800. 13) Fuel pump, injector seals, and 30-year-old vacuum/PCV lines cause rough idle and hot-start issues; a full rubber-line refresh is a weekend and $150 in parts. 14) Tire and gearing mismatch: 33-35" tires on stock 4.11 gearing with the automatic makes an already-slow truck painful and raises EGTs and trans temps; re-gearing is $2,000-$3,500 per axle pair.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (engine oil, both diffs, transfer case, trans drain-and-fill, brake fluid, coolant); cooling-system assessment and likely radiator, fan clutch, hoses, thermostat and cap; block test / combustion-gas test on the coolant and act on the result; front axle knuckle inspection with new knuckle seals and repack of birfields if any weep or clicking; new tires if age-cracked or mismatched; brake pads, rotor check, and boost accumulator if the pedal is hard; battery, belts, wiper blades; replace all accessible 30-year-old vacuum and coolant hose sections; alignment after any suspension work. Budget $1,500-$3,500 on a good example.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Head gasket if not documented as done with resurfaced head and upgraded bolts; complete suspension bushing and shock refresh including radius arm bushings, panhard, sway bar links and steering damper; power steering pump/gearbox reseal; rear main or oil pan seal if dripping; A/C system service or evaporator/expansion valve work; locker actuator repair or rewire; door lock actuators, window regulators, headliner; rust remediation on rear quarters, hatch seam and under-rear-window area before it spreads; possible re-gear if running oversize tires. Realistic 12-month spend $3,000-$7,000 depending on head gasket status.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven by rust-free body, documented head gasket and birfield service, and factory front/rear lockers (1993+ and especially 1995-1997 Collector's Edition style trucks with both lockers command a real premium). Low-mileage (sub-150k) unmolested examples with original paint, clean two-owner histories and no lift trade at strong multiples of high-mileage lifted trucks; mileage inconsistency, engine or transmission swaps of unknown origin, and heavy overland builds all compress value regardless of parts spend. Desirable colors are the factory whites, greens and the deep blues/greys with tan or grey leather; aftermarket bumper/winch/drawer builds rarely return their cost. Dry Southwest and California cars are worth a meaningful premium over Midwest/Northeast trucks, and a well-sorted driver-quality FZJ80 typically lands in the high teens to low thirties with exceptional low-mile lockered examples pushing past $45k.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-year-old truck needs a full deferred-maintenance reset regardless of how well it drives: cooling system, all fluids, front axle knuckle service, suspension bushings and shocks, brake hydraulics, and every rubber hose and seal. Even a strong example should be bought with $5,000-$8,000 set aside so the head gasket or birfields can be done on your schedule rather than on the side of Highway 1.

profiles.label: Toyota MR2 (SW20, incl. JDM Rev1–Rev5 imports)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the SW20 is a weekend-and-canyon car: a mid-engine, five-speed, analog Toyota that delivers exotic-car layout with parts-bin serviceability, and Highway 1 / Laureles Grade / Carmel Valley Road are exactly its habitat. What matters is provenance and originality — a documented, unmodified, clean-title Turbo or NA with a stamped timing-belt history is worth far more to him than a swapped, tuned, or rebuilt-title car, no matter how fast. The generation split matters: Rev1 (1991) cars have the notorious early suspension geometry and narrower rear tires, while Rev2 (late 1993+) and later JDM Rev3/4/5 cars are meaningfully better sorted. Because these are now 30+ year old Japanese sports cars that were cheap for two decades, the dominant risk is accumulated deferred maintenance, hidden accident repair, and someone else's modifications rather than inherent fragility.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt (both 5S-FE NA and 3S-GTE Turbo are belt-driven, 60k-mile/7-year interval, and the 3S-GTE is interference — a snapped belt is a bent-valve, $4k+ event). Job runs $900–1,600 done properly with water pump, tensioner, cam/crank seals; demand a dated receipt with mileage, not a verbal 'recently done.' 2) CT26 turbocharger (US/JDM Rev1–2 Turbos): shaft-seal wear past ~100–130k gives blue smoke on startup/decel, oil in the intercooler piping and boost creep. Rebuild/replace $1,200–2,200 installed; a pulled intake pipe smeared with oil is the tell. 3) Cracked turbo exhaust manifold — near-universal on high-mile 3S-GTE cars; ticking on cold start, exhaust smell in the cabin, $500–900 to replace. 4) Head gasket / overheating on Turbos that have been overboosted or run with a tired radiator; coolant loss with no visible leak, milky oil, or combustion gases in the coolant. Head gasket in situ is $2,000–3,500 because access is poor. 5) Coolant hard lines: the SW20 runs long steel pipes front-to-rear along the chassis under the rockers. They corrode from the inside and rot at the rubber-joint sections, especially on cars from salted regions and JDM imports from Hokkaido/Tohoku. Symptoms are unexplained coolant loss and wet seams under the rocker; replacement is $800–2,000. 6) Rust: rear quarter panels behind the wheel, rocker seams, the frame rails around those coolant pipes, the front trunk / battery tray floor, and the T-bar roof drain channels. California cars are usually clean; check any Midwest or JDM-import history carefully. 7) T-bar targa roofs leak and rattle — perished seals ($300–600), stained headliner, and water in the rear quarter storage bins. Hardtop cars avoid this entirely and are quieter/stiffer. 8) E153 (Turbo) and C-series (NA) transaxle: worn 2nd/3rd synchros producing crunch on fast shifts, and Turbo diffs that whine after years of clutch drops. Clutch replacement is $1,200–2,000 because the powertrain has to come out; clutch master/slave cylinders leak with age ($200–400). 9) Suspension and bushings: 30-year-old struts, collapsed lower-arm and rear-toe bushings, and worn steering rack bushings turn the mid-engine balance genuinely dangerous. Full refresh with alignment is $1,500–3,000; Rev1 1991 cars especially deserve current rubber, correct staggered tire sizing and a proper alignment. 10) Air conditioning: original R12 systems are usually dead or crudely converted; long lines, aging condenser and compressor mean $900–1,800 for a working system — and a startling number of cars have simply had A/C deleted. 11) Electrical gremlins: power window regulators and motors, pop-up headlight motors and worn gear sets, cruise control, failing ABS pump/accumulator on ABS cars (parts are scarce and $800–1,500), and corroded ground straps. 12) Interior degradation: cracked dash top, delaminating door card and sun-visor vinyl, failed HVAC blower resistor, sticky soft-touch switchgear, and sagging rear parcel/engine-bay insulation. Good used interior parts are getting expensive. 13) Modifications and swaps dominate the market: 1MZ/2GR V6 swaps, K20/K24 swaps, Gen3 3S-GTE JDM swaps, standalone ECUs, E85 tunes, boost turned up on stock internals. Each swap must be judged on workmanship (wiring, cooling, fueling, brake/clutch hydraulics, emissions legality) and each one makes California registration/smog a live question on a 1976+ vehicle. 14) Title and history: total-loss and rebuilt-title SW20s are common, as are JDM imports with rolled-back or km-to-mile-converted odometers and ambiguous mileage. Paint-meter the whole car and read the Carfax/JDM auction sheet.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (engine oil, transaxle gear oil, brake fluid flush, coolant flush with a pressure test of the hard lines); timing belt + water pump + tensioner + cam/crank seals if there is no dated receipt within 7 years/60k; tires — nearly all these cars wear old rubber, and correct-sized staggered tires plus a four-wheel alignment are safety items, not upgrades; clutch master/slave cylinders if pedal is soft or fluid is black; T-bar seals and drain cleanout; battery, belts, and any weeping hoses; get the parking brake and all lighting/pop-up headlight function correct for registration. Budget $2,500–4,500.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Suspension refresh — struts, top mounts, lower arm and rear toe-link bushings, sway bar end links ($1,500–3,000); turbo rebuild or replacement if the CT26 shows shaft play or smoke ($1,200–2,200); cracked turbo exhaust manifold ($500–900); radiator, cooling fans and thermostat on any car showing high temps in traffic ($600–1,200); A/C recommission ($900–1,800); clutch if it is original-mileage or slipping ($1,200–2,000); window regulators, blower resistor and assorted electrical tidy-up; possible fuel pump/injector service on a car that sat.
profiles.market_notes: Turbo versus NA is the single biggest price lever — a documented, unmodified, clean-title US Turbo 5-speed in the 60–100k range now trades in the mid-$20k to $40k+ band, with sub-50k hardtop Turbos higher, while NA 5-speeds are roughly half that and NA automatics are bottom-of-market. JDM Rev3–Rev5 turbos (Gen3 3S-GTE, revised suspension, later interior) carry an import premium but bring registration, parts and history-verification friction. Modified, swapped, salvage/total-loss or A/C-deleted cars — like the supercharged 1MZ example — sit in a separate $10k–18k market and effectively never recover to stock-car money; originality, service records, a working A/C, an intact interior and non-faded factory paint (red, black, Turquoise Pearl and white all do well) are what pull top bids. Mileage bands matter less than documentation: a 120k car with a folder of belts, clutch and turbo receipts beats an undocumented 70k mystery.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a typical 30+ year old SW20 needs a full 'time-based' catch-up regardless of mileage: timing belt and water pump, all coolant and brake hydraulics, fuel hoses, tires, strut and bushing rubber, and T-bar or sunroof seals. Plan $3–5k in the first year on a good car and treat A/C recommissioning and turbo refresh as probable rather than possible on Turbo examples.

profiles.label: Toyota MR2 Spyder (ZZW30, 2000–2005)
profiles.framing: This is a 2,200 lb mid-engine roadster that trades every ounce of practicality for steering feel and throttle-adjustable balance on the roads above Carmel Valley and Highway 1 — it is a weekend and fair-weather second car, not a commuter or a trip vehicle. For this buyer the correct car is a documented, unmodified, dry-climate 5-speed (2003–2005 facelift preferred for the heated glass rear window) whose oil-consumption and pre-cat history is provable rather than assumed. Mechanical simplicity and Corolla-cheap parts keep running costs low, but the two model-defining risks — 1ZZ-FE oil burning and SMT robotized-gearbox failure — can cost more than the car is worth. Coastal proximity means rust is less of a concern locally, but any Northeast/Midwest import must be inspected underneath before anything else.
profiles.weak_points: 1) 1ZZ-FE oil consumption: the pre-2003 blocks use narrow, low-tension piston rings that carbon up and can lead to a quart per 600–1,500 miles by 60–100k. Toyota revised the rings/pistons in later production, but plenty of cars still drink. A short block or ring job is $3,500–6,000 installed; ask for a documented oil-consumption test (measured quarts over a known interval) and look for oil top-up receipts in service records. 2) Pre-catalytic converters integrated into the exhaust manifold (mainly 2000–2002): the ceramic substrate breaks down, and debris is drawn back into cylinders on overlap, scoring bores and accelerating oil burn. Symptoms are rattling from the manifold, P0420/P0421 codes, and sudden consumption. Inspect/borescope through the exhaust ports; an aftermarket or replaced manifold is common and, here, a positive. 3) SMT (sequential manual, 2002–2005): the hydraulic clutch actuator and shift actuator assemblies fail, as does the accumulator and position sensor; parts are scarce and a working used actuator plus labor runs $1,500–3,000, a clutch job is worse because the actuator must be recalibrated with Techstream. Symptoms are flashing gear display, slipping/juddering engagement, refusal to select gears, and stalling at stops. SMT cars sell for materially less for this reason. 4) Clutch and shift cables on the C56 5-speed: original clutches last 80–120k; replacement is $1,200–1,900 because the powertrain has to come down. The plastic shift-cable bushings at the transaxle and shifter base crumble by 15–20 years and produce vague, notchy shifting — a $20 part but a common misdiagnosis of 'bad synchros.' Second-gear synchro wear on abused cars is real. 5) Long steel coolant pipes run the length of the car between the front radiator and the mid-mounted engine. They corrode at the clamps/underbody and the pipes themselves rot on salt-state cars; leaks appear as coolant on the belly pans and low-coolant overheating. Radiator, thermostat, and 20+ year old hoses are typical catch-up items ($600–1,500). 6) Electric power steering: the EPS motor/torque sensor and its ECU can fail, giving heavy steering and an EPS warning light; used units and control-arm-out labor put this at $400–900. 7) Soft top: 2000–2002 cars use a plastic rear window that hazes and cracks at the seams; 2003+ got heated glass. Original tops shrink, leak at the header and rear bow, and the latches wear. A quality glass-window replacement top installed is $900–1,600. Check for water staining in the footwells and behind the seats — the drains at the rear bulkhead clog and back water into the cabin and onto the ECU area. 8) ABS actuator/pump: failures are known and replacement units are expensive and increasingly scarce ($1,000–1,800). An ABS light on a car that 'just needs a sensor' should be scanned, not assumed. 9) Rust: rocker panels, jacking points, front subframe and rear suspension mounts, and the coolant pipe runs. A rusted jack point makes routine service unsafe; structural rot here is a walk-away. 10) Suspension and bushings: lower control arm and rear trailing-arm bushings, ball joints, sway bar end links, and 20-year-old shocks. A full refresh with quality dampers is $1,800–3,500; tired suspension is the single most common reason these cars feel disappointing on a test drive. 11) Engine and transaxle mounts collapse, causing shudder and driveline clunk on throttle transitions ($300–700). 12) Timing chain guides/tensioner: cold-start rattle on high-mileage 1ZZ engines, often oil-starvation related from consumption neglect; $900–1,600. 13) Catalytic converter theft is an active risk for the exposed mid/rear cat; check for a replaced or shielded cat and mismatched welds. 14) Modifications: 6-speed C60 conversions (Celica GT-S / JDM), 2ZZ-GE swaps, and turbo builds are common in this community. A 6-speed swap is a genuine improvement to highway cruising but must come with documentation of the donor box, clutch, cables/linkage, ECU handling, and who
profiles.immediate_repairs: Oil-consumption baseline (measured), fluid service including transaxle gear oil (75W-90 GL-4/Toyota LT), coolant flush and pressure test of the underbody pipes, shift-cable bushings and shifter refresh, new tires if older than six years regardless of tread (these cars are tire-sensitive and often sit on aged rubber), brake fluid flush and likely rear pads, soft-top latch/seal adjustment and drain cleanout, battery (front trunk), and a full OBD-II scan clearing/documenting any ABS, EPS, or pre-cat P0420 codes.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main seal inspection (do them together if the powertrain comes down), shocks/struts and control-arm bushings, valve cover gasket and spark plugs/coils, radiator and hoses, engine/transaxle mounts, soft top replacement if the original is shrunken or the plastic window is hazed, exhaust manifold/pre-cat replacement on a 2000–2002 car if not already done, and a headlight restoration/alignment.
profiles.market_notes: Manual 5-speed cars command a clear premium over SMT, which trade 20–35% lower on actuator-failure fear; 2003–2005 facelift cars with the heated glass rear window and standard ABS/side airbags bring more than 2000–2002. Mileage bands matter sharply — sub-30k time-capsule cars now bring $18–28k, clean 50–90k drivers $11–16k, and 120k+ or oil-burning cars single digits. Documented oil-consumption history, a replaced pre-cat/exhaust manifold, a fresh top, and original paint move price more than color, though Solar Yellow, Spectra Light Green, and Absolutely Red draw more bidders than silver or black. Engine swaps and 6-speed conversions broaden the buyer pool on enthusiast sites but cap the ceiling versus a documented, stock, low-mile example.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 20+ year old example needs a deferred-maintenance sweep regardless of mileage: all fluids including transaxle gear oil and brake fluid, coolant and radiator hoses, tires and a timing-insensitive but age-sensitive rubber refresh (bushings, mounts, top seals), plus a battery and plugs/coils. Very low-mileage cars are not exempt — dry-rotted tires, hardened top seals, stuck calipers, and crumbling shift-cable bushings are age items, not mileage items. Budget $2,500–4,000 in the first year even on a clean car, and hold the reserve separately against the oil-consumption and SMT tail risks

profiles.label: Triumph TR6 (1969–1976, US-market carbureted)
profiles.framing: The TR6 is a body-on-frame British roadster with a torquey 2.5L inline six. For a Carmel buyer it is a weekend and fair-weather car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and local British car gatherings, not a daily driver. Value depends almost entirely on the chassis frame and body metal being sound and on documented engine and driveline work. Cosmetics and options are easy to fix or buy; a rotten or cracked frame, or an engine with excessive crankshaft end float, can cost more than the car is worth. Coastal fog and salt air mean the car needs a garage. Pre-1976 cars are smog-exempt in California, so 1969–1975 examples avoid emissions testing.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Chassis frame cracking and rust at the differential mounting brackets and the rear trailing-arm (semi-trailing arm) brackets. The diff mounts tear from torque, and the brackets rust from inside the box sections. Also check the rear kick-up and the outriggers under the doors. This is the number one TR6 killer. Bracket repair and plating runs $2,500–$6,000 with the body on. A frame-off repair or replacement frame runs $10,000–$20,000+. Look for restoration photos showing the frame stripped, repaired, and painted, and for any receipts covering diff-mount reinforcement. 2) Body rust in the outer and inner sills, A-post and lower door pillars, floor pans, trunk floor, rear wheel arches, and front fender bottoms. A late-1990s restoration is now 25+ years old, so look for bubbling at seams, the lower fenders, and around the rear deck. Panel and floor repair runs $3,000–$12,000 plus paint. Ask for bare-metal photos from the restoration. 3) Crankshaft thrust washer wear causing excessive end float. The usual target is about 0.004–0.008 in. At roughly 0.012 in or more, take it seriously. If the washers drop out, the crank cuts into the block and the engine becomes scrap. Check end float with a dial indicator, or watch the front pulley while someone presses the clutch. A full rebuild runs $8,000–$15,000. Washer replacement alone is about $600–$1,500 if caught early. Ask for engine rebuild receipts showing new thrust washers and machine-shop work. 4) Front lower trunnions on the vertical links. These are brass and are meant to be filled with EP90 gear oil, not grease. Neglect causes wear, binding, and in the worst case a snapped vertical link and a collapsed front wheel. Front suspension bushings, ball joints, and steering rack mounts also wear. A full front-end refresh runs $800–$2,000. 5) Rear hubs, splined halfshafts, and differential. Rear hub bearings need a press and special tooling, at $500–$1,200 per side. Splined halfshafts bind under power and cause a clunk or rear steer. Halfshaft U-joints wear. The diff can whine, leak at the pinion seal, or clunk from worn mounts. A diff rebuild runs $1,500–$3,000. 6) Clutch release mechanism. The release fork's taper pin can shear, or the cross-shaft wears, leaving no clutch. The fix requires pulling the gearbox, at $1,500–$3,000. Master and slave cylinders leak and are inexpensive by comparison. 7) Laycock overdrive (A-type on early cars, J-type from about 1973). Failure to engage is often electrical: switch, relay, solenoid, or wiring. It can also be low oil or a worn pump or clutch. The overdrive shares oil with the gearbox. Electrical fixes are $100–$400. Overdrive rebuilds run $1,000–$2,500. Gearbox rebuilds run $1,500–$3,000. 8) Zenith-Stromberg 175CD carburetors. Diaphragms tear, emissions-era bypass valves and temperature compensators leak, and needles wear, causing poor idle and hesitation. A rebuild and synchronization runs $400–$1,000. Many cars have been converted to SU HS6 carbs, which is a common but non-original modification. 9) Cooling system. Radiators clog and the original mechanical fan is marginal in traffic or heat. Water pumps, hoses, and the expansion tank age out. Overheating risks the head gasket. A radiator and pump refresh runs $600–$1,500. 10) Lucas electrics. Poor grounds, brittle wiring harnesses, corroded bullet connectors and fuse box, tired alternator and regulator. Common symptoms are dead gauges, wipers, or overdrive. A harness replacement runs $1,000–$2,500 installed. Wiring faults are a real fire risk. 11) Brakes. Front calipers seize, rear wheel cylinders leak, and brake lines and flex hoses age out. The vacuum servo (booster) can fail. A full hydraulic refresh runs $700–$1,800. 12) Wire wheels, including aftermarket Dayton wires. Worn splines on hubs and wheels cause clunking and can wreck the hub. Spokes loosen, tubes and tires age out, and spinners seize. Hub adapters or splines run $500–$1,500, and wheels about $250–$450 each. 13) Oil leaks and en

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch master and slave cylinder rebuild or replacement', 'Rear trailing-arm and differential mount bushings (rubber, to stay original-spec)', 'Front suspension bushings and ball joints, plus trunnion inspection or replacement', 'Rear hub bearing service and halfshaft U-joints if there is play or a clunk', 'Zenith-Stromberg carb rebuild (diaphragms, needles, bypass valves)', 'Water pump and radiator recore if running warm', 'Overdrive solenoid, relay, or switch replacement if engagement is intermittent', 'Exhaust system hangers and leaks; soft top and hardtop seals']
profiles.market_notes: Chrome-bumper cars (1969–early 1974) bring more than the 1974.5–1976 rubber-bumper cars. A 1974 with overriders sits in between depending on bumper style. Working overdrive adds roughly $2,000–$3,000, and a factory hardtop adds $1,500–$3,000. Original color and a documented, photographed restoration support the top of the market, while color changes, SU carb swaps, and aftermarket wire wheels are neutral to slightly negative for purists. Rough bands: driver-quality cars sell for about $15,000–$25,000, good documented cars for $25,000–$35,000, and concours examples for $40,000+. Frame and rust condition outweighs mileage, since odometers are often unreliable on these cars.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a restored TR6 is usually 20–30 years past its restoration. Expect rubber bushings, hoses, fuel lines, brake hydraulics, and wiring connectors to need a refresh, along with tires on age. Budget for a full front and rear suspension and hydraulic catch-up, and verify that the frame repairs from the restoration have held up in a coastal climate.

profiles.label: Volkswagen GTI (Mk6, 2010–2014)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Mk6 GTI is the cheap, genuinely good daily driver: a torquey 200hp EA888 2.0T, a crisp 6-speed manual, a hatch that swallows Costco runs and a bike with the seats down, and a chassis that is happy on Highway 1 and Laureles Grade. It is not an appreciating asset and never will be, so every dollar should go toward buying a documented, stock, un-tuned car rather than chasing a rare spec. The entire risk in this generation is engine-adjacent maintenance debt — timing chain tensioner, cam follower, PCV, water pump, carbon — that a neglected car hides and a fastidious owner documents. A $11–14k car with a thick folder is worth far more than a $9k car with a clean CarFax and no receipts.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing chain tensioner (EA888 Gen1/Gen2, CCTA/CBFA): the defining failure of this engine family. The early hydraulic tensioner can lose tension on a cold start or after a hot shutdown, the chain skips teeth, and the engine bends valves — a $4,000–7,000 event. VW released revised tensioners (the 'K' / 06K109467K-series updates); 2012 cars may or may not have had it done. Symptoms: rattle for 1–3 seconds on cold start, a P0016/P0017 crank-cam correlation code. Demand a receipt for tensioner replacement or budget $900–1,600 to do it preemptively. This is the single most important piece of paper on the car. 2) High-pressure fuel pump cam follower: a small hardened bucket riding a cam lobe, meant to be inspected every 30–40k miles. When it wears through, metal enters the HPFP and the cam lobe is destroyed — $1,500–3,000. The part itself is ~$25. Look for a receipt or pull it during PPI. 3) PCV / oil separator valve (the black plastic assembly on the valve cover): diaphragm tears at 60–100k. Symptoms are rough idle, a whistle or suction noise, high crankcase vacuum that pulls the rear main seal out and causes an oil leak, and misfire codes. $350–550 installed; if it has already blown the rear main seal, add $1,000–1,500 for transmission-out seal work. 4) Plastic water pump / thermostat housing: leaks at 70–110k, often first visible as pink crust at the front of the block or a low-coolant light. $700–1,000 installed since the pump is timing-chain-driven and the job is involved. 5) Carbon buildup on intake valves: direct injection with no port wash. By 70–90k expect rough cold idle, misfires under load, and a soft midrange. Walnut blasting runs $450–800 and should recur every 60–80k. Ask when it was last done. 6) Intake manifold runner flap motor: P2015 code, check engine light, occasionally limp mode. The flap position sensor fails; a full manifold is $450–700 installed, bracket-repair kits are cheaper but a bandage. 7) Diverter valve (turbo bypass): the early diaphragm-style DV tears; revised piston-style unit (06H145710D) is a $150–250 fix. Symptoms are a flutter/whoosh, soft boost, P0299 underboost. Many have already been done. 8) DSG (DQ250 wet-clutch) if so equipped: mandatory fluid and filter service every 40k at $400–650; mechatronic unit failure is $2,500–3,800 and clutch packs are $1,800–2,500. Symptoms are shudder from a stop, hesitation in first-to-second, flare on shifts. This buyer should strongly prefer the 6-speed manual, which avoids the whole category. 9) Manual clutch and dual-mass flywheel: typically 90–130k on a non-abused car, more like 50k on a tuned one. $1,600–2,400 installed. Chatter at takeoff, rattle at idle in neutral that quiets with the pedal down, and a high engagement point are the tells. 10) Turbo K03 wastegate actuator rod: develops play and rattles at low RPM under light load; also causes boost control faults. Rebuilt/replacement turbo is $1,300–2,000; some cars only need an actuator. 11) Suspension bushings and mounts: front lower control arm bushings, sway bar end links, and rear shock mounts are all soft by 90k. Clunking over expansion joints, wandering, uneven tire wear. $700–1,400 to refresh front end properly. 12) Electrical nuisances that are near-universal: door lock actuator/microswitch failures ($250–400 per door), rear hatch handle microswitch (hatch won't open from the outside), window regulator clips, and on Autobahn cars the Xenon/AFS headlight module or ballast ($400–900). 13) Water intrusion: sunroof drains clog and wet the headliner or the driver's footwell; a soaked floor can kill the comfort control module under the seat. Lift the carpet corners and smell for mildew. 14) Oil consumption: some Gen1/Gen2 EA888s use a quart per 1,000–1,500 miles through ring/PCV issues. Ask the seller directly and check the dipstick against reported last-change mileage. 15) Tuning and modification: Stage 1/Stage 2 software plus an aggressive clutch, aftermarket diverter, or a big intake stresses t
profiles.immediate_repairs: Oil and filter with 502.00-spec synthetic; inspect (and almost certainly replace) the HPFP cam follower; full scan for stored/pending codes and ECU flash count; replace ignition coils and plugs if unknown ($250–450); replace the diverter valve if it is still the original diaphragm unit; fix any PCV whistle or rough idle; front and rear brakes if pads/rotors are marginal ($500–800); four matched tires if mismatched ($700–1,000); DSG fluid + filter immediately if automatic and no record; new wipers, cabin filter, and a battery if it is more than five years old.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Timing chain tensioner update if there is no receipt ($900–1,600); walnut-blast intake valve carbon cleaning ($450–800); water pump and thermostat housing if any seepage ($700–1,000); PCV assembly ($350–550); front control arm bushings and sway bar end links ($700–1,200); intake manifold if P2015 appears ($450–700); rear main seal if a PCV failure preceded purchase; clutch and DMF if the car is past 100k or the engagement point is high; a serpentine belt, coolant flush, and brake fluid flush as general catch-up.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission is worth a clear premium over DSG to enthusiast buyers and lowers long-term risk; DSG cars with no fluid-service history should be discounted hard. Four-door bodies sell for slightly more than two-doors to practical buyers, though enthusiasts often prefer the two-door; Autobahn (leather, sunroof, Xenons, Dynaudio) and 2013–14 Wolfsburg Edition trims add modest money. Unmodified, one- or two-owner California cars with the plaid cloth interior and documented tensioner/cam-follower/carbon work sit at the top of the range — roughly $10–15k for clean 70–110k-mile examples — while tuned, high-mile, or no-records cars fall to $6–9k and are not actually cheaper once you fund the deferred work. Color matters little except that Tornado Red, Candy White, and Carbon Steel Gray move faster than silver.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2012 with 90–120k miles is due for a cluster of age items at once: tensioner update if not done, carbon cleaning, PCV, water pump/thermostat housing, coolant and brake fluid flushes, and a front-end bushing refresh — realistically $2,500–4,000 spread over the first year. Rubber items (motor mounts, hoses, hatch struts, door seals) are 13+ years old regardless of mileage, and a California car will be rust-free but sun-baked, so expect a cracked dash trim, faded headlight lenses, and a tired battery.

profiles.label: Volkswagen Golf Alltrack (MK7.5, US 2018–2019)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Alltrack is a practical, lightly raised AWD wagon: a Subaru Outback alternative with a better chassis and, in manual form, one of the last new manual wagons sold in the US. It suits Carmel daily driving, Highway 1 and Carmel Valley roads, and occasional dirt trips to Big Sur trailheads. What matters most is a documented cooling system, documented 4MOTION fluid service (Haldex, rear diff, PTU), and an unmodified ECU. That last point is a practical California smog issue, not just a preference. The 2017 US car used pre-facelift styling but is mechanically near-identical, so the same checks apply to it.
profiles.weak_points: ['Water pump / thermostat housing (EA888 Gen3 integrated plastic thermal management module): This is the most common failure on these engines, typically between 40k and 90k miles. Symptoms are a sweet coolant smell, pink or white crust around the passenger-side lower engine area, a slowly dropping expansion tank level, and a low-coolant warning. Replacing the module with a new thermostat and coolant costs roughly $900–1,500 at an independent shop. Ask for receipts showing replacement or a warranty repair, and treat an unexplained coolant top-off history as a red flag.', 'Turbocharger (IS12-family integrated-manifold turbo): Known issues are wastegate rattle on cold start and outright turbo failures in the 50k–90k range. Symptoms include underboost codes, whistling, oil in the intercooler piping, and blue smoke. Replacement runs $2,000–3,200 at an independent shop. Some cars had turbos replaced under warranty, so get the repair order with the date and mileage. Also check whether any California emissions-warranty coverage remains by VIN.', 'Composite/plastic lower oil pan: It is vulnerable to rock strikes, which matter more on an Alltrack likely to see gravel. The drain plug threads also strip when over-torqued. Look for oily residue, gouges, or an RTV-smeared plug area. An aluminum replacement pan costs $300–700 installed. A metal pan swap is a positive sign, but ask why it was done.', 'PCV/oil separator (integrated in the valve cover on Gen3): Diaphragm failure causes a whistle or hiss at idle, rough idle, lean codes (P0171), and misfires. The rear main seal can also be stressed by excess crankcase pressure. Repair costs about $250–600. Ask for evidence of replacement on cars past about 60k miles.', 'Ignition coils and spark plugs: Coils fail intermittently and cause misfire codes (P0300–P0304). Plugs are on roughly a 40k-mile interval, and tuned cars need them sooner. Plugs cost $200–350, and a full coil set adds $150–300. Look for receipts at 40k and 80k miles.', 'Timing chain and tensioner: The Gen3 design is much improved over Gen1/2 and failures are rare. Stretch is still possible on neglected cars with long oil-change intervals. Check it with a VCDS/OBDeleven cam–crank deviation reading, and listen for a cold-start chain rattle lasting more than 2 seconds. Repair costs $1,800–3,000 if needed. Oil changes at 5k–10k miles with VW 502.00 or 504.00 oil are the key evidence.', 'Haldex Gen5 AWD coupling: The fluid is often neglected because the dealer interval is long, commonly around every 3 years. Old fluid kills the coupling pump, which leaves the car effectively FWD and may set a 4MOTION warning. A fluid service costs $150–250, a pump $600–1,000, and a full coupling more. You want receipts showing Haldex fluid changes, ideally every 20k–40k miles or 3 years.', "Angle gear / PTU (transfer case) and rear differential: The PTU is filled with 'lifetime' gear oil that cooks from exhaust heat, and it can leak at the output seals. A failed PTU is a $1,500–3,000 job. Fluid changes for the PTU and rear diff cost about $150–300 each. Look for gear-oil smell, wetness at the PTU/driveshaft flange, and records of any fluid service.", 'DQ250 6-speed DSG (automatic cars): The wet-clutch DSG is robust if fluid and filter are changed every 40k miles. Neglect leads to harsh 1–2 shifts, shudder from a stop, and mechatronic faults. A fluid/filter service costs $350–550, a mechatronic unit $1,800–2,800, and a clutch pack $2,000–3,000. Require 40k/80k service receipts.', 'Manual transmission clutch, dual-mass flywheel and shift linkage: A worn DMF shows as chatter or rattle at idle that stops when the clutch is pressed, plus vibration on takeoff. The clutch can slip in higher gears, especially on tuned cars. Clutch and DMF together cost $2,000–3,000. Shifter cables and linkage can feel notchy and respond to lubrication, and the concentric slave cylinder can leak. Ask for clutch history and whether the car has ever been tuned.', 'Panoramic sunro

profiles.market_notes: The manual gearbox is the biggest value driver. The 6-speed Alltrack has a cult following as one of the last US manual wagons, and clean examples carry a clear premium over DSG cars. SEL trim with panoramic roof, Fender audio, and the Driver Assistance package outsells S/SE on price, and 2019 is marginally preferred as the final year. Low mileage (under 50k), one-owner histories with complete dealer or independent records, and documented cooling-system and Haldex service add meaningful value. Tunes, aftermarket lifts or wheels, curbed wheels, and missing drivetrain records should pull price down, as should an expired warranty coupled with an original, unreplaced water pump.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2018–2019 Alltrack at 50k–80k miles is due or overdue for its first Haldex fluid change, PTU and rear diff oil, brake fluid, and possibly a second spark plug service. Many still have the original plastic water pump/thermostat housing, which should be budgeted as a when-not-if repair. DSG cars need proof of the 40k-mile service, and any car that was tuned should be returned to stock before its first California smog check.

profiles.label: Volkswagen Golf GTI (Mk2 / A2, 8V & 16V)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Mk2 GTI is a light, analog, manual hot hatch to drive on Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the canyon roads behind it. It is a weekend and errand car, not a show piece. The best buy is a stock, rust-free, preferably West Coast car with a recent timing belt and a clean California smog history. Engine swaps, Euro conversions and cluster swaps hurt both registrability and verifiable history. Body condition and smog eligibility matter more than mileage, because mechanical parts are cheap and plentiful while rust repair and failed-smog chasing are not.
profiles.weak_points: 1) RUST is the deal-maker or deal-breaker. Check the rear wheel arches and quarter lips, the rocker sills and jacking points, and the floor pans under the carpet. Also check the battery tray and the inner fender below it, the spare-tire well (fed by clogged sunroof and hatch drains), the lower hatch edge, the door bottoms, and the windshield frame and cowl. Paint bubbling on a lower door edge usually means rust working from inside. Canadian, Northeast and Midwest cars are often far worse underneath than the top side suggests. Repairs run $1,500 for arch patches to $8,000+ for sills and floors. Insist on lift photos and look for fresh undercoating hiding repairs. 2) TIMING BELT. The 16V engines (PL 1.8, 1987–89; 9A 2.0, 1990–92) are interference designs, so a snapped belt bends valves, a $2,500–5,000 head job. The 8V engines (HT CIS 1985–87; RV Digifant II 1990–92) are generally non-interference. Interval is about 60k miles or 5–6 years. On the 8V the water pump is belt-driven and should be done at the same time. A belt job runs $450–900. Demand a dated receipt with mileage, or treat the belt as due immediately. 3) CIS-E FUEL INJECTION (16V). Watch the fuel distributor, the differential pressure regulator, the cold-start valve and thermo-time switch, the fuel accumulator, the injector seals and inserts, and the idle stabilizer valve. Symptoms are hot-start trouble, hunting idle, rich running and a failed CO reading at smog. A rebuilt fuel distributor costs $800–1,500. A full CIS-E sort-out by a shop that actually knows it runs $600–2,000, and such shops are getting scarce. 4) DIGIFANT II (8V, 1990–92). Common faults are vacuum leaks, a worn airflow-meter potentiometer, a failed ECU coolant temp sensor (causes hard starts and rich running), the Hall sender in the distributor, a sticky idle stabilizer valve and corroded grounds. These are usually $100–600 fixes, but they cause failed smog tests and poor drivability. 5) COOLING SYSTEM. Watch for: • the brittle plastic coolant flange on the cylinder head (very common leak, $60–200) • the expansion tank cracking at its seams • radiator end-tank leaks • the fan thermo-switch and fan motor • the oil-cooler gasket on 16V cars • heater-core leaks (sweet smell, fogged glass, damp passenger carpet; $600–1,200 due to dash access). Overheating has warped many 16V heads, so ask about history. 6) OIL LEAKS AND OIL-PRESSURE WARNING. Common leak points are the valve cover gasket, cam and intermediate-shaft seals, the 16V distributor O-ring at the end of the exhaust cam, the oil pan gasket and the rear main seal. The dynamic oil-pressure warning uses two pressure switches and a buzzer. False alarms come from bad switches or wiring, but a real low-pressure warning means worn bearings or a failing oil pump. Verify with a mechanical gauge. 7) 020 FIVE-SPEED GEARBOX AND LINKAGE. Sloppy, vague shifting is usually worn shift bushings and the linkage coupler, a cheap $100–400 refresh. Grinding into 2nd or 3rd means worn synchros, and a rebuild runs $1,500–3,000. Also watch for leaks at the shift-rod and axle flange seals. The clutch cable auto-adjuster wears out. A clutch with release bearing runs $900–1,600. Check the gear-oil level, since these cars often run low from leaks. 8) SUSPENSION, STEERING AND ENGINE MOUNTS. Expect tired struts and shocks, failing strut mounts and bearings, front control-arm bushings, ball joints and tie rods. Also expect worn rear axle-beam bushings, torn CV boots and clicking outer CVs, plus a leaking power-steering rack on 16V cars. The three or four engine and transmission mounts sag, causing clunks and shift-linkage misalignment. A full refresh runs $1,500–3,500. 9) BRAKES. The 16V has rear discs. The Girling-style rear calipers seize, especially the parking-brake mechanism ($300–700 per axle). Brake hoses are typically original and over 30 years old. Check for a pulsing pedal and uneven parking-brake hold. 10) ELECTRICAL AND INSTRUMENT CLUSTER. The VDO odometer drive g

profiles.market_notes: The 16V cars (1987–92) command the premium. Late 1990–92 2.0 16V big-bumper cars on original BBS wheels sit at the top, with 8V GTIs and base Golfs well below. Rust-free, original-paint, stock and documented examples have pulled strongly ahead, with clean drivers commonly in the low-to-high teens and exceptional low-mile cars well above that. Tired, rusty or modified cars remain cheap. Engine swaps (VR6, 1.8T), Euro conversions, coilovers and cluster swaps with TMU status move a car into a separate tuner market. For a California owner they also carry smog-registration risk that should be priced as a major negative. Long-term West Coast history, timing-belt and service records, original interior condition and good colors like Tornado Red, black or white all lift value.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a sound example is now 30+ years old and usually has original or neglected rubber throughout: vacuum lines, fuel and coolant hoses, bushings, mounts and brake hoses. Expect $2,000–4,500 of baseline catch-up beyond the timing belt, before any rust repair. Budget extra time and money for CIS-E diagnosis on 16V cars, since specialist knowledge is thinning out.

profiles.label: Volkswagen Golf GTI (Mk8, 2022-2024 manual era; 2025+ Mk8.5 DSG-only)
profiles.framing: The Mk8 GTI is a practical, quick hatchback for a Carmel buyer. It should handle Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and Peninsula errands while carrying real cargo. The mechanical core (EA888 evo4 2.0T, 241 hp, VAQ front limited-slip differential, 6MT through 2024) is sound. The generation's reputation problems are mostly software and touch controls, so the priorities are an unflashed ECU, completed software and recall updates, documented 10k-mile services, and a dry cooling system. For this buyer the 2022-2024 manual cars are the target, because the 2025+ Mk8.5 is DSG-only.
profiles.weak_points: ["Infotainment and digital cockpit (MIB3) software: early 2022-2023 cars commonly show screen freezes, black screens, random reboots, laggy response, phone-projection dropouts, and lost settings. Most cases are fixed by dealer software updates, not hardware replacement. Confirm the car runs current software and look for dealer ROs mentioning infotainment or 'SVM' updates. A failed head unit or cluster out of warranty runs about $1,500-3,000.", 'Capacitive and haptic controls: the touch steering-wheel buttons on 2022-2023 cars produce accidental inputs and missed presses. MY2024 returned to physical wheel buttons. The unlit temperature/volume touch sliders and the touch light-switch panel can also misbehave. Test every wheel control, slider, and the headlight panel. A steering-wheel or switch-panel replacement runs about $600-1,500.', "Open recalls and campaigns: Mk8 Golf/GTI cars have had software-related campaigns, including rearview camera image display issues and other electrical updates. Run the VIN through NHTSA and a VW dealer. Get the dealer's printout showing completed campaigns rather than relying on the seller's word.", 'Thermostat/water pump module (EA888 family): the plastic integrated thermostat housing and water pump assembly is the most common mechanical leak. It shows as a slowly dropping coolant level, a sweet smell, or pink/purple crust under the intake side. Typical window is 40k-90k miles, but it can appear earlier. Repair runs about $800-1,400 at an independent shop. Ask for any coolant top-off history and inspect from below.', "ECU tuning and modifications: the EA888 evo4 is heavily tuned. Bench-unlock and flash tunes exist for the MG1 ECU, and downpipes, intakes, and intercoolers are common. A tune can strain the clutch, turbo, and DSG, and VW can deny warranty coverage. A dealer or VCDS/OBDeleven scan can reveal a non-OEM software version or a raised flash counter. A 'returned to stock' car may still show traces.", 'Manual clutch and dual-mass flywheel: hard launches, track use, or tuned torque wear the clutch and DMF. Symptoms are a high engagement point, slip in 3rd-4th under full boost, judder, or rattle at idle that stops when the clutch is pressed. Clutch plus DMF replacement runs about $2,000-3,200. Lessee and multi-owner cars warrant a careful clutch evaluation.', 'DSG DQ381 7-speed wet-clutch gearbox (automatic cars): fluid and filter service is due every 40k miles and costs about $400-600. Skipped service can lead to harsh low-speed engagement, shudder, or mechatronic faults. A mechatronic unit runs about $2,500-4,500. Require proof of the 40k service on any DSG car near or past that mileage.', 'VAQ electronic front limited-slip differential: generally robust, but a pump or clutch-pack fault produces a dash warning and unusual behavior when turning out of tight corners under power. Scan for VAQ fault codes. Repair is roughly $1,000-2,500.', 'Electrical sensitivity and 12V AGM battery: a weak start-stop AGM battery causes a cascade of unrelated warnings (ACC, lane assist, start-stop unavailable, infotainment glitches). A replacement must be coded or registered to the car and costs about $300-450. A 4-year-old original battery is near the end of its life.', 'Driver assist sensors (IQ.DRIVE, Travel Assist, ACC, front assist): the radar sits behind the front VW badge and the camera in the windshield. Even minor front-end repairs or a windshield replacement require calibration. A radar or camera fault after a cheap repair costs about $500-2,000. A windshield with HUD (Autobahn) plus calibration runs about $1,200-1,800.', "DCC adaptive dampers (Autobahn and some SE packages): watch for a leaking damper, knocking over Carmel's broken pavement, or DCC fault lights. A replacement damper costs about $700-1,200 per corner. Non-DCC cars use conventional struts and are cheap to service.", 'Interior rattles and trim quality: dash, door-card, and rear hatch rattles and creaks are common on Mk8 cars and show u

profiles.market_notes: Trim drives price most. The S is the value buy. The SE adds a sunroof, Harman Kardon audio, and IQ.DRIVE, and the Autobahn adds DCC, HUD, and IQ.Light LED headlights. The 2024 '380' manual-farewell cars carry a modest premium. Manuals hold a growing premium now that 2025+ is DSG-only, and clean, documented, unmodified, untuned cars sell well above flashed or modded ones. Below 50k miles is the sweet spot. Cars past the 4-year/50k-mile factory warranty discount noticeably. Kings Red and Pomelo Yellow are the desirable colors, while gray, black, and white are plentiful and priced accordingly.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 2022 car around 40k miles has usually aged past its 4-year/50k-mile warranty. As a former lease car, its free Carefree Maintenance (2 years/20k miles) likely covered the early services but little afterward. Expect to catch up the brake fluid, spark plugs, filters, the 12V battery, any outstanding software updates, and the DSG service if applicable, plus tires and front brakes on freeway-mileage examples. Plan roughly $800-1,800 of catch-up work beyond routine oil changes.
