profiles.label: Volkswagen Scirocco Mk2 (1981–1992; US-market 1982–1988, 8V and 16V)
profiles.framing: This is a light, analog, Karmann-built A1-platform hatch coupe for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and occasional longer Central Coast runs. Mechanically it is a Mk1 Golf/Rabbit with plentiful and cheap engine, brake, and suspension parts. Scirocco-specific body panels, glass, bumpers, lights, and interior trim are scarce and expensive, so rust and missing trim matter far more than engine wear. For a California buyer, the deciding factors are a US-spec, smog-legal car with its original engine, documented CIS fuel-injection health, and a rust-free structure. A modified or gray-market Euro car like the widebody G60 example is effectively unregistrable in California and is a pass for this buyer.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural and cosmetic rust is the number-one value killer. Check the front fender lips and the area behind the front wheels, the rocker sills and jacking points, and the rear wheel arches and quarter panels. Also check the lower hatch edge, the spare-tire well, the battery tray and the area under it, the A-pillar and windshield-frame base, and the floor pans under the carpet, where wet carpet from cowl, windshield-seal, or heater-core leaks rots the floors. Sunroof cars add clogged drain tubes. Proper sill or arch repair runs $2,500–8,000+, and replacement Scirocco-specific panels are hard to source. Ask for underside photos on a lift and any prior bodywork receipts.', "CIS fuel injection is a common source of hard starts, rough idle, and hot-start problems. 8V cars use K-Jetronic with a lambda frequency valve. US 16V (PL engine, 1986.5–88) cars use CIS-E/KE-Jetronic with a differential pressure regulator and idle stabilizer valve. Typical culprits are the fuel distributor, warm-up regulator, cold start valve, thermo-time switch, fuel accumulator (hot-start failures), and leaky injector seals. Cracked intake boots cause vacuum leaks. A competent CIS diagnosis with pressure gauges is $200–400. Repairs range from $300 for seals and boots to $1,500+ for a rebuilt fuel distributor. Look for receipts showing CIS pressure tests, not just 'tune-up'.", 'The fuel pumps (a main pump under the car near the tank, plus an in-tank transfer pump) and the fuel pump relay age out. They show up as whining, stalling, or no-start conditions. Expect $300–700 to replace both pumps, the filter, and the accumulator. Original rubber fuel hoses and tank-area lines can also seep, which is a fire risk worth checking at every inspection.', 'Timing belt service is critical on the 16V, which is an interference engine. A snapped belt means bent valves and $2,500–4,500 in head work. The 16V also uses a short chain at the back of the head linking the cams, which can rattle when its tensioner wears. The 1.7 and 1.8 8V engines are more forgiving but still need the belt changed on schedule. A belt and water pump job costs $500–1,000. Require a dated receipt within roughly 4 years or 40k miles, or budget for it immediately.', 'Cooling system weak spots include the plastic coolant flange at the cylinder head (cracks and leaks), the water pump, and the radiator with its plastic end tanks. Also check the fan thermo-switch (a failure overheats the car in traffic) and the expansion tank and cap. The heater core leaks sweet-smelling coolant onto the passenger floor and fogs the windshield, and replacing it is a labor-heavy $600–1,200 job. Look for coolant-system receipts and a cooling fan that cycles properly at idle.', 'Oil leaks are common from the valve cover gasket, cam and crank seals, the oil pan, and the distributor O-ring. 16V cars have an oil cooler and the dynamic oil-pressure warning system (dual pressure switches plus a buzzer). Failed switches or wiring cause nuisance alarms that owners sometimes disconnect, which masks real low-pressure problems. Expect $300–900 for a typical reseal. The car should hold oil pressure hot at idle with the warning system working.', 'The 020 five-speed transaxle tends to develop worn synchros, especially in 2nd and 3rd gear, and grinds on fast shifts. Its shift linkage bushings wear and make shifting vague or sloppy. A linkage bushing refresh is $150–400 and transforms the feel. A transaxle rebuild is $1,500–2,500. Clutch cable self-adjusters fail, and a full clutch job is about $900–1,500. The 3-speed automatic sold on 8V cars is sluggish and less desirable.', 'Front suspension clunks are typical on unrefreshed cars. Common sources are worn strut mounts and bearings, control arm and sway bar bushings, ball joints, and tie rod ends. CV boots split and throw grease, and clicking on turns means worn outer CV joints. The rear axle beam bushings also wear. A full bushing, mount, and shock refresh is $1,500–3,000. Power-steerin
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Timing belt, tensioner, and water pump if there is no dated receipt within about 4 years or 40k miles. This is mandatory on 16V cars ($500–1,000).', 'Full fluid service: engine oil, coolant flush with VW-spec coolant, transaxle gear oil, and a brake fluid flush ($300–500).', 'Fuel filter replacement and a CIS fuel pressure check (system, control, and residual pressure). Replace cracked intake boots and vacuum lines ($250–600).', 'Inspect and replace aged fuel hoses near the tank and pump. Check that the fuel accumulator holds residual pressure ($150–500).', 'Brake inspection: flush the fluid, adjust or service the rear drums and wheel cylinders, and replace any cracked rubber hoses ($300–800).', 'Tires if date codes are over 6 years old, plus an alignment check ($500–900).', 'Cooling fan
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front suspension refresh, if any clunk is present: strut mounts and bearings, control arm and sway bar bushings, tie rod ends ($1,200–2,500).', 'Shift linkage bushing kit and shift adjustment ($150–400).', 'Valve cover gasket and cam/crank seal reseal as leaks appear ($300–900).', 'CIS component work found during diagnosis, such as the warm-up regulator, cold start valve, injector seals, or idle stabilizer valve on 16V cars ($300–1,200).', 'Radiator or expansion tank replacement if the original plastic is brittle or weeping ($300–700).', 'Power window regulator repair on one or both doors ($150–800).', 'CV boot replacement, or outer CV joints if clicking ($250–700).', "Rust prevention: clear the cowl and sunroof drains, cavity-wax the sills and arches, and treat any surface rust before i
profiles.market_notes: US 16V cars (1986.5–1988) command a clear premium over 8V cars. Clean, original, documented 16Vs trade roughly $12k–25k+, while driver-grade 8Vs sit around $5k–12k. Special editions such as the Wolfsburg Edition draw extra interest. Rust-free structure, complete original Scirocco-specific trim, a five-speed manual, and continuous service records move price the most. Sub-100k-mile cars with corroborated odometer history are notably scarcer. Modified, engine-swapped, or Euro-import cars like the Rieger widebody G60 example sell to a different audience at unpredictable prices, and for a California buyer they carry registration and smog risk that outweighs any apparent bargain.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 35–40-year-old Scirocco needs a catch-up pass on rubber and fluids: timing belt, coolant hoses and flange, fuel hoses, brake hoses, intake boots, and suspension bushings. Expect $2,500–5,000 in the first year even on a good example. Cars that sat for long periods usually also need CIS fuel system attention and brake hydraulic work before they are reliable drivers.

profiles.label: Volvo 140 Series (142 / 144 / 145, 1967–1974)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 140 is a simple, durable, cheap-to-own Swedish classic for Highway 1 and Monterey Peninsula drives. It should be a usable weekend and occasional-errand car, not a restoration project. The mechanicals (B18/B20 pushrod four, M40/M41 gearbox, four-wheel discs) are nearly indestructible and well supported by parts. The real risk is structural rust hidden under fresh paint, plus a long tail of deferred maintenance and amateur modifications. Pay for a solid, dry-climate, documented car on correct carbs or injection rather than a cheaper car with filler and a Weber swap. Pre-1976 cars are exempt from California smog checks, but a straight, rust-free body cannot be cheaply bought back later.
profiles.weak_points: ['STRUCTURAL RUST is the number-one value killer at any mileage. Check these areas: front floor pans under the mats, inner and outer sills/rocker panels, jacking points, front fender bottoms behind the wheels, lower A-pillars, door bottoms, rear wheel arches, rear valance, trunk floor and spare well, and the battery tray. Also check the rear axle link and Panhard rod mounts and the front crossmember mounts. Hidden rot under a fresh repaint is common, especially after a color change. Ask for photos of the bodywork during prep. Floor or sill sections run $1,500–4,000 per area. Rotten link mounts or extensive sill work can reach $6,000–15,000+ and usually makes the car not worth repairing.', 'Windshield, rear glass, and pop-out quarter window seals harden with age (all 50+ years old by now). They leak water into the footwells and trunk, which then rots the floors from the inside. Wet carpet, musty smell, or bubbling at the lower windshield corners are the tell. Reseal each glass for $300–700. Repair any rust found in the window frames separately.', 'The B18/B20 engine is very robust but often neglected. Common issues: worn camshaft lobes and lifters, especially with low-zinc oil; solid lifters that need periodic valve lash adjustment; and leaks from the rear main seal, oil pan, timing cover and valve cover. Blue smoke points to valve guides or seals. Expect healthy compression around 140–175 psi, even across cylinders. A top-end refresh runs $1,500–3,000; a full rebuild $5,000–9,000. Ask for oil change and valve adjustment history and use high-zinc classic oil.', 'Fuel system originality and condition. A 142S has twin carburetors: SU HS6 on most markets and Zenith-Stromberg 175CD on many US 1970+ cars. Stromberg diaphragms crack and SU dashpots and needles wear. Single Weber downdraft conversions are very common and usually run acceptably, but they affect value and originality. Rebuilding the correct carbs costs $300–800; sourcing and fitting correct carbs to reverse a swap costs $800–2,000. Ethanol-degraded rubber fuel lines and the mechanical fuel pump diaphragm are fire and stalling risks. Replace them if there are no receipts.', '142E/144E/145E Bosch D-Jetronic fuel injection (1971+ in Europe, 1972–73 in the US). Aging wiring harness insulation, the MAP pressure sensor, the trigger points in the distributor, the cold-start valve, injectors and the analog ECU all cause rough running or hot-start problems. Few shops know this system. Sorting it typically costs $1,500–4,000, and good used pressure sensors and ECUs are getting scarce. Insist on a cold start, hot restart and highway test, plus receipts for any injection work.', 'M40 four-speed / M41 four-speed with Laycock J-type electric overdrive. Look for synchro wear (2nd/3rd crunch), worn shift linkage bushings and slop, and popping out of gear. On the M41, the overdrive solenoid, relay or switch can fail, or low or wrong fluid makes the overdrive slip; it shares oil with the gearbox. An overdrive rebuild runs $800–1,500; a gearbox rebuild $1,200–2,500. The cable-operated clutch has cable fraying and release bearing noise. A clutch job runs $900–1,600.', 'Driveline: the two-piece propshaft uses a rubber-mounted center support bearing that perishes. This causes a clunk on takeoff and vibration at 40–60 mph. U-joints wear. The Spicer-type rear axle commonly weeps from the pinion and axle seals, and axle bearings eventually howl. Center bearing and U-joints run $250–600. Axle seals and bearings run $400–900.', "Brakes: four-wheel discs with a dual-circuit 'triangle' split. Each circuit feeds both fronts and one rear, so the front calipers have extra pistons. There is a brake-failure warning valve/switch, a vacuum servo, and drum-in-disc rear parking brake shoes. Sticking or seized caliper pistons, leaking warning valves, cracked flex hoses, corroded hard lines, and a lazy or seized parking brake are typical. A full system refresh runs $1,200–2,500. Old rubber hoses with no recei
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Change all fluids: engine oil (high-zinc classic oil) and filter, gearbox/overdrive oil, rear axle oil, coolant', 'Flush brake fluid; inspect/replace all rubber brake hoses; free or rebuild sticking calipers; adjust the parking brake', 'Tune-up: points, condenser, cap, rotor, plugs, wires; set timing, dwell and valve lash', 'Replace rubber fuel lines and fuel filter; inspect the mechanical fuel pump; check the tank sender and vent for leaks', 'Replace coolant hoses and thermostat if undated; pressure-test the cooling system and heater valve', 'Replace tires older than ~6 years regardless of tread; check wheel bearings', 'Electrical triage: clean the fuse box, check grounds, fix horn and turn-signal indicator faults, test charging voltage', 'Fit a fire extinguisher and check the fan belt
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Reseal windshield, rear glass and pop-out quarter windows to stop floor-rotting leaks', 'Replace driveshaft center support bearing and U-joints if there is any vibration or clunk', 'Front-end refresh: ball joints, control arm bushings, tie rod ends, idler arm; alignment', 'Rear suspension bushings (trailing arms, torque rods, Panhard rod); replace lowering springs with stock-height springs if desired', 'Rebuild or properly sort carburetors (or D-Jetronic on E models); consider returning to correct factory carbs', 'Replace pinion and axle seals if weeping', 'Replace clutch cable; check overdrive solenoid and relay on M41 cars', 'Exhaust manifold gasket/downpipe and any rusted exhaust sections', 'Treat underbody and cavities (sills, doors, rear arches) with cavity wax to slow coastal-air c
profiles.market_notes: Body integrity dominates price. A genuinely rust-free, dry-climate car with records commands a large premium over a shiny repaint of unknown history. Typical drivers trade around $6,000–14,000, and exceptional examples reach $18,000–25,000+. Manual with M41 overdrive, 142E injection, and 142 GT spec are worth more than a base 142S or the BW35 automatic. The 145 wagon has its own following. Small-bumper pre-1973 cars are generally preferred over 1974 US big-bumper cars. Original colors, correct carburetion, stock suspension height and documented maintenance add value; Weber swaps, lowering springs, color changes and partial re-trims subtract.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume every rubber part is past its life unless receipted: fuel and brake hoses, glass seals, suspension bushings, and the center support bearing. Budget roughly $2,000–4,000 in the first year to bring a typical driver-grade example to a safe, reliable baseline. Any rust found during that work should be addressed before it spreads in Carmel's damp coastal air.

profiles.label: Volvo 262C Bertone Coupe (1978–1981)
profiles.framing: This is a cheap-to-buy, expensive-to-restore oddity: a Volvo 240 platform with a chopped, Bertone-assembled body, a PRV V6, and a trim/glass package that is effectively unobtainium. For a Carmel-based driver it can be a genuinely usable weekend car — 240 mechanicals under most of it, coastal-friendly torque, easy parts for the chassis — but only if the body and the 262C-specific pieces are honest, because those are what you cannot buy back. The buyer's preference for documented, unmodified cars collides head-on with this model: a large share of survivors have had the PRV replaced with a redblock four, which makes them more reliable and less valuable, and the swap quality is the whole story. Treat the purchase as buying a body and an interior; the drivetrain is negotiable, the roof, C-pillars, and glass are not.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Body rust, Bertone-specific: the cars were shipped from Gothenburg to Turin and back, and the vinyl roof plus the unique lowered roof/C-pillar seams trap moisture. Look for bubbling along the vinyl roof edges, the rear window surround, and the base of the C-pillar; roof-skin rot on a 262C is a body-shop fabrication job ($8k–$25k) because no panels exist. 2) Standard 240 rust zones apply and are cheaper but still real: front fender bottoms behind the wheel, jacking points and rocker ends, rear wheel arches, trunk floor/spare well, battery tray, and the fuel filler area. Expect $1.5k–$6k for competent localized repair. 3) Windshield and backlight surrounds: both glasses are 262C-only, the backlight especially. Rust under the seal or a chipped/delaminating rear glass is a five-figure-risk problem — check for original date-stamped glass and any leak staining on the parcel shelf. 4) PRV V6 (B27F 1978–79, B28F 1980–81) camshaft and rocker wear: chronically poor top-end oiling, especially early B27s with high-mileage or infrequent-oil-change histories. Symptoms are ticking, low vacuum, misfire, and metal in the oil; a proper top-end rebuild runs $4k–$9k, a full rebuild $8k–$14k with machine work on wet liners. 5) PRV cooling/liner interface: aluminum block with wet liners; neglected coolant leads to liner seal weeping, head gasket failure, and internal corrosion. Look for coolant loss, mayo in the filler, and receipts for correct silicate coolant. 6) Timing gear and intermediate/oil-pump drive: a stretched chain or worn drive gear is common at 100k+ and is an engine-out-ish job on a PRV. 7) K-Jetronic (CIS) fuel injection: hard hot starts, hunting idle, and rich running from a tired fuel distributor, warm-up regulator, leaking cold-start injector, dead accumulator, or perished braided fuel hoses (fire risk). Budget $600–$2,500; a fuel distributor rebuild alone is $700–$1,200. 8) Drivetrain substitutions: many survivors now run a B21/B23/B230 redblock, sometimes with an M46 4-speed + overdrive or an M47 5-speed, and often with a donor dash and wiring. Quality ranges from factory-clean to hacked. Look for correct engine mounts, an intact and untaped harness, working temp/oil/charge gauges, a BAR referee sticker and label if it's a California car, and a title that matches what's installed. 9) BW55 3-speed automatic (the factory box on most cars): slipping 1-2, delayed engagement, and cooler-line leaks; rebuilds are $2k–$3.5k and good cores are getting scarce. 10) M46 manual with Laycock J-type overdrive: overdrive that won't engage or won't drop out — usually solenoid, relay, gearlever switch, or low/contaminated fluid, but a worn OD unit is $1,200–$2,500. Confirm the OD engages and disengages under load in 4th. 11) Interior: the 262C-only leather (Amazon/beige or dark blue) shrinks and splits, elm/burl wood veneer lifts and cracks, headliner sags against the low roof, and the Bertone-specific door cards and rear buckets/bench are not reproduced. Re-trim in correct-looking hide is $4k–$9k. 12) Electrical: brittle 45-year-old insulation, corroded fuse block and ground straps, failing bulb-failure sensor causing phantom lighting faults, tired wiper/heater motors, and dead climate-control vacuum servos causing blend doors stuck on hot. 13) HVAC: original R12 systems are usually dead or crudely converted; heater core replacement means dash-out labor ($1,200–$2,000). Seat heaters (standard) often dead. 14) Chassis wear items: front control arm and sway bar bushings, worn tie rods, rear trailing-arm and panhard bushings, torque rod bushings, sagging springs, and seized rear parking-brake shoes inside the rotor hats. All cheap parts, but a full refresh is $1.5k–$3k in labor. 15) Rear axle and driveline: 1030/1031 axle whine, leaking pinion seal, dried center support bearing and worn driveshaft U-joints causing 50–65 mph vibration.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including differential and gearbox/overdrive; replace all rubber fuel lines and the CIS accumulator/filter on any injected PRV car (or the entire fuel hose run on a swapped car); new cooling hoses, thermostat, and correct coolant; tires if over 6 years old regardless of tread; brake fluid flush and rear parking-brake shoe/hardware service; reseal or replace any weeping valve cover and oil cooler lines; sort exhaust leaks and manifold studs; replace failed door/trunk/roof seals and clear all drain channels before the first wet Carmel winter; verify and repair charging system grounds; fix any inoperative wipers, lights, or bulb-failure-sensor faults for road legality. Budget $2,000–$4,500.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Front and rear suspension bushing/shock refresh and an alignment; steering rack or box seals and tie rods; driveshaft center support and U-joints; A/C system rebuild or conversion if you actually want it ($1,500–$2,500); heater core and blower if flow is weak; PRV top-end attention (cam/rocker inspection, valve stem seals) or, on a swapped car, timing belt, water pump, and injection sorting; headliner and seat leather repair; partial rust repair on rockers/arches found at PPI; possible BW55 rebuild or M46 overdrive service. Realistic 12-month spend on a $6k–$12k car: $4,000–$9,000.
profiles.market_notes: Values are driven by body integrity, originality of the 262C-specific trim (vinyl roof, C-pillar badging, glass, leather, wood), and whether the PRV is still in the car and running well. Original-drivetrain, rust-free, documented cars in the 1978 silver-over-black or the later dark blue/black schemes bring the strongest money; the first-year silver cars have a following. A redblock four-cylinder swap — even a tidy one with an M46 overdrive — typically trades at a meaningful discount to an original V6 car and narrows the buyer pool at resale, while respray-off-original-color, missing Bertone trim, or a title with a 'Title Only'/non-op notation push a car toward parts-value territory. Mileage matters less than rust receipts, photo-documented bodywork, and a stack of maintenance invoices; sub-$10k results are common and clean six-figure-mile drivers rarely clear the mid-teens.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume nothing rubber or flexible has been renewed unless there is a receipt: fuel hoses, coolant hoses, brake hoses, bushings, motor/trans mounts, and every body seal are all 40+ years old on a typical example. Plan a first-year catch-up of roughly $4,000–$8,000 covering fuel and cooling system renewal, a full suspension bushing refresh, tires, and weather sealing/drain clearing before winter storms — and set aside separate money for the first rust repair you find once the carpet and vinyl roof come up.

profiles.label: Volvo Amazon 122S Wagon (P220)
profiles.framing: This is a charming, genuinely usable 1960s wagon that the buyer will drive on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not a trailer queen. Mechanically it is simple, over-built, and fully supported by the aftermarket (VP Autoparts, Skandix, IPD), so the real questions are rust, brakes, front-end wear, and whether the car has been honestly sorted or merely made pretty. On a 4-speed non-overdrive car with a 4.10-ish final drive, 65-70 mph is a buzzy 3,400-3,700 rpm — acceptable for local use, tiring for long freeway hauls, and the single biggest driveability limit worth pricing in. Documentation matters more than shine: a repainted car with a bypassed heater, dead horn, and dead parking brake is telling you where the money went.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Structural rust is the only true value-killer. Check the front frame rails/torque boxes ahead of the firewall, the jacking points and rocker/sill closing panels, the floor pans under both front seats, the battery tray area, and — wagon-specific — the rear cargo floor, the spare-tire well, the rear spring hangers/shackle mounts, and the D-pillar/rear arch seams. A repaint in 2021 with 'spots of overspray' means the underside and seams must be photographed, not assumed. Cut-and-weld floor/rocker repair runs $1,500-$5,000+; frame-rail or spring-hanger repair can exceed the car's value. 2) Wagon tailgate rust: the lower gate's inner skin and bottom seam and the upper gate's glass frame trap water; hinges sag and the upper latch wears (rebuilt latches are available ~$150-300). A rusted lower gate is a hard-to-source, expensive panel. 3) King-pin front suspension (not ball joints): pins and bushings need grease every ~1,500 miles and are almost always neglected. Symptoms: clunk over bumps, wander, uneven front tire wear, vertical play when levered at the wheel. Proper rebuild with reaming/line-boring of the new bushings is $800-1,800 for the pair; shops that just press bushings in produce a car that binds. 4) Steering box (Bishop cam / cam-and-roller) develops 2-4 inches of play at the rim; also idler arm, tie rod ends, and the drag link. Rebuild box $500-900 exchanged, plus $300-600 in links. 5) Brakes: front Girling discs with rear drums; 1967 cars use a dual-circuit master. Expect seized caliper pistons, weeping wheel cylinders, and 30-year-old flex hoses. The parking brake acting on the rear drums seizes at the cables and levers constantly — 'parking brake doesn't work' is normal, and it is both a safety and a California-registration/inspection annoyance. Full system refresh (master, calipers, wheel cylinders, hoses, shoes, pads, cables) is $1,200-2,200. 6) B18B engine (dual SU HS6 carbs, ~95 hp): the five-main bottom end is famously durable, but the camshaft drive gear is a fiber/composite gear that strips teeth without warning, typically past 80-100k miles or after decades of age — a $60 part that requires the timing cover off ($400-800 labor); an aluminum-hub steel/fiber replacement receipt is exactly what you want to see. 7) Oil leaks: rear main and front crank seal weep, and a clogged 'flame trap' (PCV oil trap) in the intake pressurizes the crankcase and pushes oil past every seal. Cleaning/replacing the flame trap and hose is a $40 fix that prevents a $1,200 diagnosis. 8) Twin SU carbs go out of sync as throttle shafts and jet seals wear: hard cold starts, uneven idle, plug fouling, 16-18 mpg where 24-26 is normal. Rebuild/rebush the pair $500-900; many cars have been 'fixed' with a single Weber downdraft conversion, which runs but is a de-originalizing move. 9) Cooling: original radiators are usually clogged or already recored; water pump, thermostat housing corrosion, and hardened hoses are routine. Recore $400-650. Watch for overheating in traffic — a sorted Amazon should not. 10) Heater system: the box, valve, and core are buried behind the dash and the valve seizes; 'heater bypassed' is a common shortcut. Restoring heat/defrost properly means core rebuild plus box removal, $800-1,800. No defroster is a real problem in Carmel fog. 11) Electrical: many 1967 cars still have a generator/regulator (alternator conversion $350-700), plus corroded fuse block and ground straps, failed horn ring contact, dead wiper motors, and brittle cloth-loom wiring at the headlight switch and column. A dead radio/horn usually signals an un-restored harness. 12) Drivetrain: M40 4-speed is stout but the clutch hydraulics (master/slave) and the clutch cross-shaft bushings wear; second-gear synchro is the first to go. The Spicer rear axle leaks at the pinion seal and the axle-tube/backing-plate seals contaminate rear shoes. Retrofitting an M41 with Laycock J-type overdrive is the single best driveability upgrade, $2,000-3,500 installed — an
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full brake safety pass: flex hoses, wheel cylinders, caliper rebuild/replacement, fluid flush, and parking brake cables/levers freed and adjusted ($900-1,800). Replace all rubber fuel lines and inspect the tank/pump ($250-500). Flame trap/PCV service and full fluid change including gearbox and rear axle ($200-350). Twin SU sync, points/condenser/cap/rotor, valve adjustment, timing ($400-800). Front-end inspection with king-pin grease service and tie-rod/idler tightening; expect a king-pin rebuild if there is measurable play ($800-1,800). Re-commission the horn and wipers (safety/registration) and diagnose the bypassed heater ($300-900). Fresh date-coded tires if the current set is over six years old ($700-1,000). Seat-belt condition and mounting check.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Camshaft fiber-gear replacement if there is no receipt ($500-900 installed). Radiator recore and cooling-system refresh including water pump and hoses ($700-1,200). Heater core/valve restoration for real defrost ($800-1,800). Alternator conversion and fuse-block/ground-strap refresh ($500-1,000). Steering box rebuild or exchange plus idler arm ($700-1,400). Rear main/front seal and pinion-seal attention if oil consumption or drips persist ($600-1,500). Weatherstrip and tailgate seal replacement to stop cargo-floor water intrusion ($800-1,800). Seat cushion and headliner repair ($800-2,000). Strongly consider an M41 overdrive gearbox swap for freeway usability ($2,000-3,500). Localized rust repair on rockers/jack points/spare well if the PPI finds early scale ($1,500-4,000).
profiles.market_notes: Wagons (P220) command a clear premium over 122S sedans and two-doors; a 4-speed is essential, an original overdrive (M41) car adds roughly $2,000-4,000, and the rare BW35 automatic subtracts heavily. Documented rust-free dry-state provenance, photographed underside, and a receipt file move price more than paint gloss — driver-quality repainted cars with deferred mechanicals cluster around $9,000-16,000, genuinely sorted examples with overdrive, working heat, and a brake/front-end file reach $20,000-30,000, and true restorations go higher. Period colors with the split tailgate, correct 15-inch steels with hubcaps, and honest unmolested engine bays (twin SUs, not a Weber) support the top of the band; East Coast/Southeast cars carry a rust discount plus $1,200-1,800 shipping to the Monterey Peninsula. Non-functioning heater, parking brake, and horn are cheap-sounding items that reliably knock $1,500-3,000 off bidder confidence because they signal an unfinished car.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a ~58-year-old car needs a full safety re-commission regardless of cosmetics: all brake hydraulics and flex hoses, all rubber fuel lines, cooling system, weatherstrip, and date-expired tires. Budget $3,500-6,000 in the first year just to bring deferred rubber, brakes, and front-end wear current, plus $2,000-3,500 more if you want overdrive and working heat/defrost for real Monterey Peninsula use.

profiles.label: Volvo S60 (P3, 2011–2018; 2014+ facelift)
profiles.framing: This is a fast, comfortable, very safe all-weather sedan with an unusual drivetrain — Volvo's transverse 3.0L turbocharged inline-six (B6304T4) with Haldex AWD and an Aisin six-speed automatic — wrapped in one of the better-looking interiors of the era. For a Carmel-based driver it makes sense as a quiet Highway 1 commuter and weekend road-trip car, not as an appreciating asset: P3 S60s depreciate hard and are worth roughly parts-and-labor money, so the entire purchase decision hinges on documented maintenance rather than badge or color. The T6 R-Design Platinum is the desirable spec (325 hp, sport chassis, Nappa/contour seats, Harman Kardon, nav, BLIS), and the dealer-installed Polestar Performance Optimization is a factory-sanctioned flash rather than an aftermarket tune — acceptable to a 'documented, unmodified' buyer if there is a Volvo dealer receipt for it. The core risk is that a neglected example can hand you a five-figure repair (timing chain at the flywheel end, transmission, angle gear) on a car worth five figures.
profiles.weak_points: PCV / oil trap system: the SI6 crankcase ventilation box clogs with oil coke, typically 80k–130k miles, driving crankcase pressure up until it blows out the rear main seal or front crank seal, pushes oil past turbo seals, and causes a whistling/moaning idle. The dipstick or glove test is the field diagnostic; proper replacement means intake manifold off and runs $900–$1,800. If the oil trap was never done and there is a rear main leak, budget for the seal too (transmission out, $1,500–$2,500). Timing chain and guides: unlike most cars, the SI6's chain lives at the flywheel end of the engine, so chain, guide, and tensioner service requires separating engine and transmission — $3,000–$5,000. Symptom is a brief rattle or diesel-like clatter on cold start; any such noise is a hard walk-away unless the job has a receipt. Angle gear (bevel gear/PTU): the splined collar between transmission and angle gear wears and strips, especially where fluid was never changed; symptoms are a whine under load, driveline slop, or metallic glitter on the drain plug. Replacement is $1,500–$3,000 with the collar upgrade; fluid should be changed every ~30k and is almost never done. Haldex Gen IV AWD: pump strainer/filter clogs and the pump burns out, leaving front-wheel drive and a 'AWD Service Required' message; filter+fluid is a $250–$400 service every 30–40k, pump replacement $700–$1,200. Aisin AW TF-80SC six-speed: Volvo called the fluid lifetime, and it isn't. Expect torque-converter shudder at light throttle 40–60 mph, flare or clunk on the 2–3 shift, and eventual valve body/solenoid faults after 100k. Fluid+filter service is $400–$600 if done in time; a rebuilt or used unit is $3,500–$5,500. Turbo and boost plumbing: the twin-scroll turbo's wastegate actuator, bypass (diverter) valve, and charge pipe couplings leak, causing a boost-drop code, lag, or a limp-mode 'Reduced Performance' message; actuator/valve work $400–$900, turbo $2,000+. Coolant and thermostat: expansion tanks crack at the seam, thermostat housings and the coolant pipe behind the engine weep; a hot-spot overheat on this alloy six is expensive, so pressure-test it. $300–$900 typical. Water intrusion and electronics: sunroof and cowl drains plug and soak the passenger and driver footwells, which is where the CEM sits; symptoms are damp carpet padding, random warning messages, battery drain, and door/seat module faults. Cost ranges from a $150 drain cleanout to a $1,200+ module and harness repair — check under the carpet with your hand, not your eyes. Electric parking brake: the rear caliper-integrated EPB actuators seize or the module throws faults, usually after a winter car sits; $500–$900 per side including caliper. Suspension and R-Design chassis: front lower control arm bushings and sway bar end links wear by 80k, strut mounts clunk, and the R-Design's 18/19-inch wheels with low-profile tires bend on potholes and make the ride harsh. Full front control arms, links, and an alignment run $1,200–$1,800. Ignition and fuel: six coils and plugs cause rough idle/misfire codes by 90k–110k ($500–$800 to do all six properly); high-pressure fuel pump and injector faults show as long crank or fuel trim codes. Miscellaneous age items: power steering pump/rack and hose seepage (this is still a hydraulic system), front engine torque rod (dogbone) bushing collapse causing a shudder on take-off ($200–$400), A/C evaporator temp sensor and condenser leaks, and the Sensus/RTI infotainment dying or the backup camera fogging. Rust is rare on a lifelong California car but check rear subframe and rear-wheel-arch seams on any Northeast/Midwest re-registration.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up on arrival: transmission fluid and filter, angle gear fluid, Haldex fluid and filter/strainer, engine oil with a correct-spec low-ash 0W-30/5W-30, brake fluid flush, and coolant if unknown. Crankcase pressure (PCV) test and oil trap replacement if pressure is high. Tires almost always need replacing on an R-Design — a matched set of 19s is $900–$1,400 — plus an alignment. Front brake pads/rotors if under-spec, cabin and engine air filters, wiper blades, and a battery load test (these cars are hard on batteries and a weak one causes phantom module faults). Clear the sunroof and cowl drains and pull back the carpet to confirm the footwells are dry.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Spark plugs and coil pack replacement if not documented, front lower control arm bushings/ball joints and sway bar links, front engine torque rod bushing, expansion tank and any weeping coolant hoses, turbo bypass/wastegate actuator if boost codes appear, rear main or front crank seal if the PCV was neglected before you bought it, EPB actuator on one rear corner, and one or two nuisance electrical items (door module, camera, headlight ballast/bulb on the active bi-xenons at $400–$700 per side).
profiles.market_notes: T6 AWD R-Design with the Platinum package sits at the top of the P3 S60 range and commands a meaningful premium over a T5 FWD, but the whole model line is deep in depreciation — condition and records move price far more than trim. Documented transmission, angle gear, Haldex, and PCV service is worth more to an informed buyer than 20k fewer miles; a no-records 90k car and a receipted 120k car should not trade at the same number. Distinctive R-Design colors (Rebel Blue, Passion Red) and a clean one- or two-owner California history help liquidity; Polestar Performance Optimization is a mild positive only when there's a Volvo dealer invoice for it, and any non-Polestar tune, exhaust, or lowering springs is a discount. Mileage bands matter: sub-70k cars ask a premium, 70k–110k is the value sweet spot if documented, and above 120k the car is priced against its next big repair.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a decade-old Swedish turbo six arrives with every 'lifetime' fluid still original: plan a one-time $1,500–$2,500 catch-up covering transmission, angle gear, Haldex, coolant, and brake fluid, plus the PCV oil trap if pressure is high. Rubber-and-plastic age items — expansion tank, coolant hoses, control arm bushings, torque rod, sunroof drains, and the battery — should be addressed proactively rather than after they strand the car. Tires and an alignment are near-certain on an R-Design regardless of tread depth, since matched date codes on 19s are rare on cheap examples.

profiles.label: Volvo V60 T8 Polestar Engineered (SPA, Recharge Twin Engine)
profiles.framing: This is the fastest, most focused version of Volvo's last real sport wagon: a 400–455 hp plug-in hybrid with Öhlins manually adjustable dampers, Brembo front brakes, a front strut brace and a genuinely useful 50/50 estate body. For a Carmel-based buyer it is a one-car answer — quiet EV commuting to Monterey, a 30-mile electric range for town errands, and a car that can cover Highway 1 or a Bay Area run at speed in comfort. Buy it as a depreciated, warranty-backed daily driver, not as an appreciating asset: the complexity is high, dealer dependence is real, and a 2019–2021 PE (supercharger + 11.6 kWh pack) is a meaningfully different, more fragile machine than a 2022–2024 (turbo-only, 18.8 kWh, 455 hp). What matters most is documented dealer service, current software, verified high-voltage battery health, remaining factory/hybrid warranty, and a rust-free underbody if the car came from a salt state.
profiles.weak_points: 1) High-voltage battery and hybrid control system: 11.6 kWh pack on 2019–21, 18.8 kWh on 2022+. Failures are usually module-level or BMS/contactor related and announce themselves as 'Hybrid system service required,' reduced EV range, or refusal to charge. Under the 8-year/100,000-mile hybrid warranty this is free; out of warranty, module or pack replacement runs roughly $6,000–15,000+ and is dealer-only. Insist on a VIDA-based battery state-of-health/capacity report, not the driver display's guess-o-meter. 2) HV battery and engine cooling circuits: multiple electric coolant pumps, a separate battery chiller/valve block, and a PTC cabin heater. Weeping pumps, low-coolant warnings and 'reduced hybrid performance' messages appear from 40k miles; pumps are $400–900 each installed, and neglected coolant accelerates pack degradation. 3) Onboard charger (OBC) and charge port: J1772 3.7 kW (2019–21) / 6.4 kW (2022+). OBC faults produce charging aborts and stored DTCs; replacement is $1,800–3,000. Test an actual full Level 2 charge cycle, not just a plug-in handshake. 4) 12V/support battery and parasitic drain: SPA cars are notorious for flat 12V batteries after sitting, which then throw a Christmas tree of bogus faults. Expect the AGM main and (on some builds) the small support battery to be consumables at 4–6 years, $300–600 for the pair, plus a drain test if the car has sat. 5) Supercharger (2019–2021 T8 only): the Roots blower's electromagnetic clutch and bearings whine, rattle at idle, or seize; a blower assembly is $2,500–4,000 installed. 2022+ cars deleted the supercharger — one of the best reasons to prefer the later spec. 6) Timing belt on the VEA B4204T engine: rubber belt, age-sensitive, with a nominal ~10 year/150k-mile interval. A 2019–2020 car is already inside the age window; budget $1,200–2,200 and get the receipt if claimed done. Also inspect the PCV/valve-cover diaphragm (whistling, rough idle, oil weep) and the crank pulley/decoupler. 7) Fuel dilution and short-trip wear: T8s driven mostly on electricity cook the oil with fuel because the engine rarely reaches temperature. Look for 7,500-mile/annual oil changes minimum (ideally every 5,000 on a town-driven car); ask for a used-oil analysis or at least check for fuel smell and overfull dipstick level. Carbon buildup on the direct-injection intake valves shows up as cold-start stumble and misfires by 60–90k miles; walnut blasting is $700–1,200. 8) Aisin 8-speed transaxle with integrated crank-mounted starter/generator (CISG): Volvo calls the fluid lifetime; it is not. Harsh 1-2 shifts, hesitation off the line, or clunks during engine start/stop blending are warning signs. Fluid and filter service is $400–700; a transaxle or CISG failure is $6,000–9,000. 9) Electric rear axle drive (ERAD) unit: the rear wheels are motor-driven with no driveshaft. Listen for whine under EV acceleration and a growl on coast; check the reduction-gear housing for weeping oil. Replacement is a $4,000–6,000 dealer job. 10) Öhlins DFV dampers: manually adjustable, no electronic control. They leak at the shaft seals, and the adjuster collars corrode and seize in coastal/salt-state cars. Photograph all four; a full set is $2,500–4,500, but Öhlins/authorized rebuild is roughly $250–400 per corner. Also budget front lower control arm bushings and rear links at 50–80k on the stiffer PE tune. 11) Brakes and regen: gold Brembo front calipers with slotted rotors cost real money ($1,200–2,000 for front pads and rotors), while the lightly used rear rotors rust, pit and seize their pads — very common on regen-heavy PHEVs, especially Midwest cars. Brake fluid is a strict 2-year/every-other-service item on this platform. 12) Tires and wheels: 4,800+ lb curb weight on 235/40R19 or 245/35R19 performance rubber means 15–25k-mile tire life and $1,300–1,800 a set; the forged PE wheels curb easily and bend on potholes. 13) Electronics and software: Sensus (through MY2022) and Google built-in (MY2023+) both suffe
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full dealer-level scan and software update to current calibration with all open campaigns closed; load-test and likely replace the 12V AGM (and support battery) if over 4 years or if the car has sat; brake fluid flush if not documented within 2 years; rear caliper/pad service or rotor replacement if regen rust has set in; coolant level/leak check across both engine and HV battery circuits; verified full Level 2 charge cycle; four-wheel alignment and corner-balance check of the Öhlins settings; cabin filter, wiper blades, and a pano-roof drain clean-out. If oil history is thin or the car lived on electricity, an immediate oil and filter change with an oil analysis sample.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Transaxle fluid and filter service if there is no record of one; engine oil at 5,000–7,500-mile intervals rather than the optimistic factory display; spark plugs if approaching 60k; front Brembo pads and slotted rotors depending on wear; Öhlins inspection with rebuild of any weeping or seized corner; front control arm and rear link bushings if clunks appear; a set of tires ($1,300–1,800) unless recently replaced; HV battery state-of-health recheck at annual service to trend degradation while the 8-year/100k hybrid warranty is still live; timing belt on any 2019–2020 example on age alone.
profiles.market_notes: The PE was a very low-volume halo trim (a few hundred US cars per year) and wagons command a clear premium over the S60 PE sedan, but depreciation from an ~$75–80k MSRP is brutal — good cars land in the high-$30k to mid-$40k band. The biggest price movers are remaining factory warranty (48-month/50k bumper-to-bumper; staying under 50k miles matters), documented Volvo dealer service history, and model year: 2022+ cars with 455 hp, 18.8 kWh and no supercharger are worth a premium over 2019–21 400 hp cars. Colors matter less than condition, though Thunder Grey/Onyx over the PE's gold-belt charcoal Nappa is the default and the rarer Bright Dusk or Crystal White cars draw more attention; low-mile, single-owner, non-salt-state examples with clean Carfax and no accident history are the ones that clear top money. Multiple owners, lease returns, thin records, or a rust-belt address should all pull the number down.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a 27k-mile example is a calendar-maintenance car: brake fluid (2-year), 12V AGM (4–6 year), coolant condition in both circuits, and tires/rubber that age out long before they wear out. Low-mileage PHEVs typically need rear brake de-rusting, an oil change on time-based schedule regardless of miles, and a software bring-up at the dealer; any 2019–2020 car should also be priced with a timing belt on the horizon.

profiles.label: Zimmer Golden Spirit (Fox-body Mustang-based, 1980–1988)
profiles.framing: This is a coachbuilt neoclassic novelty cruiser. Fiberglass bodywork, a landau top, and Zimmer luxury trim sit on a stretched Fox-body Mustang chassis with ordinary, cheap Ford V8 and AOD mechanicals. For a Carmel driver it is a weekend and Monterey-car-week-season cruiser. Its value lives almost entirely in the condition and completeness of the Zimmer-specific body, trim, and chassis-extension work, plus a clean California smog and registration path. The Ford drivetrain is easy and inexpensive to sort, but cracked fiberglass, a rusted splice, or missing unobtainium trim can cost more than the car. Nearly all were automatics, so an automatic is the norm here and not a compromise.
profiles.weak_points: ['Chassis extension splice and Fox unibody rust: Zimmer lengthened the Fox platform ahead of the cowl to get the long hood. Inspect the welded rail extensions for cracks, poor weld penetration, rust, and sag at the splice. Also check the usual Fox rot points: front frame rails, torque boxes, floor pans under the seats, rear frame rails, and the trunk floor under the spare-tire area. Look for photos taken on a lift. Structural weld repair runs about $1,500–6,000+, and a badly rotted splice can make the car uneconomic.', 'Fiberglass body cracking and mount separation: the long front clip, fenders, running boards, and rear bodywork are hand-laid fiberglass bonded or bolted to steel. Look for spider and stress cracks around hood hinges, fender mounts, bumper brackets, and the continental spare mount, and for gaps where panels have separated from the steel substructure. Rust can also form at the steel mounting points underneath. Proper glass repair and paint usually runs $2,000–10,000, and few shops do it well.', 'Landau and padded vinyl top: the vinyl and padding trap water against the Mustang steel roof and C-pillars, causing hidden rust bubbling. Look for lifting edges, bubbles, and shrunken seams. Re-covering costs about $1,500–3,500, more if the roof needs metal repair underneath. A worn top on an 85-degree-sun or coastal-fog car deserves a careful look at the trim edges and rear window surround.', 'Cooling-system margin: the radiator and grille sit far forward of a stock Fox, with long hoses and sometimes added or relocated electric fans, so many run hot in traffic with A/C on. Watch for temperature creep at idle, weak fans, failed fan relays or thermoswitches, aged long hoses, and a clogged radiator. Water pump and timing cover leaks on the 302 are common. A radiator, fan, and hose refresh typically runs $600–1,800. Look for receipts showing a recent radiator or fan work.', 'HVAC vacuum controls and A/C: Fox HVAC defaults to defrost-only when it loses vacuum. Causes include cracked vacuum lines, a failed check valve or reservoir, or a disconnected supply under the hood, which is common on coachbuilt cars where lines were rerouted. Diagnosis is usually $150–400. If the heater core or blend door needs work, the dash comes out, at about $1,000–2,000. Many are still on R-12 or have a half-done R-134a conversion; a compressor, accumulator, and orifice-tube refresh is $1,000–2,000.', 'Engine and ignition (5.0L, plus some early cars with the 4.2L/255): 1980–85 cars are carbureted or CFI, while 1986–88 use sequential EFI with EEC-IV. On EFI and CFI cars, the distributor-mounted TFI ignition module fails with heat and causes stalling or no-restart when hot; replacement is about $100–300, ideally relocated off the distributor. Also common: intake gasket and rear main seal leaks, brittle vacuum lines, and EGR/thermactor faults that matter for smog. Pull EEC-IV codes on EFI cars.', 'AOD automatic transmission: the throttle-valve (TV) cable or rod adjustment is critical. Misadjustment causes late, soft, or slipping shifts and quickly burns the overdrive band and clutches. Symptoms include a flare on the 2–3 or 3–4 shift, no overdrive, or harsh engagement. A rebuild runs about $2,500–4,500. Look for records of a fluid and filter service and TV adjustment, and confirm the transmission type matches what the VIN and engine combination should have.', 'Rear axle and driveline: 1980–85 cars commonly use the 7.5-inch axle; later V8 cars may have the 8.8-inch. Listen for whine on decel or coast and clunks from axle bearings, the pinion seal, or U-joints. A heavier fiberglass body plus age leads to leaking seals. Typical cost is $300–800 for seals and bearings and $1,500–2,500 for a full gear rebuild. Look for receipts for gear, bearing, and U-joint work.', 'Front suspension and steering under added nose weight: the extended fiberglass nose puts extra load on the Fox MacPherson-strut front end. Check control arm bushings, ball joints, strut mounts
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil, AOD fluid and filter with TV cable verification and adjustment, rear axle gear oil, brake fluid flush, and power steering fluid', 'Cooling system refresh as needed: coolant flush, thermostat, long radiator hoses, and a fan relay or thermoswitch check, then a 20-minute idle test with A/C on', 'HVAC vacuum diagnosis and repair (lines, check valve, reservoir) to restore panel and floor modes; evaluate A/C type (R-12 vs R-134a) and charge', 'Brake inspection: flexible hoses, front pads and rotors, rear drum shoes and wheel cylinders, and a parking brake cable check', 'Ignition and fuel: cap, rotor, wires, and plugs if undocumented; TFI module check on EFI and CFI cars; rubber fuel hoses at the tank, pump, and carb or rail', 'California smog pre-test and emissi
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front suspension refresh: control arm bushings, ball joints, struts, strut mounts, tie rods, and an alignment', 'Water pump and timing cover gasket replacement if weeping', 'Intake manifold and valve cover gaskets, plus oil leak cleanup (rear main seal watch)', 'A/C compressor, accumulator, and orifice tube service or R-134a conversion done correctly', 'Landau or vinyl top re-cover with roof rust repair if bubbling appears', 'Fiberglass crack repair and localized paint at hinge and mount stress points', 'Window motors and regulators, and door hinge pin bushings', 'Rear axle seals and bearings, and U-joints if not documented', 'Re-chroming or sourcing of pitted Zimmer trim, grille, and side pipes']
profiles.market_notes: Prices hinge on cosmetic and structural condition of the Zimmer-specific work rather than drivetrain. Crack-free fiberglass, a rust-free splice and floors, a good landau top, and complete original trim and wire wheels command the premium. Most drivers trade roughly in the low-teens to mid-$20k range, with exceptional, documented, low-mile or convertible examples higher. TMU status, accident history, defrost-only HVAC, missing trim, or non-original engine and transmission pull values down hard. Later 1986–88 EFI cars are easier to live with and smog than carbureted early cars, and a clean California smog history adds real value for a CA buyer.
profiles.catchup_notes: Expect a typical example to need rubber renewal throughout: vacuum lines, fuel and coolant hoses, bushings, and brake hoses. HVAC vacuum and A/C sorting, cooling-system work for the extended front end, and AOD TV adjustment are also likely, often $2,000–5,000 in total. The bigger catch-up risks are fiberglass and paint repair, landau top re-covering, and re-chroming or sourcing Zimmer trim. These are cosmetic but expensive, and they drive the car's value.

listings.notes:
PPI checklist (2026-10-08) — BMW-experienced shop WITH A LIFT; cold start (seller not to warm it up); photos + a call with the tech.
1. Rear structure: battery box + tool tray out; diff-mount spot welds in the trunk floor; from below: subframe mounts, diff ears, subframe-to-body; cracks / old repairs / any reinforcement.
2. Cooling (no records in 26 yrs, long storage): pressure test; water pump play/weep; expansion tank, radiator necks, thermostat housing; fan clutch; coolant; any overheat history.
3. Front damage: lower lip torn; bumper support; radiator + A/C condenser behind it.
4. Gouged front wheel: balancer, check bend / crack near the spoke (seller says not cracked).
5. Identity: VIN [VIN] on windshield, door jamb, frame = the Arkansas title; LSD (diff tag or lift-and-turn test); engine is the original S52, unmodified.
6. CA smog: stored/pending codes, readiness monitors; original cats, stock exhaust.
7. Engine/drivetrain: VANOS rattle/codes; leaks (valve cover, oil filter housing, pan, rear main); clutch slip/engagement; gearbox/shifter; belts, pulleys, hose age.
8. Suspension/brakes: rear shock mounts (Z3 failure point); front control-arm + rear trailing-arm bushings; sway links; pads/rotors/fluid.
9. Body/top/interior: paint meter on every panel; rust (trunk battery area, floors — 16 yrs Arkansas); soft top + rear window + frame; window regulators; electrics/gauges; tire date codes.
Ask for: buy/don't-buy verdict; must-fix vs can-wait; rough cost for every finding.
TITLE (separate from the PPI): seller's name is not on the title (AR title -> donor parent -> school -> seller). Get photos of front+back of the title + donation + notarized purchase docs, and check with a CA registration service BEFORE paying anything.

SCOUT RECOMMENDATION 2026-09-22: Reject - hard gate unsafe_structure_or_heavy_rust.

car is a real 6-speed M66, stock, clean title, with a Carfax-documented June 2023 timing belt - the
first item on the guide's C30 checklist. Documentation is unusually good for the money.

It fails on condition. Direct review of mechanical photos 114-116 shows heavy laminating corrosion at
the rocker-to-floor pinch weld with undercoating delaminating in sheets, plus a heavily scaled
subframe. The guide's standard is "No heavy rust; light surface rust can be evaluated." Structural
extent cannot be confirmed without a lift.

- remote_auction_no_ppi: ends 2026-09-23 11:45 AM PDT in Schaumburg IL; no inspection window on the

- permanent_warning_lights: TPMS illuminated.

Cost math (app cost state, locality band 2): hammer $4,000 -> $6,370 all-in; $5,000 -> $7,462;
$6,500 -> $9,176. Budget is not the constraint. Add 2022-date-code tires, an undocumented clutch at
122k, and corrosion remediation ranging from a few hundred dollars to subframe replacement.

OPEN / UNVERIFIED: no C30 comps exist in this database, so no defensible market price read. The
auction's own signal - no reserve, 460 watchers, $2,600 at one day out with experienced bidders
talking the rust down - is the best available indication and it points at the underbody.

5. Search the phone number (Google, FB Marketplace) for reuse across car ads.
6. Jason picks the Medford PPI shop; seller drops the car off.
STOP IF: deposit to hold it, payment before seeing it, shipping/agent/escrow he picks, gift cards/Zelle, can't meet, VIN/title mismatch. No personal details beyond name until the title checks out.

2026-09-29 — next steps (from Claude)

ASK THE SELLER (sent/queued):
- Where in Jacksonville? PPI at an independent BMW shop near him, my cost; he drops it off or a mobile inspector comes to him.

PPI (I book and pay, ~$150-400 est.; brief the shop by phone):
- Rear structure: Randy Forbes reinforcement welds, trunk-floor seam rust, no prior cracking.
- The three damage areas (2005 front+rear, 02/2025 minor, 10/2025 front); signs of structural repair.
- Cooling: pressure test; water pump, thermostat, expansion tank, hoses.

- "Light tapping noise with top up"; front sway bar end links (seller says noisy).

IF DRIVING HOME (FL -> CA, ~2,700 mi) — before leaving:
cooling refresh (plastic parts) + pressure test; tires by date code (>~6 yrs = replace); oil, brake fluid, gearbox + diff oil; belt + idler/tensioner; sway bar end links; diagnose the tapping; carry coolant, belt, tools, long-tow roadside plan.

PAYMENT / PAPERWORK:

- Pay traceably: bank wire (verify details by phone), cashier's check in person, or escrow (e.g. Escrow.com). NOT Zelle/Venmo/PayPal F&F or anything he suggests.
- Title signed over with odometer + FL bill of sale; copies of everything.
